Their statement,

“We are only setting things right,”

has been interpreted as a denial of what they had acknowledged—that is: “We only do what the Messenger has commanded us to do.” It has also been interpreted as meaning: “What we do is right, and our intention is to set things right.” Both interpretations are reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, and both are true, for they say both things. They say the first to those who have not discovered their hidden intentions, and the second to themselves and to those who have discovered them. The second interpretation, however, encompasses the first, for their actions include concealing the opposite of what they outwardly profess, and they regard this as setting things right.

Mujāhid said: “They meant that befriending the disbelievers was setting things right, not causing corruption.” Al-Suddī is reported to have said: “This conduct of ours is what sets things right, whereas believing Muhammad causes corruption.” It has also been said that they meant this would serve their worldly interests: if the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gained the upper hand, they would have secured their safety by following him; and if the disbelievers gained the upper hand, they would have secured their safety from them by befriending them.

In light of these two interpretations, His words,

“Indeed, it is they who cause corruption, but they do not perceive it,”

have been explained as meaning that they do not perceive that what they have done is corruption, not reform. It has also been said that they do not perceive that Allah discloses their corruption to His Prophet. The first interpretation encompasses the second and is therefore the intended meaning, as the wording of the verse indicates.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, my Protector is Allah, who has sent down the Book, and He protects the righteous.”

He also says:

“Moses said, ‘What you have brought is sorcery. Allah will surely bring it to nothing. Indeed, Allah does not make the work of those who cause corruption prosper.’”

And Joseph said:

“Cause me to die a Muslim and join me with the righteous.”

Either of these terms may also be coupled with something more specific than itself, as in His words:

“When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption in it and to destroy crops and livestock. And Allah does not love corruption.”

This has been explained as causing corruption through disbelief, or through wrongdoing; both interpretations are correct. Allah Most High also says:

translated_text:
exaltation upon the earth or corruption.” Earlier, Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was one of those who cause corruption.”

Allah Most High also says:

“For that reason, We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a person, unless in retaliation for a life or for corruption in the land, it is as though he has killed all mankind.”

The first-mentioned killing of a person is itself a form of corruption. However, in cases of killing, the right belongs to the victim’s next of kin, whereas in cases of apostasy, waging war, and unlawful sexual intercourse, the right belongs to the public at large. This is why it is called a right belonging to Allah, and why the latter cannot be pardoned as the former can: the corruption it causes affects everyone. Allah Most High says:

“The recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be killed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides”—to the end of the verse.

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the men of ʿUraynah who apostatized, killed, and seized property. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning people under a treaty who broke their treaty and waged war. Another view is that it concerned the polytheists. Thus, He has linked corruption with apostates who wage war, treaty-breakers who wage war, and polytheists who wage war. The majority of the early and later scholars hold that it also covers highway robbers among the Muslims. The verse encompasses all these groups. Thus, whoever among them repents before being apprehended has Allah Most High’s right waived in his case.

Likewise, He has coupled “righteousness and reform with faith” in many passages, as in His words:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

“Whoever believes and sets things right—there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.”

It is well known that faith is the finest form of reform and the finest righteous deed, as stated in the authentic hadith:

“He was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, which deed is best?’ He replied, ‘Faith in Allah.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“And indeed, I am Most Forgiving to whoever repents, believes, and does

righteous deeds, and then remains rightly guided.”

He also says:

“Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds—they will enter Paradise.”

And He says:

“Except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds—for them Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds.”

Concerning accusations of unchastity, He says:

“Except those who repent thereafter and reform, for Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Concerning the thief, He says:

“But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms—Allah will accept his repentance.”

And He says:

“And the two among you who commit it—punish them both. But if they repent and reform, leave them alone.”

For this reason, according to one of their two opinions, the jurists stipulated that an accuser of unchastity must reform before his testimony can be accepted. They set a period of one year for this, just as Umar did when he gave Subaygh ibn Asal a year. Ahmad likewise adopted this approach concerning the repentance of someone who calls others to religious innovation: he is to be given a year, just as Umar gave Subaygh ibn Asal a year.

Section

If it is said:

“What has been stated about how a word’s meaning varies according to whether it is used without qualification or with qualification—in the speech of Allah, His Messenger, and everyone else—is clear, evident, and undeniable. Yet we maintain that the word ‘faith’ refers to deeds figuratively. Thus, the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Faith has sixty-odd or seventy-odd branches, the highest of which is saying “There is no god but Allah,” and the lowest of which is removing something harmful from the road,’ is figurative. His statement, ‘Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His Messengers,’ and so forth, is literal.”

This is the central argument of the Murji’ah, the Jahmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and everyone who excludes deeds from what the term “faith” encompasses.

We offer two answers. The first is a general discussion of the terminology (literal and figurative). The second concerns this particular issue: assuming that one of the two usages is figurative, which is literal and which is figurative? Is the literal usage the unqualified one, the qualified one, or are both literal? This must be established to know how the word “faith” is to be understood when used without qualification.

First, we say: Expressions that signify meanings may be classified as “literal and figurative”; the same classification may also be applied to their signification or to the meanings signified, if the terms “literal” and “figurative” are used to describe either the signified meaning or the signification. ويظهر أنه قد سقط اسم الكتاب، وهو (مجاز القرآن) كما قال الشيخ رحمه الله (١٢/ ٢٧٧): (وأول من قال ذلك مطلقا أبو عبيدة معمر بن المثنى في كتابه الذي صنفه في مجاز القرآن).
translated_text:
is that literal and figurative usage are properties of expressions. In any event, this classification is a convention introduced after the first three generations had passed. None of the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the renowned imams of learning—such as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Abū Hanīfah, and al-Shāfi‘ī—spoke in these terms. Nor did the leading scholars of language and grammar, such as al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, Abū ‘Amr ibn al-‘Alā’, and others like them.

[The first person known to have used the term “majāz” was Abū ‘Ubaydah Ma‘mar ibn al-Muthannā in his book. However, by majāz he did not mean figurative usage as distinct from literal usage] (*). Rather, by the majāz of a verse he meant an expression conveying the verse’s meaning. Accordingly, any legal theorist—such as Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī and others like him—who says, “Literal usage is distinguished from figurative usage through various methods, including an explicit statement by the scholars of language: ‘This is literal, and this is figurative,’” has spoken without knowledge. He has assumed that the scholars of language said this, whereas none of them, nor any of the early generations of the Muslim community and their scholars, said it. This is merely a later convention, most likely originating with the Mu‘tazilah and other speculative theologians like them. It is not found in the discourse of any of the early scholars of jurisprudence, legal theory, Quranic exegesis, hadith, or related disciplines.

Al-Shāfi‘ī, the first to devote a separate treatment to legal theory, did not make this classification or use the terms “literal” and “figurative.” Likewise, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan has well-known discussions in al-Jāmi‘ al-Kabīr and elsewhere concerning questions that hinge on Arabic usage, yet he did not use the terms “literal” and “figurative.” Likewise, regarding the other imams, there is no record of

لَفْظُ الْمَجَازِ فِي كَلَامِ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ إلَّا فِي كَلَامِ أَحْمَد بْنِ حَنْبَلٍ؛

" الْقُرْآنِ "

 قَالُوا:
 وَلَمْ يُرِدْ أَحْمَد بِذَلِكَ أَنَّ اللَّفْظَ اُسْتُعْمِلَ فِي غَيْرِ مَا وُضِعَ لَهُ. وَقَدْ أَنْكَرَ طَائِفَةٌ أَنْ يَكُونَ فِي اللُّغَةِ مَجَازٌ لَا فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَلَا غَيْرِهِ كَأَبِي
translated_text:
the term “majāz” in the words of any of them except Ahmad ibn Hanbal. In his Refutation of the Jahmiyyah, concerning the expressions “Indeed, We” and “We” and similar expressions in the Quran, he said: “This is an instance of majāz in the language. A man says, ‘We shall give you; We shall do such-and-such.’” He thus described this as majāz in the language.

Those of his followers who held that the Quran contains figurative usage—such as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn ‘Aqīl, Abū al-Khattāb, and others—cited this as evidence for attributing that position to him. Other followers of his denied that the Quran contains figurative usage, including Abū al-Hasan al-Kharzī, Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid, and Abū al-Fadl al-Tamīmī, son of Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī. Muhammad ibn Khuwayz Mindād and other Mālikī scholars likewise denied that the Quran contains figurative usage. Dāwūd ibn ‘Alī, his son Abū Bakr, and Mundhir ibn Sa‘īd al-Ballūtī also rejected it; the latter composed a work on the subject. Some have related two differing reports from Ahmad on this issue.

As for the other imams, none of them—neither Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, nor Abū Hanīfah—nor any of Ahmad’s early followers said that the Quran contains figurative usage. The classification of expressions into literal and figurative usage only became widespread in the fourth century AH, with its beginnings appearing in the third. I do not know of its existence in the second century, unless perhaps towards its end.

Those who denied that Ahmad and others had spoken in terms of this classification said that Ahmad’s phrase “an instance of majāz in the language” meant something permissible in linguistic usage: a single person of high standing who has assistants may say, “We have done such-and-such, and we shall do such-and-such,” and similar expressions. They said: “Ahmad did not mean by this that the expression was used in a sense other than the one for which it was coined.”

إسْحَاقَ الإسفراييني.
 وَقَالَ الْمُنَازِعُونَ لَهُ:
 النِّزَاعُ مَعَهُ لَفْظِيٌّ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا سَلَّمَ أَنَّ فِي اللُّغَةِ لَفْظًا مُسْتَعْمَلًا فِي غَيْرِ مَا وُضِعَ لَهُ لَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنَاهُ إلَّا بِقَرِينَةٍ؛ فَهَذَا هُوَ الْمَجَازُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يُسَمِّهِ مَجَازًا.
 فَيَقُولُ مَنْ يَنْصُرُهُ:
 إنَّ الَّذِينَ قَسَّمُوا اللَّفْظَ: حَقِيقَةً وَمَجَازًا قَالُوا: 
" الْحَقِيقَةُ "
 هُوَ اللَّفْظُ الْمُسْتَعْمَلُ فِيمَا وُضِعَ لَهُ. 
" وَالْمَجَازُ "
 هُوَ اللَّفْظُ الْمُسْتَعْمَلُ فِي غَيْرِ مَا وُضِعَ لَهُ كَلَفْظِ الْأَسَدِ وَالْحِمَارِ إذَا أُرِيدَ بِهِمَا الْبَهِيمَةُ أَوْ أُرِيدَ بِهِمَا الشُّجَاعُ وَالْبَلِيدُ. وَهَذَا التَّقْسِيمُ وَالتَّحْدِيدُ يَسْتَلْزِمُ أَنْ يَكُونَ اللَّفْظُ قَدْ وُضِعَ أَوَّلًا لِمَعْنَى ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ قَدْ يُسْتَعْمَلُ فِي مَوْضُوعِهِ وَقَدْ يُسْتَعْمَلُ فِي غَيْرِ مَوْضُوعِهِ؛ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الْمَشْهُورُ عِنْدَ أَهْلِ التَّقْسِيمِ أَنَّ كُلَّ مَجَازٍ فَلَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ حَقِيقَةٍ وَلَيْسَ لِكُلِّ حَقِيقَةٍ مَجَازٌ؟

 اللَّفْظُ الْمَوْضُوعُ قَبْلَ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ لَا حَقِيقَةٌ وَلَا مَجَازٌ فَإِذَا اُسْتُعْمِلَ فِي غَيْرِ مَوْضُوعِهِ فَهُوَ مَجَازٌ لَا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ. وَهَذَا كُلُّهُ إنَّمَا يَصِحُّ لَوْ عُلِمَ أَنَّ الْأَلْفَاظَ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ وُضِعَتْ أَوَّلًا لِمَعَانٍ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ اُسْتُعْمِلَتْ فِيهَا؛ فَيَكُونُ لَهَا وَضْعٌ مُتَقَدِّمٌ عَلَى الِاسْتِعْمَالِ. وَهَذَا إنَّمَا صَحَّ عَلَى قَوْلِ مَنْ يَجْعَلُ اللُّغَاتِ اصْطِلَاحِيَّةً فَيَدَّعِي أَنَّ قَوْمًا مِنْ الْعُقَلَاءِ اجْتَمَعُوا وَاصْطَلَحُوا عَلَى أَنْ يُسَمُّوا هَذَا بِكَذَا وَهَذَا بِكَذَا وَيَجْعَلَ هَذَا عَامًّا فِي جَمِيعِ اللُّغَاتِ. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ لَا نَعْرِفُ أَحَدًا مِنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ قَالَهُ قَبْلَ أَبِي هَاشِمِ بْنِ الجبائي؛ فَإِنَّهُ وَأَبَا الْحَسَنِ الْأَشْعَرِيَّ كِلَاهُمَا قَرَأَ عَلَى أَبِي عَلِيٍّ الجبائي لَكِنَّ الْأَشْعَرِيَّ رَجَعَ عَنْ مَذْهَبِ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَخَالَفَهُمْ فِي الْقَدَرِ وَالْوَعِيدِ وَفِي الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالْأَحْكَامِ وَفِي
translated_text:
Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī.

Those who disputed his position said: The disagreement with him is merely terminological. If he concedes that language contains expressions used in a sense other than that for which they were coined, whose meaning is conveyed only through a contextual indication, then this is figurative usage, even if he does not call it that.

Those who defend him reply: Those who divided expressions into literal and figurative usage said: “Literal usage” is the use of an expression in the sense for which it was coined, while “figurative usage” is its use in a sense other than that for which it was coined. Examples are the words “lion” and “donkey,” whether they refer to the animals themselves or, respectively, to a brave man and a dull-witted man. This classification and these definitions entail that an expression was first coined for a particular meaning, after which it may be used either in its assigned sense or in another sense. Hence the well-known position among those who adopt this classification is that every figurative usage must have a corresponding literal usage, whereas not every literal usage has a corresponding figurative usage.

One of their later scholars objected, saying: An expression that has been assigned a meaning but has not yet been used is neither literal nor figurative. If it is then used in a sense other than its assigned meaning, it is a figurative usage with no corresponding literal usage.

All of this would be valid only if it were known that Arabic expressions were first assigned meanings and were subsequently used in those meanings, so that their assignment preceded their use. This, in turn, would be valid only according to the view that languages arise through convention: that a group of rational people gathered and agreed to call one thing by one name and another thing by another name, and that this applies to all languages.

We know of no Muslim who expressed this view before Abū Hāshim ibn al-Jubbā’ī. Both he and Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī studied under Abū ‘Alī al-Jubbā’ī. Al-Ash‘arī, however, renounced the Mu‘tazilī school and differed with them concerning divine decree, the threat of punishment, religious designations and rulings, and concerning

صِفَاتِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَبَيَّنَ مِنْ تَنَاقُضِهِمْ وَفَسَادِ قَوْلِهِمْ مَا هُوَ مَعْرُوفٌ عَنْهُ. فَتَنَازَعَ الْأَشْعَرِيُّ وَأَبُو هَاشِمٍ فِي مَبْدَأِ اللُّغَاتِ؛

 بَعْضُهَا تَوْقِيفِيٌّ وَبَعْضُهَا اصْطِلَاحِيٌّ وَقَالَ فَرِيقٌ رَابِعٌ بِالْوَقْفِ. وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّهُ لَا يُمْكِنُ أَحَدًا أَنْ يَنْقُلَ عَنْ الْعَرَبِ بَلْ وَلَا عَنْ أُمَّةٍ مِنْ الْأُمَمِ أَنَّهُ اجْتَمَعَ جَمَاعَةٌ فَوَضَعُوا جَمِيعَ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ الْمَوْجُودَةِ فِي اللُّغَةِ ثُمَّ اسْتَعْمَلُوهَا بَعْدَ الْوَضْعِ وَإِنَّمَا الْمَعْرُوفُ الْمَنْقُولُ بِالتَّوَاتُرِ اسْتِعْمَالُ هَذِهِ الْأَلْفَاظِ فِيمَا عَنَوْهُ بِهَا مِنْ الْمَعَانِي فَإِنْ ادَّعَى مُدَّعٍ أَنَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَضْعًا يَتَقَدَّمُ ذَلِكَ فَهُوَ مُبْطِلٌ فَإِنَّ هَذَا لَمْ يَنْقُلْهُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ.

 قِيلَ:
 لَيْسَ الْأَمْرُ كَذَلِكَ؛
 بَلْ نَحْنُ نَجِدُ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُلْهِمُ الْحَيَوَانَ مِنْ الْأَصْوَاتِ مَا بِهِ يَعْرِفُ بَعْضُهَا مُرَادَ بَعْضٍ وَقَدْ سُمِّيَ ذَلِكَ مَنْطِقًا وَقَوْلًا فِي قَوْلِ سُلَيْمَانَ:
 
{عُلِّمْنَا مَنْطِقَ الطَّيْرِ}
 .
 وَفِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّمْلُ ادْخُلُوا مَسَاكِنَكُمْ}
 وَفِي قَوْلِهِ: 
{يَا جِبَالُ أَوِّبِي مَعَهُ وَالطَّيْرَ}

translated_text:
the attributes of Allah Most High, and exposed their contradictions and the unsoundness of their views, as is well known. Al-Ash‘arī and Abū Hāshim then disagreed over the origin of languages. Abū Hāshim said, “They arise through convention,” whereas al-Ash‘arī said, “They are divinely taught.” Others subsequently entered into this discussion. Some said, “They are partly divinely taught and partly conventional,” while a fourth group suspended judgment.

The point here is that no one can report that the Arabs—or, indeed, any nation—assembled a group who assigned all the names found in their language and then began using them after that assignment. What is known and established through mass transmission is simply their use of these expressions for the meanings they intended. Anyone who claims to know of an assignment preceding that usage is making a false claim, for no one has transmitted any such account.

It cannot be argued, “We know this by inference: without a prior convention, usage would not have been possible.”

The reply is: This is not so. Rather, we observe that Allah inspires animals to make sounds through which they understand one another’s intentions. Such communication is called “speech” and “saying,” as in Solomon’s words:

“We have been taught the speech of birds.”

And in Allah’s words:

“An ant said, ‘O ants, enter your dwellings.’”

And His words:

“O mountains, echo his praises, and you birds too.”

The same applies to human beings. Once a child begins to discern things, he hears his parents or caregiver utter an expression while pointing to its meaning. He thus comes to understand that the expression is used for that meaning—that is, that the speaker intends that meaning by it. He then hears one expression after another until he learns the language of the people among whom he has grown up, without their having agreed with him upon any prior assignment of meanings. Indeed, they have not even explicitly taught him the meanings of the names

although he may sometimes ask what certain names denote and be told, just as a language someone does not know may be translated for him, acquainting him with the meanings of its words. Yet if he spends some time among its speakers, he learns this without explicit instruction from any of them.

People may indeed give names to new things unknown to those before them. For example, someone may have a child and give him either an existing name or a newly coined one. The person giving the name may act alone, without agreeing with anyone else, or people may coincide in their naming. Likewise, someone may devise a tool for a craft, write a book, build a city, or do something similar, and give it a name, since it does not belong to an already familiar category with a name in the common language.

Allah has said:

“The Most Merciful taught the Quran, created man, and taught him speech.”

And:

“They will say, ‘Allah, who causes all things to speak, has caused us to speak.’”

And He said:

“Who created and fashioned, and who determined and guided.”

Thus He, glorified be He, inspires human beings to speak just as He inspires other creatures. If He, glorified be He, taught Adam all the names and presented the things named to the angels, as He has told us in His Book, we nevertheless know that He did not teach Adam every language that all people would speak until the Day of Resurrection, with those languages then being passed down to his children so that they spoke only those languages. Such a claim is plainly false. Only Adam’s children could have transmitted anything from him, peace be upon him, and in the year of the Flood Allah drowned all his descendants except those aboard the Ark. The lineages of those aboard the Ark subsequently died out, except for the descendants of Noah. They did not speak all the languages spoken by the nations that came after them. Indeed, a “single language,” such as Persian, Arabic, Greek, or Turkish, contains differences and varieties that none but Allah can enumerate; and the Arabs themselves

Not all of them left descendants; rather, the surviving descendants were Noah’s alone. All people descend from his three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. As Allah Most High said:

“And We made his descendants the sole survivors.”

Thus He left none surviving except his descendants. It is likewise reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “His sons were three.” This was related by Ahmad and others.

It is well known that these three could not possibly have spoken all these languages, nor could all these languages have been transmitted from them. Those who know one language do not know another. If there were only three original transmitters, they would have taught their children, and their children would have taught theirs. Had that been so, transmission would have remained continuous. Yet we find that, among the descendants of a single father, each tribe speaks a language unknown to the others, although their forefather is one and the same.

It cannot be argued that he taught one son one language and his other son another, for a father may have only two sons, while the languages spoken by his descendants are many times that number. The customary pattern Allah has established among human beings is that they teach their children only the language in which they themselves, or others, address them. As for languages whose speakers Allah has not yet created, they do not teach these to their children. Moreover, human beings are found uttering words they have never heard from anyone else.

translated_text:
“He presented them,” using the feminine singular pronoun. For this reason, Abū al-‘Āliya said: “He taught him the names of the angels,” because at that time there were no rational beings other than the angels; Iblīs had not yet separated from the angels, nor did he have any descendants.

‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: “He taught him the names of his descendants.” This accords with the hadith that al-Tirmidhī narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and graded authentic:

“Adam asked his Lord to show him the forms of the prophets among his descendants. He saw them, and among them he saw someone shining. He said, ‘My Lord, who is this?’ He replied, ‘Your son David.’”

Thus, He would have shown him the forms of his descendants, or some of them, together with their names. These are proper names, not names of categories.

(The second): Allah taught him the names of everything. This is the view of the majority, including Ibn ‘Abbās and his companions. Ibn ‘Abbās said: “He even taught him the words for a fart and a little fart, a bowl and a little bowl.” He meant the names of phenomena and concrete objects, in both their ordinary and diminutive forms. The evidence for this is the established report in the two Sahīh collections in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith of intercession:

“People will say, ‘O Adam, you are the father of mankind. Allah created you with His Hand, breathed into you of His spirit, and taught you the names of everything.’”

Moreover, His words, “all the names,” constitute an emphatically general expression; its scope cannot therefore be restricted by mere assertion. As for His words, “Then He presented them to the angels,” rational and non-rational beings were gathered together, so the pronoun for rational beings took precedence. This is like His saying:

“Some of them crawl on their bellies, some walk on two legs, and some walk on four.”

‘Ikrima said: “He taught him the names of general categories, not their subdivisions, such as human, jinn, angel, and bird.”

Muqātil, Ibn al-Sā’ib, and Ibn Qutayba said: “He taught him the names of the beasts, creeping creatures, and birds He had created on earth.”

اخْتَلَفَتْ اللُّغَاتُ. وَقَدْ أَوْحَى اللَّهُ إلَى مُوسَى بالعبرانية وَإِلَى مُحَمَّدٍ بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ؛ وَالْجَمِيعُ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ، وَقَدْ بَيَّنَ اللَّهُ بِذَلِكَ مَا أَرَادَ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ وَأَمْرِهِ، وَإِنْ كَانَتْ هَذِهِ اللُّغَةُ لَيْسَتْ الْأُخْرَى، مَعَ أَنَّ الْعِبْرَانِيَّةَ مِنْ أَقْرَبِ اللُّغَاتِ إلَى الْعَرَبِيَّةِ حَتَّى إنَّهَا أَقْرَبُ إلَيْهَا مِنْ لُغَةِ بَعْضِ الْعَجَمِ إلَى بَعْضٍ. فَبِالْجُمْلَةِ نَحْنُ لَيْسَ غَرَضُنَا إقَامَةَ الدَّلِيلِ عَلَى عَدَمِ ذَلِكَ؛
 بَلْ يَكْفِينَا أَنْ يُقَالَ:
translated_text:
Further evidence that these languages were not handed down from Adam is that most languages fall short of Arabic: they lack specific names for the young, dwellings, sounds, and other things associated with animals, using possessive constructions instead. Had Adam, peace be upon him, taught all these languages, he would have taught them in mutually corresponding forms.

Moreover, every people without a revealed scripture lacks names for the days of the week in its language. Its language contains only words for the day, month, and year, because these are known through sense perception and reason. Peoples therefore assigned names to them, since verbal expression follows conception. The week, however, became known only through transmitted reports. It was only through the accounts of the prophets that people learned that Allah created the heavens, the earth, and everything between them in six days, then rose over the Throne. It was prescribed for those prophets to gather on one day each week to worship Allah and thereby preserve the memory of the first week, during which Allah began creating this world. Thus, the languages of the Arabs, the Hebrews, and those who learned from them contain names for the days of the week, unlike the languages of the Turks and others like them. Their languages contain no names for the days of the week because they did not know of this and therefore had no words to express it.

It is thus clear that Allah inspired humankind to express in words what they intend and conceive, and that the first to learn this was their father Adam. They learned just as he learned, even though their languages differed. Allah revealed to Moses in Hebrew and to Muhammad in Arabic, and all of it is Allah’s speech. Through it, Allah made clear what He intended concerning His creation and His commands, although the two languages are distinct. Indeed, Hebrew is among the languages closest to Arabic—closer to it than the languages of some non-Arab peoples are to one another.

In short, our purpose is not to establish that this did not occur. Rather, it is enough for us to say:

this is not known to have occurred. Rather, inspiration suffices for speaking languages without any prior agreement. If this is called divine instruction, then let it be called divine instruction. Accordingly, anyone who claims that meanings were assigned before any of these categories of expressions were used has spoken without knowledge. What is known beyond doubt is usage itself.

These people then say that literal usage is distinguished from figurative usage by whether the expression alone is sufficient: if an expression conveys its meaning on its own, it is literal; if it conveys its meaning only with a contextual indication, it is figurative. Yet this concerns the use of an expression to convey a meaning, not any prior assignment of meaning.

Then it may be said (secondly): this division has no basis in reality. Those who distinguish between the two have no sound definition by which to tell one from the other. It is therefore clear that this division is invalid: it is a division made by people who do not properly conceive what they are saying, but instead speak without knowledge. They are thus innovators in religion who contradict reason. For they say:

“Literal usage” is the use of an expression for the meaning assigned to it, while “figurative usage” is its use for a meaning other than that assigned to it. They therefore need to establish an assignment of meaning that preceded usage, and this cannot be done.

They then divide literal usage into linguistic and customary usage. Most divide it into three categories: linguistic, scriptural, and customary. “Customary literal usage” is where an expression comes to signify a meaning through custom rather than through its linguistic designation. That meaning may be broader than its linguistic meaning, narrower than it, or distinct from it, though connected to it by an association that accounts for this usage.

The first is exemplified by words such as “neck” and “head”: they were used for the particular bodily part, then came to be used for the whole body. The second is exemplified by the word dābbah (“creature”) and similar words: it was used for anything that moved along the ground, but then came to be

used in the customary speech of some people for four-legged animals, in that of others for horses, and in that of still others for donkeys. The third category is exemplified by the words ghā’it, za’īnah, rāwiyah (water-carrier), and mazādah (waterskin). Linguistically, ghā’it denotes low-lying ground. Since people would go there to relieve themselves, they named what comes out of a person after the place where it was deposited. Za’īnah is the name of a riding animal; they then applied its name to the woman riding it. There are other similar examples.

The point is that this customary literal usage did not become literal through a group’s agreeing to transfer the expression to a new meaning. Rather, some people used it intending that customary meaning; its use then spread, and it became customary literal usage through this use. This is why some of them added the qualification “in the language in which communication takes place” to their definition of literal usage. Moreover, they themselves recognize and state that a particular usage may come to predominate for certain expressions, so that the customary meaning becomes their best-known meaning, and, when used without qualification, they signify nothing else. Customary literal usage thus supersedes linguistic literal usage. Yet the expression is literal in this newly developed customary usage without having previously been assigned to the meaning in which it is used. It is therefore clear that defining literal usage in this way is unsound.

If they say, “By ‘the meaning assigned to it,’ we mean the meaning in which it was first used,” the reply is: How can it be known that these expressions, which the Arabs used to communicate when the Quran was revealed and before then, had not previously been used for some other meaning? If they cannot establish that no such earlier usage existed, they cannot know that these are literal usages. This contradicts what they themselves agree upon. Furthermore, this would entail that no expression could be known with certainty to be literal—a conclusion no rational person would accept.

Most of them, however, say that this is a case of homonymy, not of literal and figurative usage. When one says “the head of the spring,” “the head of the road,” “the head of the people,” or “the head of the matter,” the qualifying expression here differs from the qualifying expression that indicates the meaning there. Similarly, if “a human head” is said first, this does not make our saying “a horse’s head” figurative. The same applies to other possessive constructions, such as “his hand” or “his foot.”

If it is said, “The usage is literal when the word is attached to an animal,” the reply is: there is no more reason to regard this as the literal usage than to regard “head” as literal when attached to a human. Moreover, it may be attached to small animals that most people cannot even picture and that have never occurred to the vast majority of speakers of the language. If its use in these cases is said to be literal, why should it not also be literal in “the head of the mountain,” “the head of the road,” and “the head of the spring”?

Likewise, expressions attached to a human—referring to his limbs, offspring, or dwellings—have counterparts attached to other things, including inanimate objects. Thus one says “the head of the mountain,” “the head of the spring,” “the snout of the mountain,” meaning its nose, “the mouth of the valley,” “the belly of the valley,” “the back of the mountain,” and “the belly of the earth” and “its back.” The forms with an added alif—zāhir (“outward”) and bātin (“inward”)—are also used of many things. In every case, zāhir refers to what appears and becomes evident, while bātin refers to what lies within and is hidden. The human back is called zahr because it is outward, and the human belly is called batn because it is inward.

If it is said that this usage is literal and that one figurative, this is no more justified than the reverse.

Furthermore, some nouns have been used independently by speakers of the language, such as “human” and similar words, and may then be used with the qualification supplied by a possessive construction. Examples include “the human of the eye” (its pupil), “the needle of the forearm” (its pointed bony end), and similar expressions. Even supposing that language does contain literal and figurative usage, some have claimed that this is figurative. But this is mistaken, for figurative usage is the use of an expression in a sense other than the one for which it was originally assigned. Here, however, the expression has not been used on its own; rather, it has been combined with another expression, thereby acquiring a distinct designation through the possessive construction.

Thus, if an expression were used in a possessive construction in one sense, then used in that same construction in another sense, it would be figurative. Indeed, if names such as Baalbek and Hadramawt—fused compounds originally formed as possessive constructions—are not described as figurative, then an expression used only in a possessive construction has even greater reason not to be considered figurative.

As for those who distinguish literal from figurative usage by saying that literal usage conveys a meaning without contextual indicators, whereas figurative usage conveys that meaning only with a contextual indicator; or who say, “The literal meaning is what an unqualified expression conveys, whereas the figurative meaning is conveyed only with qualification”; or who say, “The literal meaning is what first comes to mind when an expression is used without qualification, whereas the figurative meaning does not come to mind first”; or who say, “The figurative meaning can validly be denied, whereas the literal meaning cannot”—they should be asked: “What do you mean by the absence of contextual indicators and their presence?”

If this means verbal contextual indicators, such as a noun’s being used in a possessive construction or with the definite article, and its being qualified by serving as the subject of a verb, an object, the subject of a nominal sentence, or its predicate, then no noun ever occurs in connected speech without qualification. The same applies to a verb, if by its being qualified one means that it must have a subject and may be further qualified by a direct object, adverbials of time and place, an expression of purpose or accompaniment, or a circumstantial qualifier. A verb is never used without qualification. This is even more evident with particles, for a particle is used to convey a meaning through its relation to another expression.

In short, no noun, verb, or particle ever occurs in a complete utterance without qualifications that prevent it from being unqualified. If, then, a contextual indicator is something that prevents an expression from being free of every

qualification, then no expression in any human speech is free of every qualification, whether the sentence is nominal or verbal. This is why the terms kalām (“speech”) and kalimah (“utterance”) in Arabic—and indeed in other languages—are used only for qualified expressions: complete sentences, whether nominal, verbal, or vocative, if the last is regarded as a third category.

An isolated noun, verb, or particle conveying a meaning while being neither a noun nor a verb is never called a kalimah in ordinary Arabic speech. Calling it a kalimah is merely a grammatical convention, just as grammarians called certain expressions fi‘l (“verb,” literally “act”) and divided them into past, present, and imperative verbs. The Arabs never called an expression a fi‘l; rather, grammarians adopted this convention, naming the expression after what it signifies. Thus, they called an expression signifying the occurrence of an act in the past a “past verb,” and likewise for the other categories.

Similarly, wherever the term kalimah occurs in the Book and the Sunnah—or indeed in Arabic poetry and prose—it means a meaningful utterance, which grammarians call a complete sentence. Examples include the words of the Most High:

“and to warn those who say, ‘Allah has taken a son.’ They have no knowledge of this, nor did their forefathers. Grave is the utterance that comes from their mouths; they speak nothing but a lie.”

And His words, Most High:

“and He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, while the word of Allah is the highest.”

And His words, Most High:

“Come to a word common between us and you.”

And His words:

“And he made it a lasting word among his descendants.”

And His words:

“and bound them to the word of righteousness, for they were more entitled to it and worthy of it.”

And the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The truest utterance ever spoken by a poet is the saying of Labīd: ‘Indeed, everything apart from Allah is vain.’”

Since every noun, verb, or particle occurring in speech is qualified rather than unqualified, a literal expression cannot be defined as one that conveys its meaning when left unqualified and stripped of every accompanying contextual indicator.

If it is said, “Only some contextual indicators are meant, not others,” the reply is: “State the distinction between a contextual indicator with which an expression is literal and one with which it is figurative. You will never find a way to establish a sound, intelligible classification on that basis.”

Further evidence of this is that scholars have disagreed over whether, once a general expression has been specified, its use for what remains within its scope is literal or figurative. Likewise, when a command is intended to indicate recommendation, is its use literal or figurative?

They have proceeded to report differing views on this matter, as may be found in the writings of some authors on the principles of jurisprudence. Yet no one is known to have maintained this—that a general expression qualified by descriptive attributes, limits, or conditions is figurative. Rather, when some authors stated without qualification that a general expression becomes figurative once its scope has been specified, those reporting their views assumed that they meant connected specification. In those authors’ terminology, however, an expression was called a general expression that had been specified only when its scope was specified by something separate from it. As for connected specification, they never called the expression a general expression that had been specified, since it conveyed its meaning only together with the qualification, whose connection to it precluded generality. This is the terminology of many scholars of the principles of jurisprudence, and it is correct.

An expression qualified by a condition, a descriptive attribute, or the like should not be classed among cases in which generality has been specified, nor among general expressions that have been specified. Rather, one must qualify the term and say, “connected specification.” This qualified term does not fall within “specification” used without qualification.

In short, the reply is: if this is figurative, then qualifying an otherwise unqualified verb with a direct object, an expression of time or place, or a circumstantial qualifier must also be figurative. The same would apply to anything qualified by any qualification. It would follow that all speech is figurative. Where, then, is literal speech?

If it is said, “A distinction is drawn between connected and separate contextual indicators: an expression accompanied by a connected indicator is literal, whereas one accompanied by a separate indicator is figurative,” the reply is: “By ‘connected,’ do you mean something contained in the wording, or something present at the time of the utterance?”

“Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow.”

They claimed that a particular cow was intended and that its identification was deferred. This contradicts what has been widely transmitted from the early generations—the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness—namely, that they were commanded to slaughter an unspecified cow. Had they taken any cow and slaughtered it, that would have sufficed. But they made matters difficult, so Allah made matters difficult for them. The word “cow” in the verse is indefinite in an affirmative context and is therefore unrestricted. The context of the Quranic passage indicates that Allah censured them for asking what kind of cow it was. Had a particular cow been intended by the command, they would not have been blameworthy. Moreover, nothing like this has ever occurred in the commands of Allah and His Messenger: that He should command His servants concerning something specific, repeatedly leave its identity unclear to them, and not describe it from the outset by its distinguishing attributes.

They also argued that Allah deferred explaining the terms prayer, zakah, and pilgrimage, and that these terms have linguistic meanings that differ from their meanings in the Sharia. This is mistaken. Allah commanded them to pray only after they knew what was being commanded; the same applies to fasting and pilgrimage. Allah never deferred explaining any of these prescribed acts. A fuller discussion of this issue belongs elsewhere.

As for the claim that the literal meaning is what first comes to mind when an expression is used without qualification, this is among the most unsound views. The reply is: if an expression is only ever uttered with qualifications, then in every instance what first comes to mind is what that particular context indicates. As for its being unqualified, it is never used in speech entirely without qualification. Thus, there is no state in which it is wholly unqualified such that one could ask whether or not it first comes to mind. Moreover, whose mind is meant? They have become accustomed, through the speech of either their common people or their scholars, to using an expression in a particular sense. When they hear it in the Quran and hadith, they assume that it is being used in that sense. Thus, they interpret the words of Allah and His Messenger according to their own Nabataean speech and newly developed conventions. This is one way in which various groups have fallen into error. Rather, one must know the language, conventions, and customary usage in which the Quran and Sunnah were revealed, and what the Companions understood from the Messenger when they heard those expressions. For Allah and His Messenger addressed them according to that language, those conventions, and that customary usage—not according to what arose afterward.

Moreover, we have explained elsewhere that Allah and His Messenger left nothing in the Quran and hadith without explaining its meaning to those addressed, leaving them no need for anything else. We have discussed this at length elsewhere.

It has therefore become clear that the expression these people posit as free of all qualifications exists only as a mental supposition, not in actual speech. Likewise, the meaning that the logicians posit as free of all qualifications exists only as a mental supposition: nothing exists in external reality that is free of every qualification.

Thus, what they posit in dividing knowledge into conception and assent, and defining conception as the conception of a bare meaning devoid of every qualification, does not exist. Likewise, the simple elements from which they claim species are composed, and which they regard as free of every qualification, do not exist. Nor does what they posit when they claim that the Necessary Existent is existence devoid of every positive determination.

translated_text:
Thus, anyone studying these sciences must understand the nature of these attributes conceived as free of all qualifications. Assuming that they exist has led various groups astray in matters of reason and revelation. Rather, when scholars speak of the “unqualified” and the “qualified,” they mean unqualified by a particular qualification or qualified by it.

For example, they say that “slave” is unqualified in the verse concerning expiation for an oath, but qualified in the verse concerning killing. That is, it is unqualified by the requirement of faith. Otherwise, the words,

“then freeing a slave,”

already specify that it is one slave, that the slave exists, and that the slave can be freed. Those who affirm something wholly unqualified say that it is characterized by neither unity nor multiplicity, neither existence nor nonexistence, nor anything else. Rather, it is the essence considered simply as itself, as al-Rāzī explains, taking this from Ibn Sīnā and other such philosophers. Elsewhere, we have discussed qualification and its absence, universals and particulars, at length, and have explained their errors in these matters in ways that need not be discussed here.

Our concern here is only “verbal nonqualification”: uttering an expression free of every qualification. This does not occur. No one speaks except through composite, qualified discourse whose parts are interconnected. These connections constitute qualifications that preclude complete freedom from qualification.

It is therefore clear that those who distinguish between literal and figurative usage have no intelligible distinction by which two categories can be differentiated. This division is thus shown to be invalid. Accordingly, every expression found in Allah’s Book and the words of His Messenger is qualified by what clarifies its meaning. “a wall that wanted to collapse.”

They argued: “A wall is not a living creature, and only living creatures have a will. Thus, using this expression for the wall’s inclination is figurative.”

They were answered as follows: The term “will” has been used both for an inclination accompanied by awareness—the inclination of a living being—and for an inclination without awareness—that of an inanimate object. This is well-established usage in the language. People say, “This roof wants to fall,” “This land wants ploughing,” “These crops want watering,” “This fruit wants picking,” “This garment wants washing,” and similar expressions.

When an expression is used in two or more senses, it may be regarded as literal in one and figurative in another; or as literal in the meaning peculiar to each, making it a homonymous expression; or as literal in the meaning common to both. Terms of the last kind are univocal, and all general terms belong to this category. The first approach entails figurative usage, and the second entails homonymy. Both are contrary to the default assumption, so the expression must be treated as univocal.

This is how the general scope of all general terms is established. Otherwise, were someone to say, “It is literal when applied to the inclination of an inanimate object and figurative when applied to that of a living creature,” there would be no difference between the two claims except that it is used more frequently for the inclination of a living creature. In that usage, however, it is qualified by what makes clear that a living creature’s inclination is intended; here, it is qualified by what makes clear that an inanimate object’s inclination is intended.

The meaning shared by the things denoted by univocal terms is something universal and general, which exists as universal and general only in the mind. It is what is divided into species. Yet that general meaning

Whatever exists externally only in relation to something else does not exist in the mind in abstraction. This differs from the terms “human being” and “horse”: since their referents exist externally without such a relation, minds have become accustomed to conceiving what these terms denote. This is unlike conceiving what is denoted by will, knowledge, power, or unrestricted, universal existence. For these, the language has no unqualified expression denoting them. Rather, the expression “will” occurs only as qualified by the one who wills, “knowledge” only as qualified by the one who knows, and “power” only as qualified by the one who has power.

The same applies to all other accidents: since they exist only in the subjects in which they inhere, qualified by those subjects, the language likewise has expressions for them only in this qualified form. Thus, the expressions “blackness,” “whiteness,” “length,” and “shortness” occur in the language only as qualified by what is black, white, long, short, and so forth—not in abstraction from every qualification. They occur in abstraction only in the writings of those who compile works on language, because they have understood from the speech of its speakers the common meaning those speakers intend.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as Messenger has tasted the flavor of faith.”

Among the supplications is:

“Let us taste the coolness of Your pardon and the sweetness of Your forgiveness.”

Thus, the word “tasting” is used for everything one senses and whose pain or pleasure one experiences. To claim that the word applies exclusively to what occurs through the mouth is therefore an arbitrary restriction. Rather, that particular use is qualified: one says, “I tasted the food,” or “I tasted this drink.” These qualifications indicate that the tasting occurs through the mouth. Since tasting is used for what a person senses inwardly or outwardly—even scalding water is something one is said to have tasted—one says of a hot or cold drink, “I tasted its heat and its coolness.”

As for the word “garment,” it is used for everything that envelops a person and comes into close contact with him. The Most High said:

“And We made the night a garment.”

And He said:

“But the garment of righteousness—that is best.”

And He said:

“They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them.”

This also underlies the expression “He mingled truth with falsehood”: he mixed it with falsehood until it was covered over and could no longer be distinguished.

The pain of hunger thus pervades the whole hungry person—soul and body—and fear likewise envelops the body. Had it been said, “So Allah made it taste hunger and fear,” this would not have indicated that it encompassed every part of the hungry person, unlike the expression “the garment of hunger and fear.” Had He said, “So He clothed them,” the wording would not have indicated that they tasted what caused them pain. That could only be inferred through reason, from the knowledge that someone who is hungry and afraid suffers pain. “Whoever is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as his Prophet has tasted the flavor of faith.”

If it is asked, “Why, then, did He not describe the bliss of Paradise in terms of tasting?” the answer is that tasting denotes sensation in general. Someone is said to have tasted food when he has perceived its flavor, even if he has not eaten it. The bliss of the people of Paradise, however, is complete and perfect, not confined to tasting. Rather, He uses the word “tasting” in negative statements, as when He says of the people of the Fire:

“They will taste therein neither coolness nor drink.”

That is, they will not have so much as a taste of either. And He says of the people of Paradise:

“They will taste no death therein except the first death.”

The same applies to what they claim is figurative language in the Quran, such as “plotting,” “mockery,” and “ridicule” when attributed to Allah. They allege that these are figuratively given the names of the acts they requite. That is not so. Rather, the acts denoted by these words constitute injustice when directed against someone who does not deserve punishment. But when directed against someone who has inflicted such acts upon another, as punishment matching his own conduct, they constitute justice. Thus, the Most High says:

“Thus We planned for Joseph.”

He thus planned for him, just as his brothers had planned against him, as his father had said to him:

“Do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they devise a plan against you.”

And the Most High says:

“They are devising a plan, and I too am devising a plan.”

And the Most High says:

“They plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were unaware. So see what was the outcome of their plotting.”

And the Most High says:

“Those who criticize the believers who give charity voluntarily, and those who have only their meager means to give, and ridicule them—Allah ridicules them.”

is reported from Ibn ‘Abbās: while they are in the Fire, a gate of Paradise will be opened for them. They will rush toward it, only for it to be closed. Then another gate will be opened for them, and they will rush toward it, only for it to be closed. The believers will then laugh at them. The Most High says:

“So today those who believed are laughing at the disbelievers, looking on from couches. Have the disbelievers been repaid for what they used to do?”

It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basrī: “On the Day of Resurrection, the Fire will subside for them, as fat in a cooking pot subsides. They will walk forward, only for the ground to swallow them up.”

And from Muqātil: “When a wall with a gate is erected between them and the believers, with mercy on the inside and punishment on the outside, they will remain in darkness and be told: ‘Go back and seek a light.’”

Some have said: “His mocking them consists in His drawing them gradually toward their doom.” Others have said: “It consists in bringing their mockery down upon them and turning their deception and plotting back against them.” Others have said: “He shows them in this world the opposite of what He has kept hidden for them in the Hereafter.” Still others have said: “It consists in His exposing their ignorance and showing that what they did was wrong.” All of this is true, and it is mockery of them in the literal sense.

Among the well-known examples cited by those who affirm figurative language in the Quran is:

“Ask the town.”

They say that its inhabitants are meant: the governing noun has been omitted, and its dependent noun put in its place. They are answered as follows: terms such as “town,” “city,” “river,” “gutter,” and the like encompass both what occupies a place and the place itself. Sometimes the statement concerns what occupies it—namely, the inhabitants—and sometimes the place itself.

Likewise, with a river, one says, “I dug the river,” meaning the place, and “The river flowed,” meaning the water. One says, “I installed the gutter,” meaning the place, and “The gutter flowed,” meaning the water. The same applies to a town. The Most High says:

“Allah sets forth the example of a town that was safe and at peace.”

And He says:

“And how many a town

We have destroyed! Our punishment came upon it by night or while its people rested at noon.”

“Their only cry when Our punishment came upon them was: ‘Indeed, we were wrongdoers.’”

In another verse, He says:

“Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they sleep?”

Thus, He made “towns” refer to the inhabitants themselves. He also says:

“How many a town, stronger than your town which drove you out, have We destroyed! They had no one to help them.”

Here, too, they are the inhabitants. Likewise, the Most High says:

“And those towns—We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed a time for their destruction.”

The Most High also says:

“Or like the one who passed by a town that lay in ruins, its roofs fallen in.”

Here, the place is meant, not the inhabitants. Yet it must be understood that it was once inhabited: a place is only called a town if it has been built up for habitation. The word’s root sense is gathering; hence the expression, “I gathered the water in the basin,” meaning that I collected it there.

Similarly, the term “human being” encompasses both body and soul. What is said of a human being applies sometimes to one and sometimes to the other, because they are inseparably connected. The same applies to a town: when its inhabitants are punished, it falls into ruin, and when it falls into ruin, that is a punishment for its inhabitants. Whatever harm befalls either affects the other, just as whatever befalls either body or soul affects the other.

Thus, His words:

“Ask the town,”

are like His words:

“A town that was safe and at peace.”

Here, the word refers to the inhabitants, without any word being implied or omitted. Thus, even assuming that figurative usage exists in the language, there is no figurative usage in the Quran. Indeed, dividing language into literal and figurative usage is itself a newly introduced innovation of which the early generations never spoke. Later scholars hold two views on it, and the dispute is not merely verbal. Rather, the contention is that this division itself is invalid: the two categories cannot be distinguished. Consequently, every distinction they propose proves invalid, and whenever one of them proposes a distinction, another refutes it—just as the logicians claim that the attributes subsisting in the things they qualify

and necessarily belonging to them are divided into those intrinsic to their essence as it exists in external reality, those extrinsic to it but necessarily accompanying the essence, and extrinsic concomitants of existence. They propose three distinctions, all of which are invalid, because this division itself is invalid and has no basis in reality. Indeed, what they classify as intrinsic can be classified as extrinsic, and vice versa, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Their claim, “If an expression conveys its meaning without a contextual indicator, its usage is literal; if it conveys its meaning only with one, its usage is figurative,” has already been shown to be invalid. No meaningful expression conveys its meaning independently of all contextual indicators, nor does any expression require every contextual indicator.

Among the most familiar examples of figurative usage are “lion,” “donkey,” and “sea,” which they say are borrowed to describe a courageous, dull-witted, or generous person, respectively. Yet these expressions are used only within combinations and constructions, qualified by verbal elements, just as literal expressions are. An example is what Abū Bakr al-Siddīq said concerning Abū Qatāda when someone else claimed the slain man’s spoils:

“No, by Allah! Would he then turn to a lion among Allah’s lions, who fights for Allah and His Messenger, and give you his spoils?”

His words, “turn to a lion among Allah’s lions, who fights for Allah and His Messenger,” describe the man’s strength in fighting in Allah’s cause. He has identified him so precisely as to remove any ambiguity. Similarly, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Khālid is indeed a sword among Allah’s swords, which Allah has drawn against the polytheists.”

There are other such examples.

If someone says, “Verbal contextual indicators are established by linguistic convention, and their indication of meaning is literal; circumstantial indicators, however, are figurative,” the reply is:

An expression is never used without qualifications supplied by verbal elements established through linguistic convention. Moreover, the circumstances—those of the speaker and the listener—must be taken into account in all speech.

translated_text:
for when the speaker is known, aspects of his meaning can be understood that would not be understood if he were unknown, because knowing him reveals his customary manner of speaking. An expression conveys meaning only when the speaker’s language is known—that is, the customary usage he follows in his speech. An expression’s signification of a meaning is purposeful, intentional, and voluntary: the speaker intends the expression to convey that meaning.

When he habitually uses an expression to convey a particular meaning, that constitutes his linguistic usage. Thus, anyone who pays close attention to the Messenger’s expressions and what he intends by them comes to know his customary manner of speaking and understands aspects of his intent that others do not. Accordingly, whenever an expression from the Quran or hadith is mentioned, one should make a point of considering its parallel occurrences and what Allah and His Messenger meant by them. In this way, one comes to know the language of the Quran and hadith and the established manner in which Allah and His Messenger address His servants—the customary usage evident in that speech. If numerous parallels are then found in the speech of others, it becomes clear that this customary linguistic usage is shared and general, not peculiar to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; rather, it is the language of his people.

His speech must not be interpreted according to linguistic conventions that arose after him and were unknown in his speech and that of his Companions, as many people do, perhaps unaware that those conventions did not exist in his time. This is why analogy in language, even if permissible in usage, is not permissible as a basis for inference. A person may be permitted to use an expression himself for a meaning analogous to that for which they used it, provided he makes this clear—though this is disputed. But he may not take expressions whose use for particular meanings is known, assign them different meanings, and say, “They intended those other meanings by analogy with the established ones.” Rather, this is alteration and distortion.

So when he says:

“A neighbour has a greater claim by virtue of his proximity,”

a neighbour means a neighbour, not a co-owner, for this latter meaning is unknown in their language. Yet nothing in the wording entails that he is entitled to the right of pre-emption; it merely indicates that selling to him is preferable. As for “khamr” (wine), numerous texts and authentic reports establish that it was a name for every intoxicant; nabīdh was not called khamr by analogy. Likewise, they called a grave robber a thief, as ʿĀ’ishah said: “One who steals from our dead is like one who steals from our living.” They also regarded a man who commits sodomy as more culpable than one who commits unlawful intercourse with a woman.

In interpreting the Quran and hadith, one must know how their wording indicates what Allah and His Messenger intend, and how their speech is to be understood. Knowledge of the Arabic language in which we have been addressed helps us understand what Allah and His Messenger intend by their speech, as does knowledge of how expressions convey meanings. Indeed, this was the cause of most of the misguidance of the people of innovation: they came to interpret the words of Allah and His Messenger according to meanings they claimed those words conveyed, when that was not the case. They deemed one meaning literal and another figurative. Thus, the Murji’ah erred concerning the term “faith”: they deemed its application to mere assent literal, and its inclusion of deeds figurative.

They may be answered as follows: If the distinction between literal and figurative usage is invalid, there is no need for this argument. If it is valid, it does not help you; rather, it counts against you, not in your favour. For a literal expression conveys its meaning when used without qualification or any contextual indicator, whereas figurative usage conveys its meaning only through a contextual indicator. It has already become clear that wherever the term “faith” is used without qualification in the Quran and Sunnah, deeds are included within it, and the claim that deeds are excluded from it is made only

when it is qualified; this indicates that its literal meaning is conveyed by his saying:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches.”

As for the hadith of Gabriel, if by faith he meant what he mentioned together with Islam, then that is indeed so. This is certainly the meaning intended by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Likewise, when he mentioned excellence in worship, he meant excellence together with faith and Islam; he did not mean excellence devoid of faith and Islam. Even supposing that the term “faith” meant mere assent, it was used in that sense only with a contextual indicator, so it would necessarily be figurative. This is self-evident and cannot be disputed after reflection upon the Quran and hadith. This is unlike the claim that “faith” is linguistically synonymous with assent, and the claim that the Lawgiver neither changed its meaning nor transferred it to a new sense, but intended precisely what speakers of the language intended by it, without restriction or qualification. Neither of these two premises can be affirmed with certainty, so they cannot counter what is certain. How could they, when each premise has been shown to be false and among the most unsound assertions?

Furthermore, the term “faith” is no less indicative of the commanded deeds than the terms “prayer,” “fasting,” “zakah,” and “Hajj” are indicative of prayer, fasting, and Hajj as prescribed by Islamic law. This holds whether one says that the Lawgiver transferred the term to a new meaning; intended the ruling rather than the designation; intended the designation but adapted its usage as people do in customary speech; or used the designation in a qualified rather than an unrestricted sense.

 إنْ أُرِيدَ بِالْبُطْلَانِ أَنَّهُ لَا تَبْرَأُ الذِّمَّةُ مِنْهَا كُلِّهَا؛ فَكَذَلِكَ الْإِيمَانُ الْوَاجِبُ إذَا تَرَكَ مِنْهُ شَيْئًا لَمْ تَبْرَأْ الذِّمَّةُ مِنْهُ كُلِّهِ. وَإِنْ أُرِيدَ بِهِ وُجُوبُ الْإِعَادَةِ فَهَذَا لَيْسَ عَلَى الْإِطْلَاقِ. فَإِنَّ فِي الْحَجِّ وَاجِبَاتٍ إذَا تَرَكَهَا لَمْ يُعِدْ بَلْ تُجْبَرُ بِدَمِ، وَكَذَلِكَ فِي الصَّلَاةِ عِنْدَ أَكْثَرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ إذَا تَرَكَهَا سَهْوًا أَوْ مُطْلَقًا وَجَبَتْ الْإِعَادَةُ فَإِنَّمَا تَجِبُ إذَا أَمْكَنَتْ الْإِعَادَةُ وَإِلَّا فَمَا تَعَذَّرَتْ إعَادَتُهُ يَبْقَى مُطَالَبًا بِهِ كَالْجُمُعَةِ وَنَحْوِهَا.
وَإِنْ أُرِيدَ بِذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ لَا يُثَابُ عَلَى مَا فَعَلَهُ فَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ بَلْ قَدْ بَيَّنَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي حَدِيثِ الْمُسِيءِ فِي صِلَاتِهِ أَنَّهُ إذَا لَمْ يُتِمَّهَا يُثَابُ عَلَى مَا فَعَلَ وَلَا يَكُونُ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَنْ لَمْ يُصَلِّ. وَفِي عِدَّةِ أَحَادِيثَ أَنَّ الْفَرَائِضَ تَكْمُلُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ مِنْ النَّوَافِلِ؛ فَإِذَا كَانَتْ الْفَرَائِضُ مَجْبُورَةً بِثَوَابِ النَّوَافِلِ دَلَّ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يُعْتَدُّ لَهُ بِمَا فَعَلَ مِنْهَا؛ فَكَذَلِكَ الْإِيمَانُ إذَا تَرَكَ مِنْهُ شَيْئًا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ فِعْلُهُ؛ إنْ كَانَ مُحَرَّمًا تَابَ مِنْهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ وَاجِبًا فَعَلَهُ؛ فَإِذَا لَمْ يَفْعَلْهُ لَمْ تَبْرَأْ ذِمَّتُهُ مِنْهُ وَأُثِيبَ عَلَى مَا فَعَلَهُ كَسَائِرِ الْعِبَادَاتِ وَقَدْ دَلَّتْ النُّصُوصُ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يَخْرُجُ مِنْ النَّارِ مَنْ فِي قَلْبِهِ مِثْقَالُ ذَرَّةٍ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ.
وَقَدْ عَدَلَتْ 
" الْمُرْجِئَةُ "
 فِي هَذَا الْأَصْلِ عَنْ بَيَانِ الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَأَقْوَالِ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ لَهُمْ بِإِحْسَانِ وَاعْتَمَدُوا عَلَى رَأْيِهِمْ وَعَلَى مَا تَأَوَّلُوهُ بِفَهْمِهِمْ اللُّغَةَ، وَهَذِهِ طَرِيقَةُ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ؛
 وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد يَقُولُ:
 أَكْثَرُ مَا يُخْطِئُ النَّاسُ مِنْ جِهَةِ التَّأْوِيلِ وَالْقِيَاسِ.
translated_text:
for, according to the Companions and the people of the Sunnah and the community, it is not nullified by a sin alone,

the reply is:

If invalidity means that one has not fully discharged one’s obligation to perform these acts, the same applies to obligatory faith: if one leaves out any part of it, one has not discharged that obligation in full. If it means that the act must be repeated, this does not apply without qualification. Hajj includes obligations whose omission does not require repeating it; rather, they are compensated for by a sacrificial offering. Likewise with prayer, according to most scholars: if obligations are omitted inadvertently or otherwise and repetition is required, it is required only when repetition is possible. Otherwise, whatever cannot be repeated remains an outstanding obligation, as with Friday prayer and the like.

If it means that one receives no reward for what one has done, that is not so. Rather, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made clear in the hadith of the man who prayed incorrectly that someone who does not complete his prayer is rewarded for what he has done and is not like someone who has not prayed at all. Several hadiths state that obligatory acts of worship will be made complete on the Day of Resurrection through voluntary acts. If deficiencies in obligatory acts are made good through the reward of voluntary acts, this shows that one is credited for the obligatory acts one has performed. The same applies to faith: if someone leaves any part of it unfulfilled, he remains obliged to fulfill it. If it concerns something forbidden, he must repent of it; if it concerns an obligation, he must perform it. If he does not do so, his obligation remains undischarged, but he is rewarded for what he has done, just as with other acts of worship. The scriptural texts also establish that whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will be brought out of the Fire.

On this fundamental issue, the “Murji’ah” have departed from the explanations given in the Book and the Sunnah and from the statements of the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness. They have relied instead on their own opinions and on interpretations derived from their understanding of the language. This is the way of the people of innovation. Hence Imam Ahmad used to say:

“Most people’s errors arise from interpretation and analogy.”

original_text:
وَلِهَذَا تَجِدُ الْمُعْتَزِلَةَ وَالْمُرْجِئَةَ وَالرَّافِضَةَ وَغَيْرَهُمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ يُفَسِّرُونَ الْقُرْآنَ بِرَأْيِهِمْ وَمَعْقُولِهِمْ وَمَا تَأَوَّلُوهُ مِنْ اللُّغَةِ؛ وَلِهَذَا تَجِدُهُمْ لَا يَعْتَمِدُونَ عَلَى أَحَادِيثِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَالصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ وَأَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛ فَلَا يَعْتَمِدُونَ لَا عَلَى السُّنَّةِ وَلَا عَلَى إجْمَاعِ السَّلَفِ وَآثَارِهِمْ؛ وَإِنَّمَا يَعْتَمِدُونَ عَلَى الْعَقْلِ وَاللُّغَةِ وَتَجِدُهُمْ لَا يَعْتَمِدُونَ عَلَى كُتُبِ التَّفْسِيرِ الْمَأْثُورَةِ وَالْحَدِيثِ؛ وَآثَارِ السَّلَفِ وَإِنَّمَا يَعْتَمِدُونَ عَلَى كُتُبِ الْأَدَبِ وَكُتُبِ الْكَلَامِ الَّتِي وَضَعَتْهَا رُءُوسُهُمْ وَهَذِهِ طَرِيقَةُ الْمَلَاحِدَةِ أَيْضًا؛ إنَّمَا يَأْخُذُونَ مَا فِي كُتُبِ الْفَلْسَفَةِ وَكُتُبِ الْأَدَبِ وَاللُّغَةِ وَأَمَّا كُتُبُ الْقُرْآنِ وَالْحَدِيثِ وَالْآثَارِ؛ فَلَا يَلْتَفِتُونَ إلَيْهَا. هَؤُلَاءِ يُعْرِضُونَ عَنْ نُصُوصِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ إذْ هِيَ عِنْدَهُمْ لَا تُفِيدُ الْعِلْمَ وَأُولَئِكَ يَتَأَوَّلُونَ الْقُرْآنَ بِرَأْيِهِمْ وَفَهْمِهِمْ بِلَا آثَارٍ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَصْحَابِهِ وَقَدْ ذَكَرْنَا كَلَامَ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ فِي إنْكَارِ هَذَا وَجَعْلِهِ طَرِيقَةَ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ. وَإِذَا تَدَبَّرْتَ حُجَجَهُمْ وَجَدْت دَعَاوَى لَا يَقُومُ عَلَيْهَا دَلِيلٌ. وَالْقَاضِي أَبُو بَكْرٍ الْبَاقِلَانِي نَصَرَ قَوْلَ جَهْمٍ فِي 
" مَسْأَلَةِ الْإِيمَانِ "
 مُتَابَعَةً لِأَبِي الْحَسَنِ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَكَذَلِكَ أَكْثَرُ أَصْحَابِهِ. فَأَمَّا أَبُو الْعَبَّاسِ القلانسي وَأَبُو عَلِيٍّ الثَّقَفِيُّ وَأَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنُ مُجَاهِدٍ شَيْخُ الْقَاضِي أَبِي بَكْرٍ وَصَاحِبُ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ - فَإِنَّهُمْ نَصَرُوا مَذْهَبَ السَّلَفِ. وَابْنُ كِلَابٍ - نَفْسُهُ -
 وَالْحُسَيْنُ بْنُ الْفَضْلِ البجلي وَنَحْوُهُمَا كَانُوا يَقُولُونَ:
 هُوَ التَّصْدِيقُ وَالْقَوْلُ جَمِيعًا مُوَافَقَةً لِمَنْ قَالَهُ مِنْ فُقَهَاءِ الْكُوفِيِّينَ كَحَمَّادِ بْنِ أَبِي سُلَيْمَانَ وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَهُ مِثْلِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَغَيْرِهِ.
translated_text:
For this reason, you find the Mu‘tazilah, the Murji’ah, the Rāfidah, and other people of innovation interpreting the Quran according to their own opinions, reasoning, and interpretations of the language. Thus, you find that they do not rely on reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions, the Successors, or the imams of the Muslims. They rely neither on the Sunnah nor on the consensus and transmitted reports of the early generations; rather, they rely on reason and language. You find that they do not rely on works of Quranic commentary based on transmitted reports, or on works of hadith and reports from the early generations. Instead, they rely on works of literature and the works of speculative theology composed by their leading figures.

This is also the way of the heretics: they draw only on works of philosophy, literature, and language. As for works concerning the Quran, hadith, and transmitted reports, they pay them no attention. These heretics turn away from the texts of the prophets because, in their view, they do not impart knowledge, whereas the others interpret the Quran according to their own opinions and understanding, without reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions. We have already cited the statements of Ahmad and others condemning this and identifying it as the way of the people of innovation. If you carefully examine their arguments, you will find claims unsupported by evidence.

Judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī defended Jahm’s position on “the question of faith,” following Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, as did most of his followers. As for Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, Abū ‘Alī al-Thaqafī, and Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mujāhid—the teacher of Judge Abū Bakr and a companion of Abū al-Hasan—they defended the position of the early generations. Ibn Kullāb himself, al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajalī, and others like them used to say:

“Faith consists of both assent and verbal profession.”

In this, they agreed with those jurists of Kufa who held this view, such as Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān and those who followed him, including Abū Hanīfah and others.

translated_text:
Section

Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī defended Jahm’s position on “faith,” although he also defended the well-known position of Ahl al-Sunnah that one should qualify one’s profession of faith by saying, “I am a believer, if Allah wills.” For he upheld the position of Ahl al-Sunnah that no one among the people of the qiblah is to be deemed an unbeliever, that they will not remain in Hell forever, that intercession on their behalf is accepted, and other such beliefs.

In matters disputed between the people of hadith and others, he consistently defends the position of the people of hadith. Yet he was not thoroughly acquainted with the grounds for their positions, so he defends their position on the basis of principles he himself considers sound, which he received from others. This leads him into contradictions that both sides reject. Such was his approach to the question of faith: he defended Jahm’s position while also defending the qualification “if Allah wills.” Consequently, many of his followers disagreed with him over this qualification—as we shall explain when discussing his grounds for it—while most followed him in defending Jahm’s position on faith.

Anyone acquainted only with works of speculative theology, without knowing what the early generations and the imams of the Sunnah said on this subject, supposes that the position presented in those works is that of Ahl al-Sunnah. Yet it is a position held by none of the imams of the Sunnah. Indeed, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Wakī‘, and others declared those who held Jahm’s position on faith—the position defended by Abū al-Hasan—to be unbelievers. In their view, it is worse than the position of the Murji’ah. For this reason, those among the Zaydiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, and similar groups who hold al-Shāfi‘ī in high esteem have come to criticize many who claim affiliation with him

: فَإِنْ قَالُوا: فَخَبِّرُونَا مَا الْإِيمَانُ عِنْدَكُمْ؟

 الْإِيمَانُ هُوَ التَّصْدِيقُ بِاَللَّهِ وَهُوَ الْعِلْمُ،
