translated_text:
saying, “Al-Shāfi‘ī was neither a philosopher nor a Murji’ī, whereas these men are philosophers, Ash‘arīs, and Murji’ah.” Their aim is to condemn the doctrine of the Murji’ah. We shall present their principal argument, since it is well known among many later scholars who identify with the Sunnah. Al-Qādī Abū Bakr said in al-Tamhīd:

“If they ask, ‘Tell us, then: what is faith according to you?’ the answer is: ‘Faith is affirmation of Allah, which is knowledge; affirmation resides in the heart.’

“If someone asks, ‘What is your evidence for what you have said?’ the answer is: ‘The unanimous agreement of all authorities on the Arabic language that, before the revelation of the Quran and the commissioning of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—faith meant affirmation. They recognize no other meaning for faith in the language. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ‘But you would not believe us,’ meaning: ‘You would not affirm what we say.’ Likewise, people say, ‘So-and-so believes in intercession,’ and ‘So-and-so does not believe in the punishment of the grave,’ meaning that he does not affirm it.

“‘It necessarily follows that faith in the revealed Law is the faith known in the language, for Allah neither changed nor transformed the Arabic language. Had He done so, reports of this would have been transmitted so widely as to establish certainty; the community would have had abundant reasons to transmit it, and its disclosure would have prevailed over its concealment. Our knowledge that He did not do this, but instead retained the names of things and all linguistic usage as they had been, is evidence that faith in the revealed Law has its linguistic meaning.

“‘This is further clarified by the words of the Exalted:

“‘“We never sent a messenger except in the language of his people.”

“‘And His words:

“‘“Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Quran.”

“‘He thus stated that He revealed the Quran in the language of the Arabs and used its terms for what they designated among them. There is no justification for departing from the apparent meanings of these verses without evidence, especially when their wording is held to be general in scope and authoritative teaching has established that the Quran was revealed in their language. This establishes our contention: faith is what we have described, to the exclusion of all other acts of obedience, whether voluntary or obligatory.’”

These are his exact words.

translated_text:
This is the mainstay of those who defend the Jahmiyyah’s position on “the question of faith.” The majority, among Ahl al-Sunnah and others, offer several responses to this.

The first is the position of those who dispute his claim that faith is synonymous with affirmation in the Arabic language, maintaining instead that it means acknowledgment or something else.

The second is the position of those who say: Even if its linguistic meaning is affirmation, affirmation can take place through the heart, the tongue, and the other bodily faculties, as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“The private parts confirm that or belie it.”

The third is to say: It is not affirmation without qualification, but a particular affirmation subject to qualifications with which the term is coupled. This neither transfers the term to a new meaning nor alters it, for Allah has not commanded us to have faith without qualification, but rather a particular faith that He has described and explained.

The fourth is to say: Even if it means affirmation, complete affirmation residing in the heart necessarily entails the obligatory deeds of the heart and the bodily faculties. These are necessary consequences of complete faith, and the absence of a necessary consequence proves the absence of that which entails it. We also say that these necessary consequences are sometimes included within what the term denotes and sometimes fall outside it.

The fifth is the position of those who say: The term retains its linguistic meaning, but the Lawgiver has attached additional rulings to it.

The sixth is the position of those who say: The Lawgiver used it in its figurative sense; thus, it is literal in the terminology of the revealed Law, but figurative in ordinary linguistic usage.

The seventh is the position of those who say that the term has been transferred to a new meaning.

These, then, are seven positions.

(The first): The position of those who dispute that its linguistic meaning is affirmation, saying that it does not mean affirmation, but rather acknowledgment or something else.

As for his statement, “All authorities on the language unanimously agree that, before the revelation of the Quran, faith meant affirmation,” he may be asked: Who reported this consensus? How is this consensus known? In which book is this consensus mentioned?

(The second): It may be asked: By “authorities on the language,” do you mean those who transmit it, such as Abū ʿAmr, al-Asmaʿī, al-Khalīl, and others like them, or those who speak it? If you mean the former, these scholars do not transmit everything that existed before Islam with a chain of transmission. Rather, they transmit what they heard from the Arabs of their own time, and what they heard through chains of transmission from collections of poetry, Arab speech, and other material. We know of no occurrence of the term “faith” in what they transmitted, much less any consensus among them concerning it. If you mean those who used this term before Islam, we did not witness them, nor has anyone transmitted this from them to us.

(The fourth): It may be said: These scholars do not transmit statements from the Arabs saying, “This term means such-and-such.” Rather, they transmit speech heard from the Arabs and state that such-and-such is understood from it. translated_text:
affirmation, that would be no more conclusive than the transmission of the Quran from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by the Muslims as a whole. If, despite this, some Muslims may suppose that a particular meaning was intended by it when it was not, such a supposition is all the more likely on the part of these scholars concerning what they transmit from the Arabs.

(The fifth): Even supposing that they said this, they are individual transmitters whose reports do not establish mass transmission. “Mass transmission” requires the same conditions to hold at the beginning, the intervening stages, and the end of transmission. Where, then, is the mass transmission from all the Arabs before the revelation of the Quran, attesting that they knew no meaning for faith other than affirmation?

If it is said, “This undermines knowledge of the language before the revelation of the Quran,” the answer is: So be it. Given the Messenger’s explanation of the Quran with which Allah sent him, we have no need to know the language as it existed before the Quran was revealed. The Quran was revealed in the language of Quraysh, and those it addressed were Arabs who understood its intended meaning: they were the Companions. The Companions then conveyed the Quran’s wording and meaning to the Successors, until it reached us. We therefore no longer need that language to reach us through mass transmission independently of the mass transmission of the Quran.

Rather, since the Quran has reached us through mass transmission in both wording and meaning, and we know that it was revealed in their language, we know that their language contained the words “sky,” “earth,” “night,” “day,” “sun,” “moon,” and the like, with the meanings they bear in the Quran. Otherwise, if we were required to produce mass-transmitted evidence independent of the Quran for each of these words, we would be unable to do so for all of them—especially if we were required to establish that all the Arabs intended this particular meaning by a given word, for that is impossible to ascertain. translated_text:
the Quran just as they conveyed its wording. If we supposed that some people heard speech in a foreign language and translated it for us into their own language, we would have no need to know the language in which they were originally addressed.

(The sixth): He has cited no example from Arab speech to support the claim he makes about their usage. His only evidence outside the Quran consists of people saying, “So-and-so believes in intercession,” “So-and-so believes in Paradise and Hell,” “So-and-so believes in the punishment of the grave,” and “So-and-so does not believe in that.” It is well known that these were not expressions used by the Arabs before the revelation of the Quran. Rather, people began using them after the era of the Companions, when adherents of religious innovation arose among them who denied intercession and the punishment of the grave.

What they mean by this is the same as what they mean when they say, “So-and-so believes in Paradise and Hell,” and “So-and-so does not believe in that.” Although affirmation in the heart is included in what the speaker means, that alone is not his intended meaning. Rather, he means affirmation with both heart and tongue, for affirmation in the heart alone, without verbal expression, cannot be known until the person declares what is in his heart.

(The seventh): It may be said that whoever says this does not mean affirming things that are hoped for or feared without any fear or hope. Rather, he affirms the punishment of the grave and fears it, and affirms intercession and hopes for it. Otherwise, if someone affirmed that he would be punished in his grave but had no fear of that whatsoever in his heart, they would not call him a believer in it. Likewise, they call someone a believer in Paradise and Hell only if he hopes for Paradise and fears Hell—not if he is wholly indifferent to them despite knowing that they are real.

Similarly, they do not call Iblīs a believer in Allah, even though he affirms His existence and Lordship. Nor do they call Pharaoh a believer, even though he knew that Allah had sent Moses and that it was He who sent down

the signs, of which they were inwardly certain despite denying them with their tongues. Nor do they call the Jews believers in the Quran and the Messenger, even though they recognize the truth as they recognize their own sons. Nowhere in Arab speech do they call someone a believer merely because he knows that something exists which is feared and hoped for, and ought to be loved and revered, while he neither loves nor reveres it, neither fears it nor hopes for it, but instead denies and rejects it with his tongue. Indeed, even if he recognized it in his heart but denied it with his tongue, they would not say, “He affirms it.” And if he affirmed it while acting contrary to what it requires, they would not say, “He believes in it.” Thus, there is not a single example in Arab speech supporting their claim.

As for His saying:

“You would not believe us,”

we have discussed this elsewhere. This is an argument based on the Quran, and nothing in the verse indicates that “one who affirms” is synonymous with “one who believes.” The fact that one of these expressions can correctly convey this meaning does not establish that it is synonymous with the other, as we have explained at length in the relevant discussion.

(The eighth): He says, “They recognize no other meaning of faith in the language.” On what basis does he make this denial, when exhaustive knowledge of the matter is impossible? Rather, this is a statement made without knowledge.

(The ninth): There is the view of those who say that faith (īmān) is derived from security (amn), whose statements will be presented below, Allah willing. They have also reported a linguistic meaning of faith other than this, as Shaykh Abū al-Bayān said concerning the statement (1).

translated_text:
(The tenth point): Even if we suppose that faith linguistically means affirmation, it is well known that faith does not mean affirming everything, but rather something specific: what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has conveyed. Faith in the Lawgiver’s speech would therefore be more specific than faith in ordinary language. It is well known that a specific category includes qualifications not found throughout the general category. For example, if we take one species of animal—namely, the human being—it possesses both the general characteristic and a characteristic peculiar to it. Together, these are not identical to the general characteristic alone. Thus, the affirmation that constitutes faith must, at the very least, be a particular kind of affirmation in the general sense. It therefore does not have the same scope, and this entails no alteration or distortion of the language. Rather, faith in the Lawgiver’s speech combines the general with the specific, just as a human being is described as both an animal and rational.

(The eleventh point): The Quran contains no mention of faith that is both unqualified and unexplained. Rather, the term “faith” in it is either qualified or unqualified but explained.

The “qualified” is exemplified by His words:

“They believe in the unseen,”

and His words:

“But none believed Moses except some of his people’s offspring.”

The “unqualified but explained” is exemplified by His words, exalted is He:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned,”

to the end of the verse; and His words:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful,”

and similar passages; and His words:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no discomfort over what you have decided and submit fully,”

and other such verses. Wherever faith is mentioned without qualification in the Quran, He makes clear therein that a person cannot be a believer unless deeds accompany affirmation. Thus, He has made clear in

If it is said:

“Those terms retain their meanings, but certain acts have been attached to what they denote as part of the ruling, not as part of the meaning of the terms—as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and others maintain.”

The response is:

If this is correct, the same may be said of faith. He raised this objection on behalf of some of them, but then gave no sound answer to it. Instead, he claimed that this is not mentioned in the Quran. That is not so. Rather, the Quran and Sunnah are filled with evidence that a person is not accorded the status of a believer unless deeds accompany affirmation. This is explained in the Quran far more extensively than the meaning of prayer and zakah. Those were explained only by the Sunnah, whereas the meaning of faith has been explained by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations.

(The twelfth point): When it is said that the Lawgiver addressed people in the language of the Arabs, He addressed them in the language familiar to them. Their customary usage allows a term to be unqualified and general, then acquire a qualification that narrows its meaning. For example, they say, “He went to the judge,” “the governor,” or “the commander,” intending a particular person known to them. The definite article, together with their knowledge of that person, identifies him. Yet in the language, the term is generic and does not designate any particular individual. There are many similar examples.

The same applies to faith, prayer, and zakah. He addressed them using these terms with the definite article, having already explained to them that what was intended was faith possessing such-and-such characteristics, and supplication possessing such-and-such characteristics. Thus, even supposing that faith means affirmation in their language, He has made clear: “I do not regard affirmation by the heart and tongue as sufficient, let alone affirmation by the heart alone. Rather, one must act in accordance with that affirmation.” This is illustrated by His words, exalted is He:

And in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“You do not believe until you are such-and-such.”

And in His words, exalted is He:

“You will not find people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.”

And in His words:

“Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

There are many such examples in the Book and Sunnah, including his words, peace be upon him:

“The adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery.”

And his words:

“He does not believe whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.”

And other similar statements. He has thus explained to them that the affirmation without which a person cannot be a believer must be affirmation of this kind. This is clear in the Quran and Sunnah, without any alteration of the language or transfer of its terms to new meanings.

(The thirteenth point): One may instead say: He did transfer these terms to new meanings and alter their usage.

As for his statement, “Had He done so, it would have been established through mass transmission,” the response is: Yes, and it has indeed been established through mass transmission that by prayer, zakah, fasting, and Hajj, He intended their familiar meanings. By faith, He intended what He explained in His Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger as indispensable for a servant to be a believer, as in His words:

“The believers are only those…”

This is established through mass transmission in “the Quran and the collections of Sunnah.” It is likewise established through mass transmission that no one was accorded the status of a believer unless he fulfilled the obligatory duties. It is also established through mass transmission from the Prophet that he stated that whoever dies a believer will enter Paradise without being punished, whereas the defiantly sinful are not entitled to that; rather, they are liable to punishment.

Thus, the meanings and rulings associated with the term faith have been transmitted from him through more numerous independent routes than those concerning other terms. What mass transmission could be more conclusive than this? There has been every incentive to transmit and make this known, and all praise belongs to Allah. No one can transmit anything from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that contradicts this. He did, however, include them within the designation of faith in certain passages, just as he included hypocrites under that designation in certain passages, with qualifications. As for the unqualified designation, whose bearers are promised Paradise, neither group is included in it.

(The fourteenth point): Regarding his statement, “There is no reason to depart from the apparent meaning of the verses indicating that it is Arabic,” the response is:

The verses that explain what a believer is and deny faith to those who do not act are more explicit, clearer, and more numerous than these verses. Moreover, even if these verses establish that it is Arabic, what he has mentioned does not make it cease to be Arabic. Thus, when He addressed them using the terms prayer, Hajj, and others, they did not say, “This is not Arabic.” Indeed, He addressed them using the designation “hypocrites,” although linguists have stated that this designation was unknown in the pre-Islamic period. Yet they did not say that it was not Arabic, because munāfiq (hypocrite) is derived from nafaqa, meaning “to exit.” When a word is derived from their language, and its speaker adapts its usage in accordance with their customary linguistic practices, it does not thereby cease to be Arabic.

(The fifteenth point): Even if it were assumed that these expressions were not Arabic, restricting the general scope of these expressions would be no greater a departure than removing the term faith from the meaning indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations. For the texts denying faith to someone who does not love Allah and His Messenger, does not fear Allah or remain mindful of Him, performs none of the obligatory duties, and refrains from none of the forbidden things are numerous and explicit. Thus, even supposing that a verse contradicted them, restricting the scope of a few general expressions would be preferable to rejecting the many explicit texts.

translated_text:
(The sixteenth point): These people suspend judgment concerning general expressions and do not affirm their general scope, whereas the early generations say: The Messenger acquainted us with the meanings of faith and explained it to us. We know with immediate certainty what he intended by it. We know, as a matter of necessary knowledge, that someone said to possess assent, yet who does not verbally profess faith despite being able to do so, does not pray or fast, does not love Allah and His Messenger, and does not fear Allah—but instead hates the Messenger, shows him hostility, and fights him—is not a believer. Likewise, we know that the unbelievers among the polytheists and the People of the Book who knew that he was Allah’s Messenger, yet treated him in this manner, were regarded by him as unbelievers, not believers. Our certainty about this is greater than our certainty that the entire Quran contains no non-Arabic expression. Thus, even if a conflict were supposed, giving precedence to that necessary knowledge would be more appropriate.

If they say, “When someone is known to have been declared an unbeliever by the Messenger, it is thereby known that assent was absent from his heart,” they are told: This is an obstinate denial of the facts, if they mean that such people were doubtful and uncertain. But if they mean that assent unaccompanied by action is deficient and tantamount to nonexistent, this is correct. Moreover, their contention can only be established if it is first established that faith consists solely of the heart’s assent and knowledge. Yet that can only be established after accepting these premises, of which this contention is itself one. A claim cannot therefore be established by the claim itself, given the unbelief of the person concerned.

It is further said: We know with immediate certainty that the Jews and others knew that Muhammad was Allah’s Messenger, yet he judged them to be unbelievers. We therefore know, as a necessary truth of his religion, that a person may be an unbeliever despite possessing assent to his prophethood in the heart, if he does not act upon that assent by loving him, revering him, and submitting to what he brought.

Another objection that may be raised against them is this:

If what you have mentioned is correct, it supports the position of the Murjiʾa—indeed, that of the Karrāmiyya—more strongly than it supports your own. For if faith is assent, as you have stated, then assent is a kind of speech. In Arabic usage, the terms “speech,” “utterance,” and the like are applied to meaning together with wording—or, rather, to wording that conveys meaning—more frequently than they are applied to meaning detached from wording.

Indeed, neither “speech” nor any of its forms—such as a statement, affirmation, denial, command, or prohibition—is ever applied to meaning alone, without some accompanying verbal expression, gesture, or something else. Only with a qualification are these terms used in that sense. Since Allah revealed the Quran in the Arabic language, that language recognizes affirmation, denial, and other forms of speech only as meaning together with wording, or wording that conveys meaning. Hence Allah has not regarded anyone as affirming the truthfulness of the messengers merely because of the knowledge and assent within their hearts, unless they also affirm their truthfulness with their tongues.

In Arabic speech, one does not say, “So-and-so affirmed another’s truthfulness,” or “declared him a liar,” merely because he knows in his heart that the other person is truthful or lying, without saying so. Likewise, one does not say, “He commanded him,” or “forbade him,” merely because a request arose in his heart without any accompanying words, gesture, or the like.

“No ordinary human speech is permissible in this prayer of ours,”

translated_text:
Quran: ‘Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; and Allah is the Greatest.’” Reported by Muslim.

Allah Most High says:

“To Him good words ascend, and righteous deeds raise them.”

Examples of this are numerous.

In short, wherever Allah mentions in His Book that any of His creatures—whether prophets, their followers, or those who denied them—“said,” “say,” or that something is “their saying,” or uses similar expressions, He means the meaning together with the spoken wording. The terms “saying,” “speech,” and the like, together with their derivatives—past- and present-tense verbs, imperatives, verbal nouns, and active participles—are known in the Quran, the Sunnah, and all other Arabic discourse only as referring to both wording and meaning. The same applies to the various kinds of speech, such as affirmation, denial, commands, prohibitions, and so forth. No one can deny this, for the examples are too numerous to count.

There was no dispute over what “speech” denotes among the Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, or the generation after them, whether among the adherents of the Sunnah or the adherents of innovation. Rather, the first person known in Islam to have maintained that speech denotes meaning alone was ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kilāb, who lived much later—at the time of Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s ordeal. Both the scholars of the Sunnah and the scholars of innovation rejected this view of his.

It is therefore inconceivable that none of the Companions, their followers, or the generation after them should have understood what speech means—though it is the most evident characteristic of the children of Adam, as Allah Most High says, “So by the Lord of heaven and earth, it is indeed true, as surely as you speak,” and the word has countless uses—until someone came along and advanced a view about it that no Muslim or anyone else had ever expressed before him.

If they say: Allah Most High has said, “And they say within themselves,” and, “And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and fearfully,” and other such passages.

The reply is:

If what is meant is that they said it quietly with their tongues, this provides no support for their argument. This is the explanation given by the Quran commentators. They said: They would say, “Death be upon you,” and when they left, they would say among themselves—that is, to one another—“If he were a prophet, we would be punished for saying to him what we say.”

Even if we suppose that what is meant is that they said it in their hearts, this is “saying” qualified by reference to the self, like his words:

“what they say to themselves.”

Hence they said:

“Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?”

Here they used the word “saying” without qualification, meaning what they uttered with their tongues, since this refers to the secret conversations and greetings they had been forbidden to engage in. As Allah Most High says:

“Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret conversations, yet return to what they were forbidden and converse secretly in sin, aggression, and disobedience to the Messenger? When they come to you, they greet you with a greeting Allah has not used to greet you, and say within themselves, ‘Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?’”

Moreover, the first interpretation is the one held by most Quran commentators, and comparable passages support it. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘Whoever remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it.’”

This does not mean that he does not utter it with his tongue; rather, it means that he remembers Allah with his tongue. Likewise, His words:

“Remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and fearfully, and without raising your voice in speech,”

refer to remembrance with the tongue.

The word qualified by reference to the self is hadīth (discourse): one says hadīth al-nafs (inner discourse). It has not been found that they used the expressions kalām al-nafs (the self’s speech) and qawl al-nafs (the self’s saying) as they used hadīth al-nafs. and the words of Joseph:

“and You have taught me the interpretation of dreams.”

If “speech” meant what is within the self merely because He mentioned His knowledge of what is within the hearts, then He would not have mentioned His knowledge of the other kind—what is spoken aloud. If it is said, “He indicated that by implication,” the reply is, “Rather, He indicated both categories by implication.”

It does not follow from this that such communication falls within the unqualified term “speech.” There is nothing whatsoever in their language to indicate that the unqualified terms “speech” and “saying” encompass what is within the self, let alone “affirmation” and “denial.” It is thus clear that someone who does not affirm with his tongue, despite being able to do so, is not called a believer in their language, as the early generations of this Ummah—the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness—agreed. Moreover, ‘Umar’s statement, may Allah be pleased with him, “I composed in my mind a statement that I intended to deliver,” is evidence against them.

Abū ‘Ubayd said:

“Tazwīr means refining and preparing speech.” He added: “Abū Zayd said: ‘Muzawwar and muzawwaq mean the same when used of speech: well-crafted and pleasing.’”

Another said:

“‘I composed in my mind a statement’ means that I prepared it in order to deliver it.”

His wording therefore indicates that he mentally formulated what he wanted to say but had not said it. It is thus clear that it becomes a saying only when it is uttered with the tongue. Before that, it was not a saying, but something formulated within the self with the intention of saying it. Likewise, a person may plan within himself to perform Hajj, pray, travel, or do other things. The words and deeds he intends thus have a mental form conceived within the self, but they are not called words and deeds until they actually occur, just as he is not performing Hajj or praying unless those actions actually take place.

For this reason, the forbidden words and deeds a person contemplates are not recorded against him until he says or does them. Any good words or deeds he intends are recorded for him as only one good deed. Once they become actual words and deeds, he is credited with ten

“Allah has pardoned my Ummah for what they say within themselves, so long as they neither utter it nor act upon it.”

As for the verse attributed to al-Akhtal:

“Speech indeed lies within the heart;
The tongue was only made to reveal the heart.”

Some have denied that this belongs to his poetry. They said that they had searched his collected poems but had not found it. This is reported from Muhammad ibn al-Khashshāb. Others have said that its wording is: “Eloquence indeed lies within the heart.”

If someone were to support an argument with a hadith from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, recorded by both compilers of the two Sahīh collections, they would say, “This is a solitary report,” even if it were a report that scholars had unanimously affirmed as true and received with acceptance. Yet the transmission of this verse from its purported author has not been established through even one sound chain, let alone more than one, nor have scholars of Arabic received it with acceptance. How, then, can it establish even the slightest point of language, let alone what the term “speech” denotes?

Furthermore, it may be said: What is denoted by “speech,” “saying,” and similar terms is not something for which one needs to consult a poet’s words. Speakers of the language, from the earliest generations to the latest, have used these terms and understood their meanings in their language, just as they have understood what “head,” “hand,” and “foot” denote. Moreover, the evidence supplied by speakers of a language lies in their use of words to convey their meanings, not in what they state

It is therefore clear that al-Akhtal did not intend to define what “speech” denotes. Indeed, no poet intends anything of the sort. Rather—if he actually said these words—he intended what commentators on poetry have explained: speech originates in the heart, where its meaning lies. Thus, if someone says with his tongue what is not in his heart, do not trust him. This is like the statements Allah relates from the hypocrites, mentioning that they say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Hence the poet said:

“Do not admire the words of one you favor
Until, alongside his speech, there is a firm foundation.
Speech indeed lies within the heart;
The tongue was only made to reveal the heart.”

He cautioned against admiring a person’s outward words until one knows the foundation within his heart. Hence he said, “Until, alongside his speech, there is a firm foundation.” His expression “alongside his speech” proves that he called the outward utterance speech even when it is not known whether its meaning is present in the speaker’s heart. This is evidence against them. His poetry thus includes both senses. Indeed, his expression “alongside his speech” is unqualified, whereas by “Speech indeed lies within the heart,” he meant its origin and intended meaning, which the tongue reveals.

In short, anyone who needs a poet’s words to discover what “speech” denotes in the languages of the Arabs, Persians, Romans, Turks, and all other peoples is among those furthest removed from understanding the ways of acquiring knowledge. Moreover, he belongs to the later generation of poets, not the ancient poets, and he is a Christian

The “Karrāmiyya” also agree with the Murji'a and the Jahmiyya that all people’s faith is equal, and they do not qualify their profession of faith by saying “if Allah wills.” Rather, they say of anyone who outwardly professes faith, “He is truly a believer.” If he is a hypocrite, however, then according to them he will remain in the Fire forever, for only those who believe both inwardly and outwardly will enter Paradise. Whoever reports that they say hypocrites will enter Paradise has falsely attributed this to them. Rather, they say that the hypocrite is a believer because faith consists of outward speech, just as others call him a Muslim because Islam consists of outward submission. There is no doubt that the Jahmiyya’s position is more unsound than theirs in numerous respects, whether judged by revelation, language, or reason.

If it is said, “The Karrāmiyya’s position departs from the consensus of the Muslims,” the reply is: “Jahm’s position on faith likewise departs from the consensus of the Muslims before him. Indeed, the early generations declared those who held Jahm’s position on faith to be disbelievers.” People have advanced sound arguments demonstrating the falsity of the Karrāmiyya’s position, yet arguments of the same kind demonstrating the falsity of the Jahmiyya’s position are even more numerous. One example is the saying of Allah Most High:

“And among the people are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ but they are not believers.”

They say, “Allah has thus denied that the hypocrites have faith.”

We reply: This is true, for the hypocrite is not a believer, and whoever calls him a believer has gone astray. Likewise, those who possess knowledge and assent in their hearts, yet deny the Messenger and show hostility towards him—such as the Jews and others—Allah has called disbelievers. He has never called them believers, nor have any of the rulings of faith applied to them. This is unlike the hypocrite, to whom the outward rulings of faith do apply in this world. Indeed, Allah has denied faith even to someone who affirms it with his tongue and in his heart if he does not act, as Allah Most High says:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’

Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted.”’” Up to His words:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful.”

Thus, He denied faith to anyone other than these. Allah Most High also says:

“They say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Messenger, and we obey.’ Then a group of them turns away after that. Those are not believers.”

“Turning away” means turning away from obedience, as Allah Most High says:

Allah Most High also says:

“He neither believed nor prayed, but denied and turned away.”

And Allah Most High says:

It is therefore clear that “turning away” is not denial; rather, it is turning away from obedience. People are required to believe the Messenger in what he conveys and obey him in what he commands. The opposite of believing is denying, and the opposite of obedience is turning away. Hence He says:

“He neither believed nor prayed, but denied and turned away.”

Allah Most High also says:

Thus, He denied faith to those who turned away from acting, even though they had made the verbal profession. Allah Most High says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have asked his permission.”

He also says:

translated_text:
such a person has never been called a believer. Yet according to the Jahmiyyah, if knowledge is present in his heart, he is a believer whose faith is complete, equal to the faith of the prophets, whatever he might say or do. In their view, he cannot conceivably lose faith unless that knowledge leaves his heart.

Moreover, most later scholars who defended Jahm’s position endorse qualifying one’s profession of faith with “if Allah wills.” They say that “faith in the religious sense” is what a servant meets his Lord with, even though its linguistic meaning is broader. Thus, on “the question of this qualification,” they took faith to mean what they claimed it meant in religious usage, departing from its linguistic meaning. Why, then, did they not do the same regarding deeds? The scriptural evidence that obligatory deeds are part of complete faith is too abundant to count. By contrast, there is no scriptural evidence that only the faith upon which a person dies may be called faith. This is an innovated view that none of the early predecessors expressed.

These people, however, supposed that this was the reasoning of those early predecessors who qualified their profession of faith. They and others like them were not well acquainted with the statements of the early predecessors. Rather, they defend the apparent meaning of those statements using what they have learned from the speculative theologians among the Jahmiyyah and other proponents of innovation. Thus, the outward formulation remains that of the early predecessors, while its underlying meaning is the doctrine of the Jahmiyyah, whose position on faith is the most corrupt of all. Allah willing, we shall mention the statements of the early predecessors concerning “qualifying one’s profession of faith.”

Accordingly, when the unsoundness of Jahm’s position on faith began to become apparent to some followers of Abū al-Hasan, many of them disagreed with him, and some followed the early predecessors. Abū al-Qāsim al-Ansārī, al-Shahrastānī’s teacher, said in his commentary on Abū al-Ma‘ālī’s al-Irshād, after mentioning the position of his fellow scholars: “The adherents of the transmitted tradition held that faith comprises all acts of obedience

He said: “This was also the position of Abū ‘Alī al-Thaqafī, one of our earlier scholars, and Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī. Others said: ‘If someone defiantly refuses verbal affirmation, he is a disbeliever according to religious law, even if affirmation and knowledge are present in his heart.’ Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī held the same view.”

Al-Ansārī said: “I have seen in his writings that a believer is only truly a believer when he gives effect to his faith through righteous deeds, just as a scholar is only truly a scholar when he acts upon his knowledge. He cited the words of Allah Most High:

‘The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them,’

through to His words:

‘It is they who are truly the believers.’”

Abū Ishāq also said: “The essential meaning of faith in the language is affirmation, and this is only realized through knowledge and obedience to commands. Gesture and submission take the place of verbal expression.”

translated_text:
they differed concerning these, as they explained in detail. They also differed over whether matters outside affirmation itself must be added to it for the designation of faith to apply validly. These include refraining from killing the Messenger, harming him, or venerating idols. These are acts of abstention; positive acts include supporting and defending the Messenger. They said: ‘All of these are added to affirmation under religious law.’ Others said: ‘Violating these requirements constitutes major sin, but does not take a person outside faith.’”

I say: Neither of these two positions is Jahm’s position. Yet whoever says this has acknowledged that faith is not merely the heart’s affirmation, nor is it a single thing, and has maintained that revealed law has modified its meaning. This undermines their foundational premise. For this reason, the most adept exponents of this school—such as Jahm, al-Sālihī, Abū al-Hasan, and Judge Abū Bakr—held that a person does not lose the designation of faith unless knowledge departs from his heart.

Abū al-Ma‘ālī said:

“(Chapter)
On Designations and Rulings

Know that our purpose in this chapter requires us first to explain the true nature of faith.”

He said: “This is a matter on which the Muslim schools have differed widely.” He then mentioned the positions of the Khawārij, the Mu‘tazilah, and the Karrāmiyyah, before saying: “As for the positions of our scholars, the discerning scholars among our hadith scholars and speculative theologians held that faith is affirmation. This was also the position of our shaykh Abū al-Hasan—may Allah have mercy on him. His view of the meaning of affirmation varied. On one occasion, he defined it as knowledge of His existence, His having no beginning, and His divinity.

“On another occasion, he said: ‘Affirmation is an inward statement, but it includes knowledge and cannot exist without it.’ This is what it entails, for affirmation and denial, truthfulness and falsehood, are more properly associated with statements.

translated_text:
Thus, affirmation is an inward statement expressed by the tongue. Worship is described as affirmation because it gives expression to affirmation.

Some of our scholars said: ‘Affirmation is only realized through both statement and knowledge; together, they constitute a single affirmation.’ Others deemed refraining from obstinate rejection sufficient and did not make verbal acknowledgment one of the two pillars of faith. Such a person says: ‘Faith is affirmation in the heart,’ while holding that religious law requires refraining from obstinate rejection. On this basis, a disbeliever may know Allah and disbelieve only through obstinate rejection, not because he lacks the foremost element of faith.

On this basis, it is said that the Jews knew Allah and knew that Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was a prophet, but disbelieved out of obstinacy, transgression, and envy.

He said: ‘According to our shaykh Abū al-Hasan’s position, we say of everyone whom we judge to be a disbeliever that he does not know Allah at all, nor has he known His Messenger or His religion.’”

His student, Abū al-Qāsim al-Ansārī, said: “The meaning would seem to be that his faith and knowledge have no standing under religious law.”

I say:

Al-Ansārī’s explanation does not apply to this position, but rather to their view that an obstinate rejecter is a disbeliever under religious law. On that basis, disbelief would arise sometimes from the absence of faith in the heart and sometimes from obstinate rejection. Such a person would be deemed a disbeliever under religious law even though he possesses the reality of faith, namely affirmation. This necessarily entails that he is a disbeliever under religious law despite possessing faith like that of the prophets and angels. The most adept exponents of this school—such as Abū al-Hasan, the Judge, and their predecessors among Jahm’s followers—recognized that this was a contradiction that undermined their foundational premise.

They supported their position with Allah’s words:

They said: “This implies that those who do not act as faith requires have not had faith inscribed in their hearts.”

They said: “If it is said that this means they do not possess faith that suffices and is recognized as valid, or that it means they do not fulfil the obligations of faith or act as it requires, we reply: ‘This wording is general and cannot be restricted without evidence.’”

They should be answered as follows: This verse denies faith to those who show affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger. It also states that those who do not show affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger have had faith inscribed in their hearts by Allah, and that He has strengthened them with a spirit from Him. This supports the position of the Salaf: faith necessarily includes the heart’s love for Allah and His Messenger and hatred of those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.

Thus, He has promised them Paradise. All agree that the promise of Paradise applies only when one fulfils what is commanded and refrains from what is prohibited. It follows that those in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him have fulfilled the obligations by which they merit what Allah has promised the righteous and God-fearing. This indicates that the sinful are not included in this promise. This verse also indicates that no believer shows affection to the disbelievers. Yet it is well known that many people know within themselves that affirmation remains in their hearts and that they have not disbelieved the Messenger, while nevertheless showing affection to some disbelievers.

The Salaf therefore say that abandoning outward obligations is evidence that the required faith is absent from the heart. I say:

This is an issue on which al-Ashʿarī expressed two different views: does ignorance of some attributes entail ignorance of the One possessing them, or not? The correct view, held by the majority and representing his later position, is that it does not entail ignorance of the One possessing them. Counting the affirmation of the attributes as part of faith is one respect in which al-Ashʿarī differed from Jahm, for Jahm went to extremes in denying the attributes—indeed, even the names.

Abū al-Hasan said:

“Revelation then stipulated additional conditions: faith must not be accompanied by anything, whether an act or an omission, indicating the disbelief of the person responsible. Thus, religious law commands him to refrain from worshipping and prostrating before an idol; if he does so, this indicates his disbelief. Likewise, if someone kills a prophet or treats him with contempt, this indicates his disbelief. Similarly, failing to honour the written Quran or the Kaʿbah indicates his disbelief.”

He said:

“One of the things we have taken as evidence of his disbelief is that which religious law forbids to accompany faith, or requires to be joined to faith. If it occurs, this indicates to us that the affirmation which constitutes faith is absent from his heart. Likewise, whenever we declare an opponent a disbeliever on account of an interpretation he adopts, we do so only because it indicates that what constitutes faith is absent from his heart. For it is impossible for revelation to declare someone a disbeliever while faith and affirmation remain in his heart.”

The reply is:

There is no doubt that the Lawgiver does not declare someone a disbeliever while faith remains in his heart. But your claim that faith is affirmation, even when entirely devoid of all deeds of the heart, is mistaken.

{وَلَوْ كَانُوا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَالنَّبِيِّ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إلَيْهِ مَا اتَّخَذُوهُمْ أَوْلِيَاءَ}

{فَلَا وَرَبِّكَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ حَتَّى يُحَكِّمُوكَ فِيمَا شَجَرَ بَيْنَهُمْ}

{وَإِذْ يَتَحَاجُّونَ فِي النَّارِ فَيَقُولُ الضُّعَفَاءُ لِلَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا إنَّا كُنَّا لَكُمْ تَبَعًا فَهَلْ أَنْتُمْ مُغْنُونَ عَنَّا نَصِيبًا مِنَ النَّارِ قَالَ الَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا إنَّا كُلٌّ فِيهَا إنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ حَكَمَ بَيْنَ الْعِبَادِ}
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى: {وَسِيقَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلَى جَهَنَّمَ زُمَرًا حَتَّى إذَا جَاءُوهَا فُتِحَتْ أَبْوَابُهَا وَقَالَ لَهُمْ خَزَنَتُهَا أَلَمْ
translated_text:

Likewise, the Jews, Christians, Magians and other disbelievers do not possess genuine, valid faith in their hearts when we judge them to be disbelievers.

Allah Most High said:

“Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

And He said:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning whatever disputes arise between them”—to the end of the verse.

Thus Allah made these matters conditions for the status of believer to apply. This establishes that faith is knowledge subject to conditions without which it has no validity.”

The reply is:

If you say that He added conditions to the heart’s knowledge before the status or designation of believer can apply, this would not be Jahm’s position. Rather, it would be the position of those who regard faith as analogous to prayer and pilgrimage: although these terms linguistically mean supplication and intention, the Lawgiver added further requirements, either for their religious status alone or for both their religious status and their designation. Whoever holds this position has conceded that the status of believer mentioned in the Quran and Sunnah is not established merely by the heart’s affirmation; those conditions must also be fulfilled.

Accordingly, he cannot regard a sinful person as a believer without evidence establishing this, merely by saying that the person possesses affirmation in the heart. Those who define faith as the heart’s affirmation say that no disbeliever in the Fire possesses any affirmation of Allah whatsoever—neither Iblīs nor anyone else.

Yet Allah Most High said:

“When they dispute in the Fire, the weak will say to those who were arrogant, ‘We used to follow you, so can you spare us any portion of the Fire?’ Those who were arrogant will say, ‘We are all in it. Allah has indeed judged between His servants.’”

And He Most High said:

“Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups. When they reach it, its gates will be opened, and its keepers will say to them, ‘Did there not

come to you messengers from among yourselves, reciting to you the verses of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?’ They will say, ‘Yes, but the decree of punishment has come into effect against the disbelievers.’”

They have thus acknowledged that the messengers came to them, recited to them the verses of their Lord, and warned them of the meeting of this Day of theirs. They therefore know Allah, His Messenger and the Last Day, yet they remain disbelievers in the Hereafter.

Allah Most High said:

“Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers will ask them, ‘Did no warner come to you?’ They will say, ‘Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, “Allah has sent down nothing.”’”

They thus denied His existence and denied His sending down revelation. In the Hereafter, however, they acknowledge all of this.

Allah Most High said:

“If only you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord! He will say, ‘Is this not the truth?’ They will say, ‘Yes, by our Lord.’ He will say, ‘Then taste the punishment for your disbelief.’”

And He Most High said:

“The agony of death brings the truth: ‘This is what you were trying to evade.’”

Then, further on, He says:

“You were certainly heedless of this. Now We have removed your veil, and today your sight is sharp.”

There are many other verses indicating that the disbelievers will know their Lord in the Hereafter. If mere knowledge were faith, they would be believers in the Hereafter.

If they say, “Faith in the Hereafter is of no benefit; reward is only for faith in this world,” the reply is:

This is correct. But if faith is nothing more than mere knowledge, its essential nature does not change. If deeds are not part of faith, then someone who possesses this knowledge in the Hereafter lacks nothing of faith. Yet the most they claim is that, when he died, his heart contained no affirmation of the Lord whatsoever. The Quranic texts indicate in several places that the disbelievers affirmed the Lord in this world. Even Pharaoh, who openly displayed denial, inwardly affirmed Him.

Allah Most High said:

“They denied them, though their souls were certain of them, out of injustice and arrogance.”

And as Moses said to Pharaoh: “He said, ‘You certainly know

“Our Lord, destroy their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.”

Allah said:

When Pharaoh said:

Allah said:

Thus, He described him as disobedient, not as inwardly lacking knowledge, just as He said:

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

Likewise, He said concerning Iblīs:

“So the angels prostrated, all of them together, except Iblīs; he was arrogant and became one of the disbelievers.”

He described him only in terms of refusal, arrogance and opposition to the command; He did not describe him as lacking knowledge. In several places, Allah has also stated that the disbelievers acknowledged the Creator, as in His saying:

“If you ask them who created them, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’”

They should then be asked: When you say that faith is affirmation in the heart, on the tongue, or both, do you mean affirmation in general terms, or must it include the details? If someone affirms that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah but does not know Allah’s attributes, is he a believer or not? If they consider him a believer, they should be told: If he then learns of those attributes and denies them, he is no longer a believer, by the consensus of the Muslims. Thus, some faith is more complete than other faith.

If they say that he is not a believer, their position entails that no one is a believer until he knows in detail everything the Messenger conveyed. Yet it is well known that most of the Muslim community do not know all of that. They hold, however, that faith varies in degree only in its continuity.

Abū al-Maʿālī said:

“If someone says, ‘Your principle entails that the faith of someone engrossed in his sinful conduct is like the faith of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’

we reply: ‘What makes his faith superior to that of everyone else is the continuity of his affirmation and Allah’s protection of him from the intrusion of doubts and the stirrings of misgivings. Affirmation is an accident that does not persist. It occurs in uninterrupted succession in the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, whereas in others it is present at certain times and absent during periods of interruption. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has a number of instances of affirmation, while others have only some of them. His faith is therefore greater and better.’”

He said: “If faith were described as increasing and decreasing, with this meaning intended, that would be sound.”

I say: This, then, is what, in their view, makes the Prophet’s faith superior to that of others. Yet it is well known that this is utterly unsound in many respects, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Section

Those among the later scholars who championed Jahm’s doctrine concerning faith said—as did al-Qādī Abū Bakr, whose exact wording follows:

> If someone asks, “What is Islam according to you?” he is told: “Islam is compliance and submission. Every act of obedience through which the servant complies with his Lord and submits to His command is Islam. Faith is one of the constituent qualities of Islam. All faith is Islam, but not all Islam is faith.”
>
> If he asks, “Why do you say that Islam means what you have described?” he is told: “Because of the words of Allah Most High:
>
> ‘The Bedouins say, “We believe.” Say, “You have not believed; rather, say, ‘We have submitted.’”’
>
> He denied them faith while affirming their Islam. What He affirmed meant only compliance and submission. Another example is His saying:
>
> ‘And they offer you peace.’
>
> Anyone who submits to something has surrendered, although this expression is most often used of someone who submits to Allah and His Prophet.”

I say: Besides being false and contrary to the Book and the Sunnah, what they have stated is self-contradictory. They have made faith one of the constituent qualities of Islam: all acts of obedience are Islam, yet none of them is faith except affirmation.

Although the Murji’ah say that faith includes Islam, they maintain that faith is affirmation by the heart and the tongue. The Jahmiyyah, however, make it affirmation by the heart alone. Thus, neither the two testimonies of faith, nor prayer, nor zakat, nor any other such acts form part of faith. And it has already

As for the contradiction, when they say, “Faith is one of the constituent qualities of Islam,” someone who possesses faith has attained only one of those qualities, not the entirety of the Islam that is obligatory. Yet they have said, “All faith is Islam, but not all Islam is faith.” If they mean that all faith constitutes the Islam that Allah has commanded, this contradicts their statement that faith is one of its constituent qualities: they have made faith part of Islam, not identical with it. But if they say, “All faith is Islam,” meaning that it is obedience to Allah and part of the Islam that is obligatory—and this is what they mean—then they should be told:

On this basis, there would be as many instances of Islam as there are acts of obedience. The two testimonies of faith alone would constitute Islam; prayer alone would constitute Islam; and zakat would constitute Islam. Indeed, every dirham you give to a poor person would constitute Islam, every prostration would constitute Islam, every day you fast would constitute Islam, and every glorification of Allah you utter, whether during prayer or otherwise, would constitute Islam.

“You have not believed; rather, say, ‘We have submitted.’”

He thus affirmed Islam for them while denying them faith. Furthermore, if you exclude the defiantly sinful from the designation of Islam, doing so is more objectionable than excluding them from the designation of faith. You have therefore fallen into the gravest error for which you censured the Mu‘tazilah. For the Quran and Sunnah deny them the designation of faith far more emphatically than they deny them the designation of Islam, and the designation of faith carries greater weight in the Quran and Sunnah.

If, however, you say, “Rather, anyone who performs an act of obedience is called a Muslim,” it follows that someone who performs an act of obedience without uttering the two testimonies of faith is a Muslim. Likewise, someone who affirms the truth in his heart without expressing it with his tongue must, according to you, be a Muslim. For, according to you, faith is Islam, so whoever possesses faith has attained Islam. Thus, according to you, someone who utters the two testimonies of faith without performing any deeds would be a Muslim.

You also cite His words:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted.”’”

You say, “He denied them faith and affirmed Islam for them.”

The response is: This verse is evidence against you. By affirming Islam for them despite their lack of faith, He showed that faith is not a constituent part of Islam. Were it part of Islam, they could not be Muslims without possessing it.

They say, “The word dīn (religion) is derived from tadayyun (religious devotion), and its meaning is close to that of Islam.”

The response to them is: If this is your position, then your statement, “Every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer,” contradicts it. When you say, “Every believer is a Muslim,” you do not mean that he has pronounced the two testimonies of faith or fulfilled any of the five pillars. Rather, you mean that he has performed an act of obedience—an inward act of obedience. Yet this is not what is meant by a Muslim in the Quran and Sunnah, nor among the leading scholars, early or later. You then cite the verse as evidence, although the Bedouins had merely manifested outward Islam by pronouncing the two testimonies of faith, whether truthfully or falsely. Allah thus affirmed Islam for them but not faith. Someone unfamiliar with the reality of the matter might therefore suppose that this is the position of the early generations, supported by the Quran and Sunnah: that every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer. Yet the difference between the two positions is greater than that between the early generations’ position and that of the Muʿtazilah concerning faith and Islam. For the Muʿtazilah’s position on faith and Islam is far closer to that of the early generations than the Jahmiyyah’s position is. Their position that those who pray toward the qiblah will remain eternally in Hell, however, is further from the early generations’ position than that of the Jahmiyyah.

The later scholars who championed Jahm’s position on “the question of faith” profess the position of the early generations on this matter, on qualifying one’s profession of faith, on denying faith in the heart where the Quran denies it, and on similar matters. In all this, however, their agreement with the early generations is merely verbal. Otherwise, their position differs utterly from that of the early generations; no position is further removed from theirs.

Section

Among the Quranic proofs that faith, when mentioned without qualification, necessarily entails deeds is the saying of the Most High:

“Only those believe in Our signs who, when reminded of them, fall down in prostration and glorify their Lord with praise, and are not arrogant.”

He thus denies faith to anyone other than these. Whoever, when reminded by the Quran, fails to perform the prostration Allah has prescribed for him is not among the believers. The prostrations of the five daily prayers are obligatory by agreement of the Muslims. As for prostration upon recitation, its obligation is disputed. Those who consider it obligatory may cite this verse as evidence, but this is not the place to discuss that issue in detail. This verse is like His saying:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives.”

And His saying:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned.”

And His saying:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have asked his permission.”

Further evidence is His saying, Most High:

“Allah has pardoned you. Why did you grant them permission before it became clear to you who was truthful and you knew who the liars were?”

“Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission to be excused from striving with their wealth and their lives. And Allah knows well those who fear Him.”

“Only those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day ask your permission, and whose hearts are filled with doubt, so they waver in their doubt.”

This verse is like His saying:

Among its opposites are showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, and seeking his permission to abstain from jihad. “And Allah knows well those who fear Him,”

indicates that those who fear Him are the believers.

The Prophet’s following sayings fall into the same category:

“One who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is not a believer while committing it.”

“He whose neighbor is not safe from his harm does not believe.”

“You will not believe until you love one another.”

“None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his child, his father, and all people.”

“None of you believes until he loves for his brother the good that he loves for himself.”

“Whoever cheats us is not one of us, and whoever takes up arms against us is not one of us.”

translated_text:
Section

When faith is qualified by being mentioned alongside Islam or righteous deeds, everyone agrees that it may refer to the faith within the heart. But does it also include what is conjoined with it, making this a case of mentioning the specific after the general? Or, when the two are mentioned together, does the other term fall outside what faith denotes, while remaining a necessary implication of it, according to the position of Ahl al-Sunnah? Or is it neither a part nor a necessary implication of faith? People hold three views on this, as will be explained, Allah willing.

This occurs with most terms: what they denote varies according to whether they are used without qualification or with qualification. Examples include the terms “what is right” and “what is wrong.” When these are used without qualification, as in His saying, exalted is He:

“He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong,”

and His saying:

“You are the best nation brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong,”

and His saying:

“The believing men and believing women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong,”

“what is right” includes every good, and “what is wrong” includes every evil.

Yet a term may be mentioned alongside something more specific than itself, as in His saying:

“There is no good in much of their private conversation, except in that of those who enjoin charity, what is right, or reconciliation between people.”

Here He distinguishes what is right from charity and reconciliation between people—just as He distinguishes the terms faith and deeds, and the terms faith and Islam. Likewise, in His saying, exalted is He:

“Indeed, prayer restrains one from indecency and wrongdoing,”

He distinguishes

between the two, although indecency is included in “what is wrong” in His saying:

“They forbid what is wrong.”

Then He mentions two things alongside wrongdoing in His saying:

“Indeed, Allah commands justice, excellence, and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression.”

Here He distinguishes oppression from the other two, although it is included in wrongdoing in the two passages cited earlier.

The term “worship” is another example. When worshipping Allah is commanded without qualification, it includes everything Allah has commanded. Relying upon Him and seeking His help are among the things He has commanded. They are therefore included in such statements as:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

And His saying:

“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him.”

And His saying:

“O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, We have sent down the Book to you in truth, so worship Allah with sincere devotion to Him.”

“Say, ‘It is Allah I worship, with sincere devotion to Him.’”

And His saying:

“Do you command me to worship other than Allah, you ignorant people?”

Yet another term may be mentioned alongside worship, as in His saying:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

And His saying:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

And Noah’s saying:

“Worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me.”

Likewise, when the expression “obedience to Allah” is used on its own, it includes everything He has commanded, and obedience to the Messenger is included in obedience to Him. Similarly, when the term “piety” is used on its own, it includes carrying out every command and refraining from everything forbidden.

Talq ibn Habīb said: “Piety means acting in obedience to Allah, upon light from Allah, hoping for Allah’s mercy; and refraining from disobedience to Allah, upon light from Allah, fearing Allah’s punishment.”

This is its meaning in His saying:

“Indeed, the pious will be amid gardens and rivers,

in a seat of honour, near a Sovereign, Perfect in Power.”

Yet another term may be mentioned alongside piety, as in His saying:

“Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him.”

“And provide for him from where he does not expect.”

“And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient—Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

And His saying:

“Fear Allah, in whose name you appeal to one another, and honour the ties of kinship.”

And His saying:

“Fear Allah and speak upright words.”

And His saying:

“Fear Allah and be with the truthful.”

And His saying:

“Fear Allah as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims.”

And other such passages.

His saying:

“Fear Allah and speak upright words”

is like His saying:

“Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that over which He has made you trustees.”

And His saying:

“The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and so have the believers. All have believed in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’ And they say, ‘We hear and obey. Grant us Your forgiveness, our Lord; to You is the final return.’”

He thus mentions their statement alongside faith, just as He mentions upright speech alongside piety. It is well known that when piety is mentioned without qualification, it includes upright speech. Likewise, when faith is mentioned without qualification, it includes hearing and obeying Allah and the Messenger.

The same applies to His saying:

“Believe in Allah and His Messenger.”

When belief in Allah is mentioned without qualification with reference to the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, it includes belief in the Messenger. Likewise, His saying:

“All have believed in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”

When belief in Allah is mentioned without qualification, it includes belief in these associated matters. The same applies to His saying:

“And those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you.”

And His saying:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham’”—and the rest of the verse.

And when it is said:

“So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet,”

belief in His Messenger includes belief in all the Books, messengers and prophets. The same applies when it is said:

“And believe in His Messenger; He will grant you a double share of His mercy.”

And when it is said:

“Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that over which He has made you trustees,”

belief in Allah and His Messenger includes belief in all of that. Spending is also included in His saying in the other verse:

“Believe in Allah and His Messenger,”

just as upright speech is included in such words of His as:

“And We have certainly enjoined those who were given the Scripture.”

Likewise, when “righteousness” is mentioned without qualification, it encompasses everything Allah has commanded, as in His saying:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and the wicked will be in Hellfire.”

And His saying:

“Rather, righteousness is in one who fears Allah.”

And His saying:

“Rather, righteousness is in one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture and the prophets; who gives wealth, despite his love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the stranded traveller, those who ask, and to free those in bondage; who establishes prayer and gives zakah; those who fulfil their promises when they make them; and those who are patient in poverty, hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and those are the ones who are pious.”

Thus, when righteousness is mentioned without qualification, it denotes the same as piety; and when piety is mentioned without qualification, it denotes the same as righteousness. Yet the two may be mentioned together, as in His saying, Exalted is He:

“Cooperate in righteousness and piety.”

Likewise, when “sin” is mentioned without qualification, it includes every sinful act. Yet it may be mentioned alongside transgression, as in His saying, Exalted is He:

“And do not cooperate in sin and transgression.”

Likewise, when “sins” are mentioned without qualification, they include neglecting any obligation and committing any forbidden act, as in His saying:

“O My servants

who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.”

Yet it may be mentioned alongside another term, as in His saying:

“Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affairs.”

Likewise, when “guidance” is mentioned without qualification, it encompasses both the knowledge with which Allah sent His Messenger and acting upon it. It therefore includes everything Allah has commanded, as in His saying:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

What is meant is a request both to know the truth and to act upon it. The same applies to His saying:

“A guidance for the pious.”

This means that they know what it contains and act upon it, and that is why they have become successful. Likewise, the people of Paradise say:

“Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this.”

He guided them by inspiring them with beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds. Yet guidance may be mentioned alongside being chosen, as in His saying:

“And We chose them and guided them to a straight path.”

And in His saying:

“He was grateful for His favours; He chose him and guided him.”

“Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns to Him.”

Likewise, He, Exalted is He, says:

“It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth.”

Here, guidance means faith, and the religion of truth means Islam. When guidance is mentioned without qualification, however, it is like faith mentioned without qualification: it includes both.

When “misguidance” is mentioned without qualification, it encompasses anyone who has strayed from guidance, whether deliberately or out of ignorance, and it follows that he will be punished. Thus He says:

“Indeed, they found their forefathers astray, so they hasten to follow in their footsteps.”

And He says:

“Our Lord, we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they led us astray from the path. Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great curse.”

And He says:

“Whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer.”

Yet misguidance may be mentioned alongside waywardness and wrath, as in His saying:

“Your companion has not gone astray

And in His saying:

“Not those who have incurred Your wrath, nor those who have gone astray.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, the criminals are in error and blazing fires.”

Likewise, when “waywardness” is mentioned without qualification, it encompasses every act of disobedience to Allah, as in His saying concerning Satan:

“I will surely lead them all astray, except Your chosen servants among them.”

Yet it may be mentioned alongside misguidance, as in His saying:

“Your companion has not gone astray, nor has he become wayward.”

Likewise, when the term “poor” is used on its own, it includes the needy; and when “needy” is used on its own, it includes the poor. When the two are mentioned together, however, each refers to a distinct group. Examples of the first usage are His sayings:

“If you conceal your charity and give it to the poor, that is better for you.”

“Its expiation is to feed ten needy people.”

An example of the second is His saying:

“Charitable alms are only for the poor and the needy.”

These terms vary in meaning according to whether they are unqualified or qualified, used in isolation or alongside other terms. Sometimes, when used on its own, one term is broader than the other, as with “faith” and “what is right” in relation to deeds and truthfulness, and “wrongdoing” in relation to indecency, transgression, and the like.

At other times, the terms are equal in their breadth and specificity, as with “faith,” “righteousness,” and “piety,” or “poor” and “needy”: whichever is used without qualification encompasses what the other encompasses.

The same applies to “recitation.” When used without qualification, as in His saying:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture recite it as it should be recited,”

it includes acting upon it. This is how the Companions and their successors, such as Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and others, explained it. They said: “‘They recite it as it should be recited’ means that they follow it as it should be followed: they regard as lawful what it declares lawful, regard as unlawful what it declares unlawful, act upon its clear verses, and believe in its ambiguous verses.”

It has also been said that the word here means following, as in His saying:

“And by the moon when it follows the sun.”
