As Abū ʿAbd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said: “Those who taught us the Quran—ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, and others—told us that whenever they learned ten verses from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, they would not proceed beyond them until they had learned the knowledge and practice they contained. They said: ‘Thus we learned the Quran, knowledge, and practice together.’”

In His saying:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture recite it as it should be recited,”

the Scripture has been interpreted as referring to the Quran, and also to the Torah.

Muhammad ibn Nasr related through his established chain of transmission that Ibn ʿAbbās explained “recite it as it should be recited” as meaning: “They follow it as it should be followed.”

It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he explained “recite it as it should be recited” as meaning: “They regard as lawful what it declares lawful, regard as unlawful what it declares unlawful, and do not distort its words from their proper places.”

Concerning “recite it as it should be recited; those are the ones who believe in it,” Qatādah said: “Those are the Companions of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They believed in Allah’s Book and affirmed its truth, regarded as lawful what it declares lawful, regarded as unlawful what it declares unlawful, and acted upon its contents. It has been related to us that Ibn Masʿūd used to say: ‘Reciting it as it should be recited means regarding as lawful what it declares lawful and regarding as unlawful what it declares unlawful, and that we recite it as Allah revealed it, without distorting its words from their proper places.’”

Concerning “recite it as it should be recited,” al-Hasan said: “They act upon its clear verses, believe in its ambiguous verses, and leave whatever they find difficult to understand to the one who knows it.” Mujāhid explained it as: “They follow it as it should be followed”; and in another narration: “They act upon it as they should.”

Yet recitation may also be mentioned alongside something else, as in His saying:

“Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish prayer. Indeed, prayer restrains one from indecency and wrongdoing.”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others said: “Reciting the Book means performing all acts of obedience to Allah.” Prayer was then singled out for mention, as in His saying:

“And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer,”

and His saying:

“So worship Me and establish prayer

for My remembrance.”

Likewise, the expression “following what Allah has revealed” encompasses all acts of obedience, as in His sayings:

“Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord, and do not follow any protectors besides Him.”

“Whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer misery.”

“This is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they lead you away from His way.”

Yet He may mention something else alongside it, as in His sayings:

“This is a blessed Book which We have revealed, so follow it and fear Allah, that you may receive mercy.”

“Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord—there is no god but Him—and turn away from the polytheists.”

“Follow what is revealed to you, and be patient until Allah judges, for He is the best of judges.”

Likewise, when the term “the righteous” is used without qualification, it includes every God-fearing person, whether among those foremost in good deeds or those who take a middle course. When mentioned alongside “those brought near,” however, its meaning is more specific. Concerning the first usage, Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire.”

Concerning the second, He says:

“No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyīn. And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyīn is? A record inscribed, witnessed by those brought near.”

This is a vast subject, an exhaustive treatment of which would be lengthy. It is among the most beneficial matters for understanding what words signify in general, and the words of the Quran and Sunnah in particular. Through it, many misconceptions over which people have disputed extensively are dispelled. Among these is “the question of faith and Islam”: the dispute over what these two terms denote was the first disagreement to arise that caused the Muslim community to split. This also applies to the statements of the early generations and the imams of the Sunnah concerning the definition of faith. Sometimes they say, “It is speech and action.” Sometimes they say, “It is speech, action, and intention.” Sometimes they say, “Speech, action, intention, and adherence to the Sunnah.” And sometimes they say, “Speech of the tongue, belief in the heart, and action of the limbs.” All of these are correct.

When they say “speech and action,” speech includes the speech of both the heart and the tongue. This is what is understood by the terms “saying,” “speech,” and similar expressions when used without qualification. There are four views concerning what “speech” and “saying” denote when used without qualification. The position of the early generations, the jurists, and the majority is that these terms encompass both verbal expression and meaning, just as the term “human being” encompasses both soul and body.

Another view holds that what the term denotes is verbal expression alone: meaning is not part of what it denotes, but is instead what that verbal expression signifies. This is the view of many speculative theologians among the Muʿtazilah and others, and of a group of those who identify with the Sunnah. It is also the view of the grammarians, because their discipline concerns verbal expressions.

Another view holds that what the term denotes is meaning alone, and that applying “speech” to verbal expression is figurative, because the expression signifies that meaning. This is the view of Ibn Kullāb and his followers.

Another view holds that it is a term shared by verbal expression and meaning. This is the view of some later Kullābīs. The point here is that those among the early generations who said, “Faith is speech and action,” meant the speech of the heart and tongue, and the actions of the heart and limbs. Those who wished to specify belief thought that “speech” would be understood to mean only outward speech, or feared that it might be understood that way, so they added “belief in the heart.”

Those who said, “Speech, action, and intention,” held that “speech” encompasses both belief and the speech of the tongue, whereas “action” might not be understood to include intention, so they added it. Those who added adherence to the Sunnah did so because none of this is beloved to Allah unless it accords with the Sunnah. The others did not mean every kind of speech and action; they meant only those words and deeds prescribed by Allah. Their purpose, however, was to refute the “Murji’ah,” who made faith speech alone, so they said, “Rather, it is speech and action.”

Those who described it as having “four components” explained what they meant. Thus, when Sahl ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Tustarī was asked, “What is faith?” he replied:

“Speech, action, intention, and adherence to the Sunnah. For if faith consists of speech without action, it is disbelief; if it consists of speech and action without intention, it is hypocrisy; and if it consists of speech, action, and intention without adherence to the Sunnah, it is innovation.”

Section

Coordinating one thing with another in the Quran and in speech generally implies a distinction between the two elements, while both share in what is predicated of them. This distinction has degrees. The greatest is when they are entirely distinct: neither is identical to the other, nor part of it, nor known to be its necessary concomitant. Examples include His saying:

“He created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six days,”

and similar passages; His saying:

“and Gabriel and Michael”;

and His saying:

“And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion.”

This is the most common case.

Next is when there is a necessary connection between them, as in His saying:

“Do not mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth”;

His saying:

“And whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him and follows a path other than that of the believers”;

and His saying:

“And whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers.”

Whoever disbelieves in Allah has disbelieved in all of these. Thus, the latter element necessarily accompanies the former. In the preceding verse, the former element is a necessary concomitant, for whoever opposes the Messenger after guidance has become clear to him has followed a path other than that of the believers. There is disagreement regarding the second.

As for His saying:

“Do not mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth,”

the two necessarily accompany one another. Whoever mixes truth with falsehood, making it confused with it, obscures the truth to the extent that he makes falsehood apparent, so that the truth becomes confused. And whoever conceals the truth needs to put in its place

falsehood, thereby mixing truth with falsehood. This is why anyone among the People of the Book who conceals what Allah has revealed must necessarily put forward some falsehood. The same applies to the “people of innovation”: you will find no one who abandons any part of the Sunnah that must be believed and acted upon without falling into an innovation, nor anyone who follows an innovation without abandoning something of the Sunnah. As the hadith states:

“No people introduce an innovation without abandoning an equivalent part of the Sunnah.”

It was narrated by Imam Ahmad.

Allah Most High has said:

“They forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of, so We stirred up enmity and hatred among them.”

When they abandoned a portion of what they had been reminded of, they replaced it with something else, and enmity and hatred arose among them. Allah Most High has also said:

“Whoever turns away from the Reminder of the Most Merciful, We assign to him a devil who becomes his companion.”

That is, from the Reminder revealed by the Most Merciful. Allah Most High has also said:

“Whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer.”

“But whoever turns away from My Reminder will have a life of hardship, and We shall raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.”

And He has said:

“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow any allies besides Him. How little you take heed!”

He thus commanded people to follow what He revealed and forbade its opposite: following allies besides Him. Whoever does not follow one of these two follows the other. This is why He said:

“and follows a path other than that of the believers.”

The scholars said: Whoever does not follow their path follows a path other than theirs. They therefore deduced from this that following their path is obligatory, and that no one may depart from what they have unanimously agreed upon.

Likewise, whoever does not do what is commanded does some of what is forbidden, and whoever does what is forbidden does not do everything that is commanded. Thus a person cannot do everything he has been commanded to do while doing some of

what is forbidden. Nor can he refrain from everything that is forbidden while neglecting some of what he has been commanded to do. Refraining from what is forbidden is itself among the things commanded, while neglecting what is commanded is among the things forbidden. Thus, whatever distracts him from an obligation is forbidden, and whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation he must do. Hence, when the term “command” is used without qualification, it includes prohibition. When it is qualified by an accompanying reference to prohibition, prohibition is as discussed above.

Thus, when Allah Most High says of the angels:

“They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them,”

this includes their avoiding anything He forbids them. As for His words:

“and they do what they are commanded,”

it has been said that this means they do not go beyond what they are commanded to do. It has also been said that they do it at its appointed time, neither before nor after it.

It may be said, however, that He did not say, “and they do nothing except what they are commanded.” Rather, that is indicated by His words:

“They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.”

It has also been said that they do not disobey what He commanded them in the past, and they do what they are commanded in the future. Yet it may be said that this verse describes what will happen: what they are commanded to do here is not past; rather, it all concerns the future. For He says:

“Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire,”

and the measures by which one protects oneself necessarily lie in the future.

It may also be said that failing to do what is commanded sometimes results from disobedience to the one issuing the command, and sometimes from inability. When someone is both capable and willing, the commanded act within his power necessarily takes place. Thus, His words, “They do not disobey,” mean that they do not refuse to obey, while His words, “and they do what they are commanded,” mean that they are capable of doing so. They are incapable of none of it; rather, they do it all. It follows that everything they are commanded to do necessarily takes place.

This may also imply that they do only what they are commanded to do, just as someone may say, “I do what I have been commanded to do,” meaning, “I carry it out without adding to it or falling short of it.”

Moreover, regarding His words:

“They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them,”

if He has forbidden them some other action, that prohibition falls within His command. If He has not forbidden it, they cannot be blamed for doing what they have not been forbidden to do. The point is that the term “command,” when used without qualification, includes prohibition. An example is His saying:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

That is, those who hold authority to command. Whoever holds authority to command also holds authority to prohibit, and must be obeyed in both respects. Thus, prohibition is included within command.

Moses said to al-Khidr:

“You will find me patient, if Allah wills, and I will not disobey any command of yours.”

“He said, ‘Then if you follow me, do not question me about anything until I myself mention it to you.’”

This prohibited him from asking questions until al-Khidr himself spoke to him about the matter. When al-Khidr made a hole in the ship, Moses said to him:

“Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a dreadful thing!”

Thus, he questioned him before al-Khidr himself spoke about it. Concerning the boy, he said:

“Have you killed an innocent soul who had killed no one? You have certainly done a terrible thing!”

Again, he questioned him before al-Khidr himself spoke about it. Concerning the wall, he said:

“If you had wished, you could have taken payment for it.”

This, too, is a request in meaning, for a question or request may take a conditional form. You might say, “If you were to stay with us, we would honour you,” or, “If you spend tonight with us, you will be doing us a kindness.” Another example is Adam’s saying:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.”

And Noah’s saying:

“My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. Unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers.”

There are many such examples. Hence Moses said:

“If I question you about anything after this, then do not keep me as your companion.”

This indicates that he questioned him on all three occasions before al-Khidr himself spoke to him about the matter. This was disobedience to his prohibition, and it fell within the scope of Moses’ words:

“And I will not disobey any command of yours.”

This shows that whoever disobeys a prohibition disobeys a command. Another example is the saying of Allah Most High:

“Surely, His is the creation and the command.”

Here, prohibition is included within command. Other examples are His sayings:

“So let those who oppose his command beware,”

and:

“It is not for a believing man or woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair.”

His prohibition is included in this.

The jurists have differed concerning a man who says to his wife, “If you disobey my command, you are divorced”: if he forbids her something and she disobeys him, does this fall within his “command”? There are two opinions. One holds that it does not, because a prohibition is essentially different from a command. The other holds that it does, because customary usage understands this expression to mean disobedience to both commands and prohibitions. This is the correct view, because the customary meaning mentioned here is also a literal meaning in language and religious usage. Whenever anyone uses “command” without qualification—as in “Obey so-and-so’s command,” “So-and-so obeys another’s command,” or “He does not disobey his command”—it includes prohibition, since whoever prohibits something commands that it be left undone.

For this reason, He, glorified be He, says:

“Do not mix truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know.”

He did not say, “Do not conceal the truth.” Thus, He did not state a separate prohibition for each, because the two necessarily go together. This is not the wāw expressing combination, which the Kufan grammarians call wāw al-sarf, as some may suppose. That would mean, “Do not combine the two,” leaving either one, on its own, unprohibited.

Moreover, that construction occurs only where the distinction is apparent, as in His sayings:

“While Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strive and made evident those who are steadfast,”

and:

“Or He could destroy them for what they have earned, though He pardons much.”

“And those who dispute Our signs may know that they have no escape.”

Another instance of conjoining something that necessarily entails what precedes it is the saying of Allah Most High:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

For when they obey

the Messenger, they have obeyed Allah, as He, Most High, says:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah.”

If someone whom Muhammad’s message has reached obeys Allah, he must necessarily obey the Messenger, for there is no obedience to Allah except through obedience to him.

The third is conjoining a part of something with the whole, as in His sayings:

“Maintain the prayers and the middle prayer.”

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus son of Mary.”

“Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael.”

“And He caused you to inherit their land, their homes, their wealth, and land you had not trodden.”

The fourth is conjoining references to the same thing because the two descriptions differ, as in His saying:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who decreed and guided, and who brought forth the pasture.”

And His saying:

“Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them, and those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and are certain of the Hereafter.”

Poetry contains examples said to involve conjunction merely because the wording differs, such as:

“He found her words to be lies and falsehood.”

Some people claim that something similar occurs in the Book of Allah, citing His words, “a law and a way.” This is mistaken: such usage occurs neither in the Quran nor in eloquent speech. At most, the examples people cite involve words with different meanings. Some, for instance, have claimed that the following is an example of this:

“How dear are Hind and the land where Hind dwells—
And Hind, from whom separation and distance keep me apart.”

They claimed that the two words have the same meaning, citing this as evidence for their claim that the law

Na’y (“separation”) is broader in meaning than buʿd (“distance”), for na’y encompasses separation over distances both short and long; it is thus akin to parting. Buʿd, however, is used only when the distance separating things is great. Allah, Most High, says:

“They prevent others from it and keep away from it.”

They are censured for their avoidance and withdrawal, whether they were near or far. Not all of them were distant—especially according to those who say that this verse was revealed concerning Abū Tālib. Al-Nābighah said:

“And the trench was like a basin dug in hard, virgin ground.”

The word nu’y here means a trench dug around a tent so that water drains into it rather than entering the tent. That is, the trench had become like a basin: it lay alongside the tent, not far from it.

 فَقَوْلُهُ صَدَقُوا أَيْ فِي قَوْلِهِمْ:
 آمَنُوا؛
 كَقَوْلِهِ:
 
{قَالَتِ الْأَعْرَابُ آمَنَّا قُلْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنُوا وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا أَسْلَمْنَا وَلَمَّا يَدْخُلِ الْإِيمَانُ فِي قُلُوبِكُمْ}
 إلَى قَوْلِهِ: 
{إنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَرْتَابُوا وَجَاهَدُوا بِأَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَنْفُسِهِمْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الصَّادِقُونَ}
 أَيْ هُمْ الصَّادِقُونَ فِي قَوْلِهِمْ: آمَنَّا بِاَللَّهِ بِخِلَافِ الْكَاذِبِينَ الَّذِينَ قَالَ اللَّهُ فِيهِمْ: {إذَا جَاءَكَ الْمُنَافِقُونَ قَالُوا نَشْهَدُ إنَّكَ لَرَسُولُ اللَّهِ
translated_text:
whether these deeds fall under this designation.”

He also said:

“Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he ought, while being a believer.”

He thus made deeds inseparable from this designation, and this designation inseparable from deeds.

The point here is that praise is established only for faith accompanied by deeds, not for faith devoid of deeds. Once it is acknowledged that abandoning deeds incurs blame and punishment, their dispute serves no purpose; it becomes merely a verbal dispute. Even so, their wording is mistaken and contrary to the Quran and Sunnah. If, however, they say that abandoning deeds does a person no harm, this is outright disbelief.

Some people attribute this view to them, reporting that they say: “Allah has prescribed obligations for His servants, but He did not intend them to perform them, and abandoning them does them no harm.” This may be the position of the extremists who say that none of those who affirm Allah’s oneness will enter the Fire. Yet I know of no particular individual to whom I can attribute this statement. People merely report it in books without identifying who said it. It may be the statement of someone who has no share of good, for many openly sinful people and hypocrites say: “No sin causes harm where there is faith,” or “where there is affirmation of Allah’s oneness.” In some writings refuting the Murji’a, they are described in these terms.

This is also indicated by His words, exalted is He, at the end of the verse:

“It is they who have been truthful, and it is they who are truly pious.”

His words “have been truthful” mean truthful in their claim to have believed. This is like His saying:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted,” for faith has not yet entered your hearts.’”

And then:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful.”

That is, they are truthful in saying, “We believe in Allah,” unlike the liars of whom Allah said:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah’

and Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are surely liars.”

He, exalted is He, also said:

“Among the people are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ yet they are not believers.

“They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive only themselves, though they do not realize it.

“In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease; and they will have a painful punishment because they used to lie.”

The word rendered “they used to lie” has two well-known readings. For they lied when they said, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” and inwardly denied the Messenger, even though they outwardly affirmed him.

He, exalted is He, also said:

“Alif Lām Mīm.

“Do people think they will be left to say, ‘We believe,’ without being tested?

“We certainly tested those before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful, and He will surely make evident the liars.”

He thus made clear that He must test people—that is, examine them and put them to trial. The expression “I tested the gold” is used when one puts gold into the fire to separate it from whatever is mixed with it. This is also the meaning in Moses’ words:

“This is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will.”

That is, Your testing, examination, and trial: just as You test Your servants with prosperity and adversity to distinguish those who are steadfast and grateful from others, and You test them by sending messengers and revealing scriptures to distinguish the believer from the disbeliever, the truthful from the liar, and the hypocrite from the sincere. You thus make this a cause of some people’s going astray and others’ being guided.

The Quran contains many such passages, describing the believers as truthful and the hypocrites as liars, because both groups professed with their tongues, “We believe.” Whoever substantiates his words with his deeds is a truthful believer, while whoever says with his tongue what is not in his heart is a lying hypocrite. He, exalted is He, said:

“What befell you on the day the two armies met was by Allah’s permission, so that He might make evident the believers,

“and make evident those who acted hypocritically. They were told, ‘Come, fight in the cause of Allah, or defend.’ They said, ‘Had we known there would be fighting, we would have followed you.’ That day they were closer to disbelief than to faith, saying with their mouths what was not in their hearts. And Allah knows best what they conceal.”

So when He said in the verse on righteousness:

“Those are the ones who have been truthful, and those are the God-fearing,”

this indicated that they were truthful in saying, “We believe,” for this was the declaration they were commanded to make and which they used to utter. They were not commanded to declare, “We are righteous,” or, “We are virtuous.” Rather, when a man says, “I am righteous,” he is praising himself. Thus, Zaynab bint Jahsh was originally named Barrah (“righteous”), but people said, “She is praising herself,” so the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, named her Zaynab.

This differs from professing faith by saying, “We believe,” for they were obliged to say this. He, exalted is He, said:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what Moses and Jesus were given, and what the prophets were given from their Lord.’”

Likewise, near the beginning of Āl ‘Imrān:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us, and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what Moses, Jesus, and the prophets were given from their Lord.’”

He, exalted is He, also said:

“The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, as do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’”

His words, “We make no distinction,” show that they said, “We believe, and we make no distinction.” Hence He said:

“And they say, ‘We hear and obey.’”

They thus combined their declaration, “We believe,” with their declaration, “We hear and obey.”

In the verse on righteousness, He said:

“And those are the God-fearing.”

He thus identified the righteous with the God-fearing when these terms are used independently and without qualification. Yet He distinguished between them when they are paired and qualified, in His words:

“And cooperate in righteousness and piety.”

This verse indicates that faith, righteousness, and piety denote the same thing when used without qualification: the believers are the God-fearing, and they are the righteous.

For this reason, the authentic hadiths on intercession state:

“Whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will come out of the Fire.”

Some versions say, “An atom’s weight of good.” This accords with His words, exalted is He:

“So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

That atom’s weight of good is an atom’s weight of faith. These believers—the righteous and the God-fearing—are those who attain complete felicity. They are the people of Paradise who have been promised entry into it without punishment. It is this group that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, referred to when he said:

“Whoever cheats us is not one of us, and whoever takes up arms against us is not one of us.”

Such a person is not one of these; rather, he is among the sinners subject to the threat of punishment, like others of their kind.

Section

This category follows the same pattern as “the names of Allah, the names of His Book, the names of His Messenger, and the names of His religion.” Allah, exalted is He, says:

“Say, ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.’”

He, exalted is He, also says:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names.”

And Allah, exalted is He, says:

“He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the seen. He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.”

“He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Most Holy, the Source of Peace, the Giver of Security, the Guardian, the Almighty, the Compeller, the Supremely Great. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him.”

“He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

All His names agree in referring to His holy Self, while each name also signifies an attribute distinct from that signified by another name. Thus, “the Almighty” signifies His Self together with His might; “the Creator” signifies His Self together with His act of creating; and “the Especially Merciful” signifies His Self together with His mercy. His Self necessarily entails all His attributes. Accordingly, each name signifies His Essence together with the attribute particular to that name through complete signification; either of the two through partial signification; and another attribute through necessary implication.

The same applies to “the names of His Book”: the Quran, the Criterion, the Book, Guidance, Clarification, Healing

and Light, and the like, follow this same pattern. The same applies to “the names of His Messenger”: Muhammad, Ahmad, al-Māhī (the Effacer), al-Hāshir (the Gatherer), al-Muqfī (the Successor), the Prophet of Mercy, the Prophet of Repentance, and the Prophet of Battle. Each name signifies a praiseworthy attribute of his distinct from that signified by another.

The same applies to the accounts recounted repeatedly in the Quran, such as the account of Moses and others. Their purpose is not to provide entertainment, but to convey lessons, as Allah, exalted is He, says:

“There was certainly in their stories a lesson for those of understanding.”

What occurred was a single event with various aspects. It is therefore expressed in different ways, each expression indicating an aspect from which those who reflect may draw a lesson. This is not repetition in any sense.

The same applies to “the names of His religion,” which Allah and His Messenger have commanded. It is called faith, righteousness, piety, goodness, religion, righteous action, the straight path, and the like. In itself it is one, but each name signifies an attribute distinct from that signified by another. That attribute is the primary meaning of the term, while the rest originally followed from it as necessary implications; the term then came to signify the rest through partial signification.

For “faith” is rooted in the faith within the heart, and it necessarily involves “two things”: the heart’s affirmation, acknowledgment, and knowledge. This is called the speech of the heart. Al-Junayd ibn Muhammad said: “Affirming Allah’s oneness is the speech of the heart, and reliance upon Him is the action of the heart.” Thus, faith must include the heart’s speech and action, followed by the body’s speech and action. It must include actions of the heart, such as loving Allah and His Messenger, fearing Allah, loving what Allah and His Messenger love, hating what Allah and His Messenger hate, devoting one’s deeds sincerely to Allah alone, the heart’s reliance upon Allah alone, and other actions of the heart that Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory and included within faith.

translated_text:
The heart is the foundation. Whatever knowledge and will it contains necessarily extend to the body; the body cannot fail to carry out what the heart wills. Hence the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said in an authentic hadith:

“Indeed, within the body is a piece of flesh: when it is sound, the rest of the body is sound, and when it is corrupt, the rest of the body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.”

Abū Hurayra said: “The heart is a king, and the limbs are its soldiers. When the king is good, its soldiers are good; when the king is corrupt, its soldiers are corrupt.”

Abū Hurayra’s statement offers an approximate analogy, whereas the Prophet’s words, peace and blessings be upon him, explain the matter more clearly. Even when a king is righteous, his soldiers have a will of their own by which they may disobey him. The reverse is also possible: they may be righteous while he is corrupt, or corrupt while he is righteous. The heart is different: the body follows it and never departs from its will, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When it is sound, the rest of the body is sound, and when it is corrupt, the rest of the body is corrupt.”

Thus, when the heart is sound through the faith within it—both knowledge and the heart’s actions—the body must necessarily be sound in outward speech and deeds, embodying faith in its full sense. As the leading scholars of hadith have said: “It is speech and action: inward and outward speech, and inward and outward action.” The outward follows the inward and is inseparable from it: whenever the inward is sound, the outward is sound; when it is corrupt, the outward is corrupt.

For this reason, one of the Companions said of a man fidgeting in prayer: “Had this man’s heart been humble, his limbs would have been humble.” The heart’s faith must therefore include love for Allah and His Messenger, and Allah and His Messenger must be dearer to a person than anything else. Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and sparing their women. Indeed, he was one of those who spread corruption.”

And He said:

The same applies to the Jews of whom Allah said:

Likewise, many of the polytheists, of whom Allah said:

“It is not you they disbelieve; rather, the wrongdoers deny Allah’s signs.”

Thus, these people erred on “two fundamental points”:

First, they assumed that faith consists solely of assent and knowledge, unaccompanied by any action, state, movement, will, love or reverent fear within the heart. This is among the gravest errors of the Murjiʾah altogether. For the “deeds of the heart”—which some Sufis call states and stations, stages of those journeying to Allah, stations of those who know Allah, or other names—include matters that Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory, and these belong to obligatory faith. They also include matters that He loves but has not made obligatory, and these belong to recommended faith.

The first category is indispensable for every believer. Whoever confines himself to it is among the righteous, the people of the right; whoever fulfils it and also fulfils the second is among the foremost, those brought near to Allah.

These deeds include loving Allah and His Messenger—indeed, loving Allah and His Messenger more than anything else, and loving Allah, His Messenger and jihad in His cause more than one’s family and wealth. They also include fearing Allah alone rather than created beings, placing one’s hope in Allah alone rather than created beings, relying on Allah alone rather than created beings, and turning to Him

with reverent fear of Him, as the Most High said:

“This is what you were promised—for everyone who repeatedly turned to Allah and kept His commandments.”

“Who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart turned to Him.”

These deeds also include loving and hating for Allah’s sake, and showing loyalty and enmity for Allah’s sake.

Second: they assumed that whenever the Lawgiver declares someone a disbeliever who will remain in the Fire forever, this can only be because his heart contains no knowledge or assent whatsoever. In this they contradicted sensory experience, reason, revelation, and what people of sound natural disposition and the great majority of rational thinkers agree upon. A person may recognize that someone else has the truth, yet deny it out of envy, a desire to exalt himself above that person, or personal desire. That desire drives him to wrong the other person and reject what he says by every means, even though he knows in his heart that the other person has the truth.

Most of those who rejected the messengers knew that they had the truth and were truthful. Yet they rejected them either out of envy, a desire for supremacy and leadership, or attachment to their existing religion and the benefits it afforded them, such as wealth, leadership, friendship with certain people, and other things. They saw that following the messengers would mean abandoning desires dear to them or facing things they disliked. They therefore rejected the messengers and opposed them, becoming among the most extreme disbelievers, like Iblīs and Pharaoh, despite knowing that they themselves were following falsehood and that the messengers had the truth.

For this reason, the disbelievers offer no sound argument that undermines the messengers’ truthfulness. They rely only on the fact that the messengers’ message conflicts with their desires, as when they said to Noah:

“Should we believe you when the lowliest people follow you?”

It is well known that his being followed by the lowliest people does not undermine his truthfulness; rather, they disliked associating with those people

just as the polytheists asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to send away the weak, such as Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās, Ibn Masʿūd, Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, Bilāl, and others like them. This took place in Mecca, before the Ahl al-Suffa (the people of the sheltered platform) were among the Companions. Then Allah, blessed and exalted is He, revealed:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face. You are in no way accountable for them, nor are they in any way accountable for you, that you should drive them away and thus become one of the wrongdoers.”

“Thus We have tested some of them through others, so that they might say, ‘Are these the ones Allah has favoured from among us?’ Does Allah not know best those who are grateful?”

Likewise, Pharaoh said:

“Should we believe in two mortals like ourselves, while their people are our servants?”

Pharaoh also said:

“Did we not raise you among us as a child, and did you not spend years of your life among us?”

“And you committed that deed of yours, and you were one of the ungrateful.”

Similarly, the Arab polytheists said:

“If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land.”

Allah Most High said:

“Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary to which fruits of every kind are brought as provision from Us?”

Likewise, the people of Shuʿayb said to him:

“Does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our forefathers worshipped, or that we should no longer do as we please with our wealth?”

Similarly, the polytheists generally said:

“We found our forefathers following a religion, and we are following in their footsteps.”

These statements and others like them are not arguments that undermine the messengers’ truthfulness. Rather, they show that the messengers’ message conflicted with their wishes, desires, and customs. That was why they did not follow them. All these people were disbelievers. Indeed, Abū Tālib and others loved the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and wanted his word to prevail. They bore him no envy and knew that he was truthful, but they knew that in

following him they would have to abandon their forefathers’ religion and incur the censure of Quraysh. They could not bear to abandon that custom or endure such censure. Thus, their refusal to believe was not because they did not know that believing in him was right, but because of their own desires. How, then, can it be said that every disbeliever disbelieves only because he lacks knowledge of Allah?

The Jahmiyyah were not content merely to declare every disbeliever ignorant of the truth; they went so far as to say that he does not know that Allah truly exists. For them, disbelief is not ignorance of just any truth, but ignorance of this particular truth.

Yet we, like everyone else, see many disbelievers who inwardly know that Islam is true. They explain what prevents them from believing: hostility from their families; financial support they receive from them, which would be cut off; fear that, if they believed, they would not enjoy the same standing among Muslims as they do within their own religion; and other such personal interests. They explain that these are what prevent them from believing, despite knowing that Islam is true and their own religion is false.

The same occurs with every matter of truth: there are people who know in their hearts that it is true, yet outwardly deny it and show hostility towards those who uphold it, thinking that this will bring them some benefit or ward off some harm.

Allah Most High said:

“O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. Whoever among you takes them as allies is indeed one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”

“So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening to ally themselves with them, saying, ‘We fear that a turn of fortune may strike us.’ But perhaps Allah will bring victory or a decree from Himself, and they will then regret what they concealed within themselves.”

“And those who believe will say, ‘Are these the ones who swore their most solemn oaths by Allah that they were indeed with you?’ Their deeds have come to nothing, and they have become losers.”

And the Quran commentators agree that these verses were revealed concerning people who outwardly professed Islam but had a disease in their hearts. They feared that the Muslims would be defeated and therefore allied themselves with disbelievers among the Jews, Christians and others because of the fear in their hearts—not because they believed that Muhammad was lying and that the Jews and Christians were telling the truth. The best-known report concerning this is:

“‘Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I have allies among the Jews, but I declare before Allah that I renounce allegiance to the Jews.’ ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy then said, ‘But I am a man who fears reversals of fortune, and I will not renounce allegiance to the Jews.’ Then this verse was revealed.”

Among the Murji’ah, who said that faith consists of affirmation in the heart and profession with the tongue, and that deeds are not part of it, were a group of jurists and devout worshippers from Kufa. Their position was not like Jahm’s: they recognized that a person cannot be a believer without verbally professing faith when able to do so. They also recognized that Iblīs, Pharaoh and others were disbelievers despite the affirmation in their hearts. Yet if they exclude the actions of the heart from faith, Jahm’s position necessarily follows from theirs; and if they include them in faith, they must also include bodily actions, since these necessarily follow from the actions of the heart.

These people, however, had scriptural arguments that made the matter unclear to them. They observed that Allah distinguished between faith and deeds in His Book, saying in several places:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds”.

They also observed that Allah addressed people as believers before they had performed the deeds, saying:

“O you who believe, when you rise to pray, wash your faces and your arms up to the elbows.”

“O you who believe, when the call is made for prayer on Friday”.

translated_text:
They also said:

“If a man believed in Allah and His Messenger one morning, then died before any deeds became obligatory upon him, he would die a believer and be among the people of Paradise. This shows that deeds are not part of faith.”

They also said:

“We concede that faith increases in the sense that whenever Allah revealed a verse, affirming it became obligatory, and this affirmation was added to the affirmation that preceded it.”

But according to them, once Allah’s revelation was complete, faith no longer varied in degree. Rather, everyone’s faith is equal: the faith of the foremost early believers, such as Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, is equal to that of the most wicked people, such as al-Hajjāj, Abū Muslim al-Khurāsānī and others.

Both the theologians and the jurists among the Murji’ah say that deeds may figuratively be called faith, because action is the fruit and consequence of faith, and because deeds are evidence of it. They say that the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Faith has sixty-odd or seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road.”

are figurative.

The Murji’ah fall into three categories. The first are those who say that faith consists solely of what is in the heart. Some of these include the actions of the heart within faith; these constitute most of the Murji’ah groups. Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī recorded their views in his book, mentioning many groups whose enumeration would be lengthy. We have, however, outlined their principal views. Others do not include the actions of the heart within faith, such as Jahm and those who followed him, including al-Sālihī. This is the position he and most of his followers defended.

The second position is that faith consists solely of verbal profession. No one before the Karrāmiyyah is known to have held this view.

The third is that faith consists of affirmation in the heart and profession with the tongue. This is the well-known position of the jurists and devout worshippers among them. They erred in several respects:

" أَيْضًا "
 لَوْ قُدِّرَ أَنَّهُ عَاشَ فَلَا يَجِبُ عَلَى كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الْعَامَّةِ أَنْ يَعْرِفَ كُلَّ مَا أَمَرَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ وَكُلَّ مَا نَهَى عَنْهُ وَكُلَّ مَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ بَلْ إنَّمَا عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَعْرِفَ مَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ هُوَ وَمَا يَحْرُمُ عَلَيْهِ فَمَنْ لَا مَالَ لَهُ لَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَعْرِفَ أَمْرَهُ الْمُفَصَّلَ فِي الزَّكَاةِ. وَمَنْ لَا اسْتِطَاعَةَ لَهُ عَلَى الْحَجِّ لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَعْرِفَ أَمْرَهُ الْمُفَصَّلَ بِالْمَنَاسِكِ وَمَنْ لَمْ يَتَزَوَّجْ لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَعْرِفَ مَا وَجَبَ لِلزَّوْجَةِ فَصَارَ يَجِبُ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ تَصْدِيقًا وَعَمَلًا عَلَى أَشْخَاصٍ مَا لَا يَجِبُ عَلَى آخَرِينَ.
 وَبِهَذَا يَظْهَرُ الْجَوَابُ عَنْ قَوْلِهِمْ:
 خُوطِبُوا بِالْإِيمَانِ قَبْلَ الْأَعْمَالِ.
 فَنَقُولُ:
translated_text:
(First): their assumption that the faith Allah has made obligatory upon His servants is the same for them all, and that whatever faith is obligatory upon one person must equally be obligatory upon everyone. But this is not so. Allah imposed requirements of faith upon the followers of earlier prophets that He did not impose upon the community of Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), and He imposed requirements of faith upon the community of Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) that He did not impose upon others. The faith required before the entire Quran had been revealed was not the same as the faith required after its revelation. Nor is the faith required of someone who knows in detail what the Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) conveyed the same as that required of someone who knows it only in general terms. Faith necessarily entails believing the Messenger in everything he conveyed. Yet someone who believed the Messenger and died immediately afterwards was required to have no more faith than that.

As for someone whom the Quran and hadiths have reached, together with the detailed reports and commands they contain, he is required to affirm them in detail, report by report and command by command. This is not required of someone whose only obligation was faith in general terms because he died before anything further reached him.

Moreover, even supposing that he lived, not every ordinary person is required to know everything the Messenger commanded, everything he prohibited, and everything he conveyed. Rather, each person need only know what is obligatory upon him personally and what is forbidden to him. Someone who has no wealth is not required to know the Messenger’s detailed instructions concerning zakah. Someone who lacks the means to perform Hajj is not required to know his detailed instructions concerning its rites. Someone who has not married is not required to know what is owed to a wife. Thus, some people are required to fulfil obligations of faith, in both affirmation and action, that others are not.

This makes clear the answer to their statement:

“They were addressed with the command to have faith before they were commanded to perform deeds.”

We reply:

translated_text:
If you say, “They were commanded to have faith before those deeds became obligatory,” then before those deeds became obligatory, they were not part of faith. They possessed the faith required of them before the additional obligations were imposed upon them. Once the command was revealed, however, if they did not acknowledge its obligatory nature, they were not believers. Hence Allah Most High says:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by those who are able to make their way there. But whoever disbelieves—Allah is indeed free of need of all creation.”

This is why Hajj is not mentioned in most hadiths that mention Islam and faith, such as the hadith of the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays, the hadith of the man from Najd said to have been Dimām ibn Tha‘labah, and others. Hajj is mentioned in the hadiths of Ibn ‘Umar and Gabriel because it was the last of the five obligations to be prescribed. Before it became obligatory, it was not included in faith or Islam. Once it became obligatory, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) included it within faith when that term was used on its own, and within Islam whether that term was mentioned alongside faith or used on its own. We shall mention, Allah willing, when Hajj became obligatory.

Likewise, their statement, “Someone who believed and died before deeds became obligatory upon him died a believer,” is correct. He fulfilled the faith required of him, while deeds had not yet become obligatory upon him. This must be understood, for it dispels a misconception that has arisen among both groups.

Thus, when it is said, “Obligatory deeds are part of faith,” the faith that is obligatory varies; it is not one and the same for everyone.

The people of the Sunnah and hadith say: “All good deeds, both obligatory and recommended, are part of faith”—that is, part of faith made complete through recommended deeds, not obligatory faith. A distinction is drawn between obligatory faith and complete faith

The sufficient form includes only the obligatory acts, while the complete form also includes the recommended acts.” The term “completeness” may refer either to obligatory completeness or to recommended completeness.

As for their statement that Allah distinguishes between faith and deeds in various passages, this is correct. We have explained that when faith is mentioned on its own, Allah and His Messenger include within it the deeds that have been commanded. Deeds may also be mentioned alongside faith, and we have given many comparable examples. This is because the foundation of faith is what resides in the heart, and outward deeds necessarily follow from it. It is inconceivable for the obligatory faith of the heart to exist in the complete absence of deeds performed by the limbs. Rather, whenever outward deeds are deficient, this is due to a deficiency in the faith within the heart. Thus, faith encompasses both the underlying reality and its necessary consequences, even though its foundation lies in the heart. Where deeds are mentioned alongside faith, the intended meaning is that faith in the heart alone does not suffice: righteous deeds must accompany it.

There are two views concerning expressions of this kind. Some say that the conjoined element was already included in the preceding term, but was then mentioned by its particular name to single it out, lest anyone suppose that it had not been included in the first term. They say that this applies whenever a specific term is conjoined to a general one, as in His words:

“Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel, and Michael”

and His words:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary”

and His words:

“And those who believe and do righteous deeds and believe in what has been sent down to Muhammad—and it is the truth from their Lord”.

Thus, belief in what was sent down to Muhammad is singled out after His words, “Those who believe”. This verse was revealed concerning the Companions

and other believers.

And His words:

“Maintain the prayers, especially the middle prayer.”

And His words:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him, inclining to the truth, and to establish prayer and give zakah.”

Prayer and zakah are themselves acts of worship. Thus, His words, “believed and did righteous deeds,” are like His words:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, devoting their religion sincerely to Him, inclining to the truth, and to establish prayer and give zakah.”

For He intended, first, that worship should be devoted to Allah alone, not to anyone else. He then commanded prayer and zakah so that it would be known that these are two obligatory acts of worship, and that sincere worship in general does not suffice without them. Likewise, He mentions faith first because it is the indispensable foundation, then mentions righteous deeds because they too are indispensable to the completeness of religion. Thus, no one should suppose that mere faith unaccompanied by righteous deeds suffices.

Likewise, His words:

“Alif, Lām, Mīm. This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for those mindful of Allah, who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them; and who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and are certain of the Hereafter. Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.”

It has been said that the latter are the People of the Book who believed in what was sent down to him and what was sent down to those before him, such as Ibn Salām and others like him, and that they constitute a category distinct from those previously mentioned, who believe in the unseen.

It has also been said that these are all those mentioned earlier, who believed in what was sent down to him and what was sent down before him. He, glorified be He, is One, yet He joined some of His attributes to others with conjunctions. Likewise, His words, “and the middle prayer,” refer to the afternoon prayer.

When descriptions are grammatically definite, they serve to clarify and imply praise or blame. You say, “This man is the one who did such-and-such, and he is the one who did such-and-such, and he is the one who did such-and-such,” enumerating his merits. Thus, alongside grammatical agreement, such descriptions may be joined by conjunctions or placed in the accusative or nominative.

This interpretation is correct. For if those who believe in the unseen did not believe in what was sent down to him and what was sent down before him, they would neither be upon guidance from their Lord, nor successful, nor mindful of Allah. Likewise, if those who believe in what was sent down to him and what was sent down before him were not among those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what Allah has provided for them, they would neither be upon guidance from their Lord, nor successful, nor mindful of Allah.

This shows that all these descriptions apply to the rightly guided, Allah-fearing people who followed the guidance of the Book sent down to Muhammad. Thus, this description is joined to the earlier one even though it is already included within it. The purpose, however, is to describe their faith: they believe in everything Allah sent down to His prophets, making no distinction between any of them. Otherwise, if only belief in the unseen were mentioned, someone who believes in some revelation and rejects some might say, “We believe in the unseen.”

 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ أَحْمَد بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ وَغَيْرُهُ:
 لَمْ يَكُنْ مِنْ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ مُنَافِقٌ وَإِنَّمَا كَانَ النِّفَاقُ فِي قَبَائِلِ الْأَنْصَارِ؛ فَإِنَّ مَكَّةَ كَانَتْ لِلْكُفَّارِ مُسْتَوْلِينَ عَلَيْهَا فَلَا يُؤْمِنُ وَيُهَاجِرُ إلَّا مَنْ هُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ دَاعٍ يَدْعُو إلَى النِّفَاقِ؛ وَالْمَدِينَةُ آمَنَ بِهَا أَهْلُ الشَّوْكَةِ؛ فَصَارَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِهَا عِزٌّ وَمَنَعَةٌ بِالْأَنْصَارِ فَمَنْ لَمْ يُظْهِرْ الْإِيمَانَ آذَوْهُ. فَاحْتَاجَ الْمُنَافِقُونَ إلَى إظْهَارِ الْإِيمَانِ مَعَ أَنَّ قُلُوبَهُمْ لَمْ تُؤْمِنْ؛ وَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى افْتَتَحَ الْبَقَرَةَ وَوَسَطَ الْبَقَرَةِ وَخَتَمَ الْبَقَرَةَ بِالْإِيمَانِ بِجَمِيعِ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ الْأَنْبِيَاءُ؛

{قُولُوا آمَنَّا بِاللَّهِ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إلَيْنَا وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إلَى إبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطِ وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَى وَعِيسَى وَمَا أُوتِيَ النَّبِيُّونَ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإِنَّمَا هُمْ فِي شِقَاقٍ}

 الْآيَةَ تَارَةً. وبـ 
{قُلْ يَا أَيُّهَا الْكَافِرُونَ}
translated_text:
people came to fall into “three categories”: believers, disbelievers who openly professed their disbelief, and hypocrites. This differed from their situation when he was in Mecca, for there were no hypocrites there.

For this reason, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others said: There were no hypocrites among the Emigrants; hypocrisy existed only among the tribes of the Ansār. Mecca was under the control of the disbelievers, so only a true believer would embrace faith and emigrate. There was no incentive there for hypocrisy. In Medina, however, those who wielded power had embraced faith, and through the Ansār the believers gained strength and protection. Anyone who did not profess faith would suffer harm at their hands. The hypocrites therefore needed to profess faith, although their hearts did not believe.

Allah Most High opened Surah al-Baqarah, addressed its middle, and concluded it with belief in everything the prophets brought. At its beginning He said what has already been quoted, and in its middle He said:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah and in what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, and what Moses and Jesus were given, and what the prophets were given by their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.’ If they believe as you believe, then they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, they are only in opposition,” and the rest of the verse.

At its end He said:

“The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, as do the believers. All believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers: ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’ They say, ‘We hear and obey. We seek Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return,’”

and the following verse.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The two verses at the end of Surah al-Baqarah: whoever recites them in a night, they will suffice him.”

As for the verse in the middle of the surah, it is established in the Sahīh that “he used to recite it in the two units of prayer before the dawn prayer, together with ‘Say, O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you,’ and the rest of the verse, on some occasions; and ‘Say, O disbelievers’

According to the view of these scholars, it may be said: Righteous deeds conjoined with faith are included within faith, and their conjunction with it is that of the particular with the general—either to mention something specifically after mentioning it generally, or because its conjunction indicates that it was not included in the general term.

It has also been said: Rather, deeds are not originally part of faith, for the foundation of faith is what resides in the heart. They are, however, necessary consequences of it, so whoever does not perform them has no faith: the absence of a necessary consequence entails the absence of that which necessitates it. Nevertheless, in the Lawgiver’s usage, deeds have come to be included within the term “faith” when it is used without qualification, as previously illustrated by the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When deeds are conjoined with faith, they are mentioned lest anyone imagine that faith alone, without the righteous deeds necessarily entailed by it, secures the promised reward. Their mention therefore singles them out and makes them explicit, so that it may be known that the reward promised in the Hereafter—Paradise without punishment—is only for those who believe and do righteous deeds, not for those who claim faith but do not act.

In more than one passage, Allah, glorified is He, has made clear that anyone who truthfully says, “I believe,” must fulfil what is obligatory. Restricting faith to such people indicates its absence from all others.

The Jahmiyyah raise an objection here, mentioned by Abū al-Hasan in his book al-Mūjaz: the Quran denies faith to anyone other than such people, as in His words:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned.”

Yet it does not say that these deeds are part of faith. They say: “We therefore maintain that whoever does not perform these deeds is not a believer, because their absence indicates the absence of knowledge from his heart.”

This may be answered in several ways:

translated_text:
First:
You have conceded that these deeds are necessary consequences of faith in the heart, so that when they are absent, no faith remains in the heart. This is precisely the point at issue. Once this is conceded, whether they are necessary consequences or constituent parts is merely a verbal dispute.

Second:
Some texts explicitly state that they are constituent parts, such as his saying:

“Faith has sixty-odd or seventy-odd branches.”

Third:
If you say that anyone who lacks these things is a disbeliever entirely devoid of faith, then your position is that of the Khawārij. Yet you stand at one extreme and the Khawārij at the other—how, then, can you agree with them? These things include establishing prayer, paying zakah, fasting Ramadan, performing Hajj, jihad, submitting to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, and other duties whose neglect you do not regard as disbelief. If you do declare those who neglect them to be disbelievers, your position becomes that of the Khawārij.

Fourth:
The claim that the absence of some of these deeds necessarily means that a person’s heart contains no affirmation whatsoever that the Lord truly exists is self-evidently false.

Fifth:
If this is established for these deeds, it is established for all other obligations, and the substantive disagreement is thereby resolved.

translated_text:
Section

The second error of the Murji’ah is their assumption that faith in the heart consists solely of affirmation, excluding deeds of the heart, as discussed earlier concerning the Jahmiyyah among the Murji’ah.

Their third error is their assumption that faith in the heart can be complete without any deeds. Thus, they regard deeds as the fruit and outcome of faith, relating the two as cause and effect, but do not regard deeds as inseparable from faith. The truth, however, is that complete faith in the heart necessarily entails corresponding outward action. It is impossible for complete faith to reside in the heart without outward action.

Consequently, they posit situations that cannot occur, because they fail to grasp the connection between the body and the heart. For example, they posit a man whose heart contains faith equal to that in the hearts of Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, yet who never prostrates to Allah even once, does not fast Ramadan, commits incest with his mother and sister, and drinks wine during the daytime in Ramadan. They say, “This is a believer whose faith is complete.” All other believers reject this in the strongest terms.

I then met al-Zuhrī and told him what they were saying. He replied, “Glory be to Allah! People have already begun engaging in these disputes. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

‘The one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is not a believer while doing so, nor is the one who drinks wine a believer while drinking it.’”

I then met al-Hakam ibn ‘Utbah and said to him, “‘Abd al-Karīm and Maymūn heard that some Murji’ah visited you, presented their views to you, and that you accepted what they said.”

“They were commanded only to worship Allah with sincere devotion to Him, inclining to truth, to establish prayer and give zakah. That is the upright religion.”’”

In al-Umm, in the chapter “Intention in Prayer,” al-Shāfi‘ī, may Allah be pleased with him, cited the hadith narrated by ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, as evidence that no prayer is valid without an intention:

“Actions are only by intentions.”

He then said: “The Companions, the Successors after them, and those whom we have known unanimously held that faith consists of speech, deeds and intention; none of these three suffices without the others.”

Hanbal said: “Al-Humaydī narrated to us, saying: ‘I was informed that some people say: Whoever acknowledges the obligation of prayer, zakah, fasting and Hajj, yet does none of these until he dies, and prays with his back to the qiblah until he dies, is nevertheless a believer so long as he does not deny their obligation—if he knows that, despite abandoning these things, he still has faith, provided that he acknowledges the obligatory duties and the requirement to face the qiblah.’

“I said: ‘This is blatant disbelief, contrary to the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the scholars of the Muslims. Allah Most High said:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah with sincere devotion to Him,”

“to the end of the verse.’”

Hanbal said: “I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: ‘Whoever says this has disbelieved in Allah, rejected His command, and rejected what the Messenger brought from Allah.’”

I say: As for their citing his statement concerning the slave woman, “Free her, for she is a believer,” this is one of their well-known arguments. Ibn Kullāb also cited it as evidence. He held that faith consists of both inward assent and verbal profession, so his position was closer to the truth than that of Jahm and his followers. This, however, provides no proof, because

outward faith, on which rulings in this world are based, does not necessarily entail the inward faith that makes a person among the blessed in the Hereafter. For the hypocrites referred to in the words:

“‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ but they are not believers,”

are outwardly believers: they pray with the people, fast, perform Hajj, and fight in military campaigns. Muslims intermarry with them and inherit from them, and they inherit from Muslims, as was the case with the hypocrites during the time of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not apply to the hypocrites the rulings applicable to those who openly professed disbelief, whether regarding marriage, inheritance, or similar matters. Indeed, when ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl—one of the most notorious hypocrites—died, his son ‘Abd Allāh, one of the finest believers, inherited from him. Likewise, whenever any of them died, their believing heirs inherited from them; and when an heir of one of them died, they inherited from him alongside the Muslims.

The jurists have differed over whether the hypocritical unbeliever who conceals his unbelief may inherit and be inherited from, holding two views. The correct view is that he may inherit and be inherited from, even if he is known to be inwardly a hypocrite, as was the practice of the Companions during the Prophet’s lifetime, peace and blessings be upon him. This is because inheritance is based on outward allegiance, not on the love within people’s hearts. If it depended on that, there would be no way to ascertain it. When the rationale underlying a ruling is hidden or variable, the ruling is attached to its presumed indicator: here, the allegiance to Muslims that a person outwardly displays. Thus, the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him:

“A Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, nor does a disbeliever inherit from a Muslim,”

did not include the hypocrites, even though in the Hereafter they will be in the lowest depths of the Fire. Rather, they inherited and were inherited from. “The hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He deceives them. When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off before people, and they remember Allah only a little.”

In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! He watches the sun until, when it is between the two horns of a devil, he rises and pecks out four units of prayer, remembering Allah only a little during them.”

They would accompany the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, on military campaigns, just as Ibn Ubayy went on the campaign against Banū al-Mustaliq, during which he said:

“If we return to Medina, the more honourable will surely expel the more contemptible from it.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Zayd ibn Arqam reported:

“We set out with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, on a journey during which the people suffered hardship. ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy said to his companions, ‘Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him.’ He also said, ‘If we return to Medina, the more honourable will surely expel the more contemptible from it.’

“I went to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and informed him. He sent for ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy and questioned him, and he swore the most solemn oath that he had done no such thing. Nevertheless, outwardly, the rulings applicable to believers apply to them. This makes clear the answer to many objections raised concerning this matter. For many later scholars recognize only two categories among those who profess Islam: the upright and the sinful. They have disregarded the rulings concerning hypocrites, although hypocrites have continued to exist and will continue to exist until the Day of Resurrection. Hypocrisy has many branches, and the Companions used to fear hypocrisy for themselves.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks, he lies; when he promises, he breaks his promise; and when he is entrusted with something, he betrays that trust.”

Muslim’s wording adds:

“Even if he fasts, prays, and claims to be a Muslim.”

In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Amr reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever possesses four traits is a pure hypocrite, and whoever possesses one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when he is entrusted with something, he betrays that trust; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he behaves wickedly.”

At first, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would offer funeral prayers for them and seek forgiveness for them, until Allah forbade him to do so, saying:

“Never offer the funeral prayer for any of them who dies, nor stand at his grave.”

He also said:

“Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them—even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them.”

He therefore no longer offered funeral prayers for them or sought forgiveness for them, but their lives and property remained inviolable

, and he did not deem lawful against them what he deemed lawful against disbelievers who did not profess faith, but openly professed disbelief rather than faith. For he, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. Once they say this, they safeguard their lives and property from me, except by right of that testimony, and their reckoning rests with Allah.”

When he said to Usāmah ibn Zayd, “Did you kill him after he had said, ‘There is no god but Allah’?” Usāmah replied, “He only said it to seek protection.” He said, “Why did you not cut open his heart?” He also said, “I have not been commanded to probe people’s hearts or cut open their bellies.”

Whenever permission was sought to kill a man, he would say, “Does he not pray? Does he not pronounce the testimony of faith?” If he was told, “He is a hypocrite,” he would reply, “Even so.”

Thus, his ruling, peace and blessings be upon him, concerning their lives and property was the same as his ruling concerning those of others: he deemed none of them lawful to take except on outwardly evident grounds, even though he knew that many of them were hypocrites. There were others whose hypocrisy he did not know. Allah Most High said:

“Among the Bedouins around you are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those hardened in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a tremendous punishment.”

When one of them died, Muslims who did not know that he was a hypocrite would offer the funeral prayer for him, while those who knew that he was a hypocrite would not. Whenever someone died, ‘Umar would not offer the funeral prayer for him until Hudhayfah did so, because Hudhayfah knew their identities.

Allah Most High also said:

“O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them. Allah knows best their faith. If you know them to be believers, do not send them back to the disbelievers.”

Here He commanded that they be examined, and said, “Allah knows best their faith.”

translated_text:
And when Allah Most High commanded the freeing of a believing slave as an expiation, people were not required to free only someone whom they knew to have faith in his heart. That would be like telling them: “Kill everyone except those whom you know to have faith in their hearts.” They were not commanded to probe people’s hearts or cut open their bellies. Thus, if they saw a man outwardly professing faith, they were permitted to free him.

When the owner of the slave girl asked the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, “Is she a believer?” he meant only the outward profession of faith by which a Muslim is distinguished from a disbeliever. Likewise, someone bound by a vow was not required to free only someone whom he knew to have faith in his heart, for he cannot know this in all cases; indeed, no created being can.

Here is Allah’s Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, the most knowledgeable of all creation, yet Allah says to him:

“Among the Bedouins around you are hypocrites, and among the people of Medina are those hardened in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ruled concerning these people just as he did concerning the other believers. Had the funeral of one of them been brought before him, he would have offered the funeral prayer. He was forbidden to offer that prayer only for those whose hypocrisy he knew. Otherwise, he would have been required to probe people’s hearts and know their innermost secrets, something no human being can do.

Thus, when Allah exposed them in Surah Barā’ah through His repeated words, “And among them,” “And among them,” he came to know the hypocrisy of some whose hypocrisy he had not previously known. Allah described them by characteristics that people knew they possessed, but people had not been certain that these characteristics necessarily indicated their hypocrisy. Some suspected it, and some knew it, but their hypocrisy was not known to the community at large, unlike their situation once the Quran was revealed.

Thus, when Surah Barā’ah was revealed, they concealed their hypocrisy. They could no longer display it from time to time as they had been able to do before. Allah Most High revealed:

“If they do not desist
