—the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and those who spread rumors in Medina—We will surely set you against them; then they will remain your neighbors there only a short while. Accursed, wherever they are found, they will be seized and killed mercilessly. This was Allah’s established way with those who passed away before, and you will find no change in Allah’s established way.”

When they were threatened with death if they displayed their hypocrisy, they concealed it. Hence the jurists disagreed over whether a zindīq should be invited to repent.

Some said that he should. Those who held this view cited the hypocrites whose outward professions the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, accepted, leaving their affairs to Allah.

The response to this is that such was the case initially. Afterward, Allah revealed:

“Accursed, wherever they are found, they will be seized and killed mercilessly.”

They then knew that if they displayed their hypocrisy as they had previously done, they would be killed, so they concealed it.

A zindīq is a hypocrite. Those who hold that he should be executed do so only when it becomes apparent that he is concealing hypocrisy. They argue: “His repentance cannot be known, because the most he can do is outwardly profess what he professed before; he had already been professing faith while being a hypocrite. If their repentance were accepted, there would be no way to put them to death, yet the Quran has threatened them with death.”

The point is that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke of that slave girl’s faith only in terms of the outward faith upon which outward legal rulings depend. Indeed, it is established that when Saʿd testified that a man was a believer, the Prophet said:

“Or a Muslim.”

Yet that man outwardly displayed as much faith as the slave girl, and more. A distinction must therefore be drawn between the outward rulings concerning believers, which people apply in this world, and the judgment concerning their reward and punishment in the Hereafter. translated_text:
be a believer inwardly, according to the consensus of all who face the qiblah. Even the Karrāmiyyah, who call a hypocrite a believer and say, “Faith is the spoken declaration,” maintain that only inward faith benefits a person in the Hereafter. Some have reported that they regard hypocrites as inhabitants of Paradise, but this misrepresents their position. Their disagreement concerned only the designation, not the ruling, owing to the Murji’ah’s misconception that faith is neither divisible nor admits of degrees.

For this reason, the most the jurists required of a slave whose emancipation fulfils an expiation was outward action. They therefore disagreed over whether emancipating a young child suffices. There are two well-known positions among the early generations, both transmitted from Ahmad.

One position holds that emancipating the child does not suffice, because faith consists of speech and action, whereas the child has not personally embraced faith; his status as a believer merely follows that of his parents for the purposes of worldly rulings. No one, however, stipulated that the slave must be known to be a believer inwardly.

The other position holds that emancipating the child does suffice, because emancipation belongs to outward legal rulings, and the child’s status follows that of his parents. Just as he inherits from them and the funeral prayer is offered for him—and it is offered only for a believer—so too may he be emancipated.

Likewise, since the time of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, hypocrites who did not reveal their hypocrisy have had the funeral prayer offered for them upon their death and have been buried in Muslim cemeteries. In the cemetery used by the Muslims during his lifetime and those of his caliphs and Companions, everyone who outwardly professed faith was buried, even if inwardly a hypocrite. Nowhere in the lands of Islam did hypocrites have a cemetery separating them from the Muslims, as Jews and Christians have separate cemeteries.

Those buried in Muslim cemeteries had the funeral prayer offered for them by the Muslims. Yet, according to the explicit text of the Quran, it is impermissible to offer the funeral prayer for someone known to be a hypocrite. It is thus clear that this was based on outward faith, while Allah takes charge of what is concealed within. The Prophet used to

This establishes that the funeral prayer may be offered, and forgiveness sought, for anyone not known to be an unbeliever inwardly, even if he practises an innovation or has committed sins. If the imam or people of knowledge and religious commitment refrain from offering “the funeral prayer” for someone who openly practises innovation or wickedness, as a deterrent, this does not make it unlawful to pray for him or seek forgiveness for him. Indeed, concerning those for whom he declined to offer the funeral prayer—the one who misappropriated war booty, the one who killed himself, and the debtor who left no means of repaying his debt—the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Offer the funeral prayer for your companion.”

It is also reported that he would privately seek forgiveness for a man, even though he publicly refrained from doing so to deter others from following that man’s course, as related in the report concerning Muhallam ibn Jaththāmah.

In the Quran and Sunnah, those who outwardly profess Islam fall into only two categories: believers and hypocrites. The hypocrite is in the lowest depths of the Fire, while the other is a believer. His faith may, however, be deficient, so that the unqualified designation does not apply to him, or his faith may be complete. This will be discussed, Allah willing, when addressing Islam and faith and the designations applied to sinful members of the Muslim community. The point here, however, is that no one is to be deemed an unbeliever inwardly merely because of a sin he commits or an innovation he introduces—even if he calls others to it—unless he is a hypocrite.

As for someone who believes in his heart in the Messenger and what he brought, but has mistakenly adopted certain innovations through misinterpretation, he is not an unbeliever at all. The Khawārij were among the most conspicuous in their innovation, their fighting against the Muslim community, and their declaring it unbelieving. Yet none of the Companions deemed them unbelievers—neither ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib nor anyone else. Rather, they passed judgment

The same applies to the rest of the seventy-two sects: whoever among them is a hypocrite is inwardly an unbeliever; whoever is not a hypocrite, but inwardly believes in Allah and His Messenger, is not inwardly an unbeliever, even if he errs in interpretation, whatever his error may be. Some of them may possess a trait of hypocrisy without possessing the hypocrisy that places its bearer in the lowest depths of the Fire.

Whoever maintains that every one of the seventy-two sects commits unbelief that places it outside Islam has contradicted the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them all—as well as the consensus of the four imams and other imams. None of them declared every one of the seventy-two sects unbelievers. Rather, some of them declared certain groups unbelievers on account of particular doctrines, as has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The imams only declared the person in question an unbeliever because the supposed case is one that cannot actually occur. It is impossible for a man to perform none of what he has been commanded to do—prayer, zakat, fasting, and pilgrimage—while committing whatever forbidden acts he can, such as praying without ablution or in a direction other than the qiblah, and marrying his mother, yet still be inwardly a believer. Rather, he would only act in this way because his heart lacks faith.

For this reason, the followers of Abū Hanīfah would declare various categories of people unbelievers for saying such-and-such, because of the contempt it expressed. or not? For this reason, later jurists posited a case that cannot actually occur: if a man acknowledges that prayer is obligatory, but refuses when called upon to pray, is summoned to repent three times under threat of execution, and still does not pray until he is put to death, does he die an unbeliever or a sinful Muslim? They hold two views on this.

This hypothetical case is untenable. It is contrary to human nature for a man to believe that Allah has made prayer obligatory upon him and will punish him for abandoning it, yet submit to being killed rather than prostrate once before Allah, without any excuse for not doing so. No human being would ever do this. Indeed, anyone who acknowledges that prayer is obligatory will pray if beaten; matters will not reach the point of execution. The reason is that being killed is so grave a harm that a person will endure it only for something of great importance, such as remaining faithful to a religion which he believes he would be lost if he abandoned. He therefore remains steadfast until he is killed, whether that religion is true or false. But if he believes that the act is obligatory upon him, both inwardly and outwardly, performing the prayer can never be harder for him than enduring execution.

A comparable example would be to suppose that a man from Ahl al-Sunnah is told, “Ask Allah to be pleased with Abū Bakr and ʿUmar,” but refuses until he is killed, despite loving them both, believing in their excellence, and having no excuse that prevents him from asking Allah to be pleased with them. This would never happen.

Likewise, suppose that a man bears witness, inwardly and outwardly, that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and is asked to make that declaration, with no fear or desire prompting him to refuse, yet refuses until he is killed. It is impossible for such a person inwardly to bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. This is why outward profession is part of the faith without which a person cannot be saved, according to the general body of earlier and later scholars, from the first generations to the last, except for the Jahmiyyah—Jahm and those who agreed with him. If, however, he is assumed to have an excuse because he is unable to speak, or because he is afraid of people who, if

he openly professed Islam, would harm him, or for a similar reason, then he may remain silent while retaining faith in his heart, like someone compelled to utter words of unbelief. Allah Most High says:

“Except for one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith. But those who open their hearts to unbelief—upon them is wrath from Allah, and theirs will be a tremendous punishment.”

This verse is among the proofs that the position of Jahm and his followers is false. For Allah includes everyone who utters words of unbelief among those subject to the punishment threatened against unbelievers, except someone who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith.

If it is objected, “But Allah Most High says, ‘But those who open their hearts to unbelief,’” the response is: this agrees with the beginning of the verse, for whoever disbelieves without compulsion has opened his heart to unbelief. Otherwise, the beginning of the verse would contradict its end. If “whoever disbelieves” meant only someone who opens his heart to unbelief—which occurs without compulsion—the exception would not have been confined to someone who is compelled. Rather, it would have had to include both the compelled and the uncompelled, provided they had not opened their hearts to unbelief. When someone willingly utters words of unbelief, he has opened his heart to them, and that utterance is unbelief. This is also indicated by the words of Allah Most High:

“The hypocrites fear lest a surah be revealed about them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, ‘Go on mocking; Allah will surely bring out what you fear.’”

“If you ask them, they will surely say, ‘We were only talking idly and joking.’ Say, ‘Was it Allah, His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking?’”

“Make no excuses; you have disbelieved after having believed. If We pardon a group of you, We will punish another group because they were evildoers.”

Thus, He states that they disbelieved after having believed, despite their saying, “We uttered words of unbelief without believing in them; we were only talking idly and joking.” He makes clear that mocking Allah’s verses is unbelief. This can only come from someone who has opened his heart to such speech. Had there been faith in his heart, it would have prevented him from speaking these words.

And the Quran makes clear that faith in the heart necessarily entails outward action commensurate with it, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“They say, ‘We believe in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey.’ Then a group of them turns away after that. Such people are not believers.”

“When they are called to Allah and His Messenger for him to judge between them, a group of them turns away.”

“But if the right is on their side, they come to him in submission.”

Up to His words:

“The only response of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger for him to judge between them, is to say, ‘We hear and we obey.’ It is they who are successful.”

Thus, He denied faith to those who turn away from obeying the Messenger, and stated that when believers are called to Allah and His Messenger for him to judge between them, they hear and obey. He thereby made clear that this is a necessary consequence of faith.

Section

If it is objected:

“If faith, understood without qualification, encompasses everything that Allah and His Messenger have commanded, then whenever any part of that is absent, faith is invalidated. This would require declaring those who commit sins to be unbelievers, as the Khawārij maintain, or holding that they will remain in the Fire forever and denying them the designation of faith altogether, as the Mu‘tazilah maintain. Both these positions are worse than that of the Murji’ah, for the Murji’ah include scholars and devout worshippers whom the Muslim community remembers favourably. As for the Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah, Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, across all their groups, unanimously condemn them.”

The response is:

First, it should be understood that the position on which no one from Ahl al-Sunnah has agreed with the Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah is that those who commit major sins will remain in the Fire forever. This position is one of the well-known religious innovations. The Companions, those who followed them in righteousness, and all the other imams of the Muslims agreed that no one with an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will remain in the Fire forever. They also agreed that our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will intercede for those who commit major sins among his community for whom Allah permits him to intercede. In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that he said:

“Every prophet has a supplication that is answered, and I have reserved my supplication as intercession for my community on the Day of Resurrection.”

These hadiths are cited in their respective places. Some people have attributed a contrary view on this matter to the Companions, as

translated_text:
in the report from Ibn ‘Abbās that a murderer’s repentance is not accepted. Yet this misrepresents the Companions, for none of them said that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not intercede for those who commit major sins, nor that they would remain in the Fire forever. Rather, according to one of the two reports from Ibn ‘Abbās, he said that a murderer’s repentance is not accepted. Two positions are likewise reported from Ahmad ibn Hanbal concerning the acceptance of a murderer’s repentance. Disagreement over repentance, however, is distinct from disagreement over remaining in the Fire forever. Murder involves the rights of another human being, and this is why disagreement arose concerning it.

As for the claim that if any part of faith is lost, all of it is lost, this is not conceded. This is the very premise from which innovations concerning faith arose: they supposed that whenever any part of faith is lost, all of it is lost and nothing remains.

The Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah then said: “Faith consists of everything that Allah and His Messenger have commanded”—that is, faith understood without qualification, as the people of hadith have stated. They said: “If any part of it is lost, a person retains no faith whatsoever and will therefore remain in the Fire forever.”

The Murji’ah, despite the differences among their groups, said: “Neither major sins nor neglecting outward obligations diminishes faith in any way, for if any part of it were lost, nothing would remain. It must therefore be a single entity in which the righteous and the wicked are equal.”

Yet the statements of the Messenger and his Companions indicate that some faith may be lost while some remains, as in his saying:

“Whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will come out of the Fire.”

For this reason, Ahl al-Sunnah and the people of hadith hold that faith varies in degree. The majority of them say that it increases and decreases. Some say that it increases but do not say that it decreases, as is reported from Mālik in one of the two reports from him. Others say that it varies in degree, as did ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak. Indeed,

translated_text:
the use of the terms “increase” and “decrease” with reference to faith is established from the Companions, and no Companion is known to have disagreed.

Thus, through numerous well-known chains, transmitters have related from Hammād ibn Salamah, from Abū Ja‘far, from his grandfather ‘Umayr ibn Habīb al-Khatmī, a Companion of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said: “Faith increases and decreases.” He was asked: “How does it increase, and how does it decrease?” He replied: “When we remember Allah, praise Him and glorify Him, that is its increase; when we become heedless and forget, that is its decrease.”

Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ayyāsh narrated from Harīz ibn ‘Uthmān, from al-Hārith ibn Muhammad, that Abū al-Dardā’ said: “Faith increases and decreases.”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Yazīd narrated to us: Harīz ibn ‘Uthmān narrated to us, saying: ‘I heard our elders—or some of our elders—relate that Abū al-Dardā’ said: “Part of a servant’s understanding is to watch over his faith and any decrease in it. Part of a servant’s understanding is to know whether faith is increasing or decreasing. And part of a man’s understanding is to know from which direction Satan’s incitements come to him.”’”

Ismā‘īl ibn ‘Ayyāsh narrated from Safwān ibn ‘Amr, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Rabī‘ah al-Hadramī, that Abū Hurayrah said: “Faith increases and decreases.”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Yazīd ibn Hārūn narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Talhah narrated to us, from Zubayd, from Dharr, who said: ‘ ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb used to say to his companions: “Come, let us increase in faith.” They would then remember Allah, Mighty and Majestic.’”

Abū ‘Ubayd said in al-Gharīb, concerning the report from ‘Alī: “Faith first appears as a speck in the heart, and whenever faith increases, the speck grows.” This is narrated from ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from ‘Amr ibn Hind al-Jumalī, from ‘Alī. Al-Asma‘ī said: “A lumzah is like a small dot, or something similar.”

وَقَالَ أَحْمَد بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ:
 حَدَّثَنَا وَكِيعٌ عَنْ شَرِيكٍ عَنْ هِلَالٍ عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عكيم قَالَ: سَمِعْت ابْنَ مَسْعُودٍ يَقُولُ فِي دُعَائِهِ: اللَّهُمَّ زِدْنَا إيمَانًا وَيَقِينًا وَفِقْهًا.
 وَرَوَى سُفْيَانُ الثَّوْرِيُّ عَنْ جَامِعِ بْنِ شَدَّادٍ عَنْ الْأَسْوَدِ بْنِ هِلَالٍ قَالَ:
 كَانَ مُعَاذُ بْنُ جَبَلٍ يَقُولُ لِرَجُلِ: اجْلِسْ بِنَا نُؤْمِنُ نَذْكُرُ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى وَرَوَى أَبُو الْيَمَانِ: حَدَّثَنَا صَفْوَانُ عَنْ شريح بْنِ عُبَيْدٍ أَنَّ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ رَوَاحَةَ كَانَ يَأْخُذُ بِيَدِ الرَّجُلِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِهِ فَيَقُولُ: قُمْ بِنَا نُؤْمِنُ سَاعَةً فَنَحْنُ فِي مَجْلِسِ ذِكْرٍ. وَهَذِهِ الزِّيَادَةُ أَثْبَتَهَا الصَّحَابَةُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَنُزُولِ الْقُرْآنِ كُلِّهِ.
 وَصَحَّ عَنْ عَمَّارِ بْنِ يَاسِرٍ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 ثَلَاثٌ مَنْ كُنَّ فِيهِ فَقَدْ اسْتَكْمَلَ الْإِيمَانَ الْإِنْصَافُ مِنْ نَفْسِهِ وَالْإِنْفَاقُ مِنْ الْإِقْتَارِ؛ وَبَذْلُ السَّلَامِ لِلْعَالِمِ ذَكَرَهُ الْبُخَارِيُّ فِي 
" صَحِيحِهِ "
 وَقَالَ جُنْدُبُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ وَابْنُ عُمَرَ وَغَيْرُهُمَا: تَعَلَّمْنَا الْإِيمَانَ ثُمَّ تَعَلَّمْنَا الْقُرْآنَ فَازْدَدْنَا إيمَانًا وَالْآثَارُ فِي هَذَا كَثِيرَةٌ رَوَاهَا الْمُصَنِّفُونَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ عَنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ فِي كُتُبٍ كَثِيرَةٍ مَعْرُوفَةٍ.
 قَالَ مَالِكُ بْنُ دِينَارٍ:
 الْإِيمَانُ يَبْدُو فِي الْقَلْبِ ضَعِيفًا ضَئِيلًا كَالْبَقْلَةِ؛ فَإِنْ صَاحِبُهُ تَعَاهَدَهُ فَسَقَاهُ بِالْعُلُومِ النَّافِعَةِ وَالْأَعْمَالِ الصَّالِحَةِ وَأَمَاطَ عَنْهُ الدَّغَلَ وَمَا يُضْعِفُهُ وَيُوهِنُهُ أَوْشَكَ أَنْ يَنْمُوَ أَوْ يَزْدَادَ وَيَصِيرَ لَهُ أَصْلٌ وَفُرُوعٌ وَثَمَرَةٌ وَظَلَّ إلَى مَا لَا يَتَنَاهَى حَتَّى يَصِيرَ أَمْثَالَ الْجِبَالِ. وَإِنْ صَاحِبَهُ أَهْمَلَهُ وَلَمْ يَتَعَاهَدْهُ جَاءَهُ عَنْزٌ فَنَتَفَتْهَا أَوْ صَبِيٌّ فَذَهَبَ بِهَا وَأَكْثَرَ عَلَيْهَا الدَّغَلَ فَأَضْعَفَهَا أَوْ أَهْلَكَهَا أَوْ أَيْبَسَهَا كَذَلِكَ الْإِيمَانُ
translated_text:
Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Wakī‘ narrated to us, from Sharīk, from Hilāl, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Ukaym, who said: ‘I heard Ibn Mas‘ūd say in his supplication: “O Allah, increase us in faith, certainty and understanding.”’”

Sufyān al-Thawrī narrated from Jāmi‘ ibn Shaddād, from al-Aswad ibn Hilāl, who said: “Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal used to say to a man: ‘Sit with us and let us strengthen our faith by remembering Allah Most High.’”

Abū al-Yamān narrated: “Safwān narrated to us, from Shurayh ibn ‘Ubayd, that ‘Abd Allāh ibn Rawāhah would take one of his companions by the hand and say: ‘Come, let us strengthen our faith for a while, for we are in a gathering of remembrance.’” The Companions affirmed this increase after the Prophet’s death, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and after the entire Quran had been revealed.

It is authentically reported that ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir said: “Whoever possesses three qualities has attained completeness of faith: being fair even at one’s own expense, spending despite poverty, and offering the greeting of peace to the scholar.” Al-Bukhārī cited this in his Sahīh.

Jundub ibn ‘Abd Allāh, Ibn ‘Umar and others said: “We learned faith, then we learned the Quran, and so our faith increased.” Reports concerning this are numerous. Authors who have written on this subject have transmitted them from the Companions and the Successors in many well-known books.

Mālik ibn Dīnār said: “Faith first appears in the heart weak and small, like a tender plant. If its possessor tends it, watering it with beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds, and removing the weeds and whatever weakens and saps it, it will soon grow or increase, developing roots, branches, fruit and shade without limit, until it becomes like mountains. But if its possessor neglects it and fails to tend it, a goat may come and pluck it out, or a child may carry it away, or he may let weeds proliferate around it, weakening it, destroying it or causing it to wither. Such is faith.”

Khaythamah ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān said: “Faith grows fat in times of abundance and lean in times of drought. Its abundance is righteous deeds, and its drought is sins and disobedience.”

One of the early generations was asked: “Does faith increase and decrease?” He replied: “Yes. It increases until it becomes like mountains, and decreases until it becomes like specks of dust.”

In the authentic hadith narrated by Hudhayfah:

“A man will be spoken of in these terms: ‘How strong he is! How clever he is! How intelligent he is!’ Yet there will not be a mustard seed’s weight of faith in his heart.”

In another authentic hadith narrated by him:

“Trials are presented to hearts as a reed mat is woven, reed by reed. Any heart that absorbs them is marked with a black spot, while any heart that rejects them is marked with a white spot, until hearts become of two kinds: one white like a smooth stone, unharmed by any trial for as long as the heavens and the earth endure; the other dusky black, like a cup tipped over, neither recognizing good nor rejecting evil, except as dictated by the desires it has absorbed.”

The hadith concerning the seventy thousand who enter Paradise without being brought to account is sufficient evidence. Indeed, it is among the strongest proofs that faith increases and decreases, for it describes them as possessing strong and increased faith through those qualities which indicate the strength of their faith and their reliance upon Allah in all their affairs.

Abū Nu‘aym narrated through al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, from Yazīd ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Yazanī: “Abū Rāfi‘ heard a man relate that he had asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about faith. He replied: ‘Would you like me to tell you what true faith is?’ The man said: ‘Yes.’ He said: ‘When you do wrong or wrong anyone—your male slave, your female slave, or anyone else—you grieve and are distressed by it.

Al-Bazzār said:
Muhammad ibn Abī al-Hasan al-Basrī narrated to us: Hāni’ ibn al-Mutawakkil narrated to us: ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sulaymān narrated to us, from Ishāq, from Anas, who attributed the following to the Prophet:

“Three qualities, when present in a person, make him deserving of reward and bring his faith to completion: good character by which he lives among people, scrupulousness that restrains him from disobeying Allah, and forbearance with which he counters the foolishness of the ignorant.”

And:

“Four things are signs of wretchedness: eyes that shed no tears, hardness of heart, expectations of a long life, and greed for worldly things.”

The first qualities indicate increased and stronger faith, while the latter four indicate its weakness and decrease.

Abū Ya‘lā al-Mawsilī said:
‘Abd Allāh al-Qawārīrī and Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd narrated to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Zuray‘ and Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd narrated to us, saying: ‘Awf narrated to us: ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Muzanī told me—Yazīd added in his narration, “in the mosque of Basra”—: A man whom he named, but whose name ‘Awf forgot, told me:

“I was in Medina, in a mosque where ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb was present. He asked some of those sitting with him: ‘What did you hear the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say about Islam?’

“One replied: ‘I heard him say: “Islam began as a young camel, then became two-toothed, then four-toothed, then six-toothed, then fully mature.”’

“‘Umar said: ‘After full maturity comes nothing but decline.’”

This is how Abū Ya‘lā recorded it in the “Musnad of ‘Umar,” though it would be more appropriate to record it in the musnad of this unidentified Companion.

Abū Sulaymān said: Whoever does good during his night is rewarded during his day, and whoever does good during his day is rewarded during his night.

And the Quran explicitly affirms this increase in several verses, as in His words, Exalted is He:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them.”

This increase occurs whenever the verses are recited to them, at whatever time; it is not their assent to them when they were first revealed. This is something the believer experiences: when the verses are recited to him, his understanding of the Quran and knowledge of its meanings bring into his heart knowledge pertaining to faith that was not there before. It is as though he had never heard the verse until that moment. His heart also acquires a desire for good and a fear of evil that were not there before. Thus his knowledge of Allah and his love of obeying Him increase. This is an increase in faith.

Allah, Exalted is He, also says:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

This increase occurred when they were threatened with the enemy, not when a verse was revealed. They increased in certainty, reliance upon Allah, steadfastness in jihad, and devotion to Allah alone, fearing not created beings but the Creator alone.

Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Whenever a surah is revealed, some of them say, ‘Which of you has this increased in faith?’ As for those who believe, it increases them in faith, and they rejoice.”

“But as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds impurity to their impurity.”

This “increase” is not merely assent to the fact that Allah revealed the surah. Rather, it increases their faith according to what it entails. If it commands jihad or something else, their eagerness increases; if it prohibits something, they refrain from it and come to dislike it. Hence He says:

“And they rejoice.”

Rejoicing is something beyond mere assent. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture rejoice in what has been revealed to you, while among the factions are those who reject part of it.”

Rejoicing in this is part of the increase in faith. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Say, ‘In Allah’s bounty and His mercy—in that let them rejoice.’”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“And on that Day

the believers will rejoice in Allah’s victory.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“We have appointed only angels as keepers of the Fire, and have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those given the Scripture may become certain and those who believe may increase in faith.”

And He says:

“It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers so that they might increase in faith alongside their existing faith.”

This verse was revealed when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions returned from al-Hudaybiyyah. Thus He made tranquility a cause of increased faith. Tranquility is reassurance within the heart, distinct from the heart’s knowledge and assent. Hence He said concerning the day of Hunayn:

“Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down forces you did not see.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“As one of two, when they were in the cave, he said to his companion, ‘Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us.’ Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with forces you did not see.”

No Quranic revelation had come down on the day of Hunayn or on the day in the cave. Rather, He sent down His tranquility and reassurance in the face of fear of the enemy. Thus, when He sent down tranquility into their hearts upon their return from al-Hudaybiyyah, so that they might increase in faith alongside their existing faith, this indicated that the additional faith was a state, quality, and action of the heart, such as its reassurance, calm, and certainty.

Certainty may relate to action and reassurance, just as it may relate to knowledge. Likewise, the doubt that contradicts certainty may concern knowledge or the heart’s reassurance. Hence the transmitted supplication says:

“O Allah, grant us such fear of You as will stand between us and disobedience to You; such obedience to You as will bring us to Your Paradise; and such certainty as will ease for us the calamities of this world.”

In the hadith of al-Siddīq, reported by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī, and others from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he said:

“Ask Allah for well-being and certainty, for after certainty no one has been given anything

better than well-being; so ask Allah Most High for both.”

Thus, certainty in the face of calamities, beyond knowing that Allah has decreed them, consists in the heart’s calm, reassurance, and submission. This is part of complete faith in divine decree, both its good and its evil, as He, Exalted is He, says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. Whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

Alqamah said—and this is also reported from Ibn Mas‘ūd—“This is a man who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, so he is content and submits.” As for His words, “He guides his heart,” His guidance of the person’s heart is an increase in his faith, just as He, Exalted is He, says:

“As for those who are guided, He increases them in guidance.”

And He says:

“They were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance.”

The term “faith” most often occurs in the Quran with a qualification. In such cases, the expression does not encompass everything Allah has commanded. Rather, it is understood to entail its necessary consequences and the fulfillment of all that He has commanded; in that case, the unqualified term encompasses it. He, Exalted is He, says:

“Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that over which He has made you trustees. Those among you who believe and spend will have a great reward.”

“Why do you not believe in Allah when the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are believers?”

“It is He who sends down clear signs to His servant to bring you out of darkness into light.”

And He, Exalted is He, says at the end of the surah:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger. He will grant you a double share of His mercy, provide you with a light by which to walk, and forgive you. Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Some commentators have said that the first verse addresses Quraysh, and that the second addresses the Jews and Christians. This is not so, for Allah has never addressed the disbelievers by saying, “O you who believe.” Then, after that, He said: “So that the People of the Scripture may know that they have no power

The increase in faith that Allah commands and that His believing servants attain can be understood in several respects:

First: the distinction between general and detailed requirements. Although all people must believe in Allah and His Messenger, and every community must commit itself in general to whatever its messenger commands, it is clear that what became obligatory after the entire Quran had been revealed was not obligatory at the outset. Nor is every individual required to believe in the same details of what the Messenger conveyed as someone whom further reports have reached. Whoever knows the Quran, the prophetic teachings, and their meanings must believe in their details to an extent not required of others.

If a man believes in Allah and the Messenger, inwardly and outwardly, then dies before learning the religious laws, he dies as a believer who has fulfilled the faith required of him. Yet neither the faith required of him nor the faith he actually attained is like the faith of someone who learned those laws, believed in them, and acted upon them. Rather, the latter’s faith is more complete both in what is required and in what is attained: the faith required of him is more complete, and the faith he actually attains is more complete.

Allah Most High says:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you.”

This refers to the legislation of commands and prohibitions. It does not mean that every member of the Muslim community is required to fulfill everything required of all its other members, or that each has actually done so. Third: knowledge and affirmation themselves vary in strength, firmness, and freedom from doubt and uncertainty. This is something everyone can observe within himself. Even when people perceive the same thing through their outward senses—for example, when they sight the crescent moon—some see it more clearly than others. The same applies to hearing the same sound, smelling the same scent, and tasting the same kind of food. Likewise, the heart’s knowledge and affirmation vary to an even greater extent, in numerous respects. People differ in their knowledge of the meanings they believe in—the meanings of the Lord’s names and His speech—far more than they differ in their knowledge of other things.

Fourth: affirmation that entails action of the heart is more complete than affirmation that does not. Thus, knowledge upon which a person acts is more complete than knowledge upon which he does not act. Suppose two people know that Allah is true, His Messenger is true, Paradise is real, and Hell is real. If this knowledge produces in one of them love and fear of Allah, longing for Paradise, and flight from Hell, while in the other it does not, then the first person’s knowledge is more complete. The strength of an effect indicates the strength of its cause, and these responses arise from knowledge. Knowing what is loved entails seeking it, and knowing what is feared entails fleeing from it. If the necessary consequence does not occur, this indicates weakness in that which entails it. This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Being told is not like seeing for oneself.”

This was not because Moses doubted Allah’s report. Rather, even when someone is certain that the person informing him is truthful, he may not picture what he has been told as he would upon seeing it for himself. Indeed, his heart may be too occupied to picture it, even though he believes it. Clearly, seeing it for himself gives him a conception of what was reported that he did not have when merely told about it. Thus, this affirmation is more complete than the former affirmation.

Fifth: actions of the heart—such as love for Allah and His Messenger, fear of Allah Most High, hope in Him, and the like—are all part of faith, as established by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the agreement of the early generations. People differ enormously in these respects.

Sixth: outward actions, together with inward actions, are also part of faith, and people differ in them.

Seventh: someone who remembers in his heart what Allah has commanded him and keeps it present in mind, rather than being heedless of it, is more complete than someone who affirms it but is heedless of it. Heedlessness is incompatible with complete knowledge, while affirmation, remembrance, and keeping things present in mind perfect knowledge and certainty. This is why ʿUmayr ibn Habīb, one of the Companions, said:

“When we remember Allah, praise Him, and glorify Him, our faith increases; when we become heedless, forget, and neglect our duties, it decreases.”

That is indeed so. Muʿādh ibn Jabal used to say to his companions:

“Sit with us for a while, that we may grow in faith.”

Allah Most High says:

“And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his own desires.”

And He says:

“And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers.”

And He says:

“He who fears Allah will heed the reminder, but the most wretched will avoid it.”

Then, whenever a person recalls what he previously knew and acts upon it,

he gains knowledge of something else that he had not known before and comes to understand meanings of Allah’s names and signs that he had not previously understood. As stated in the report:

“Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah grants him knowledge of what he did not know.”

This is something every believer experiences within himself. In the Sahīh, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The one who remembers his Lord and the one who does not remember his Lord are like the living and the dead.”

Allah Most High says:

“When His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith.”

This is because they increase their knowledge of what they had not previously known and increase their actions based on that knowledge. They also increase their remembrance of what they had forgotten and their actions in response to that reminder. The same applies to the signs that people witness throughout the horizons and within themselves.

Allah Most High says:

“We will show them Our signs throughout the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.”

That is, that the Quran is true. Then Allah Most High says:

“Is it not enough that your Lord is a witness over all things?”

For Allah has borne witness in the Quran to what He has related, and the believer has believed it. He then showed them signs throughout the horizons and within themselves that point to the very things He related in the Quran. These signs thus made clear to them that the Quran is true, in addition to what they had already attained.

Allah Most High also says:

“Have they not looked at the heaven above them—how We built it and adorned it, and how it has no rifts? And the earth—We spread it out, set firm mountains upon it, and caused every delightful kind of plant to grow in it, as an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns to Allah.”

Both the signs in creation and the recited verses provide insight and a reminder: insight dispels blindness, and reminders dispel heedlessness. Thus, one who did not know is given insight and comes to know, while one who knew but forgot is reminded. A person may read a surah many times—even Sūrat al-Fātihah—and, in the course of doing so, meanings become apparent to him that had never occurred to him before, as though it had been revealed at that very moment. He then believes in those meanings, and his knowledge increases

and so do his deeds. This occurs in everyone who reads the Quran reflectively, unlike someone who reads it heedlessly. Moreover, whenever a person does something he has been commanded to do, he recalls that command and affirms it. At that moment, an affirmation arises in his heart of which he had previously been heedless, even though he had neither disbelieved nor denied it.

The eighth point:

A person may disbelieve and deny certain things without knowing that the Messenger taught or commanded them. Had he known this, he would not have disbelieved or denied them. Rather, his heart is firmly convinced that the Messenger speaks only the truth and commands only what is right. Then he hears the verse or hadith, reflects upon it, has its meaning explained to him, or comes to understand it in some other way. He then believes what he previously disbelieved and recognizes what he previously denied. This is a new affirmation and a new faith through which his faith increases. Before this, he was not a disbeliever, but ignorant.

Although this resembles the case of general and detailed belief—where the heart has neither denied nor affirmed any particulars, neither recognized nor rejected them, so that detailed understanding follows general belief in a heart free of preconceptions—many people, including people devoted to learning and worship, hold numerous detailed beliefs in their hearts that contradict what the Messenger brought, without knowing that they contradict it. Once they learn this, they retract them.

Anyone who introduces an erroneous statement into religion or performs an erroneous deed while believing in the Messenger—or who, if he knew what the Messenger said and believed it, would not depart from it—falls into this category. Every person who introduces a religious innovation while intending to follow the Messenger falls into this category. Thus, someone who knows what the Messenger brought and acts upon it is more complete in faith than someone who has erred concerning it. Someone who comes to know what is correct after having erred, and then acts upon it, is more complete in faith than someone who has not done so.

Section

Allah has affirmed in the Quran that Islam may exist without faith, in His words, Exalted is He:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted,” for faith has not yet entered your hearts. If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish the reward of your deeds in the least.’”

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections that Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave gifts to a group—in another narration, ‘made a distribution’—but left one of them without anything, although he was the one I admired most. I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, why have you passed over so-and-so? By Allah, I certainly consider him a believer.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, ‘Or a Muslim.’ I said this three times, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, repeated his response to me three times. Then he said, ‘I give to a man even though another is dearer to me than he is, for fear that Allah might cast him face down into the Fire.’”

In another narration:

“He struck me between my neck and shoulder and said, ‘Are you arguing with me, Saʿd?’”

As for this Islam, whose adherents Allah has described as not yet having faith enter their hearts: is it an Islam for which they are rewarded, or is it of the same kind as the Islam of the hypocrites?

There are two well-known views on this among the early and later scholars.

The first is that it is an Islam for which they are rewarded and which takes them out of disbelief and hypocrisy. This is reported from al-Hasan, Ibn Sīrīn, and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī

translated_text:
Mujāhid, who said concerning the verse,

‘The Bedouins say, “We believe.” Say, “You have not believed; rather, say, ‘We have submitted.’”’

‘We have submitted for fear of being taken captive or killed.’”

However, this chain of transmission is disconnected: Sufyān did not live to meet Mujāhid.

Those who held that this Islam is like the Islam of the hypocrites, for which they receive no reward, argued: “Allah denied them faith, and anyone denied faith is a disbeliever.”

They also said: “Islam is faith: every Muslim is a believer, and every believer is a Muslim. Anyone who regards the gravely sinful as Muslims but not believers must consequently exclude them from the words of the Exalted:

‘O you who believe, when you rise for prayer,’

and His words:

‘O you who believe, when the call to prayer is made on Friday,’

and similar passages. For they are addressed as believers, not as Muslims; anyone who is not a believer is therefore not included.”

The answer to this is as follows: those early scholars who said that such people had passed out of faith into Islam did not say that no faith whatsoever remained in them. Rather, that is the position of the Khawārij and the Muʿtazila.

Those of Ahl al-Sunnah who expressed this view say that the gravely sinful will be brought out of the Fire through intercession, and that they possess faith by virtue of which they will be brought out of the Fire. Nevertheless, they are not unreservedly called believers, because faith in its unqualified sense is that by which a person merits reward and entry into Paradise, and these people do not possess such faith.

They are, however, included in addresses to believers, because such addresses encompass anyone who has entered into faith, even if he has not perfected it. Indeed, he is addressed precisely so that he may do what completes his faith. How, then, could he have completed it before being addressed? Otherwise, we would have established that the commanded act was part of faith before the address, whereas it only became part of faith after they were commanded to perform it. “The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives,”

and similar passages. For, in the first place, the address “O you who believe” outwardly includes anyone who professes faith, even if he is inwardly a hypocrite. How, then, could it exclude someone who is not a hypocrite, even if he is not a true believer?

The reality is that someone who is not a true believer may be described as a Muslim who possesses faith that prevents him from remaining in the Fire forever. This is agreed upon among Ahl al-Sunnah. But may he be called a believer without qualification? This is where they differed. Some said: “He is called a Muslim, but not a believer.” Others said: “Rather, he is called a believer.”

The precise position is to say that he is a believer whose faith is deficient: a believer by virtue of his faith, and a flagrant sinner by virtue of his major sin. He is not accorded the unqualified designation of a believer, for the Quran and Sunnah deny him that unqualified designation. Nevertheless, the designation of faith includes him in the commands of Allah and His Messenger, since these impose obligations and prohibitions upon him, which bind him just as other duties do. The question concerns only the unqualified designation of praise.

Accordingly, the address to believers encompasses “three groups.” It includes the true believer. It also includes the hypocrite with respect to the outward rulings applicable to him, even though hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire in the Hereafter. Inwardly, neither Islam nor faith is ascribed to him, while outwardly he is accorded Islam and outward faith. It also includes those who have submitted, even though the reality of faith has not entered their hearts; nevertheless, they possess a portion of faith and Islam for which they are rewarded.

translated_text:
They may, moreover, neglect the obligations imposed upon them without having committed major sins for which they would be punished like those guilty of major sins; rather, they are punished for neglecting their obligations. Such people include the Bedouins mentioned in the verse and others like them. They said, “We believe,” without fulfilling what they were commanded to do, inwardly or outwardly. Neither had the reality of faith entered their hearts, nor had they striven in Allah’s cause, although the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had called them to strive.

Alternatively, they may be among those guilty of major sins who are liable to the threatened punishment, such as those who pray, pay zakat, and strive in Allah’s cause, yet commit major sins. These people do not leave Islam; rather, they are Muslims. There is, however, a terminological disagreement concerning them: may they be called believers? We shall discuss this, Allah willing.

As for the “Khawārij” and the “Mu‘tazilah,” they exclude them from the designations of both faith and Islam, since they regard faith and Islam as one and the same. Thus, in their view, whoever leaves faith also leaves Islam. The Khawārij, however, say that they are disbelievers, whereas the Mu‘tazilah say that they are neither Muslims nor disbelievers, placing them in an intermediate position between the two.

The evidence that the Islam mentioned in the verse is an Islam for which they are rewarded, and that they are not hypocrites, is His saying:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted,” for faith has not yet entered your hearts.’”

He then says:

“If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish the reward of your deeds in the least.”

This indicates that if they obey Allah and His Messenger while possessing this Islam, Allah will reward them for their obedience. The hypocrite’s deeds, however, are of no avail in the Hereafter.

Furthermore, He describes them in terms contrary to those used to describe the hypocrites. He describes the hypocrites as having disbelief in their hearts and concealing the opposite of what they outwardly display, as the Most High says:

“And among the people

are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ but they are not believers. They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none but themselves, though they do not realize it. In their hearts is a disease, and Allah has increased their disease”—and the following verses.

He also says:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.’ Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars.”

Thus, in the Quran, He describes the hypocrites as liars who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts, and as having disbelief in their hearts for which they will be punished. He does not describe these people in any such terms. Rather, when they claimed to believe, He said to the Messenger:

“Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted,” for faith has not yet entered your hearts. If you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not diminish the reward of your deeds in the least.’”

Denying them the unqualified designation of faith does not entail that they are hypocrites, as illustrated by His saying:

“They ask you about the spoils of war. Say, ‘The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger.’ So fear Allah, set matters right among yourselves, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers.”

Then He says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord; those who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them. It is they who are truly believers.”

It is well known that not everyone who lacks these qualities is thereby a hypocrite destined for the lowest depths of the Fire. Rather, such a person has not fulfilled the requirements of obligatory faith, and so the designation is denied to him, just as other designations are denied to someone who neglects some of what is required of him. Likewise, the Bedouins had not fulfilled the requirements of obligatory faith, so the designation was denied to them for that reason, even though they were Muslims possessing a measure of faith for which they would be rewarded. This is the condition of most people when they first enter Islam; indeed, it is the condition of most of those who have not come to know

the realities of faith. For if a man is fought until he accepts Islam—as the disbelievers used to be fought until they accepted Islam—or accepts Islam after being taken captive, or hears about Islam and comes to embrace it, he is a Muslim committed to obeying the Messenger, although knowledge of the realities of faith has not yet entered his heart. Such knowledge comes only to someone for whom its means have been made available: through understanding the Quran, through close association with people of faith and following their example in word and deed, or through special guidance that Allah grants him.

A person may perceive aspects of Islam’s excellence that draw him to embrace it. Even if he was born into it and raised among its people, he loves it because some of its merits and some of the faults of the disbelievers have become apparent to him. Yet many such people may fall into doubt when they hear objections that cast doubt upon Islam, and they do not strive in Allah’s cause. Such a person is therefore not included in His words:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause.”

Yet he is not inwardly a hypocrite concealing disbelief. Thus, he is neither among those who are truly believers nor among the hypocrites. Nor is he among those who commit major sins. Rather, he performs outward acts of obedience but does not fulfil the realities of faith that would make him truly a believer.

Such a person possesses some faith, but he is not among those who are truly believers, and he is rewarded for the acts of obedience he performs. Hence Allah Most High says:

“Rather, say, ‘We have submitted.’”

Hence He also says:

“They regard their acceptance of Islam as a favour to you. Say, ‘Do not regard your acceptance of Islam as a favour to me. Rather, it is Allah who has favoured you by guiding you to faith, if you are truthful.’”

That is, truthful in your claim:

“We believe.”

He is saying: if you are truthful, then it is Allah who has favoured you by guiding you to faith; and this

implies that they may be truthful in saying:

“We believe.”

Their truthfulness may mean either that they possess the qualities described in His words:

“They believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

Or it may mean that they were not like the hypocrites, but possessed some faith, even though they were not entitled to make an unqualified claim to faith. This is the more likely interpretation—and Allah knows best—for He said concerning the women whose faith was examined:

“If you know them to be believers, then do not send them back to the disbelievers.”

Yet it is impossible to rule out their experiencing doubt in the future. Moreover, Allah declared only the hypocrites to be liars, not others. He did not declare these people to be liars, but said:

“You have not believed.”

This is like the saying:

“None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”

And the sayings:

“A person who commits adultery is not a believer at the time he commits it.”

“He whose neighbour is not safe from his harm does not believe.”

Yet such people are not hypocrites. The context of the verse indicates that Allah censured them because, in their ignorance and coarseness, they regarded their acceptance of Islam as a favour, and declared what was within themselves despite Allah’s knowledge of it. For Allah Most High said:

“Say, ‘Are you teaching Allah about your religion, when Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth?’”

Had there been nothing of religion in their hearts, they would not have been teaching Allah about their religion, for outward Islam is recognizable to everyone.

The preposition bā’ is used in His words:

“Are you teaching Allah about your religion?”

because the verb carries the sense of informing and telling. It is as though He said: “Are you informing Him and telling Him about your religion, when He knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth?”

The context of the verse indicates that what they informed Allah of was what Allah related of their words:

“We believe.”

For they were reporting what was in their hearts.

The Quran commentators also mention the following:

“When these two verses were revealed, they came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, swearing that they were believers and were speaking truthfully. Then Allah Most High revealed: ‘Say, are you teaching Allah about your religion?’”

This indicates that they had been sincere from the outset in entering the religion, for after the verse was revealed they had undertaken no further striving that would bring them within the description given in the verse. They had merely made a statement. Allah, glorified be He, said:

“Faith has not yet entered your hearts.”

The expression lammā (“not yet”) negates something whose occurrence is near and which usually does occur, as in His words:

“Or do you think you will enter Paradise while Allah has not yet made evident those among you who have striven?”

Al-Suddī said: “This verse was revealed concerning the Bedouins of Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Aslam, Ashjaʿ and Ghifār. They are those whom Allah mentioned in Sūrat al-Fath. They used to say, ‘We believe in Allah,’ to secure their own safety. But when they were summoned to set out for al-Hudaybiyah, they stayed behind, and this verse was revealed concerning them.”

It is reported from Muqātil:

“They lived between Mecca and Medina. Whenever a detachment sent by the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed through their territory, they would say, ‘We believe,’ to safeguard their lives and property. When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, set out for al-Hudaybiyah, he summoned them to accompany him, but they did not go with him.”

Mujāhid said: “It was revealed concerning the Bedouins of Banū Asad ibn Khuzaymah.” Someone else described their circumstances, saying:

“They came to Medina in a year of drought and outwardly professed Islam, although they were not believers. They fouled the roads of Medina with excrement and drove up prices there. They would claim credit before the Messenger of Allah

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying, ‘We have come to you with our belongings and dependants.’ This verse was then revealed concerning them.”

Regarding His words:

“They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam. Say, ‘Do not consider your acceptance of Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred a favor upon you by guiding you to faith, if you are truthful.’”

Qatādah said: “They claimed credit before the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when they came, saying, ‘We have accepted Islam without fighting. We did not fight you as such-and-such tribes did.’ So Allah said to His Prophet:

‘They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam. Say, “Do not consider your acceptance of Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred a favor upon you by guiding you to faith.”’”

Muqātil ibn Hayyān said:

“They were the Bedouins of Banū Asad ibn Khuzaymah. They said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, we have come to you without fighting and have left our clans and possessions behind. Every Arab tribe fought you before reluctantly entering Islam. This therefore gives us a claim upon you.’ So Allah Most High revealed:

‘They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam. Say, “Do not consider your acceptance of Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred a favor upon you by guiding you to faith, if you are truthful.”’”

Thus it is He who has bestowed this favor upon you. Concerning them Allah revealed:

“And do not render your deeds worthless.”

It is also said concerning the major sins to which a threat of the Fire is attached: each incurs that punishment for whoever commits it and dies persisting in it without repenting.

All of this makes clear that they were not inwardly disbelievers, yet neither had they attained the faith required of them. Sūrat al-Hujurāt mentions these categories of people. He said:

“Indeed, most of those who call out to you from behind the chambers do not understand.”

He did not describe them as disbelievers or hypocrites. Nevertheless, there is reason to fear that such people may fall into disbelief and hypocrisy. This is why some of them apostatized: their hearts had not been suffused with the sweetness of faith. After that, He said: “O you who believe, if there comes to you

an evildoer with news, verify it,” and so on. This verse was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn ‘Uqbah, who had lied in his report.

The exegetes said:

“This verse was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn ‘Uqbah. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent him to Banū al-Mustaliq to collect their zakat. There had been enmity between him and them in the pre-Islamic period. He travelled part of the way, then returned to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying, ‘They have withheld the zakat and wanted to kill me.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then mobilized a force against them, whereupon this verse was revealed.”

This account is well known through numerous chains of transmission. Allah Most High then said in the continuation of the passage:

“And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he were to obey you in much of the matter, you would surely suffer hardship.”

Allah Most High also said:

“If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other,” and so on.

He then forbade them to ridicule one another, to disparage one another, and to call one another offensive names. He said:

“Wretched is the designation of sinful disobedience after faith.”

It has been said that this means: do not call someone an evildoer or a disbeliever after he has come to faith. This interpretation, however, is weak. Rather, the meaning is: what an evil designation it is for you to be evildoers after having believed. Likewise, Allah Most High said concerning the man who lied:

“If an evildoer comes to you with news, verify it.”

Thus, He called him an evildoer. In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“Reviling a Muslim is sinful disobedience, and fighting him is disbelief.”

That is, if you revile a Muslim, ridicule him, and disparage him, you deserve to be called evildoers. In the verse concerning accusations of unchastity, He said:

“And never accept their testimony, for it is they who are the evildoers.”

evildoers, you will have deserved the designation of sinful disobedience after faith. Moreover, when they called one another offensive names, they were not saying, “Evildoer! Disbeliever!” For when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, arrived in Medina, some of them were already calling others by nicknames.

A group of exegetes said concerning this verse: “Do not address someone, after he has embraced Islam, by the religion he followed before Islam—for example, saying to a Jew who has become Muslim, ‘You Jew!’” This is reported from Ibn ‘Abbās and a group of the Successors, including al-Hasan, Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr, ‘Atā’ al-Khurāsānī, and al-Qurazī. ‘Ikrimah said: “It means saying to someone, ‘You disbeliever! You hypocrite!’” ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Zayd said: “It means calling someone by his deeds, such as saying, ‘You fornicator! You thief! You evildoer!’” In the commentary transmitted by al-‘Awfī from Ibn ‘Abbās, he said: “It means reproaching someone who has repented for sins he previously committed.”

It is well known that calling someone a disbeliever, a Jew, a fornicator, a thief, or by other names referring to wrongdoing is not the same as calling him an evildoer. Thus, His words,

“Wretched is the designation of sinful disobedience,”

do not mean calling the person being reviled an evildoer, for calling him a disbeliever is more serious. Rather, the one who reviles becomes an evildoer, in accordance with the saying:

“Reviling a Muslim is sinful disobedience, and fighting him is disbelief.”

He then said:

“And whoever does not repent—it is they who are the wrongdoers.”

Thus, He designated them wrongdoers if they did not repent of that, even though they remained included among those called believers. He then mentioned the prohibition of backbiting, followed by the prohibition of boasting about lineage, and said:

“Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”

He then mentioned the Bedouins’ statement:

“We have believed.”

Thus, the surah forbids these acts of disobedience and sins, which involve transgression against the Messenger and against

the believers. The Bedouins mentioned in it are of the same kind as the hypocrites.

Those guilty of reviling others and sinful disobedience, those who called out from behind the chambers, and others like them are not hypocrites. Hence the exegetes said that they were those summoned to join the expedition in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. Although they were guilty of major sins, they were not inwardly disbelievers and hypocrites.

Ibn Ishāq said:

“When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, intended to perform ‘umrah—the ‘umrah of al-Hudaybiyah—he summoned the desert dwellers and Bedouins around Medina to accompany him, fearing that his people might engage him in battle or bar his way. Many of them, however, were reluctant to join him.”

They are those whom Allah meant by His words:

“Those Bedouins who remained behind will say to you, ‘Our possessions and families kept us occupied, so ask forgiveness for us.’”

That is: ask Allah to forgive us for staying behind rather than accompanying you.

“They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts.”

That is, they do not care whether you ask forgiveness for them or not. This is the condition of a sinful person who is unconcerned about his sin. Concerning the hypocrites, however, He said:

“And when it is said to them, ‘Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you,’ they turn their heads aside, and you see them turning away in arrogance.”

“It is all the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them: Allah will never forgive them.”

He did not say anything like this about these Bedouins. Rather, the verse indicates that, had they been sincere in requesting forgiveness, the Messenger’s asking forgiveness for them would have benefited them. He then said:

“You will be called to face a people of great military might; you will fight them, or they will submit. If you obey, Allah will grant you a good reward; but if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment.”

Thus Allah promised them a reward for obeying the one calling them to jihad and threatened them with punishment for turning away from obedience to him. This is like the way others guilty of sins and major offenses are addressed, unlike someone who is a disbeliever

translated_text:
inwardly, for he does not deserve a reward merely for obeying the command until he first believes. Nor is the threat against him merely for turning away from obedience in jihad, for his disbelief is graver than that. All this indicates that these people belong to the sinful members of the Muslim community. Sinful disobedience may consist either in neglecting obligations or in committing forbidden acts. Since these people neglected the jihad Allah had made obligatory upon them, and experienced a degree of doubt that weakened their faith, they were not among the truthful whom He described, even though they were sincere in inwardly adhering to the religion of Islam.

The exegetes’ statement, “They were not believers,” denies them the faith that Allah denied them, just as He denied it to the fornicator, the thief, the drinker, the person whose neighbour is not safe from his harm, the person who does not love for his brother the good he loves for himself, and the person who does not submit to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, and others like them.

Support for this may be drawn from His words:

“How evil is the name of sinful disobedience after faith!”

Likewise, in the saying:

“Reviling a Muslim is sinful disobedience, and fighting him is disbelief.”

Thus He condemned anyone who exchanged the designation of faith for that of sinful disobedience. This indicates that a sinfully disobedient person is not called a believer, and therefore that these Bedouins belong to the category of those guilty of major sins, not that of the hypocrites.

As for the report that they embraced Islam for fear of being killed or taken captive, this was also how people other than the Emigrants and Helpers embraced Islam: they did so out of hope and fear. Such was the conversion of those of Quraysh who were set free after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had subdued them, and the conversion of those whose hearts were being won over, both among them and among the people of Najd. Not everyone who embraced Islam out of hope or fear was among the hypocrites who are in the lowest depths

of the Fire; rather, they enter Islam and obedience without harbouring rejection of the Messenger or hostility towards him in their hearts. Yet their hearts have neither been illuminated by the light of faith nor gained clear insight into it. Such a person’s Islam may improve until he becomes one of the believers, as happened with most of those set free after the conquest. He may instead remain among the sinful members of the Muslim community. Among them is one who becomes a doubting hypocrite:

“When Munkar and Nakīr ask him, ‘What do you say about this man who was sent among you?’ he replies, ‘Ah, ah! I do not know. I heard people saying something, so I said it too.’”

The statement of those who said that they embraced Islam without fighting has already been mentioned: their Islam was better than that of others; Allah condemned them only because they presented their acceptance of Islam as a favour, and revealed concerning them, “Do not invalidate your deeds”; and they belong to the category of those guilty of major sins.

Furthermore, He says:

“But say, ‘We have submitted,’ for faith has not yet entered your hearts.”

The expression “not yet” is used only to negate something whose occurrence is expected and anticipated, as in His words:

“Or do you think that you will enter Paradise when Allah has not yet made evident those among you who strive and those who are steadfast?”

And His words:

“Or do you think that you will enter Paradise when the like of what befell those who passed away before you has not yet come upon you?”

Thus, His words, “Faith has not yet entered your hearts,” indicate that faith is expected to enter their hearts. A person who initially enters Islam may not yet have faith in his heart, but it develops later, as stated in the hadith:

“A man would embrace Islam at the beginning of the day out of desire for worldly gain, yet before the day ended, Islam would be dearer to him than everything upon which the sun rises.”

For this reason, faith subsequently entered the hearts of most of those who embraced Islam out of hope and fear. And His words, “But say, ‘We have submitted’”

Yet obedience to Allah and His Messenger does not benefit a hypocrite until he first believes. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others cited this verse as evidence that one qualifies a profession of faith by saying “if Allah wills,” but not a profession of Islam, and that those guilty of major sins leave faith and enter Islam.

Al-Maymūnī said:

“I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal his opinion about saying, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills.’ He replied, ‘I say, “A believer, if Allah wills,” and I say, “A Muslim,” without qualification.’ I asked Ahmad, ‘Do you distinguish between Islam and faith?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ I asked him, ‘What evidence do you cite?’ He recited:

‘The Bedouins say, “We believe.” Say, “You have not believed; rather, say, ‘We have submitted.’”’

Al-Shālanjī said:

“I asked Ahmad about someone who says, ‘I regard myself as a believer in terms of legal rulings and inheritance, but I do not know my standing before Allah.’ He replied, ‘He is not a Murji’ite.’”

Abū Ayyūb Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Hāshimī said:

He replied, “The Prophet’s hadith, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicates this.” He then cited his words:

“Take out of the Fire anyone in whose heart there is such-and-such a weight [of faith]. Take out anyone in whose heart there is such-and-such a weight [of faith].”

“This indicates it.”

‘Īsā al-Ahmar and his position on irjā’ were mentioned in Abū ‘Abd Allāh’s presence. He said, “Yes, that is a pernicious view.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said, “Mu’ammal narrated to us: Hammād ibn Zayd narrated to us: I heard Hishām say, ‘Al-Hasan and Muhammad would say, “A Muslim,” but hesitated to say, “A believer.”’”

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “Did anyone other than Suwayd narrate it?”

He replied, “Not to my knowledge.”

I also heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh say, “Faith consists of words and deeds.”

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “What about the hadith that is narrated:

‘Free her, for she is a believer’?”

He replied, “Not everyone includes the words, ‘She is a believer.’ They say, ‘Free her.’”

He said, “Mālik, who heard it from this shaykh, Hilāl ibn ‘Alī, does not include the words, ‘For she is a believer.’”

وَ 
" الْمُعْتَزِلَةُ "

translated_text:
and some of them did say that she was a believer; when she affirms that, she has the legal status of a believing woman. That is what it means.

I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, “Do you distinguish between faith and Islam?”

He replied, “People have differed over this. Hammād ibn Zayd, they reported, used to distinguish between faith and Islam.”

He was asked, “Who are the Murji’ah?”

He replied, “Those who say that faith consists of words without deeds.”

I say: Ahmad ibn Hanbal never meant that such a person had been stripped of all faith, leaving him with none, as the Khawārij and Mu‘tazilah maintain. Indeed, he explicitly stated in several places that those who commit major sins possess faith by virtue of which they will be brought out of the Fire. He cited as evidence the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Bring out of the Fire anyone in whose heart there is a speck’s weight of faith.”

That view is neither his position nor that of any of the imams of Ahl al-Sunnah. Rather, they all agree that sinful people who are not hypocrites possess some faith by virtue of which they will be brought out of the Fire. This is what distinguishes them from the disbelievers and hypocrites. Yet possessing some faith does not necessarily mean that a person comes within the unqualified, praiseworthy designation of “believer.” The bearer of the revealed Law denied this designation to such people, saying:

“No adulterer is a believer at the time he commits adultery.”

He also said:

“None of you believes until he loves for his brother the good that he loves for himself.”

And he said:

“He whose neighbour is not safe from his harm does not believe.”

He swore to this repeatedly. He also said:

“A believer is one whom people trust with their lives and property.”

The Mu‘tazilah, however, deny such a person the designation of faith altogether, as well as that of Islam. They say, “He possesses nothing of faith or Islam,” and, “We place him in a position between two positions.” They maintain that he will remain in the Fire forever and will not be brought out of it through intercession. This is precisely what they were reproached for.

{الْإِسْلَامُ: أَنْ تَشْهَدَ أَنْ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ وَتُقِيمَ الصَّلَاةَ وَتُؤْتِيَ الزَّكَاةَ وَتَصُومَ رَمَضَانَ وَتَحُجَّ الْبَيْتَ}
