translated_text:
constitute the foundation of faith, is disbelief in Allah and what He has said, and ceasing to believe in Him and affirm His truthfulness. The opposite of faith that consists of deeds, rather than acknowledgment, is a disbelief that does not amount to disbelief in Allah that takes one outside the religion. Rather, it is disbelief consisting in the neglect of deeds, just as deeds themselves constitute faith, though not the faith that consists of acknowledging Allah.

Since someone who abandons the faith that consists of acknowledging Allah is a disbeliever who must be called upon to repent, whereas someone who abandons the faith that consists of deeds—such as zakat, Hajj, and fasting—or abandons restraint from drinking wine and unlawful sexual intercourse has lost only part of his faith, we do not hold that the latter must be called upon to repent. Nor do those who disagree with us among Ahl al-Sunnah and the people of innovation who say that faith consists of affirmation and deeds, with the sole exception of the Khārijites. Likewise, our saying that he is a disbeliever with respect to his neglect of deeds does not require that he be called upon to repent, nor does it exempt him from the prescribed punishments.

Just as the loss of faith that consists of deeds does not require calling him to repent or exempting him from the prescribed punishments and legal rulings, since the foundation of his faith remains, likewise our applying the designation of disbelief to him with respect to his deeds does not require us to call him to repent or exempt him from those punishments and rulings. For he has not committed the fundamental disbelief that consists of denying Allah or what He has said.

They said:

Knowledge of Allah is faith, and ignorance of Him is disbelief. Performing the obligations is also faith, yet ignorance of them before they were revealed is not disbelief. This is because the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, acknowledged Allah when He first sent His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to them, although they did not know the obligations subsequently imposed upon them. Their ignorance of those obligations was not disbelief. Then Allah revealed the obligations to them, and their acknowledgment and observance of them constituted faith. Whoever denies them disbelieves only because he rejects what Allah has conveyed as false. Had no communication come from Allah, ignorance of them would not have made a person a disbeliever. Even after that communication had come, any Muslim whom it had not reached would not be a disbeliever because of his ignorance of them,

“Disbelief short of disbelief, wrongdoing short of wrongdoing, and wickedness short of wickedness.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

They said:

Atā spoke truly. A disbeliever may be called a wrongdoer, and a sinful Muslim may also be called a wrongdoer. Thus, there is wrongdoing that takes a person outside the religion of Islam, and wrongdoing that does not.

Allah Most High said:

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing.”

And He said:

“Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong.”

He then cited the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim, who said:

“When the verse ‘Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing’ was revealed, the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, found this difficult and said, ‘Which of us has not wronged himself?’

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘That is not what it means. Have you not heard the words of the righteous servant: “Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong”? It refers only to associating partners with Allah.’”

Muhammad ibn Yahyā narrated to us: al-Hajjāj ibn al-Minhāl narrated to us, from Hammād ibn Salamah, from Alī ibn Zayd, from Yūsuf ibn Mihrān, from Ibn Abbās, who reported that whenever Umar ibn al-Khattāb entered his house, he would open the Quran and read from it. One day, he entered and began reading, until he reached this verse:

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing,”

to the end of the verse. He put on his sandals, took his cloak, and went to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, saying: “Abū al-Mundhir, I came across this verse earlier: ‘Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing.’ Yet we know that we do wrong and commit misdeeds.”

He replied: “Commander of the Faithful, that is not what it means. Allah says: ‘Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong.’ It refers only to associating partners with Allah.”

Muhammad ibn Nasr said:

Likewise, wickedness is of two kinds: wickedness that takes a person outside the religion, and wickedness that does not. Thus, a disbeliever is called wicked, and a sinful Muslim is also called wicked. Allah mentioned Iblīs, saying:

“He rebelled against his Lord’s command.”

That wickedness on his part constituted disbelief. Allah Most High also said:

“As for those who are wicked, their refuge is the Fire.”

He means the disbelievers, as is shown by His words:

“Whenever they wish to leave it, they will be returned to it, and it will be said to them, ‘Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.’”

A sinful Muslim is also called wicked, without being excluded from Islam. Allah Most High said:

“Those who accuse chaste women of adultery and then fail to produce four witnesses—flog them with eighty lashes, and never accept their testimony. It is they who are the wicked.”

And He Most High said:

“Whoever undertakes Hajj during these months must abstain from sexual relations, wickedness, and disputing during Hajj.”

The scholars explained that wickedness here means acts of disobedience.

They said:

Since wrongdoing is of two kinds and wickedness is of two kinds, disbelief likewise is of two kinds:

These, then, are two positions, both broadly reported from Ahmad ibn Hanbal among the hadith scholars who shared his views. Ismā‘īl ibn Sa‘īd al-Shālanjī related that he asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about someone who persists in major sins, pursuing them with all his effort, yet has not abandoned prayer, zakat, or fasting: “Is someone in this condition considered persistent in sin?”

He replied: “He is persistent in sin. His case is like that described in the Prophet’s words:

‘An adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer.’

“He leaves the sphere of faith and comes within the sphere of Islam. It is also like his words:

‘He does not drink wine while he is a believer, nor does he steal while he is a believer.’

“And it is like the statement of Ibn ‘Abbās concerning Allah’s words:

‘Those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are the disbelievers.’”

I said to him: “What is this disbelief?”

He replied: “Disbelief that does not take a person outside the religion. Just as faith has degrees, some lower than others, so too does disbelief, until it reaches something concerning which there is no disagreement.”

Ibn Abī Shaybah said, concerning the words, “An adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer”: “He does not possess complete faith; rather, his faith is deficient.”

He said: “I also asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about ‘Islam and faith.’ He replied: ‘Faith consists of speech and deeds, while Islam is affirmation.’”

He said: “Abū Khaythamah held the same view. Ibn Abī Shaybah said: ‘There can be no Islam without faith, and no faith without Islam.’”

He said:

“As for the Mu‘tazilah, they hold that faith comprises all acts of obedience, and that whoever falls short in any of them is a sinner, neither a believer nor a disbeliever. These are the true adherents of Mu‘tazilism, who advocate the intermediate position between the two positions.”

He then cited the arguments of the Murji’ah, followed by those of the people of the Sunnah. He refuted the Khawārij’s practice of declaring sinners disbelievers by citing the prescribed punishments for adultery, theft, and similar offenses, the right of mutual inheritance, and the hadith of ‘Ubādah:

He said:

“Faith has degrees, some higher than others. Someone whose faith is deficient is not like someone whose faith is complete. Allah Most High says:

‘The believers are only those whose hearts tremble at the mention of Allah.’

‘It is they who are the true believers.’

“The same applies to the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

‘A believer is one from whom people feel safe, and a Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand Muslims are safe.’

“He means a true believer and a true Muslim. Another example is his saying:

‘The believers most complete in faith.’

“It is well known that one cannot be more complete unless another is less complete.

This is a difficult question requiring explanation and elaboration. The relationship of Islam to faith resembles that between the two testimonies of faith: each is connected to the other in meaning and ruling. And concerning giving effect to faith through deeds, He says:

“But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds—for them will be the highest ranks.”

Someone whose outward conduct consists of the deeds of Islam, but who has no underlying firm belief in the unseen, is a hypocrite whose hypocrisy takes him outside the religion. Someone whose conviction is belief in the unseen, but who does not act according to the requirements of faith and the ordinances of Islam, is a disbeliever whose disbelief is incompatible with monotheism. Whoever believes in the unseen matters that the messengers have conveyed from Allah and acts upon Allah’s commands is both a believer and a Muslim. Were this not so, it would be possible for a believer not to be called a Muslim, and for a Muslim not to be called a believer in Allah. Those who face the qiblah have unanimously agreed that every believer is a Muslim, and every Muslim believes in Allah, His angels, and His books.”

He thereby affirmed both the deeds of the limbs in outward dealings and the deeds of the heart in intentions. Deeds stand in relation to faith as the lips do to the tongue: speech cannot function properly without both, for the lips bring the letters together and the tongue gives expression to speech. He said:

They come together in a single servant who is both a Muslim and a believer. The convictions of the heart that he mentioned describe that servant’s heart, while the outward actions he mentioned describe his body.

He also said:

The community is agreed that if a servant believes in all the convictions of the heart mentioned in the description of faith in the hadith of Gabriel, but does not perform the actions mentioned in the description of Islam, he is not called a believer. Likewise, if he performs everything by which Islam was described but does not hold the beliefs by which faith was described, he is not a Muslim. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has informed us that the community will not agree upon misguidance.

I say:

It appears that he meant by this the consensus of the Companions and those who followed them. Alternatively, he meant that such a person is not called a believer for the purposes of legal rulings, and that he is not a Muslim if he denies any of these pillars, or knows that the Messenger conveyed them but does not believe him. Or perhaps he did not count the dissent of those who follow their own inclinations as genuine disagreement. Otherwise, Abū Tālib was certainly familiar with their views. This—and Allah knows best—is what he intended, for he devoted “Chapter Thirty-Three” to explaining Islam and faith in detail and elucidating the convictions underlying the heart’s dealings according to the doctrine of the people of the Community.

What he has said is better than what many others have said, but two points are disputed.

The first is that a Muslim deserving of reward must possess the obligatory faith set out in detail in the hadith of Gabriel.

The second is the claim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, uses the designation “believer” rather than “Muslim,” in statements such as “Or a Muslim,” because the person is not among the distinguished and most excellent believers. It is as though he were saying: because he is not among the foremost who are brought near to Allah, but among the righteous who follow the middle course.

Both these points are contested by the majority of scholars. They say: It was not because that man was not among the distinguished and most excellent believers—such as the foremost who are brought near to Allah—that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said of him, “Or a Muslim.” If that were so, he would be denying the unqualified designation of faith to the righteous, Allah-fearing people who follow the middle course and are promised Paradise without punishment, since they belong to those on the right rather than the foremost who are brought near to Allah. But this is not the case. Rather, those on the right, together with the foremost who are brought near to Allah, are all believers promised Paradise without punishment. Everyone of this description is a believer by the agreement of Muslims, both those of the Sunnah and those of innovation.

If it were permissible to deny someone faith because another person’s faith was superior, faith would be denied to most of Allah’s pious allies, and indeed to many of the prophets. This is utterly untenable. It resembles the claim that a designation is denied because its recommended perfection is absent. We have already explained that nothing of this kind occurs in the words of Allah or His Messenger.

Rather, this hadith specifically concerns someone described as a Muslim but not a believer. He must therefore fall below the rank of the righteous who follow the middle course and are destined for Paradise. His faith must fall short of the faith of all these people, so he cannot have fulfilled all the faith that they were commanded to have. Then, if he is capable of attaining that faith but neglects what is obligatory, he deserves blame. If, however, it is supposed that he is incapable of attaining the faith that characterizes these people, then he is unable to attain faith like theirs, and this would not have been obligatory for him. “Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double share of His mercy and grant you a light by which you may walk.”

And He said:

“Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

Hence it has been said: “Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah grants him knowledge of what he did not know.” This kind of thing lies beyond people’s power, although even the outward and inward deeds within their power depend on Allah’s bounty, His assistance, and His enabling them to perform them.

Things, however, fall into two categories: those whose very nature places them within people’s power, through Allah’s assistance, such as standing and sitting; and those whose very nature places them beyond their power.

If it is said that Allah grants those who obey Him strength in their hearts and bodies, enabling them to do what others cannot, this too is true and falls within the same meaning.

Allah Most High said:

“When your Lord revealed to the angels, ‘I am with you, so strengthen those who believe.’”

He also said:

“When you encounter a force, stand firm.”

Thus He commanded them to stand firm, while revealing to the angels that they are to instill this steadfastness in the believers.

translated_text:
to whom Allah has given wealth but no knowledge, who handles his wealth recklessly, without knowledge: he does not fear his Lord in its use, maintain his ties of kinship with it, or recognize Allah’s right over it—he occupies the worst rank; and a servant to whom Allah has given neither wealth nor knowledge, who says, ‘If I had wealth, I would act with it as so-and-so does’—he is judged according to his intention, so the two are equal in their burden of sin.”

Ibn Mājah’s wording is:

“This community may be compared to four men: a man to whom Allah has given wealth and knowledge, who applies his knowledge to his wealth, spending it as is right; and a man to whom Allah has given knowledge but no wealth, who says, ‘If I had what this man has, I would do as he does.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘The two are equal in reward. And a man to whom Allah has given wealth but no knowledge, who handles his wealth recklessly, spending it improperly; and a man to whom He has given neither knowledge nor wealth, who says, “If I had wealth like this man’s, I would do as he does”—the two are equal in their burden of sin.’”

Likewise, two people whose hearts are equal in faith—in knowledge, affirmation, love, strength, state, and station—may be equal even though one performs bodily deeds that the other is physically incapable of performing. As a report states:

“The believer’s strength lies in his heart, and his weakness in his body; the hypocrite’s strength lies in his body, and his weakness in his heart.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“The strong man is not the one who overpowers others in wrestling; rather, the strong man is the one who controls himself when angry.”

He also said:

“I saw myself drawing water from a well. Then Ibn Abī Quhāfah took the bucket and drew one or two bucketfuls, though there was weakness in his drawing—may Allah forgive him. Then Ibn al-Khattāb took it, and it turned into, in

his hand, a large bucket. I have never seen a man of such prowess draw water as he did; he continued until the people had watered their camels and settled them at their resting places.”

Thus, he described Abu Bakr as weaker. Whether he meant the brevity of his tenure or his inability to match ʿUmar’s strength, there is no doubt that Abu Bakr was stronger in faith than ʿUmar, while ʿUmar was stronger in action. As Ibn Masʿūd said:

“We have enjoyed strength and honour ever since ʿUmar embraced Islam.”

Strength of faith is greater and more complete than strength in action. A person of faith may have the reward of another’s deeds recorded for him: a reward equal to that for ʿUmar’s conduct as ruler is recorded for Abu Bakr, since it was he who appointed him as his successor. In the Musnad, it is reported through two chains of transmission from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was weighed against the community and outweighed it. Then Abu Bakr was weighed against the community and outweighed it. Then ʿUmar was weighed against the community and outweighed it.”

During the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and after his death, ʿUmar gained through Abu Bakr faith and knowledge that he had not previously possessed. Abu Bakr encouraged him to do the good he did and exerted himself to help him do it. Someone who helps bring about an action, while firmly resolved that it should be done, is like the one who performs it. As established in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever equips a warrior has himself gone on campaign, and whoever takes good care of his family in his absence has himself gone on campaign.”

He also said:

“Whoever directs someone to a good deed will have a reward like that of the one who performs it.”

And he said:

“Whoever provides a fasting person with food to break his fast will have a reward like his.”

Al-Tirmidhī also narrated:

“Whoever consoles someone afflicted by a calamity will have a reward like his.”

These and other reports show that two people may be equal in outward deeds—or indeed, one may surpass the other—yet the one whose outward deeds are inferior may be superior before Allah because the faith in his heart is superior. But when they differ in the faith within their hearts, the one inferior in that respect can never be superior before Allah

even if Allah has not bestowed upon the one of lesser rank the faith He has bestowed upon the superior, nor granted his heart the means of attaining that superior faith that He has granted the one of lesser rank.

For this reason, Allah has favoured some prophets over others, even if the superior has performed fewer deeds than the one of lesser rank. Thus, Allah favoured our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—whose prophethood lasted twenty-odd years—over Noah, who remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty. He also favoured the community of Muhammad, who worked from the afternoon prayer until sunset, over those who worked from the beginning of the day until the midday prayer, and over those who worked from the midday prayer until the afternoon prayer. Allah gave the community of Muhammad a double reward, while giving each of the others a single reward, because the faith in their hearts was more complete and superior. The others did more work, but these received a greater reward. This is His bounty, which He grants to whomever He wills through the means He has graciously bestowed upon them and with which He has distinguished them.

The same applies to all others whom Allah Most High favours: He favours them through the means by which they deserve a greater reward. Thus, He may endow one of two people with a capacity through which he attains knowledge, and a capacity through which he attains certainty, patience, reliance upon Allah, sincere devotion, and other qualities by which Allah grants him distinction. He favours him in reward only because of the faith with which He has favoured him.

As Allah Most High says:

“A group among the People of the Scripture said, ‘Believe in what has been revealed to the believers at the beginning of the day, then reject it at its end, so that they may turn back.’”

“‘And trust only those who follow your religion.’ Say, ‘True guidance is Allah’s guidance.’ Do you fear that anyone should be given the like of what you have been given, or that they should argue against you before your Lord? Say, ‘All bounty is in Allah’s hand.’”

He says in another verse:

“Allah knows best where to place His message.”

And He says:

“Allah chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind.”

And He says:

“He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.”

{أَنْ هَدَاكُمْ لِلْإِيمَانِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ صَادِقِينَ}

translated_text:
And the causes of forgiveness and punishment have already been explained elsewhere. Likewise, He provides for whomever He wills without measure, and it is known that He may favour whomever He wills with the means of provision. If there are aspects of faith beyond the capacity of many people, with which Allah favours whomever He wills, then these are among the things through which Allah grants them superiority. Others are described as lacking that faith, not by way of blame, but to indicate this distinction, for blame attaches only to neglecting something commanded or doing something forbidden.

On Abū Tālib’s account, however, it would be said that such people are Muslims, not believers, in one respect, while they are believers in another. On this view, someone may be described as lacking faith because he lacks the recommended degree of perfection—indeed, even the perfection that makes one superior to someone who lacks it, though it may lie beyond human capacity. He may even be described as lacking a perfection obligatory for someone else, although it is neither obligatory nor recommended for him. Yet such usage is not known in the Lawgiver’s speech. The only known usage there is that describing someone as lacking faith invariably entails blame; thus, only someone guilty of a sin is described in this way.

It therefore becomes clear that his words, “Or a Muslim,” express a withholding of judgment as to whether that person has fulfilled the inward and outward obligations, as the vast majority have said.

One group says that he may be a hypocrite with no faith whatsoever. These are the people who say that the Bedouins mentioned were hypocrites with no faith whatsoever. This is the view defended by a group including Muhammad ibn Nasr. Most, however, say that these people were not among the hypocrites none of whose deeds are accepted, although they had an element of hypocrisy. Rather, they possessed an assent to the truth that allowed whatever they did for Allah to be accepted from them. This is why He described them as Muslims, and why He said:

“that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful”

just as

they say the same of the adulterer, the thief, and others who are described as lacking faith despite possessing assent to the truth. This is the soundest of the three views concerning them. Abū Tālib regarded those deserving blame for neglecting an obligation as being among those whose hearts were to be reconciled and who were given nothing, while regarding that man as a believer surpassed in excellence by someone else.

The majority, however, say that affirming Islam for them but not faith is like affirming it for that man: he was a Muslim, not a believer. In both cases, they are blameworthy, not merely surpassed in excellence by others. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The believers most perfect in faith are those best in character.”

Yet he did not deny faith to those below them. Allah Most High also said:

“Those among you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal to the others. They are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterwards. Yet Allah has promised the finest reward to all.”

Thus, He affirmed faith for both the more excellent and the less excellent. This is agreed upon among Muslims. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“When a judge strives to reach a judgment and is correct, he has two rewards; if he strives and errs, he has one reward.”

He said to Saʿd ibn Muʿādh when he passed judgment concerning Banū Qurayzah:

“You have indeed judged them according to the judgment of the King from above the seven heavens.”

He would also say to someone whom he sent out with an army or a military detachment:

“If you besiege the people of a fortress and they ask you to let them surrender on the basis of Allah’s judgment, do not let them surrender on that basis, for you do not know what Allah’s judgment concerning them is. Rather, let them surrender on the basis of your judgment and that of your companions.”

These three hadiths are in al-Sahīh (the Authentic Collection). The hadith of Solomon, peace be upon him, also contains the words: “And I ask You for a judgment that accords with Your judgment.” These and other texts demonstrate what was agreed upon by the Companions and those who followed them

" أو مُسْلِمٌ "
 وَكَسَائِرِ مَنْ نُفِيَ عَنْهُ الْإِيمَانُ مَعَ أَنَّهُ مُسْلِمٌ كَالزَّانِي وَالشَّارِبِ
translated_text:
in righteousness: that Allah may distinguish one of two people by enabling him to exercise independent reasoning through which he attains knowledge beyond the other’s reach. He thus receives two rewards, while the other, being unable to attain that knowledge, receives one reward and incurs no sin. The knowledge with which the former has been distinguished, and his acting upon it inwardly and outwardly, constitute an increase in his faith. This faith is obligatory for him because he is capable of it, whereas the other is incapable of it and is therefore not obliged to attain it. Thus, the former has been favoured with faith that is obligatory for him but not for someone incapable of attaining it.

This applies throughout the Muslim community in disputed matters of belief and practice. When one person is granted knowledge of the actual truth while the other strives but is unable to reach it, both are praiseworthy, rewarded believers. Yet Allah has distinguished the former with a measure of obligatory faith by which He has favoured him over the latter. The one who errs deserves neither blame nor punishment, even though the former would be blamed and punished if he did what the latter did. Similarly, Allah has distinguished our Prophet’s community with a revealed law by which He has favoured it. Were we to neglect anything He has commanded us in that law, this would be grounds for blame and punishment, whereas the prophets before us are not blamed for leaving it undone. Nevertheless, Allah has favoured Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, over the other prophets, and his community over the other communities, without this entailing any blame for any prophet or for the communities that followed them.

Furthermore, a person is obliged to fulfil only those requirements of faith of which he is capable. If he fulfils them, he deserves the Paradise Allah has promised. If such a person were called a Muslim but not a believer, it would follow that among those promised Paradise are people called Muslims but not believers—such as the Bedouins, the man concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Or a Muslim,” and all the others who are denied the designation of faith despite being Muslims, such as the adulterer and the drinker of wine

and the thief, the person whose neighbour is not safe from his harm, the person who does not wish for his brother the good he wishes for himself, and others besides them. Yet that is not the case. Allah has linked the promise of Paradise only to the designation of faith, not to the designation of Islam, although He has made Islam obligatory and declared that it is the religion He has approved and that He accepts no other religion. Nevertheless, He has not said that Paradise has been prepared for the Muslims, nor that Allah has promised the Muslims Paradise. Rather, He has mentioned this only in connection with faith, as in His words:

“Allah has promised the believing men and believing women Gardens beneath which rivers flow.”

Thus, He links this promise to faith mentioned either without qualification or qualified by righteous deeds, as in His words:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the best of creation.”

“Their reward with their Lord is Gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow.”

And His words:

“Give glad tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that they will have Gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with fruit from them, they will say, ‘This is what we were provided with before.’”

And His words:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, establish prayer and give zakah will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.”

And His words:

“As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and grant them more from His bounty.”

And His words:

“As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them into mercy and bounty from Him and guide them to Himself on a straight path.”

And His words:

“Those who believe and do righteous deeds—We will admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever. They will have purified spouses there, and We will admit them into deep shade.”

And in the other verse:

“Who is more truthful in speech than Allah?”

And He says:

“As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full. Allah does not love the wrongdoers.”

And He says:

“Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward.”

And He says:

“So whoever believes and mends his ways

will have no fear, nor will they grieve.” And He says:

“Those who believe and do righteous deeds—We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity—they are the people of Paradise, where they will abide forever.”

There are many verses to this effect. The promise of Paradise, mercy in the Hereafter, and deliverance from punishment is linked to the designation of faith, whether mentioned without qualification or qualified by righteous deeds and the like. As explained earlier, faith mentioned without qualification includes doing what Allah and His Messenger have commanded. This promise has not been linked to the designation of Islam.

If someone who fulfils as much of faith as he is able, but cannot know its details, could be called a Muslim without being called a believer, he would be among the people of Paradise. Paradise would then be deserved by someone called a Muslim even though he was not called a believer. But this is not the case: Paradise has been linked only to the designation of faith.

This is also among the evidence cited by those who say that not every Muslim is among the believers promised Paradise. Were that the case, the promise of Paradise would have been linked to the designation of Islam, just as it has been linked to faith, to “piety” and “righteousness,” as in His words:

“Indeed, the righteous will be amid Gardens and rivers.”

And His words:

“Indeed, the virtuous will be in bliss.”

It has also been linked to the designation of the friends of Allah, as in His words:

“Indeed, the friends of Allah will have no fear, nor will they grieve.”

“Those who believe and are mindful of Allah.”

“For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. There is no changing the words of Allah. That is the supreme triumph.”

Since the designation of Islam is not used in this way, it is clear that what it denotes does not necessarily entail what faith denotes, whereas the designations of righteousness, piety, and the friends of Allah do. The designation of Islam therefore includes those subject to the threat of punishment, even though Allah rewards them for their obedience. For example, someone may have both faith and hypocrisy in his heart, with the latter making him deserving of punishment. Allah punishes such a person but does not leave him in the Fire forever, because his heart contains an atom’s weight of faith or more.

The same applies to all others who commit major sins: their faith is deficient. If someone has a trait of hypocrisy in his heart, he will be punished for it unless Allah pardons him, but he will not remain in the Fire forever. These people are Muslims but not believers, although they possess faith. Yet they also possess hypocrisy, which is contrary to faith. Thus, calling them believers is no more warranted than calling them hypocrites, especially if they are closer to disbelief than to faith.

In the rulings of this world, they are included under the designation of faith, just as the outright hypocrite is—and with greater reason, since they possess faith by virtue of which they are included in Allah’s address:

“O you who believe!”

For this commands them to do what benefits them and forbids them from doing what harms them, and they need such guidance. If the faith they possess entails their inclusion in the wording of this address, there is nothing further to discuss. Otherwise, they are no worse off than the outright hypocrite. That hypocrite, too, is commanded to perform these deeds; they benefit him in this world, and by virtue of them he will be gathered with the believers on the Day of Resurrection. Through them he will be distinguished from the followers of other religions on the Day of Resurrection, just as he was distinguished from them in this world. But at the moment of truth, a barrier will be erected:

“Then a wall will be erected between them, with a gate: within it is mercy, and outside it is punishment.”

“They will call out to them, ‘Were we not with you?’ They will reply, ‘Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, waited and doubted, and were deluded by wishful thinking until Allah’s command came. And the Deceiver deceived you about Allah.’”

“So today no ransom will be accepted from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your abode is the Fire; it is your refuge. What an evil destination!”

Allah Most High has also said:

“Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire, and you will never find a helper for them.”

“Except those who repent, mend their ways, hold fast to Allah, and devote their religion sincerely to Allah. Those will be with the believers, and Allah will grant the believers a great reward.”

For this reason, Allah Most High said concerning these people:

He did not say that this alone makes them believers, since He did not mention faith in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers. Rather, they are with the believers. He mentioned only righteous deeds and performing them sincerely for Allah, and said:

Thus, the same ruling applies to them. Elsewhere, He has explained that believers differ in rank: whoever fulfils the requirements of obligatory faith deserves reward, whereas whoever possesses a trait of hypocrisy and commits major sins is among those threatened with punishment. Allah will benefit him through his faith and bring him out of the Fire by virtue of it, even if it amounts only to a mustard seed’s weight. Yet this does not entitle him to the unqualified designation of believer, to which the promise of Paradise without punishment is attached.

To complete this explanation: some people may possess both a branch of faith and a branch of disbelief or hypocrisy, yet be called Muslims, as Ahmad explicitly stated. They said: “Disbelief that does not take one out of Islam; disbelief less than outright disbelief, wickedness less than outright wickedness, and wrongdoing less than outright wrongdoing.”

This is also among the evidence al-Bukhārī cited in his Sahīh. In the “Book of Faith,” with which he opened his Sahīh, he established the position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah and included a refutation of the Murji’ah. He was among those who championed the Sunnah and the community—the way of the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness.

The scholars agree that the designation “Muslims” applies outwardly to the hypocrites, because they outwardly submitted and performed outward deeds: prayer, zakat, pilgrimage, and jihad in their outward forms. Thus, the Prophet applied the outward rulings of Islam to them. They also agree that whoever possesses no faith whatsoever falls under the words of Allah Most High:

“Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire.”

The word has two readings: dark and darak. Abū al-Husayn ibn Fāris said: “Paradise has ascending ranks, and the Fire has descending depths.” Al-Dahhāk said: “Daraj refers to levels one above another, while dark refers to levels one below another.”

There is no doubt that he is the most fearful of Allah in this community and the most knowledgeable of His limits. Likewise, he said:

“I have reserved my supplication as intercession for my community on the Day of Resurrection. It will reach, if Allah wills, whoever dies without associating anything with Allah.”

He also said:

“I hope that you will constitute half the people of Paradise.”

Ahmad and others used these and similar texts as evidence for using a conditional qualification when affirming one’s faith, as we shall discuss in its proper place.

The point is that the best of the believers occupy the highest ranks of Paradise, while the hypocrites occupy the lowest depths of the Fire, even though they were outwardly Muslims in this world and subject to the outward rulings of Islam.

Thus, someone who possesses both faith and hypocrisy is called a Muslim, for he is no worse than a complete hypocrite. If his hypocrisy predominates, he does not deserve the designation of believer; rather, the designation of hypocrite is more fitting for him. Something containing both white and black, but more black than white, is more rightly called black than white. As Allah Most High says:

“That day they were nearer to disbelief than to faith.”

If, however, his faith predominates, but he also possesses hypocrisy for which he deserves the threatened punishment, he is likewise not among the believers promised Paradise. This supports what Muhammad ibn Nasr reported from Ahmad, although I myself have not found it in the statements of Ahmad that have reached me, nor was it mentioned by al-Khallāl or others like him.

The proponent of this view argues as follows:

Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, denied him faith, I deny him faith just as the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did. The Messenger denied it only to someone who committed a major sin. As for a believer who commits a minor sin, it is expiated through his good deeds and his avoidance of major sins. Nevertheless, his faith is deficient compared with that of someone who avoids minor sins. He has therefore not fulfilled the faith required of him, but has mixed it with sins that are expiated through other deeds. His rank is consequently lower than that of someone who has not committed such sins.

As for those to whom the Messenger denied faith, we deny it to them just as the Messenger did. Although they possess assent and the foundation of faith, they have abandoned enough of its requirements to deserve being denied the designation of faith. Hypocrisy and faith, or disbelief and faith, may coexist in a person. According to those who hold this view, faith without qualification is that which entitles its possessor to the promise of Paradise.

Various groups among the “followers of desires”—the Khārijites, Mu‘tazilites, Jahmiyyah, and Murji’ah, both Karrāmī and non-Karrāmī—say that faith and hypocrisy cannot coexist in a person. Some even claim consensus on this. Abū al-Hasan mentioned such a consensus in some of his books. This is where they went wrong, contradicting the Quran, the Sunnah, and the reports from the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, as well as plain reason.

In their view, it is inconceivable that the same person should enter both Paradise and Hell; rather, whoever enters one cannot enter the other. Hence they denied that anyone could leave Hell or that intercession could be made for any of its inhabitants.

It is reported that the extreme Murji’ah agreed with them on this principle, but took the opposite position, saying that those who commit major sins enter Paradise and do not enter Hell.

As for Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, and the other Muslim groups—hadith scholars, jurists, and practitioners of speculative theology, including the Murji’ah among the jurists, the Karrāmiyyah, the Kullābiyyah, the Ash‘ariyyah, and the Shī‘ah, both their Murji’ah and non-Murji’ah groups—they say:

Allah may punish a person in Hell and then admit him to Paradise, as the authentic hadiths explicitly state. Such a person has evil deeds for which he was punished and good deeds on account of which he entered Paradise. All agree that he has both disobedience and obedience to his credit. These groups did not disagree about his fate; rather, they disagreed over what to call him.

The Murji’ah, both Jahmī and non-Jahmī, said that he is a believer whose faith is complete. Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah hold that he is a believer deficient in faith; otherwise, he would not have been punished. Likewise, all Muslims agree that he is deficient in righteousness and piety. But may he be called a believer without qualification? There are two views on this, and the correct approach is to distinguish between contexts.

If the question concerns worldly rulings, such as whether freeing him would fulfil an obligation of expiation, the answer is that he is a believer. The same applies if the question is whether he is included in passages addressed to believers. But if the question concerns his standing in the Hereafter, the answer is:

A person of this kind is not among the believers

who are promised Paradise. Rather, he possesses faith that prevents him from remaining in Hell forever and through which he will enter Paradise after being punished in Hell, unless Allah forgives his sins. Hence some have said: “He is a believer by virtue of his faith and an evildoer by virtue of his major sin,” or, “A believer deficient in faith.”

Those among Ahl al-Sunnah and the Mu‘tazilah who do not call him a believer say that the designation of wickedness is incompatible with the designation of faith, because Allah says:

“How wretched is the name of wickedness after faith!”

And:

“Is one who is a believer like one who is an evildoer?”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“Reviling a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.”

According to this principle, a person may possess a branch of disbelief while also possessing faith. This explains the reports in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called many sins disbelief, although the person committing them may possess more than an atom’s weight of faith and therefore will not remain in Hell forever. For example, he said:

“Reviling a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief.”

And:

“Do not revert after me to being disbelievers, striking one another’s necks.”

This is widely reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through several chains of transmission in the Sahīh. During the Farewell Pilgrimage, orders were given for it to be proclaimed among the people. Thus, he called those who strike one another’s necks without right disbelievers, and called this act disbelief.

Nevertheless, Allah Most High said:

“If two groups of believers fight one another, make peace between them,”

up to His words:

“The believers are but brothers.”

He thus made clear that they had not departed from faith altogether, but that they possessed something constituting disbelief: this particular trait. As some of the Companions said: “A lesser form of disbelief.”

Likewise, the Prophet said:

“If someone says to his brother, ‘You disbeliever!’ one of them has incurred that charge.”

He called him his brother at the very moment those words were spoken, while stating that one of them had incurred that charge. Had either of them departed from Islam altogether, he would no longer have been his brother. Rather, he possesses an element of disbelief.

The same applies to his statement in the authentic hadith:

“No man knowingly claims descent from someone other than his father without committing disbelief.”

And in another hadith:

“Whoever disowns his lineage, however tenuous the connection, has disbelieved in Allah.”

Among the passages of the Quran whose wording was abrogated was:

“Do not disown your fathers, for disowning your fathers is disbelief on your part.”

The rights of parents are coupled with Allah’s right in such statements as:

“Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final return.”

And:

“Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him and that you be good to your parents.”

A person’s father is the source from which he was created, and his child is among his earnings, as Allah says:

“Neither his wealth nor what he earned will avail him.”

Denying one’s parents is therefore a branch of disbelief. By denying that from which his Lord created him, he has denied his Lord’s creation of him. In the language of those before us, the Lord was called “Father,” so this involves disbelief in Allah in this respect. Yet this is not like denying the Creator altogether. We shall discuss the remaining hadiths, if Allah wills.

The purpose here is to state a “comprehensive principle” upon which an understanding of the scriptural texts can be built, and by which people’s disputes can be referred back to the Book and the Sunnah. People have disputed extensively over various aspects of what faith and Islam denote, because these two terms occur so frequently and are discussed so much. The more a term is discussed—being used without qualification in one place, with one qualification elsewhere, and with another qualification in yet another place—the more this can cause aspects of its meaning to become unclear. Then, the more widely it is heard, the greater the number of people who become confused about it.

One reason for this is that a person hears some instances of its use but not others. What he hears may be qualified in a way that confines it to a particular meaning, so he assumes that it has that same meaning wherever else it occurs. translated_text:

Muslims—both those who follow the Sunnah and those who follow religious innovations—agree on the obligation to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and the Last Day. They agree on the obligation of prayer, zakah, fasting, and pilgrimage. They agree that whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will enter Paradise and will not be punished, and that whoever does not believe that Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is Allah’s Messenger to him is a disbeliever. These and similar matters are the foundations of religion and the principles of faith upon which those who profess Islam and faith agree.

Their disagreement, beyond this, concerning certain rulings relating to the threat of punishment or certain meanings of particular terms is a minor matter compared with what they agree upon. Nevertheless, those who oppose the clear truth of the Book and the Sunnah are recognized by the majority of the Muslim community as adherents of religious innovation and are attested to be astray. They enjoy neither an honourable reputation nor general acceptance within the Muslim community, as is the case with the Khawārij, the Rāfidah, the Qadariyyah, and others like them. The disagreements among the people of knowledge and the Sunnah concern only subtle matters that elude most people. Yet whatever they dispute must be referred back to Allah and His Messenger.

Referring “the question of Islam and faith” back to Allah and His Messenger establishes that, although what each of these two terms denotes is obligatory, no one merits Paradise unless he is both a believer and a Muslim. The truth concerning this is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained in the hadith of Gabriel: he distinguished “three levels” within the religion and among its adherents. The first is Islam, the middle is faith, and the highest is excellence. Whoever reaches the highest level

“Then We granted the Book as an inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants. Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those who, by Allah’s permission, are foremost in good deeds. That is the great bounty.”

The Muslim who has not fulfilled the obligations of faith is the one who wrongs himself. The one who follows a middle course is a believer without qualification: he fulfils his obligations and avoids what is forbidden. The one foremost in good deeds is the person of excellence, who worships Allah as though he sees Him. Allah, glorified be He, also mentions this threefold division of people in the Hereafter in Surahs al-Wāqi'ah, al-Mutaffifīn, and Hal Atā, mentioning the disbelievers as well. Here, however, He confines the division to those chosen from among His servants.

Abū Sulaymān al-Khattābī said:

“This question is among those on which people most often err. Al-Zuhrī said, ‘Islam is the declaration of faith, while faith is deeds,’ citing the verse as evidence. Others held that Islam and faith are one and the same, citing His words:

‘So We brought out whoever was there of the believers. But We found there only one household of Muslims.’”

Al-Khattābī said: “Two scholars discussed this matter, each adopting one of these two views. The later of them refuted his predecessor and wrote a book against him extending to two hundred leaves.”

I say: Of the two men to whom al-Khattābī referred, I think the earlier was Muhammad ibn Nasr. Among the scholars of the Sunnah and hadith, he is the one I know to have discussed at length the view that Islam and faith are one and the same. I know of no one before him who treated this subject at length. As for the other, who refuted him, I think he was … (1), but I have not come across his refutation.

The view al-Khattābī preferred is that of those who distinguished between the two, such as Abū Ja'far, Hammād ibn Zayd, and 'Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī. It is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others. I know of no early scholar who disagreed with them by holding that Islam itself is identical to faith itself. Thus, the general position of Ahl al-Sunnah was the one these scholars expressed, as al-Khattābī mentioned.

Likewise, Abū al-Qāsim al-Taymī al-Asbahānī, his son Muhammad—the commentator on Muslim—and others stated that the preferred view among Ahl al-Sunnah is that the designation “believer” should not be applied without qualification to a thief or a fornicator, as the scriptural text indicates.

In his Commentary on al-Bukhārī, al-Khattābī made statements implying that Islam and faith are inseparable despite their distinct designations. [Al-Baghawī also mentioned this in Sharh al-Sunnah, saying: “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used ‘Islam’ to designate outward deeds and ‘faith’ to designate inward belief. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This is Gabriel, who came to teach you your religion.”

Both affirmation and action are encompassed by each of the terms Islam and faith. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

And His words:

“And I have approved Islam as your religion.”

And His words:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him.”

He thus made clear that the religion He approves and accepts from His servants is Islam. Religion can receive His approval and acceptance only when affirmation accompanies action.

I say: Although the distinction made by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith of Gabriel implies that excellence is the highest level, that excellence encompasses faith, and that faith encompasses Islam, it does not establish the reverse. Even supposing that it indicated their inseparability, it explicitly shows that what one term denotes is not what the other denotes. The precise explanation, however, is that their meanings differ depending on whether they occur separately or together, as we have explained. Whoever understands this will find many difficulties resolved in numerous areas where various groups have gone astray—concerning the question of faith and other matters.

His statement that religion can receive approval and acceptance only when affirmation accompanies action indicates that faith must accompany action. This establishes that faith is obligatory in all circumstances, but it does not establish that the action constituting religion is not called Islam. If faith is a condition for its acceptance, it does not follow that faith necessarily accompanies it. Even if faith necessarily accompanied it, it would not follow that faith forms part of what the term Islam denotes.

translated_text:
Shaykh Abū ʿAmr ibn al-Salāh said:

Concerning the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah,” and the rest of the passage, and “Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers,” and the rest of the passage, he said:

This explains the foundation of faith, namely inward affirmation, and the foundation of Islam, namely outward submission and compliance. Outwardly, a person’s status as a Muslim is established by the two testimonies of faith. He mentioned the four alongside them only because they are Islam’s most manifest and principal rites. By performing them, a person completes his submission; abandoning them suggests that he is undoing the bond of his compliance, or that it is coming undone.

The term faith also encompasses the practices used to explain Islam in this hadith, as well as all other acts of obedience, because they are fruits of inward affirmation—which is the foundation of faith—and serve to sustain, complete, and preserve it. Thus, in the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained faith as the two testimonies, prayer, zakat, fasting, and giving one-fifth of the spoils of war.

For this reason, the unqualified designation “believer” does not apply to someone who commits a major sin or neglects an obligatory duty. A designation denoting completeness applies to the complete instance and is not ordinarily used for a deficient one without qualification. It was therefore permissible to deny him this designation without qualification in the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The adulterer is not a believer while committing adultery.”

The term “Islam” also encompasses the “foundation of faith,” namely affirmation, and the “foundation of acts of obedience,” for all of this is submission.

He said: From what we have explained and established, it follows that Islam and faith overlap in some respects and differ in others, and that every believer is a Muslim, but not

every Muslim is a believer. He said:

This is a thorough explanation that reconciles the various texts concerning faith and Islam, about which those discussing them have so often erred. What we have established accords with the positions of the great majority of scholars, both the scholars of hadith and others.

In response, it may be said:

What he has stated—may Allah have mercy on him—accords with the previously explained statements of the imams and with what the Quran and Sunnah indicate, making it clear that the majority hold that every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer.

His statement that the hadith mentions the foundation of faith and the foundation of Islam may be challenged as follows: the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, answered the questions about faith and Islam by giving what amounts to a definition of each. Thus, what he mentioned corresponds to faith and Islam themselves, not merely to their foundations. Faith, therefore, means believing in what he mentioned, both inwardly and outwardly. However, his description of faith includes Islam, just as excellence in worship includes faith.

As for the statement, “The foundation of submission is outward Islam,” Islam is submission and obedience to Allah, both outwardly and inwardly. This is the religion of Islam with which Allah is pleased, as the texts of the Quran and Sunnah indicate. Whoever submits outwardly but not inwardly is a hypocrite whose outward profession is accepted, for one has not been commanded to cut open people’s hearts.

Furthermore, if Islam encompasses the inward affirmation that constitutes the foundation of faith, it necessarily follows that every Muslim is a believer. This contradicts what has been reported from the majority. Nevertheless, Islam must involve an affirmation through which the foundation of faith is attained; otherwise, a person would not be rewarded for it. Thus, he is

then both a Muslim and a believer. It must therefore be clarified who the Muslim who is not a believer is, and how he falls within Islam. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This was Gabriel, who came to teach you your religion.”

His statement, “Islam consists of the five pillars,” does not refer to someone who performs them without sincerity to Allah, but rather with hypocrisy. It refers instead to someone who performs them as commanded, both inwardly and outwardly. He identified these five as Islam because they are the purely devotional acts of worship owed to Allah Most High by every servant capable of performing them. Other duties are either collective obligations serving a benefit—once that benefit is secured, the obligation lapses—or concern people’s rights against one another, even though fulfilling them may also bring one nearer to Allah, and other such matters.

These other duties follow from the five pillars, as in his statements:

“A Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe.”

“The best of Islam is to provide food and greet with peace those you know and those you do not know.”

And there are other statements to this effect. These five, then, are the pillars and foundations, just as faith has its pillars and foundations.

The statement, “Acts of obedience are the fruits of inward affirmation,” can mean two things. It can mean that they necessarily follow from it: whenever inward faith exists, they exist. This is the position of the early generations and Ahl al-Sunnah. Or it can mean that inward faith may give rise to them, yet may be complete and perfect even when they are absent. This is the position of the Murjiʾah among the Jahmiyyah and others. We have already explained that they erred in three respects:

(First): Their assumption that faith in the heart can be complete without the deeds of the heart—affirmation without such deeds of the heart as love of Allah, awe and fear of Him, reliance upon Him, and longing to meet Him.

(Third): Their claim that anyone whom the Lawgiver declares a disbeliever is declared so only because his heart lacks affirmation of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He. Many later scholars do not distinguish between the positions of the early generations and the views of the Murjiʾah and Jahmiyyah, because these are intermingled in the writings of many of them. Such a person inwardly holds the Jahmiyyah’s and Murjiʾah’s view of faith, yet venerates the early generations and the scholars of hadith. He therefore imagines that he can reconcile the two, or reconcile the statements of those like himself with those of the early generations.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī said:

“A third group—the overwhelming majority of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah and the scholars of hadith—maintained that the faith to which Allah called His servants and which He made obligatory upon them is Islam, which He established as the religion, approved for His servants, and called them to embrace. It is the opposite of disbelief, which He abhors. He said:

‘He does not approve disbelief for His servants.’

And He said:

‘I have approved Islam as your religion.’

And He said:

‘Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam.’

And He said:

‘What of one whose heart Allah has opened to Islam, so that he follows a light from his Lord?’

Thus Allah praised Islam in the same way that He praised faith, making it a designation of praise and commendation. He stated that whoever embraces Islam follows a light and guidance from his Lord, and that it is His religion, which He has approved. Whatever He has approved, He has loved and praised. He also means that every believer is a Muslim and that every Muslim must possess some faith. This is correct and agreed upon. translated_text:
faith,” as [nasr] (1). Indeed, I know of no one among the early generations who said this. What is well known from a number of early and later scholars, however, is that the believer entitled to Allah’s promise is the Muslim entitled to Allah’s promise. Thus every Muslim is a believer, and every believer is a Muslim. The meaning of this is agreed upon by early and later scholars—indeed, by all the sects of the Muslim community. They all say that the believer promised Paradise must be a Muslim, and the Muslim promised Paradise must be a believer. Everyone, from the earliest generations to the latest, who enters Paradise without punishment is both a believer and a Muslim.

Furthermore, Ahl al-Sunnah do not say: “Those who leave the Fire and enter Paradise possess some measure of that.” The dispute concerns only the application of the designation. Reports from the early generations affirming that faith consists of speech and action have been transmitted in such numbers as to establish certainty, whereas no such statement concerning Islam has been transmitted from them. However, the overwhelming majority held that Islam encompasses the entire religion, not merely the verbal profession, contrary to the apparent meaning of what is reported from al-Zuhrī. They therefore said that prayer, zakat, fasting, Hajj, and the other commanded deeds are part of Islam just as they are part of faith. He consequently assumed that they regarded the two as one and the same, but that is not so. They agree that faith necessarily entails Islam, yet the inclusion of Islam within faith does not mean that the two are identical.

As for Islam, he has no evidence that it necessarily entails faith when the term is used without qualification. Whether it entails the faith that is obligatory or the perfection of faith is disputed, and he has no evidence that it necessarily entails faith. Nevertheless, the prophets whom Allah described as Muslims were all believers, and Allah also described them as believers. Even had He not mentioned this about them, we would still know with certainty that all the prophets are believers.

translated_text:
Likewise, the earliest forerunners were both Muslims and believers.

Even if it were assumed that Islam necessarily entails the faith that is obligatory, the most that could be said is that the two necessarily accompany one another: every Muslim is a believer, and every believer is a Muslim. This is correct if what is meant is that every Muslim who enters Paradise possesses the faith that is obligatory. It is also agreed upon if what is meant is that every Muslim who is rewarded for his worship must possess the foundation of faith. Thus, every Muslim is a believer, even if this is not the faith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, denied to those who do not love for their brothers what they love for themselves, to those who commit major sins, and to the Bedouins and others.

If it is said that Islam and complete faith necessarily accompany one another, it does not follow that they are identical. They are like the soul and the body: among us, no soul is found except with a body, and no living body is found except with a soul, yet neither is identical to the other. Faith is like the soul, for it resides in the soul and is connected to the body, while Islam is like the body, which cannot be alive without the soul. This means that the two necessarily accompany one another, not that the two terms designate the same thing. The Islam of the hypocrites is like a dead body—a body without a soul. Every living body has a soul, but souls differ, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Souls are assembled troops: those that recognize one another unite, and those that do not recognize one another are at odds.”

Not everyone who performs prayer with his body has a heart illuminated by remembrance of Allah, humble devotion, and understanding of the Quran, even though he is rewarded for his prayer and, under the rulings applicable in this world, his obligation is discharged. Outward Islam is thus like the outward performance of prayer, while faith is like the knowledge of Allah, humble devotion, and reflection upon the Quran that reside in the heart during prayer. will also manifest humble devotion in his limbs, but the converse does not hold. Hence the saying:

“Beware of hypocritical humility.”

This is when the body displays humble devotion while the heart does not. When the heart is sound, the whole body is sound; yet the body’s engagement in worship does not mean that the heart is fulfilling its inward realities.

With regard to “faith” and “Islam,” people fall into three ranks: those who wrong themselves, those who follow a middle course, and those foremost in good deeds. Someone who is a Muslim outwardly and inwardly, yet wrongs himself, must possess faith, though he has not fulfilled what is obligatory. The converse does not hold, and the same applies in the other case. This will be discussed, Allah willing.

The verses cited as evidence by Muhammad ibn Nasr establish that Islam is obligatory, that it is Allah’s religion, that Allah loves it and is pleased with it, and that it is His only religion. All of this is true. Yet none of it establishes that Islam is identical to faith. Nor does it establish that Islam alone makes a person one of the people of Paradise, as he mentioned when presenting the evidence for the first position. Allah has promised the believers Paradise in numerous verses, but He has not attached this promise to the designation “Islam.” Thus, His praise of Islam, His making it obligatory, and His love for it indicate that it is included within faith and forms part of it. All the adherents of the Sunnah agree on this. They say:

Every believer is a Muslim, and everyone who fulfils the obligatory requirements of faith has fulfilled the obligatory requirements of Islam. The dispute, however, concerns the converse.

Similarly, Allah loves prayer, commands it, makes it obligatory, and praises both it and those who perform it in numerous passages. Yet this does not establish that what the term “prayer” designates is identical to what the term “faith” designates. Rather, prayer is included within faith. Thus, every believer performs prayer, but not everyone who prays while committing major sins is necessarily a believer.

All the evidence he cited from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, distinguishes between what “faith” and “Islam” designate when they are mentioned together, as in the hadith of Gabriel and elsewhere. It also shows that when the term “faith” is used without qualification, it includes Islam.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hāmid said in his book on the foundations of religion:

“We have already stated that faith consists of speech and deeds. As for Islam, Ahmad’s statements admit of two reported positions. The first is that it is like faith. The second is that it consists of speech without deeds. This latter position is his explicit statement as transmitted by Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd.”

He said: “The correct view is that the school has only one reported position: that Islam consists of speech and deeds. His statement that Islam consists of speech may mean that it does not require the deeds stipulated as conditions of faith. Prayer is not a condition of Islam, since his explicit statement is that a person does not become a disbeliever by abandoning prayer.”

He said: “We have established that Islam and faith are two terms designating two meanings, and we have mentioned the disagreement among the jurists.”

It had previously been stated that Islam and faith are two terms designating different meanings, and that Mālik, Sharīk, and Hammād ibn Zayd held this view, distinguishing between Islam and faith.

He said: “The followers of al-Shāfiʿī and the followers of Abū Hanīfah said that they are two terms with the same meaning.”

He said: “This implies that a person may cease to be designated a believer while remaining a Muslim. This happens when he commits the major sins mentioned in the report: he loses the designation of faith, yet remains a Muslim. If he repents of this, he returns to the faith he previously possessed. Committing minor sins does not deprive him of the designation of faith; rather, it continues to apply to him.”

 إنَّ الْأَعْمَالَ الظَّاهِرَةَ الْمَأْمُورَ بِهَا لَيْسَتْ مِنْ الْإِسْلَامِ فَقَوْلُهُ بَاطِلٌ بِخِلَافِ التَّصْدِيقِ الَّذِي فِي الْقَلْبِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا لَيْسَ فِي النُّصُوصِ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّهُ مِنْ الْإِسْلَامِ بَلْ هُوَ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ وَإِنَّمَا الْإِسْلَامُ الدِّينُ كَمَا فَسَّرَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِأَنْ يُسْلِمَ وَجْهَهُ وَقَلْبَهُ لِلَّهِ فَإِخْلَاصُ الدِّينِ لِلَّهِ إسْلَامٌ وَهَذَا غَيْرُ التَّصْدِيقِ ذَاكَ مِنْ جِنْسِ عَمَلِ الْقَلْبِ وَهَذَا مِنْ جِنْسِ عِلْمِ الْقَلْبِ.
 وَأَحْمَد بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ وَإِنْ كَانَ قَدْ قَالَ فِي هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ:
 إنَّ الْإِسْلَامَ هُوَ الْكَلِمَةُ فَقَدْ قَالَ فِي مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ: إنَّ الْأَعْمَالَ مِنْ الْإِسْلَامِ وَهُوَ اتَّبَعَ هنا الزُّهْرِيَّ رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ فَإِنْ كَانَ مُرَادُ مَنْ قَالَ ذَلِكَ إنَّهُ بِالْكَلِمَةِ يَدْخُلُ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ وَلَمْ يَأْتِ بِتَمَامِ الْإِسْلَامِ فَهَذَا قَرِيبٌ.
 وَإِنْ كَانَ مُرَادُهُ أَنَّهُ أُتِيَ بِجَمِيعِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَعْمَلْ فَهَذَا غَلَطٌ قَطْعًا بَلْ قَدْ أَنْكَرَ أَحْمَد هَذَا الْجَوَابَ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ مَنْ قَالَ:
 يُطْلِقُ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَعْمَلْ مُتَابَعَةً لِحَدِيثِ جِبْرِيلَ فَكَانَ يَنْبَغِي أَنْ يَذْكُرَ قَوْلَ أَحْمَد جَمِيعِهِ.
 قَالَ إسْمَاعِيلُ بْنُ سَعِيدٍ:
 سَأَلْت أَحْمَد فِي الْإِسْلَامِ وَالْإِيمَانِ فَقَالَ: 
" الْإِيمَانُ "
 قَوْلٌ وَعَمَلٌ وَالْإِسْلَامُ الْإِقْرَارُ.
 وَقَالَ:
 وَسَأَلْت أَحْمَد عَمَّنْ قَالَ فِي الَّذِي قَالَ جِبْرِيلُ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إذْ سَأَلَهُ عَنْ الْإِسْلَامِ فَإِذَا فَعَلْت ذَلِكَ فَأَنَا مُسْلِمٌ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 نَعَمْ.
 فَقَالَ قَائِلٌ:
 وَإِنْ لَمْ يَفْعَلْ الَّذِي قَالَ جِبْرِيلُ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَهُوَ مُسْلِمٌ أَيْضًا؟
 فَقَالَ:
 هَذَا مُعَانِدٌ لِلْحَدِيثِ.
translated_text:
contains abundant evidence against those who say that Islam is merely the verbal profession. Numerous proofs show that deeds are part of Islam; indeed, all the texts indicate this. Whoever says that the prescribed outward deeds are not part of Islam holds a false view. This differs from the heart’s affirmation of truth: nothing in the texts indicates that this is part of Islam; rather, it is part of faith. Islam is religious submission, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained it: submitting one’s face and heart to Allah. Thus, devoting one’s religion sincerely to Allah is Islam. This differs from affirming the truth: the former belongs to the heart’s deeds, while the latter belongs to its knowledge.

Although Ahmad ibn Hanbal said on this occasion that Islam is the verbal profession, elsewhere he said that deeds are part of Islam. Here he followed al-Zuhrī, may Allah have mercy on him. If someone who says this means that a person enters Islam through the verbal profession without having fulfilled Islam completely, this is close to the truth. But if he means that the person has fulfilled Islam entirely even without performing any deeds, this is certainly mistaken. Indeed, following the hadith of Gabriel, Ahmad rejected this answer—the statement that the designation applies to a person even if he performs no deeds. He should therefore have quoted Ahmad’s statement in full.

Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd said:

“I asked Ahmad about Islam and faith. He replied: ‘Faith consists of speech and deeds, while Islam is acknowledgment.’”

He also said:

“I asked Ahmad about someone who made the following statement concerning Gabriel’s exchange with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he asked him about Islam—‘If I do that, am I a Muslim?’ to which he replied, ‘Yes.’ Someone then said: ‘Even if he does not do what Gabriel mentioned to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is he still a Muslim?’ Ahmad replied: ‘Such a person is contradicting the hadith.’”

فَقَدْ جَعَلَ أَحْمَد مَنْ جَعَلَهُ مُسْلِمًا إذَا لَمْ يَأْتِ بِالْخَمْسِ مُعَانِدًا لِلْحَدِيثِ مَعَ قَوْلِهِ:

 وَحَدِيثُ سَعْدٍ يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ مُسَمَّى الْإِيمَانِ أَفْضَلُ وَلَكِنْ حَدِيثُ عُمَرَ لَمْ يَذْكُرْ الْإِسْلَامَ إلَّا الْأَعْمَالَ الظَّاهِرَةَ فَقَطْ وَهَذِهِ لَا تَكُونُ إيمَانًا إلَّا مَعَ الْإِيمَانِ الَّذِي فِي الْقَلْبِ بِاَللَّهِ وَمَلَائِكَتِهِ وَكُتُبِهِ وَرُسُلِهِ فَيَكُونُ حِينَئِذٍ بَعْضُ الْإِيمَانِ فَيَكُونُ مُسَمَّى الْإِيمَانِ أَفْضَلَ كَمَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ حَدِيثُ سَعْدٍ فَلَا مُنَافَاةَ بَيْنَ الْحَدِيثَيْنِ:
 وَأَمَّا تَفْرِيقُ أَحْمَد بَيْنَ الْإِسْلَامِ وَالْإِيمَانِ فَكَانَ يَقُولُهُ تَارَةً وَتَارَةً يَحْكِي
translated_text:
Thus, Ahmad regarded anyone who called a person a Muslim despite his failure to fulfil the five pillars as contradicting the hadith, even though Ahmad himself said that Islam is acknowledgment. This indicates that acknowledgment marks one’s initial entry into Islam, and that one has not fulfilled the obligations of Islam until one fulfils the five pillars. Applying the designation is conditional upon fulfilling them, for he censured anyone who did not follow the hadith of Gabriel.

Moreover, in most of his answers, he judged someone who abandoned prayer to be a disbeliever; indeed, he also did so for abandoning other pillars. Muslims unanimously agree that a disbeliever is not a Muslim. It is therefore clear that he did not mean that Islam consists merely of speech without deeds. Even supposing that he did mean this, it would imply that abandoning any of the four pillars does not constitute disbelief. Most reports from him, however, indicate the contrary. Those who do not judge someone who abandons these pillars to be a disbeliever—such as al-Shāfi‘ī, Mālik, Abū Hanīfa and others—nevertheless regard them as part of Islam. How, then, could Ahmad not regard them as part of Islam, when his position on their inclusion in Islam is stronger than that of others?

It has also been reported that he considered the hadith of Sa‘d to conflict with the hadith of ‘Umar and gave preference to the hadith of Sa‘d. Al-Hasan ibn ‘Alī said:

“I asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal: ‘Which is stronger: faith or Islam?’ He replied: ‘There is this hadith of ‘Umar, but I prefer the hadith of Sa‘d.’”

It seems that he understood the hadith of ‘Umar to indicate that deeds are what the term Islam denotes, which would make what it denotes superior, whereas the hadith of Sa‘d indicates that what the term faith denotes is superior. Yet the hadith of ‘Umar mentions only outward deeds in its description of Islam. These do not constitute faith unless accompanied by the heart’s faith in Allah, His angels, His Books and His messengers. They then constitute part of faith, so what the term faith denotes is superior, as the hadith of Sa‘d indicates. There is therefore no contradiction between the two hadiths.

As for Ahmad’s distinction between Islam and faith, he would sometimes affirm it, and at other times report
