Were that so, such people would be included in His words:

“Allah has promised believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow,”

and similar passages in which they are promised Paradise without punishment.

Furthermore, the Prophet has denied them this designation on more than one occasion. Indeed, he said:

“Fighting a believer is disbelief.”

And he said:

“Do not become disbelievers after me, striking one another’s necks.”

If he cites His words:

“And if two groups of believers fight one another,”

or similar passages as evidence, the response is: all these people are called believers only with the qualification that they have committed these acts, so that the duties imposed on them and on others may be stated.

Likewise, regarding his statement, “The deficiency is not in their acknowledgment that Allah is the Truth and that what He says is truthful,” the response is: rather, deficiency does occur in the faith within their hearts, in their understanding and knowledge. How could faith in Allah, His names, and His attributes be identical in all hearts? Or how could believing that He knows all things, has power over all things, and is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful, Almighty, All-Wise, and severe in punishment not be part of faith in Him? No Muslim could say that believing these things is not part of faith in Him, nor claim that people are equal in this respect.

As for his statement that Islam decreases just as faith decreases, this too is true, as the authentic hadiths indicate. Whoever falls short in any aspect of prayer, zakat, fasting, or Hajj has diminished his Islam accordingly.

Whoever says that Islam consists only of the declaration of faith, intending thereby that it neither increases nor decreases, is mistaken. The refutation offered by those who regard Islam and faith as identical is directed only at these people, for their view of Islam resembles the Murji’ah’s view of faith. Thus, people have adopted “three views” concerning faith and Islam:

The Murji’ah say that Islam is superior because it includes faith.

Others say that faith and Islam are identical. These include the Muʿtazilah, the Khawārij, and a group among the adherents of hadith and the Sunnah. Muhammad ibn Nasr attributed this view to the majority of the latter, but that is not the case.

The third view is that faith is more complete and superior. This is what the Book and the Sunnah indicate in numerous places, and it is what has been transmitted from the Companions and the Successors who followed them in righteousness.

translated_text:
Some among those who hold this view say that Islam consists merely of the verbal declaration, and that deeds are not part of Islam.

The correct view is that Islam comprises all outward deeds. Ahmad ruled out qualifying one’s profession of Islam with “if Allah wills” only on the basis of al-Zuhrī’s statement that Islam is the declaration of faith. This is how al-Athram, al-Maymūnī, and others transmitted his position.

According to his other response, however, in which he did not adopt the view that Islam is the declaration alone, one qualifies one’s profession of Islam just as one qualifies one’s profession of faith. A person cannot assert with certainty that he has fulfilled everything commanded of him in Islam. Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe,”

and:

“Islam is built upon five pillars,”

asserting with certainty that one has fulfilled all five without deficiency, as commanded, is like asserting with certainty that one possesses faith.

Allah Most High has said:

“Enter into Islam completely.”

That is, enter into Islam in its entirety—into all its prescribed duties.

The reasoning Ahmad and other early scholars gave concerning the designation of faith also applies to the designation of Islam. If Islam means the declaration of faith, no qualification is made, as Ahmad and others explicitly stated. If it means performing all outward obligations, then qualifying one’s profession of Islam is like qualifying one’s profession of faith.

Everyone who pronounces the two testimonies of faith becomes a Muslim, distinct from Jews and Christians, and subject to the rulings of Islam that apply to Muslims. This, therefore, is something that can be affirmed with certainty, without qualification. It was for this reason that al-Zuhrī said, “Islam is the declaration of faith.” Ahmad and others agreed with him on that point. In agreeing with him, Ahmad did not mean that the Islam required of a person consists of the declaration alone: al-Zuhrī was far too learned to be unaware of this. Accordingly, Ahmad did not give this answer in his second response, lest it be thought that Islam consists of nothing but the declaration. Thus, when al-Athram said

translated_text:
to Ahmad, “Then if someone says, ‘I am a Muslim,’ does he make no qualification?”

He replied, “Yes, he makes no qualification when he says, ‘I am a Muslim.’”

I then said to him, “Am I to say, ‘This person is a Muslim,’ when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe,’ although I know that people are not safe from him?”

He then cited the report of Ma‘mar from al-Zuhrī, who said, “We therefore consider Islam to be the declaration of faith, and faith to be deeds.”

Ahmad thus explained that when Islam means the declaration of faith, no qualification is made. Wherever this is what is understood by the word Islam, no qualification is made. If this meaning were intended by “faith”—as it is in His words,

“then the freeing of a believing slave”—

what is meant is simply someone who outwardly professes Islam. For the faith upon which worldly rulings depend is outward faith, which is Islam. Thus, in outward rulings, both terms refer to the same thing.

Accordingly, when al-Athram mentioned to Ahmad that the Murji’ah cited as evidence the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“Free her, for she is a believer,”

he answered that the intended meaning was that she was to be treated as a believing woman under worldly rulings. He did not mean that she was a believer in Allah’s sight who, if she met Him with this declaration alone, would deserve to enter Paradise without entering the Fire. The believer in the unqualified sense in Allah’s Book is the one promised Paradise without entering the Fire, provided he dies upon his faith.

This is why Ibn Mas‘ūd and other early scholars would require anyone who testified to his own faith to testify that he would enter Paradise—meaning, if he died in that state. For he already knew that no one enters Paradise unless he dies a believer.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal rejected Ibn ‘Amīrah’s report that ‘Abd Allāh had abandoned the practice of qualifying his profession of faith. For when Ibn Mas‘ūd was told, “Some people say, ‘We are believers,’” he replied, “Why did you not ask them whether they are in Paradise?”

In another version, he said, “Why did they not say, ‘We are the people of Paradise’?” In yet another version, he was told, “This man claims to be a believer.” He replied, “Then ask him whether he is in Paradise or in the Fire.” They asked him, and he answered, “Allah knows best.” ‘Abd Allāh then said to him, “Why did you not leave the first matter to Allah, just as you left the second?”

“Whoever says, ‘I am a believer,’ is an unbeliever; whoever says, ‘I am learned,’ is ignorant; and whoever says that he is in Paradise is in the Fire.” This is narrated from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb through several disconnected chains, in reports transmitted by Qatādah, Nu‘aym ibn Abī Hind, and others.

The objection that the Murji’ah raise against Ibn Mas‘ūd—and which they say Yazīd ibn ‘Amīrah raised with him until he recanted—is that a person knows his present state but does not know in what state he will die. Because of this objection, many came to say that a believer is someone whom Allah has foreknown would end his life in faith, and an unbeliever is someone whom Allah has foreknown to be an unbeliever, and that no account is taken of his condition before that. This is the basis upon which they qualify their profession of faith. This is one of the two views held by Ahmad’s followers and others, and it is the view of Abū al-Hasan and his followers.

But this was not what Ahmad and the other early scholars intended. Rather, they meant that faith in the unqualified sense includes carrying out what has been commanded. Thus, saying, “I am a believer,” is like saying, “I am a friend of Allah,” “I am a God-fearing believer,” “I am among the righteous,” and similar statements.

Ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, was not unaware that Paradise is only for those who die as believers, or that a person does not know in what state he will die.

 هَذَا التَّوَقُّفُ يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّك لَا تَشْهَدُ لِنَفْسِك بِفِعْلِ الْوَاجِبَاتِ وَتَرْكِ الْمُحَرَّمَاتِ. فَإِنَّهُ مَنْ شَهِدَ لِنَفْسِهِ بِذَلِكَ شَهِدَ لِنَفْسِهِ أَنَّهُ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْجَنَّةِ إنْ مَاتَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَلِهَذَا صَارَ الَّذِينَ لَا يَرَوْنَ الِاسْتِثْنَاءَ لِأَجْلِ الْحَالِ الْحَاضِرِ بَلْ لِلْمُوَافَاةِ لَا يَقْطَعُونَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ يَقْبَلُ تَوْبَةَ تَائِبٍ كَمَا لَا يَقْطَعُونَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى يُعَاقِبُ مُذْنِبًا فَإِنَّهُمْ لَوْ قَطَعُوا بِقَبُولِ تَوْبَتِهِ لَزِمَهُمْ أَنْ يَقْطَعُوا لَهُ الْجَنَّةَ وَهُمْ لَا يَقْطَعُونَ لِأَحَدِ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْقِبْلَةِ لَا بِجَنَّةِ وَلَا نَارٍ؛ إلَّا مَنْ قَطَعَ لَهُ النَّصُّ.
 وَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 الْجَنَّةُ هِيَ لِمَنْ أَتَى بِالتَّوْبَةِ النَّصُوحِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ السَّيِّئَاتِ.
 قَالُوا:
 وَلَوْ مَاتَ عَلَى هَذِهِ التَّوْبَةِ لَمْ يُقْطَعْ لَهُ بِالْجَنَّةِ وَهُمْ لَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ فِي الْأَحْوَالِ بَلْ يَجْزِمُونَ بِأَنَّ الْمُؤْمِنَ مُؤْمِنٌ تَامُّ الْإِيمَانِ وَلَكِنَّ عِنْدَهُمْ الْإِيمَانَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ هُوَ مَا يُوَافِي بِهِ فَمَنْ قَطَعُوا لَهُ بِأَنَّهُ مَاتَ مُؤْمِنًا لَا ذَنْبَ لَهُ قَطَعُوا لَهُ بِالْجَنَّةِ فَلِهَذَا لَا يَقْطَعُونَ بِقَبُولِ التَّوْبَةِ لِئَلَّا يَلْزَمُهُمْ أَنْ يَقْطَعُوا بِالْجَنَّةِ وَأَمَّا أَئِمَّةُ السَّلَفِ فَإِنَّمَا لَمْ يَقْطَعُوا بِالْجَنَّةِ لِأَنَّهُمْ لَا يَقْطَعُونَ بِأَنَّهُ فَعَلَ الْمَأْمُورَ وَتَرَكَ الْمَحْظُورَ وَلَا أَنَّهُ أَتَى بِالتَّوْبَةِ النَّصُوحِ وَإِلَّا فَهُمْ يَقْطَعُونَ بِأَنَّ مَنْ تَابَ تَوْبَةً نَصُوحًا قَبِلَ اللَّهُ تَوْبَتَهُ.
وَجِمَاعُ الْأَمْرِ أَنَّ الِاسْمَ الْوَاحِدَ يُنْفَى وَيُثْبَتُ بِحَسَبِ الْأَحْكَامِ الْمُتَعَلِّقَةِ بِهِ فَلَا يَجِبُ إذَا أُثْبِتَ أَوْ نُفِيَ فِي حُكْمِ أَنْ يَكُونَ كَذَلِكَ فِي سَائِرِ الْأَحْكَامِ وَهَذَا فِي
translated_text:
For Ibn Mas‘ūd was far above such a misunderstanding. What he meant was: “Ask him whether he will be in Paradise if he dies in this state.” It was as though he had said: “Ask him whether, in this state, he would be among the people of Paradise.” When the man replied, “Allah and His Messenger know best,” he said: “Why did you not leave the first matter to Allah, just as you left the second?”

His meaning was: your hesitation shows that you do not attest that you have fulfilled your obligations and refrained from what is forbidden. Anyone who attests to this about himself thereby attests that he will be among the people of Paradise if he dies in that state.

For this reason, those who qualify their profession of faith not because of their present state, but because of the state in which they will die, do not affirm with certainty that Allah accepts a penitent’s repentance, just as they do not affirm with certainty that Allah Most High will punish a sinner. If they were certain that He accepted someone’s repentance, they would have to be certain that this person would enter Paradise. Yet they do not affirm that any particular person among those who face the qiblah will enter either Paradise or the Fire, except someone whose fate is explicitly established by a scriptural text.

When told, “Paradise is for whoever sincerely repents of all sins,” they reply, “Even if he were to die in this state of repentance, one could not affirm with certainty that he would enter Paradise.” They do not qualify their statements concerning present states; rather, they assert categorically that a believer is a believer whose faith is complete. In their view, however, the faith that counts before Allah is the faith with which a person dies. Thus, if they were certain that someone died a believer, free of sin, they would be certain that he would enter Paradise. This is why they do not affirm with certainty that repentance is accepted: otherwise, they would have to affirm with certainty that the person would enter Paradise.

The leading scholars of the early generations, by contrast, refrained from affirming that someone would enter Paradise only because they could not be certain that he had fulfilled what was commanded and avoided what was forbidden, or that he had sincerely repented. Otherwise, they did affirm with certainty that Allah accepts the repentance of whoever sincerely repents.

The essence of the matter is that the same designation may be denied or affirmed according to the judgments associated with it. Its affirmation or denial with respect to one judgment does not necessarily entail the same with respect to all other judgments. This occurs in

the speech of the Arabs and of all other peoples, because the intended meaning is understood. For example, hypocrites may be counted among the believers in one passage, while in another it is said that they are not of their number. Allah Most High says:

“Allah certainly knows those among you who hinder others and those who say to their brothers, ‘Come to us,’ and who hardly ever join the fighting.”

“Begrudging you their help, when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like someone overcome by the throes of death. But when fear departs, they lash you with sharp tongues, greedy for good things. Those have not believed, so Allah has rendered their deeds worthless, and that is easy for Allah.”

Here He counted these hypocrites among the believers, though they feared the enemy, shrank from fighting, discouraged others, and disparaged the believers. Yet in another verse He says:

“They swear by Allah that they are of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid.”

“If they could find a refuge, caves, or somewhere to slip into, they would turn to it, rushing headlong.”

The sin of these latter people is less grave, for they did not harm the believers either by discouraging them or by lashing them with sharp tongues. Rather, they swore by Allah that they were believers inwardly, in their hearts; the believers already knew that outwardly they were of their number. So Allah declared their claim false and said:

“But they are not of you.”

In the other passage, however, He said:

“Allah certainly knows those among you who hinder others.”

Thus, the address encompasses someone who is outwardly a Muslim and a believer without actually being a believer: among you are people of this description who do not believe, and whose deeds Allah has instead rendered worthless. Such a person is of your number outwardly, but not inwardly.

For this reason, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked for permission to kill some of the hypocrites, he said:

“People must not say that Muhammad kills his Companions.”

For outwardly they were counted among his Companions by those who did not know the true state of affairs. Yet among his Companions who truly were his Companions there was no hypocrisy

Two conflicting pieces of evidence existed in his case: the bed and the resemblance. Outwardly, the stronger claim to paternity belongs to the man to whose bed the child was born. This is also because the relationship underlying the bed is manifest and lawful, whereas fornication is a hidden matter that is not known and must be concealed, not disclosed. As he said:

“The adulterer gets the stone.”

This resembles the expressions “May your mouth be filled with dust” (1) and “May your mouth be filled with grit” (2). That is, you must remain silent rather than disclose fornication, for Allah hates such disclosure. Since she could veil herself from him without harm, he instructed her to do so because of the apparent evidence that he was not, in reality, her brother.

Thus, the same designation may be denied for one legal ruling and affirmed for another. He is a brother for purposes of inheritance, but not for purposes of mahram status. Likewise, a child born of fornication, according to some scholars, and the son of a woman who has undergone mutual imprecation with her husband, according to all but a few dissenting scholars, is not regarded as a son for purposes of inheritance and similar rulings, yet is regarded as a son with respect to the prohibition of marriage and mahram status.

The term “marriage,” and other such terms, when used in a command, encompasses the complete act—in this case, both the contract and intercourse—as in His words:

“Marry those women who please you,”

and His words:

“Until she marries a husband other than him.”

In a prohibition, however, it encompasses both the incomplete and the complete act. Thus, even the contract alone is prohibited, without intercourse, as in His words:

“Do not marry women whom your fathers married.”

This is because the purpose of one who issues a command is to secure a benefit, and that benefit is attained only through consummation. Similarly, if someone says, “Buy me some food,” the intended purpose is achieved only through both purchasing it and taking possession of it. The purpose of one who issues a prohibition, however, is to avert harm; hence every constituent part of the act falls within the prohibition, because its occurrence is itself harmful.

and likewise, lineage and inheritance depend on its complete form, whereas the prohibition of marriage arises from even the slightest cause, including breastfeeding. Similarly, anything that has a beginning and a complete form may sometimes be denied because its complete form is absent, and sometimes affirmed because its initial form is present.

Thus, the word “men” encompasses males, even young children, in such words of Allah as:

“If they are siblings, both men and women, the male shall have the share of two females.”

But it does not encompass young children in such words of His as:

“And the oppressed among men, women, and children who say, ‘Our Lord, take us out of this town whose people are oppressors.’”

Emigration and jihad are activities undertaken by those capable of them. Had He mentioned only oppressed men, it might have been thought that children were not included, since they are not among those suited to undertake these activities and are weak. He therefore mentioned them by their particular designation to clarify their excuse for not emigrating and the obligation of jihad.

Likewise, faith has a beginning and a complete form, as well as outward and inward aspects. When worldly rulings concerning rights and prescribed punishments—such as the protection of life and property, inheritance, and worldly penalties—are attached to faith, they are attached to its outward manifestation. It cannot be otherwise, since making these rulings depend on the inward reality is impossible. Even if this were sometimes possible, it would be difficult both to ascertain that reality and to act upon it. One cannot know it in a manner that establishes it outwardly, nor can one punish someone whose inward reality one knows.

It was on these two grounds that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) refrained from punishing the hypocrites. Among them were some whom he did not know, as Allah has stated. As for those whom he knew, had he punished any of them, that person’s people would have become angry on his behalf, and people would have said:

“Muhammad kills his companions.”

translated_text:
aversion to Islam, since the offence was not outwardly apparent and commonly known.

When he contemplated punishing those who stayed away from prayer, the presence of women and children in the houses prevented him.

As for faith in its initial form, it is to this that commands and prohibitions are addressed. Thus, when Allah says:

“O you who believe, when you rise for prayer”

and similar words, this is outwardly a command to everyone who professes faith, and inwardly an address to everyone who knows himself to affirm the Messenger’s truthfulness—even if he is sinful and has failed to fulfil inward and outward obligations. If the expression “those who believe” includes such people, there is nothing further to discuss. If it does not include them, that is because of their sins. Their sins, however, cannot prevent them from being commanded to perform good deeds which, if they perform them, will be a means of their receiving mercy. If they neglect them, they remain subject to the command and to punishment for neglecting them—a punishment for abandoning faith. These duties also bind the disbeliever, but his performance of them is not valid until he believes. Likewise, the outright hypocrite’s performance of them is not inwardly valid until he believes.

As for someone who possesses the beginnings of faith, his performance is valid, because he inwardly acknowledges the obligation of what the Messenger has made obligatory and the prohibition of what he has forbidden. This is the basis of validity.

As for faith in its complete form, it is to this that the promises of Paradise, support, and deliverance from the Fire relate. These promises are only for those who do what is commanded and refrain from what is forbidden. Whoever performs some duties and neglects others is rewarded for what he performs and punished for what he neglects. Such a person does not fall under the designation of a believer who deserves praise and commendation without blame or punishment.

When the Messenger denied someone faith, he denied it with respect to this ruling, for he said this by way of warning. Such a warning consists only in denying that which entails reward and averts punishment. Hence, the negation of faith found in the Quran and Sunnah

translated_text:
with respect to those who commit sins occurs only in statements of warning and censure, not in commands and prohibitions or in rulings pertaining to this world.

The designations of Islam, faith, and excellence are praiseworthy and desirable because of the good outcome awaiting those who possess these qualities. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that this good outcome belongs to those who possess them in the manner he described. Thus, whoever denied them faith—or both faith and Islam—without declaring them disbelievers denied these only with regard to the rulings of the Hereafter, namely reward, not with regard to worldly rulings.

The Muʿtazilah, however, thought that when the designation was denied, all its constituent parts were denied as well. They therefore held that such people possessed no faith or Islam whatsoever and would remain in the Fire forever. This contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations. Had they possessed nothing of faith or Islam, none of the rulings applicable to believers and Muslims would have applied to them; rather, they would have been like the hypocrites.

Yet the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus establish a distinction between the hypocrite who inwardly rejects the Messenger’s truthfulness and the sinful believer. The Muʿtazilah thus equated those who commit sins with the hypocrites in the rulings of this world and the Hereafter, denying them Islam and faith. Indeed, they may affirm these outwardly for the hypocrite while denying them to the sinner both inwardly and outwardly.

If it is said:

When Allah sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, anyone who followed him and believed in what he brought was a believer and a Muslim; if he died, he would be among the people of Paradise. Thereafter, “faith and Islam” increased until Allah Most High said:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you.”

The same applies to faith: the detailed faith mentioned in the hadith of Gabriel was not commanded at the outset, when Allah revealed Sūrat al-ʿAlaq and Sūrat al-Muddaththir. Rather, this came in the Medinan surahs, such as al-Baqarah and al-Nisāʾ. Accordingly, it does not follow that this detailed faith was obligatory for those who came before us.

Thus, a man may be a Muslim who worships Allah alone, associating nothing with Him, possesses the faith made obligatory upon him, and is among the people of Paradise, yet does not possess the faith mentioned in the hadith of Gabriel. Of such a person, however, it is said that he possesses the faith and Islam he was commanded to have.

A man may also be a Muslim who worships Allah as commanded, worships no one else, fears Him and hopes in Him, yet the following have not penetrated his heart: that Allah and His Messenger should be dearer to him than anything else; that Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause should be dearer to him than all his family and wealth; that he should love for his brother what he loves for himself; that he should fear Allah and no one else; and that he should rely upon Allah alone. All these are aspects of obligatory faith, but they are not necessarily entailed by Islam. Islam is submission, which includes humbling oneself before Allah alone, obeying Him, and worshipping Him alone. This may include fearing Him and hoping in Him.

for oneself—these are realities distinctive of faith. Whoever does not possess them is not truly among the believers, even though he may be a Muslim. The same applies to his heart trembling when Allah is mentioned, and to his faith increasing when His verses are recited to him.

If it is asked, “Is lacking this faith a sin?” the answer is:

If the revelation making it obligatory has not reached a person, his failure to fulfil it is not a sin. But if that revelation has reached him and he does not act upon it, his failure is sinful, provided he is capable of fulfilling it. Many people—or most of them—do not possess these detailed aspects of faith, although they fulfil the obedience required in Islam, and when they commit sins, they repent and seek forgiveness for them. They do not know that these realities of faith within the heart are obligatory, or even that they belong to faith. Indeed, many among them who know of these realities consider them recommended, supererogatory acts, if they acknowledge their obligation.

“Islam” thus encompasses someone who outwardly professes Islam but possesses no faith at all: the outright hypocrite. It also encompasses someone who outwardly professes Islam and has a general inward belief, but does not fulfil everything obligatory in either respect. These are the defiantly disobedient, each of whom may possess a trait of hypocrisy. It also encompasses someone who fulfils the requirements of Islam and the faith they entail, but does not fulfil obligatory faith in its entirety. Such people are not defiantly disobedient people who neglect an outward obligation or commit an outwardly forbidden act. Nevertheless, they have neglected some obligatory realities of faith—knowledge and deeds of the heart, followed by actions of some bodily faculties—for which they are blameworthy.

{لَيْسَ وَرَاءَ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ مِثْقَالُ حَبَّةِ خَرْدَلٍ}
 فَإِنَّ مُرَادَهُ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَبْقَ بَعْدَ هَذَا الْإِنْكَارِ مَا يَدْخُلُ فِي الْإِيمَانِ حَتَّى يَفْعَلَهُ الْمُؤْمِنُ؛
 بَلْ الْإِنْكَارُ بِالْقَلْبِ آخِرُ حُدُودِ الْإِيمَانِ لَيْسَ مُرَادُهُ أَنَّ مَنْ لَمْ يُنْكِرْ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَعَهُ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ حَبَّةُ خَرْدَلٍ:
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ: لَيْسَ وَرَاءَ ذَلِكَ " فَجَعَلَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ ثَلَاثَ طَبَقَاتٍ وَكُلٌّ مِنْهُمْ فَعَلَ الْإِيمَانَ الَّذِي يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ لَكِنَّ الْأَوَّلَ لَمَّا كَانَ أَقْدَرَهُمْ كَانَ الَّذِي يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ أَكْمَلَ مِمَّا يَجِبُ عَلَى الثَّانِي وَكَانَ مَا يَجِبُ عَلَى الثَّانِي أَكْمَلَ مِمَّا يَجِبُ عَلَى الْآخَرِ وَعُلِمَ بِذَلِكَ أَنَّ النَّاسَ يَتَفَاضَلُونَ فِي الْإِيمَانِ الْوَاجِبِ عَلَيْهِمْ بِحَسَبِ اسْتِطَاعَتِهِمْ مَعَ بُلُوغِ الْخِطَابِ إلَيْهِمْ كُلِّهِمْ.
translated_text:
This is the “hypocrisy” that the early generations feared for themselves, for someone in this condition may possess a trait of hypocrisy.

Beyond this are the faith and its attendant deeds by which Allah has distinguished those brought near to Him above the righteous, the people of the right. This may consist of recommended acts. A believer may also be favoured through aspects of faith and Islam that are obligatory for him but not for others. Hence the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart—and that is the weakest faith.”

In another hadith:

“Beyond that there is not even a mustard seed’s weight of faith.”

He means that beyond this rejection, nothing belonging to faith remains for the believer to do. Rather, rejecting evil in the heart is the final boundary of faith. He does not mean that someone who fails to reject it has not even a mustard seed’s weight of faith. This is why he said, “Beyond that.”

He thus placed believers in three ranks, each fulfilling the faith obligatory upon him. However, because the first has the greatest ability, what is obligatory upon him is more complete than what is obligatory upon the second; and what is obligatory upon the second is more complete than what is obligatory upon the last. This establishes that people differ in the faith obligatory upon them according to their ability, even though the divine command has reached them all.

Section

As for “qualifying one’s profession of faith” by saying, “I am a believer, if Allah wills,” people hold “three” views: some consider it obligatory, some prohibit it, and some permit either course according to two different considerations. This last view is the soundest.

Those who prohibit it are the Murji’ah, the Jahmiyyah, and others like them who regard faith as a single thing that a person knows he possesses, such as affirmation of the Lord and similar convictions within his heart. One of them says:

“I know that I am a believer just as I know that I have pronounced the two testimonies of faith, that I have recited al-Fātihah, that I love the Messenger of Allah, and that I hate the Jews and Christians. My saying, ‘I am a believer,’ is therefore like my saying, ‘I am a Muslim,’ or, ‘I have pronounced the two testimonies of faith and recited al-Fātihah,’ or, ‘I hate the Jews and Christians,’ and similar present realities that I know with certainty. Just as it is not permissible to say, ‘I have recited al-Fātihah, if Allah wills,’ neither should one say, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills.’ But if someone is uncertain about it, he says, ‘I did it, if Allah wills.’”

They said that whoever qualifies his profession of faith in this way doubts his faith, and they called such people “the doubters.”

They said:

“Faith followed by unbelief, whose possessor then dies an unbeliever, is not faith. It is like a prayer that someone invalidates before completing it, or a fast that someone breaks before sunset. Such a person is an unbeliever in Allah’s sight, because He knows the state in which he will die.”

They said the same regarding unbelief. This is the reasoning adopted by many later Kullābīs and others who wish to defend the well-known statement of the people of the Sunnah and hadith, “I am a believer, if Allah wills,” while also maintaining that faith admits of no degrees, and that a person does not doubt the faith he presently possesses, but only his future faith.

Added to this is their assertion that Allah’s love, pleasure, displeasure, and hatred are beginningless. Are these His will, or are they other attributes? They hold “two views” on this.

Most of their early scholars say that pleasure, displeasure, anger, and similar attributes are distinct from will, just as hearing and sight are distinct from knowledge. The same applies to friendship and enmity. All these are eternal, beginningless attributes according to Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb and those who followed him among the speculative theologians and the adherents of the legal schools—the Hanbalīs, Shāfi‘īs, Mālikīs, and others.

They said:

translated_text:
are reducible to will, and will accords with knowledge. The meaning, then, is that Allah has willed from eternity to reward these people after their belief and to punish Iblīs after his unbelief. This meaning is sound, for Allah wills to create everything He knows He will create.

Those who affirm these as distinct attributes say that His love, too, corresponds to whom He wills to reward: He loves everyone He wills to reward and hates everyone He wills to punish. This, in turn, accords with His knowledge. According to them, He does not become pleased with anyone after having been displeased with him, nor does He rejoice at a servant’s repentance after accepting it; rather, He has rejoiced at his repentance from eternity. They understand rejoicing as either will or pleasure. The meaning is that He has willed from eternity to reward him, or has been pleased from eternity with the one He wills to reward. Likewise, according to them, His anger is not specific to the Day of Resurrection as opposed to the time before it. Rather, His anger is beginningless, whether understood as will or as something else.

These people say:

“If Allah knows that a person will die an unbeliever, He has willed from eternity to punish him. Thus, the faith that person once possessed is invalid and of no benefit; its existence is as good as its nonexistence. Such a person is therefore not a believer at all. If Allah knows that he will die a believer, He has willed from eternity to reward him, and the unbelief he committed is as good as nonexistent. Thus, according to them, this person was never an unbeliever at all.”

On this basis, they qualify their profession of faith with “if Allah wills.” Some of their leading scholars, such as Abū Mansūr al-Māturīdī, likewise qualify a declaration of unbelief, since their reasoning applies equally to both. However, the vast majority of the imams hold that a declaration of unbelief is not to be qualified in this way, and that doing so is an innovation not known to have been practised by any of the early generations. Nevertheless, it is a necessary consequence of their position.

But the following objection may be raised: if saying “He is a believer” means the same as saying “He is in Paradise,” you nevertheless say of an unbeliever, “He is an unbeliever,” without saying “He is in the Fire” unless you make this conditional upon his dying in unbelief. This shows that he is certainly an unbeliever at present, even though he may become a believer. The same applies to a believer, whether one is speaking of oneself or of someone else.

Thus, if it were said of a Jew or a Christian, “This man is an unbeliever,” someone holding this view would add, “If Allah wills,” unless he knew that the man would die an unbeliever. According to these people, no one knows anyone to be a believer unless he knows that he will die upon faith. This view was held by many scholastic theologians who followed Ibn Kullāb, and many followers of the imams agreed with them. Yet it was not the view of any of the early generations—neither the four imams nor anyone else. Nor did any of those early scholars who qualified their profession of faith with “if Allah wills” base their practice on this reasoning: neither Ahmad nor anyone before him.

A group who had originally qualified their profession of faith in imitation of the early generations carried the reasoning behind this view further. They had inherited this qualification from the early generations. The people of Syria were stern in their opposition to the Murji’ah. Muhammad ibn Yūsuf al-Firyābī, a companion of al-Thawrī, served as a frontier guard at Ascalon when it was still inhabited and was among the finest Muslim frontier strongholds. When one of them is told, “There is no doubt about this,” he replies, “Yes, there is no doubt about it. But if Allah wills to change it, He will change it.” Thus, by saying “if Allah wills,” they mean that it may change in the future, even though there is no doubt about it at present. It is as though, for them, a reality can be affirmed without this qualification only if it does not change. This resembles what those others say about faith: that faith is what Allah knows will not change, so that the person possessing it dies upon it.

That view, however, was advanced by people of learning and religion through independent reasoning and reflection. Those who qualify everything in this way, by contrast, learned this practice from some followers of their shaykh. The shaykh to whom they affiliate themselves, known as Abū ‘Amr ‘Uthmān ibn Marzūq, did not endorse this kind of qualification. Rather, he followed the practice of his predecessors in this matter. Some of his companions introduced it after him.

Their shaykh was affiliated with Imam Ahmad and was a follower of ‘Abd al-Wahhāb, the son of Shaykh Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī. Abū al-Faraj was a student of Judge Abū Ya‘lā. Although all these men were affiliated with Imam Ahmad, they agreed with Ibn Kullāb on the foundational principle for which Ahmad censured the Kullābiyyah and on account of which he ordered that al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī be shunned. A group of followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī and Abū Hanīfa likewise agreed with Ibn Kullāb on this principle, including Abū al-Ma‘ālī al-Juwaynī, Abū al-Walīd al-Bājī, Abū Mansūr al-Māturīdī and others.

Their views on various questions concerning the divine attributes and related matters—such as the question of the Quran: does He, glorified be He, speak by His will and power, or is the Quran inseparably inherent in His essence?—together with their position on the qualification “if Allah wills,” are founded upon that principle.

translated_text:
Likewise, al-Ash'arī and his followers based their position on that principle, for all of these were Kullābīs who say:

“Allah has not spoken by His will and power; He does not become pleased with anyone after he believes, or angry with anyone after he disbelieves; nor does He rejoice in a person’s repentance after he repents.”

Thus, they agreed with the early generations that the Quran is the uncreated speech of Allah. They then said that it is eternal and that He did not speak it by His will and power. They subsequently disagreed about this eternal speech: is it a single meaning, or eternal letters despite their occurring in succession? Their views and those of others have been discussed at length elsewhere.

This later group objects to saying “with certainty” about anything. Their excessive use of the qualification “if Allah wills” has led them to reject this expression, even when they are certain of the substance of what they say. Thus, they firmly affirm that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah and that Allah is their Lord, yet they will not say “with certainty.” A group of them met with me, and I reproached them for this and refused to do what they requested until they said “with certainty.” They brought me a book containing hadiths claiming that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade a person to say “with certainty.” These are fabricated, invented hadiths forged by some later individuals.

The point here is that, when qualifying one’s profession of faith with “if Allah wills” was justified on such grounds, some people extended that rationale to matters in which, by the consensus of the Muslims, such qualification is impermissible. They reasoned that, if Allah knows that things existing now will change their conditions, their present attributes should be qualified with “if Allah wills.” Thus, they say, “This is small, if Allah wills,” because Allah may make it large. They say, “This person is insane, if Allah wills,” because Allah may make him sane. And concerning an apostate they say:

translated_text:
“This person is a disbeliever, if Allah wills,” because he may repent. Those who qualified their profession of faith with “if Allah wills” on this basis thought that this was the position of the early generations.

These people and other speculative theologians like them defend the widely recognized teachings of Islam, just as the Muʿtazilah, the Jahmiyyah, and other speculative theologians do. Thus, they defend the existence of the Creator, prophethood, resurrection, and similar matters. Alongside this, they defend the widely recognized positions of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, as do the Kullābiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, the Ashʿariyyah, and others like them. They defend the positions that the Quran is the uncreated speech of Allah; that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter; that those who face the qiblah do not become disbelievers through sin, nor will they remain in the Fire forever; that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will intercede for those who commit major sins; that the trial of the grave is real, as is its punishment; and that the Pool of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the Hereafter is real. They defend other such positions widely known to be among the foundational beliefs of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah. They likewise defend the caliphates of the four caliphs, the excellence of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and similar matters.

Yet many speculative theologians, in much of what they defend, are not acquainted with the true teachings of Islam on those matters, with what the Sunnah has brought, or with the positions held by the early generations. They therefore defend the well-known positions of the early generations, but not on the grounds upon which those positions were actually based. Instead, they use other grounds received from people of innovation outside their ranks. Consequently, their discourse contains the very contradictions, inconsistencies, and errors for which the early generations condemned such discourse and its practitioners. Indeed, their statements condemning this kind of discourse are numerous.

the Book and the Sunnah is false and untrue, and therefore contradicts both revealed law and reason.

“And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.”

When these people learned that Ahl al-Sunnah were known to qualify their profession of faith with “if Allah wills,” they thought this could only make sense if faith meant the faith upon which a servant dies and with which he meets his Lord. They therefore supposed that this was what faith meant to the early generations and began attributing this position to them. Yet none of the early generations held this position. Rather, these people attributed it to them on the basis of their own supposition, because they thought that the early generations’ statements could only be explained on this basis. They claim that the foundational doctrine of Jahm concerning faith, which they have defended, is the position of the discerning scholars and speculative thinkers among the scholars of hadith.

Such misrepresentation frequently occurs concerning the positions of the early generations: a speculative thinker opposes their position and sets out his argument against it without understanding what they actually held. Someone who knows these thinkers’ arguments but not those of the early generations, or who venerates them because he sees them as superior to himself, then says, “This is the position of the discerning scholars,” or, “The discerning scholars have said…” Yet the position in question may be false, contradicting reason as well as revealed law. This occurs frequently in the discourse of some innovators and some heretics.

Those whom Allah has granted knowledge and faith know that whatever depth of understanding and attainment the later generations possess falls short of that of the early generations, in both knowledge and practice. Anyone versed in theoretical and rational questions, as well as practical matters, knows that the position of the Companions is always sounder than that of those who came after them, and that whenever anyone introduces a novel position into Islam, it is mistaken, while someone before him has already arrived at the correct position.

 وَأَنَّ ذَلِكَ هَلْ هُوَ شَرْطٌ فِي صِحَّةِ الْإِيمَانِ وَحَقِيقَتُهُ فِي الْحَالِ وَكَوْنُهُ مُعْتَدًّا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ بِهِ وَفِي حُكْمِهِ فَمَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ ذَلِكَ شَرْطٌ فِيهِ يُسْتَثْنَوْنَ فِي الْإِطْلَاقِ فِي الْحَالِ؛ لَا أَنَّهُمْ يَشُكُّونَ فِي حَقِيقَةِ التَّوْحِيدِ وَالْمَعْرِفَةِ؛
 لَكِنَّهُمْ يَقُولُونَ:
 لَا يَدْرِي أَيَّ الْإِيمَانِ الَّذِي نَحْنُ مَوْصُوفُونَ بِهِ فِي الْحَالِ هَلْ هُوَ مُعْتَدٌّ بِهِ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ؟ عَلَى مَعْنَى أَنَّا نَنْتَفِعُ بِهِ فِي الْعَاقِبَةِ وَنَجْتَنِي مِنْ ثِمَارِهِ.
 فَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ:
 أَمُؤْمِنُونَ أَنْتُمْ حَقًّا؟ أو تَقُولُونَ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ؟ أو تَقُولُونَ نَرْجُو؟ فَيَقُولُونَ نَحْنُ مُؤْمِنُونَ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ يَعْنُونَ بِهَذَا الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ تَفْوِيضَ الْأَمْرِ فِي الْعَاقِبَةِ إلَى اللَّهِ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى وَإِنَّمَا يَكُونُ الْإِيمَانُ إيمَانًا مُعْتَدًّا بِهِ فِي حُكْمِ
translated_text:
Abū al-Qāsim al-Ansārī reported that, after mentioning the position of Abū al-Hasan and his followers concerning faith and affirming that it is the heart’s assent, Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī said:

“Some of our scholars hold that faith is contingent upon one’s final state: true faith requires that one meet his Lord with it and end his life upon it. Others do not make this a condition of faith in the present.”

Al-Ansārī said:

“After mentioning that most leading scholars of the early generations used to say, ‘Faith consists of knowledge in the heart, affirmation with the tongue, and action with the limbs,’ he said: ‘Most of these scholars hold that faith is contingent upon one’s final state. Those who hold this position apply it only to someone concerning whom no report states that he is among the people of Paradise. As for someone concerning whom such a report exists, they affirm his faith with certainty, as with the ten Companions.’”

He then said:

“The position chosen by the discerning scholars is that faith is assent. We have already mentioned their differing views concerning its dependence upon one’s final state: whether this is a condition for faith to be valid and real in the present, and for it to be recognized by Allah and in His judgment.

“Those who make this a condition qualify their present profession of faith with ‘if Allah wills.’ This is not because they doubt the reality of their affirmation of Allah’s oneness and their knowledge of Him. Rather, they say: ‘It is not known whether the faith we presently possess is recognized by Allah—that is, whether we shall benefit from it in the end and reap its fruits.’

“When they are asked, ‘Are you truly believers? Or do you say, “If Allah wills”? Or do you say, “We hope so”?’ they reply, ‘We are believers, if Allah wills.’ By this qualification, they mean to entrust the ultimate outcome to Allah, glorified and exalted is He. Faith is only recognized as such in the judgment of

{وَعَدَ اللَّهُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَالْمُؤْمِنَاتِ جَنَّاتٍ}

 فَهَؤُلَاءِ - يَعْنِي الْقَائِلِينَ بِالْمُوَافَاةِ جَعَلُوا الثَّبَاتَ عَلَى هَذَا التَّصْدِيقِ وَالْإِيمَانَ الَّذِي وَصَفْنَاهُ إلَى الْعَاقِبَةِ وَالْوَفَاءَ بِهِ فِي الْمَآلِ شَرْطًا فِي الْإِيمَانِ شَرْعًا لَا لُغَةً وَلَا عَقْلًا.
 قَالَ:
 وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ سَلَفِ أَصْحَابِ الْحَدِيثِ وَالْأَكْثَرِينَ؛
 قَالَ:
 وَهُوَ اخْتِيَارُ الْإِمَامِ أَبِي بَكْرِ بْنِ فورك؛
 وَكَانَ الْإِمَامُ مُحَمَّدُ ابْنُ إسْحَاقَ بْنِ خُزَيْمَة يَغْلُو فِيهِ وَكَانَ يَقُولُ:
 مَنْ قَالَ: أَنَا مُؤْمِنٌ حَقًّا فَهُوَ مُبْتَدِعٌ.
وَأَمَّا مَذْهَبُ سَلَفِ أَصْحَابِ الْحَدِيثِ كَابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ وَأَصْحَابِهِ وَالثَّوْرِيِّ
translated_text:
Allah when it is a mark of success and a sign of salvation. If, however, its possessor—Allah forbid—is among the wretched in Allah’s judgment, then the faith with which he is presently adorned is merely held on loan.”

He said:

“Those who adopt this position see no difference between saying, ‘I am a believer, certainly destined for Paradise,’ and saying, ‘I am truly a believer.’”

I say:

This follows only according to those who understand faith to encompass fulfilling obligations and abstaining from prohibited acts. Whoever dies in this state is among the people of Paradise. But according to the position of the Jahmiyyah and the Murji’ah—the position defended by these advocates of Jahm’s doctrine—a person unquestionably dies in faith and, in their view, possesses perfect faith, yet they also count him among those guilty of major sins who enter the Fire. Thus, meeting his Lord with faith does not necessarily mean that he is among the people of Paradise. This consequence of their position demonstrates its falsity, for Allah has promised the believers Paradise.

They likewise said:

“Especially since Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says:

‘Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens’

—to the end of the verse.”

He said:

“These people—meaning those who make faith contingent upon one’s final state—have made perseverance in this assent and the faith we have described until the end, and remaining true to it at one’s final outcome, a condition of faith in religious law, though not in language or reason.”

He said:

“This is the position of the early hadith scholars and of the majority.”

He said:

“It is also the position chosen by Imam Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak. Imam Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzayma went to great lengths in upholding it and used to say: ‘Whoever says, “I am truly a believer,” is an innovator.’”

As for the position of the early hadith scholars, such as Ibn Masʿūd and his companions, al-Thawrī

 قُلْنَا الْإِيمَانُ هُوَ التَّصْدِيقُ لُغَةً وَشَرْعًا غَيْرَ أَنَّ الشَّرْعَ ضَمَّ إلَى التَّصْدِيقِ أَوْصَافًا وَشَرَائِطَ:
 مَجْمُوعُهَا يَصِيرُ مَجْزِيًّا مَقْبُولًا كَمَا قُلْنَا فِي الصَّلَاةِ وَالصَّوْمِ وَالْحَجِّ وَنَحْوِهَا وَالصَّلَاةُ فِي اللُّغَةِ: هِيَ الدُّعَاءُ غَيْرَ أَنَّ الشَّرْعَ ضَمَّ إلَيْهَا شَرَائِطَ.
 فَيُقَالُ:
 هَذَا يُنَاقِضُ مَا ذَكَرُوهُ فِي مُسَمَّى الْإِيمَانِ فَإِنَّهُمْ لَمَّا زَعَمُوا أَنَّهُ فِي اللُّغَةِ التَّصْدِيقُ وَالشَّرْعُ لَمْ يُغَيِّرْهُ أَوْرَدُوا عَلَى أَنْفُسِهِمْ.
translated_text:
and Ibn 'Uyaynah, most of the scholars of Kufa, Yahyā ibn Sa'īd al-Qattān—as he reports from the scholars of Basra—and Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other imams of the Sunnah—they would qualify their affirmation of faith with “if Allah wills.”

This is established from them by mass transmission. Yet none of them said: “I make this qualification on account of one’s final state, and because faith refers only to that with which a servant meets his Lord.” Rather, their leading scholars explicitly stated that they made this qualification because faith includes performing obligatory duties. They would therefore not attest to having fulfilled these, just as they would not attest to their own righteousness and piety. This is something they do not know, and doing so would amount to declaring themselves pure without knowledge. We shall mention their statements on this, if Allah wills.

As for one’s final state, I know of none of the early scholars who explained the qualification on this basis. However, many later hadith scholars among the followers of Ahmad, Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, and others do explain it this way, as do their theologians, such as Abū al-Hasan al-Ash'arī and most of his followers. But this is not the position of the early hadith scholars.

He then said:

“If someone asks: ‘If you say that the faith commanded in religious law is what you have described, together with its conditions, and that this is not derived from language, how can you consistently maintain that faith retains its linguistic meaning?’

We reply: ‘Faith means assent, both linguistically and in religious law. However, religious law has added qualities and conditions to assent; taken together, these receive reward and acceptance. This is like what we have said concerning prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, and similar acts. Prayer, in its linguistic sense, means supplication, but religious law has added conditions to it.’”

It may be said in reply: This contradicts what they have stated concerning what the term “faith” denotes. For when they claimed that its linguistic meaning is assent and that religious law has not changed it, they raised the following objection against themselves:

How, then, can deeds be excluded from what faith denotes in religious law?

This is indeed what happened. These were the people of Mecca who had opposed Allah and His Messenger before the conquest. Most of them believed and became friends of Allah and His Messenger.

Ibn Kullāb and his followers based their position on the premise that friendship is an eternal attribute inherent in Allah’s Essence, namely His will, love, pleasure, and the like. It therefore means His will to reward a person after death. This, in turn, follows Allah’s knowledge: anyone whom He knows will die a believer has always been a friend of Allah, because Allah has always willed to admit him to Paradise. The same applies to enmity.

The majority, however, say: Although friendship and enmity involve Allah’s love and pleasure, hatred and displeasure, He, glorified be He, is pleased with a person and loves him after he believes and does righteous deeds. He only becomes displeased and angry with him after he disbelieves, as Allah Most High says:

He thus states that their deeds angered Him. Likewise, He says:

“When they provoked Our wrath, We took vengeance upon them.”

The commentators explain this as: “They angered Us.” Allah Most High also says:

“If you are grateful, He is pleased with that for you.”

In the authentic hadith recorded in al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine has openly challenged Me to war. When I love him, I become his hearing with which

he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he strikes, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him; if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. He thus tells us that His servant continues to draw near to Him through voluntary acts of worship until He loves him. Then He says: “When I love him, I become such and such.” This shows that His love for His servant comes only after the servant does what He loves.

The Quran also indicates this. Allah Most High says:

“Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.”

The words “Allah will love you” express the consequence of the command “follow me.” This is equivalent to the consequence of a condition, which is why the verb is in the jussive mood. This is the reward for their deed—following the Messenger: He rewards them for that by loving them. The consequence of a condition, the reward for a deed, and the effect of a cause can only come afterward, not beforehand. This is like His words, Most High:

And His words, Most High:

There are many such examples. Likewise, He says:

He therefore encourages them to act by promising them this, just as He encourages them through everything else He promises them. Recompense for a deed comes after the deed. Likewise, His words:

“When you were called to faith but disbelieved.”

He, glory be to Him, abhors them when they are called to faith but disbelieve. Similar to this are His words:

“Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a victory near at hand.”

His words, “Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you,” make clear that He was pleased with them at that time. The particle idh (“when”) denotes a time in the past. Thus, it is known that He was pleased with them at that time because of that deed, and rewarded them for it. An effect cannot precede its cause, and something assigned to a particular time cannot precede that time.

Even if He was pleased with them in some respect, this particular pleasure resulting from the pledge came about only then. As established in an authentic hadith, He will say to the people of Paradise:

“O people of Paradise, are you pleased?”

They will reply: “Our Lord, how could we not be pleased when You have given us what You have given no one else among Your creation?”

He will say: “Shall I not give you something better than that?”

They will reply: “Our Lord, what could be better than that?”

He will say: “I bestow My pleasure upon you, and I shall never be displeased with you thereafter.”

This indicates that it is at that time that they receive this pleasure, which will never be followed by displeasure. It also indicates that other instances of His pleasure may be followed by displeasure.

In the two Sahīh collections, in the hadith of intercession, each of the messengers says:

“My Lord has become angry today with an anger the like of which He has never had before and will never have again.”

And in the authentic hadith collections, it is narrated through several chains from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

that he said:

“Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than does a man who has lost his mount in a desolate, deadly wilderness, with his food and drink upon it. He searches for it but cannot find it, so he lies down awaiting death. Then, when he wakes, there is his mount, with his food and drink upon it.”

In another narration: “How great do you think his joy at finding it would be?”

They replied: “Immense, O Messenger of Allah!”

He said: “Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than this man does at recovering his mount.”

Likewise, He laughs at two men, one of whom kills the other, yet both enter Paradise. He also laughs at the last person to enter Paradise, who says: “Are You mocking me, when You are the Lord of all worlds?”

He replies: “No, but I have power to do whatever I will.” All of this is in the Sahīh.

The qunūt supplication includes:

“Take me into Your care among those You have taken into Your care.”

It is inconceivable to ask for something that is beginningless. Allah Most High has said:

“My Protector is Allah, Who has sent down the Book, and He takes care of the righteous.”

And He said:

“Allah is the Protector of those who are mindful of Him.”

His taking them into His care is thus a recompense for their righteousness and mindfulness of Him, and results from it; it therefore cannot precede it. Although they became righteous and mindful of Him only through His will, power, bounty and kindness, this care is nevertheless tied to their being mindful of Him and righteous. This indicates that His taking them into His care follows that, just as His being with those who are mindful of Him and righteous, through His help and support, does not precede their becoming mindful of Him and righteous.

The same applies to mercy. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Most Merciful shows mercy to those who show mercy. Show mercy to those on earth, and the One above the heaven will show mercy to you.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “An authentic hadith.”

Likewise, His words:

“If you are grateful, He is pleased with that for you.”

He made His pleasure with it dependent upon gratitude, as a consequence depends upon its condition and an effect upon its cause. A consequence only comes after its condition.

The second basis for qualifying one’s profession of faith is that faith in its full sense entails doing everything Allah has commanded His servant to do and abstaining from everything He has forbidden. If a man says, “I am a believer,” in this sense, he has testified that he is among the righteous and God-fearing who fulfil everything they have been commanded to do and abstain from everything they have been forbidden, and thus that he is one of Allah’s allies. This amounts to declaring oneself pure and testifying to something about oneself that one does not know. If this testimony were true, he ought also to testify that he will enter Paradise if he dies in this state. Yet no one testifies that he himself will enter Paradise. His testimony that he is a believer is therefore like his testimony that he will enter Paradise if he dies in this state.

This was the basis adopted by the majority of the early generations who qualified their profession of faith, although they permitted leaving it unqualified when a different meaning was intended, as we shall explain, if Allah Most High wills.

Al-Khallāl also related this answer through al-Fadl ibn Ziyād. He said: Al-Fadl added: I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh say: Sulaymān ibn Harb understood this as referring to acceptance. He would say, “We perform deeds, but we do not know whether they will be accepted from us.”

I say: Acceptance depends on performing the deed as commanded. Whoever fears Allah in his deed and performs it as commanded has had it accepted from him. Yet he cannot be certain of its acceptance because he cannot be certain that he has performed it fully, as commanded. As the Most High said:

“And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful.”

‘Ā’ishah asked, “O Messenger of Allah, does this mean a man who commits adultery, steals, drinks wine, and is afraid?”

He replied, “No, daughter of al-Siddīq. Rather, it is a man who prays, fasts, gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him.”

translated_text:
Ibn Mas‘ūd concerning qualification in faith, because faith consists of words and deeds, and deeds mean action. We have made the verbal profession, but we fear that we may have fallen short in our deeds. I therefore prefer that one qualify one’s profession of faith by saying, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills.’”

He said: I also heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh being asked about the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And we shall, if Allah wills, join you.”

“What does the qualification refer to here?”

He replied, “To the places of burial. He does not know whether he will be buried in the place whose occupants he greeted or elsewhere.”

[It is also related from al-Maymūnī that he asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh about his position and opinion concerning the statement, “A believer, if Allah wills.” He replied, “I say, ‘A believer, if Allah wills,’ and, ‘A believer, I hope,’ because one does not know whether one’s deeds have discharged one’s obligations as required.”] (*)

Statements like these occur frequently in the words of Ahmad and others like him. This accords with what has already been explained: a believer in the unqualified sense is someone who fulfils his obligations and deserves Paradise if he dies in that state. Someone who falls short by neglecting what is commanded or doing what is forbidden is not called a believer without qualification. A believer in the unqualified sense is a righteous, Allah-fearing person, a close friend of Allah. Thus, saying, “I am certainly a believer,” is like saying, “I am certainly righteous, Allah-fearing, and a close friend of Allah.”

Nevertheless, Ahmad and other early scholars disliked a man asking another, “Are you a believer?” They also disliked answering this question, because it was an innovation introduced by the Murji’ah to support their position. A man knows that he is not a disbeliever; indeed, he finds that his heart affirms what the Messenger brought, so he says, “I am a believer.” This is then used to establish that faith is assent: you are certain that you are a believer, yet you are not certain that you have done everything you were commanded to do. They would therefore affirm faith in a qualified sense that did not entail testifying to their own perfection. Thus, the correct view is that one may say, “I am a believer,” without adding “if Allah wills,” if this is the sense intended. However, one should accompany this statement with something clarifying that one does not mean complete faith in its unqualified sense. This is why Ahmad disliked giving an unqualified answer without first adding that qualification.

Al-Marwadhī said:

“Abū ‘Abd Allāh was asked, ‘Should we say, “We are the believers”?’ He replied, ‘We say, “We are Muslims.”’”

He also said:

“I asked Abū ‘Abd Allāh, ‘Should we say, “We are believers”?’ He replied, ‘Rather, we say, “We are Muslims.”’”

Nevertheless, he did not condemn someone who omitted the qualification if that person did not intend what the Murji’ah intended—that faith consists merely of words. Rather, he dislikes omitting it because he knows that there is faith in his heart, even though he is not certain that his faith is complete.

Al-Khallāl said:

“Ahmad ibn Asram al-Muzanī informed me that Abū ‘Abd Allāh was asked, ‘What if a man asks me, “Are you a believer?”’ He replied, ‘Your asking me this is an innovation.’ He does not doubt his faith—or he said, ‘We do not doubt our faith.’”

Al-Muzanī said:

“What I remember is that Abū ‘Abd Allāh said, ‘I say as Tāwūs said: “I believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His Messengers.”’”

translated_text:
Al-Khallāl said:

“Harb ibn Ismāʿīl and Abū Dāwūd informed me. Abū Dāwūd said: ‘I heard Ahmad say: I heard Sufyān—meaning Ibn ʿUyaynah—say that when he was asked, “Are you a believer?” he would not answer the question, but would say, “Your asking me this is an innovation, and I do not doubt my faith.” He also said, “If one says, ‘if Allah wills,’ this is not objectionable, nor does doubt enter into it.”’”

Thus, it is reported from Ahmad that he said, “We do not doubt our faith,” and that the questioner does not doubt the faith of the person questioned. This is an even stronger statement. Yet he is certain only that he acknowledges and accepts as true what the Messenger brought; he is not certain that he is fulfilling his obligations. It is therefore clear that Ahmad and others among the early generations were certain, without doubt, of the faith present in the heart in this situation. They understood the qualification “if Allah wills” to refer to faith in its unqualified sense, which includes doing what is commanded.

They also argued that this qualification is permissible concerning matters about which one has no doubt. This is a “second rationale”: even though we do not doubt the faith within our hearts, the Sunnah has established the use of this qualification concerning things known to exist, because of the wisdom it contains.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Hārūn reported:

“I asked Abū ʿAbd Allāh about adding ‘if Allah wills’ when affirming one’s faith. He replied: ‘Yes, this qualification is used not out of doubt, but out of fear and caution concerning one’s deeds. Ibn Masʿūd and others used it, and this is the position of al-Thawrī. Allah Most High says:

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his Companions:

“Indeed, I hope to be the most mindful of Allah among you.”

And he said concerning the deceased:

“And upon it you will be resurrected, if Allah wills.”’”

Ahmad thus explained that he adds this qualification out of fear and caution concerning his deeds: he fears that he may not have fully accomplished what he was commanded to do, so he takes the precaution of adding “if Allah wills.” He said, “Not out of doubt,” meaning, without

Al-Khallāl said:

Muhammad ibn Abī Hārūn also informed me that Hubaysh ibn Sindī related to them concerning this question. Abū ʿAbd Allāh said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said when he stood by the graves: ‘We shall indeed join you, if Allah wills.’ Yet he had already been informed of his impending death and knew that he would die. “A man also asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘If one of us wakes up in a state of major ritual impurity, may he fast?’ He replied, ‘I do that, and then I fast.’ The man said, ‘You are not like us: Allah has forgiven your past and future sins.’ He replied, ‘By Allah, I do indeed hope to be the most fearful of Allah among you.’

“There are many such examples, all involving certainty.”

He said:

An elderly man came to him and asked him about faith. He told him, “It consists of words and deeds; it increases and decreases.”

The man asked, “Should I say, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills’?”

He replied, “Yes.”

The man said, “They tell me that I am in doubt.”

He replied, “What an evil thing they have said!”

Then the man left, and he said, “Bring him back.” He asked him, “Do they not say that faith consists of words and deeds, and that it increases and decreases?”

He replied, “Yes.”

He said, “These people themselves make this qualification.”

The man asked, “How so, Abū ʿAbd Allāh?”

He replied, “Tell them: ‘You maintain that faith consists of words and deeds. You have uttered the words, but you have not fulfilled the deeds. This qualification therefore concerns those deeds.’”

“Should one make this qualification when professing faith?”

He replied:

“Yes. I say, ‘I am a believer, if Allah wills.’ I make this qualification with certainty, not doubt.”

He then said:

“Allah says, ‘You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety.’ Allah Most High has thus declared that they will enter the Sacred Mosque.”

Ahmad thus made clear in his statement that he makes this qualification while remaining certain of the faith he presently possesses: he affirms it with his tongue, and his heart has no doubt about it. He makes the qualification because deeds are part of faith, and he is not certain that he has performed them fully; rather, he doubts this. Thus, he denied doubt and affirmed certainty regarding what he knows with certainty about himself, while affirming doubt regarding what he does not know to be present. He explained that this qualification is recommended concerning the latter—what a person does not know whether he has fulfilled or not—and is also permissible concerning what he knows with certainty.

Thus, even if he made the qualification concerning the very faith present in his heart, it would be permissible, as in the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“By Allah, I do indeed hope to be the most fearful of Allah among you.”

This concerns something present, not future: his being the most fearful of Allah among us. He does not hope to become the most fearful of Allah among us; rather, he hopes that, at the time of making this statement, he is the most fearful of Allah among us. Similarly, when a believer performs a deed, he hopes that Allah has accepted it from him and fears that He has not accepted it from him.

As Allah Most High says:

“And those who give what they give while their hearts tremble, knowing that they will return to their Lord.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is the man who prays, fasts, and gives charity, yet fears that it will not be accepted from him.”

Acceptance is a present or past matter, yet he entertains both hope and fear concerning it. This is because, when something has a future outcome, whether praiseworthy or blameworthy, and a person considers it possible that it has or has not occurred, he may be said to hope for it or to fear it. Hope and fear thus relate to the present and the past because the desired or dreaded outcome lies in the future. translated_text:
accepted it, in which case he will be deprived of its reward. Likewise, he fears that Allah may have become displeased with him for his disobedience and may therefore punish him for it.

When someone is pursuing a desired end—as with a merchant or a courier whom he has sent to attend to some business at a particular time—once that time has passed, he says, “I hope that so-and-so has taken care of that matter.” Its completion lies in the past, but the joy, happiness, and other desired benefits it brings him lie in the future.

At the time when pilgrims customarily enter Mecca, someone may say, “I hope they have entered.” Concerning a military detachment dispatched against the disbelievers, one may say, “We hope that Allah has granted the believers victory and spoils.” At the time when the Nile in Egypt rises, one may say, “We hope that the Nile has risen,” just as someone present in Egypt at such a time says, “We hope that the Nile will rise high this year.” When rain falls in some areas, someone who owns land and wishes for rain on it may be told, “I hope the rain has been widespread, and I hope that such-and-such a tract of land has received rain.” This is because what one hopes for is something whose occurrence brings joy and delight, whereas what one dreads is something whose occurrence causes pain.

This is connected to knowing what has happened, and that knowledge lies in the future. When someone learns that the Muslims have been victorious, that the pilgrims have entered, or that rain has fallen, he rejoices, and other objectives of his are thereby fulfilled. If matters turn out otherwise, that desired and welcome outcome is not attained. Thus, he says, “I hope” and “I fear,” because what brings joy or distress is connected to learning what has happened, and this lies in the future.

Likewise, the happiness and salvation sought through faith lie in the future. Thus, the qualification “if Allah wills” is made concerning present faith on this account, because the goal sought through it lies in the future. Moreover, every future outcome one seeks is contingent upon Allah’s will

translated_text:
even if one is certain that it will occur, since nothing in the future can occur except by Allah’s will.

Thus, our statement, “This will happen, if Allah wills,” is true, for it will happen only if Allah wills. The wording merely makes its occurrence conditional; making something conditional does not necessarily imply doubt. Rather, that depends on the speaker’s knowledge: sometimes he is doubtful, and sometimes he is not. Since doubt frequently accompanies this expression because people do not know how things will turn out, some have supposed that doubt forms part of its meaning. That is not so.

In His words,

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills,”

no doubt on Allah’s part is conceivable, nor indeed on the part of His Messenger, who was being addressed, or the believers. Hence Thaʿlab said: “This is a qualification made by Allah concerning something He knows, whereas created beings make such qualifications concerning what they do not know.”

Abū ʿUbaydah and Ibn Qutaybah said that in (“if”) here means idh (“when”), that is, “when Allah willed.” The point of this is to express the certainty of the action through in, just as it is expressed through idh. Strictly speaking, however, idh is an adverb specifying time, whereas in is a conditional particle.

If it is objected that the Arabs say, “When the unripe dates turn red, come to me,” but do not say, “If the unripe dates turn red,” the answer is: The purpose here is to specify the time of coming as the time when the dates turn red. They therefore use the temporal adverb that conveys certainty. The word in does not specify a time; it merely expresses a condition, linking the second action to the first. The parallel to the matter under discussion would be their saying, “The unripe dates will turn red and become sweet, if Allah wills.” This is true, and it is analogous to the expression in question.

If it is objected: Some people sought to avoid this meaning and took the qualification to refer to something uncertain. Thus al-Zajjāj said concerning “You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque”: that is, He commanded you

translated_text:
to do so. It has also been said that the qualification concerns security and fear: that is, “You will surely enter it in safety”; as for entering itself, there is no doubt about that. Another view is: “You will surely enter, all or some of you,” because He knew that some of them would die. The qualification thus concerns the fact that not all of them would enter.

The answer is that the proponents of all these views have fallen into the very difficulty they sought to escape, while also departing from the meaning conveyed by the Quran. They have thus distorted its meaning without gaining anything thereby. As for the interpretation, “Allah commanded you to do so,” He, glorified be He, already knew whether He would command them or not. His knowledge that He would command them to enter it is just like His knowledge that they would enter. They have therefore attached the qualification to something the wording does not indicate, although Allah’s knowledge encompasses both what is explicitly stated and what is implicit.

The same applies to their security and fear: He knows whether they will enter in safety or in fear. He stated that they would enter in safety, knowing that they would indeed enter in safety. Neither matter, then, involved any doubt on Allah’s part, nor indeed on the part of His Messenger.

As for the view, “All or some of them,” the answer is that what is made conditional upon His will is the entry of those intended by the wording. If He intended all of them, then all of them must enter it. If the majority were intended, then it is their entry that is made conditional upon His will. What He did not intend cannot be made conditional by in (“if”); rather, what is made conditional by in is what will occur. This was a promise whose fulfilment was certain. Thus, when ʿUmar said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah:

“Did you not tell us that we would come to the House and circumambulate it?”

He replied, “Yes. But did I tell you that you would come to it this year?”

He said, “No.”

He replied, “You will certainly come to it and circumambulate it.”

If it is asked, “Why did He not make the other promises in the Quran conditional in this way?” the answer is: Because this verse was revealed after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions had returned

{رُوِيَ أَنَّهُ رَأَى فِي الْمَنَامِ قَائِلًا يَقُولُ: لَتَدْخُلُنَّ الْمَسْجِدَ الْحَرَامَ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ فَأَصْبَحَ فَحَدَّثَ النَّاسَ بِرُؤْيَاهُ وَأَمَرَهُمْ بِالْخُرُوجِ إلَى الْعُمْرَةِ فَلَمْ تَحْصُلْ لَهُمْ الْعُمْرَةُ ذَلِكَ الْعَامَ فَنَزَلَتْ هَذِهِ الْآيَةُ}

 وَكَانَ قَوْلُهُ:
 
{إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ}
 هُنَا تَحْقِيقًا لِدُخُولِهِ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ يُحَقِّقُ ذَلِكَ لَكُمْ؛

" الصَّحِيحَيْنِ

 إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَاهَدُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ فُرْسَانًا أَجْمَعُونَ}
