Beyond this is the view of those who say: “There is no punishment at all; it is merely a threat with no reality behind it.” This is among the views of heretics and disbelievers. Some of them may cite His words:

“With this Allah warns His servants.”

Such a person should be told: A warning can inspire fear only if there is something fearsome that could actually befall the person being warned. If nothing could happen, there can be no genuine warning; all it amounts to is deluding frightened people with something unreal, as a small child may be deluded. It is well known that this cannot frighten rational, discerning people, for once they know that there is nothing to fear, their fear disappears.

This resembles the claim of the philosophizing “heretics,” the Qarmatians, and their like: that the Messengers, may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them, addressed people with outward promises and threats that have no underlying reality, but are merely parables intended to convey the soul’s condition after its separation from the body. According to them, although the promises and threats presented to people have no reality, they are held out solely for their worldly benefit, since people cannot be set right in any other way.

The falsity of “this view” is part of the elementary knowledge of the Messengers’ religion. Moreover, if matters were so, the intelligent among the Messengers’ closest followers would have known it. Once they knew it, they would cease to observe the commands and prohibitions, just as happens among the inner circles of the heretical philosophers and the Qarmatians—the Ismā‘īlīs, the Nusayrīs, and their like. For anyone among them who attains mastery in knowledge

and spiritual understanding is, in their view, no longer bound by commands and prohibitions: forbidden things become permissible for him, and obligations cease to bind him. Their rancor then becomes apparent, their secrets are exposed, and people at large discover the true nature of their hidden religion. Thus they came to be called the Bātiniyyah (esotericists), because they conceal beliefs contrary to what they outwardly profess.

If—Allah forbid—the religion of the Messengers were like this, its closest adherents would have known this and revealed its hidden teachings. Those possessed of knowledge and discernment would then have regarded it as akin to the religion of the Bātiniyyah. Yet it is self-evident that the Companions, who knew the Messenger’s inner and outward life better than anyone else and understood his purposes and intentions most fully, were the most steadfast of the entire community in obeying his commands—in private and in public—and maintained this obedience until death. Those closest to him and most intimately acquainted with his inner life—such as Abū Bakr and ʿUmar—were the most steadfast in obedience, privately and publicly, and the most diligent in fulfilling their obligations and avoiding what was forbidden, inwardly and outwardly.

In certain respects, the heretics among the Sufis have resembled these people. They hold that the spiritual wayfarer must perform what is commanded and refrain from what is forbidden until, as they claim, he attains spiritual knowledge and realization. At that point, religious obligations cease to bind him. They interpret the words of the Most High accordingly:

“And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.”

They claim that “certainty” means the spiritual knowledge they profess to possess. Here, however, certainty means death and what follows it, as the Most High says of the people of Hell:

“And we used to indulge in vain discourse with those who indulged in it,
And we used to deny the Day of Judgment,
Until certainty came to us.
So the intercession of intercessors will not benefit them.”

Al-Hasan al-Basrī said: “Allah has appointed no endpoint for His believing servants short of death.”

ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ تَنَازَعَ النَّاسُ فِي اسْمِ الْمُؤْمِنِ وَالْإِيمَانِ نِزَاعًا كَثِيرًا، مِنْهُ لَفْظِيٌّ،
translated_text:
and he recited this verse. Another example is the Prophet’s statement (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) when ʿUthmān ibn Mazʿūn died: “As for ʿUthmān ibn Mazʿūn, certainty has come to him from his Lord.”

These people may initially witness the divine decree—the cosmic reality—and suppose that the ultimate aim of one who possesses spiritual knowledge is to witness the decree and lose awareness even of this witnessing. In that state of witnessing, no distinction is made between what is commanded and what is forbidden, between what Allah loves and what He hates, or between His allies and His enemies.

One of them may say: “The spiritual knower first witnessed obedience and disobedience, then witnessed obedience without disobedience”—meaning obedience to the divine decree. Thus one of their shaykhs said: “I disbelieve in a Lord who can be disobeyed.” When he was told concerning a certain wrongdoer, “This man’s wealth is unlawful,” he replied: “Even if he has disobeyed the command, he has obeyed the will.”

They then advance “to the third state of witnessing”: neither obedience nor disobedience. This is the state of witnessing of those who profess the oneness of existence. This is the furthest extreme of the heresy of the innovators—the Jahmiyyah among the Sufis—just as Qarmatianism is the furthest extreme of Shiite heresy. These two forms of heresy closely resemble one another. Both contain forms of disbelief not found in the religion of the Jews, the Christians, or the Arab polytheists. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
and much of it substantive. The leading jurists did not dispute any of the rulings we have mentioned, although some were more knowledgeable about the religion and more steadfast in upholding it than others. Rather, they disputed terminology: whether faith increases and decreases; whether a profession of faith may be qualified; whether deeds form part of faith; and whether a sinful Muslim is a believer whose faith is complete.

What is transmitted from the Companions, the leading scholars of the generation that followed them, and the majority of the early generations—and is the position of the scholars of hadith and the view ascribed to Ahl al-Sunnah—is that faith consists of words and deeds, increasing through obedience and decreasing through disobedience, and that it is permissible to qualify one’s profession of faith. Thus, Umayr ibn Habīb al-Khatmī and other Companions said: “Faith increases and decreases.” He was asked: “How does it increase and decrease?” He replied:

“When we remember Allah, praise Him, and glorify Him, that is its increase. When we become heedless, forget, and neglect our duties, that is its decrease.”

These, then, are the expressions transmitted from the majority of them. Some of them, and many later scholars, would say: “Words, deeds, and intention.” Others would say: “Words, deeds, intention, and following the Sunnah.” Still others would say: “Speech of the tongue, conviction of the heart, and action of the bodily members”—that is, the limbs.

Some transmitted this last formulation as a saying traced back to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), in the collection attributed to Abū al-Salt al-Harawī, from Alī ibn Abī Mūsā al-Ridā. However, it is among the sayings fabricated and falsely attributed to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), according to the agreement of the scholars versed in his hadith.

There is no substantive difference between these expressions. Rather, in the usage of the early generations, the unqualified terms “words” and “deeds” encompass what is affirmed by the heart and spoken by the tongue, as well as the actions of the heart and the limbs. translated_text:
without conviction in the heart is the speech of hypocrites, and this is only called “words” with a qualification, as Allah Most High says:

“They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts.”

Likewise, actions of the limbs without actions of the heart are among the deeds of hypocrites, which Allah does not accept.

Thus, the formulation used by the early generations encompasses both inward and outward words and deeds. However, since some people might not understand that intention is included, some of them added: “And intention.” Others then explained that words, deeds, and intention are not accepted merely as such, but must conform to the Sunnah. This, too, is true. Those who said “words and deeds” intended to explain that faith encompasses these categories, not to specify the qualities those words and deeds must possess.

Likewise, whoever said, “Conviction of the heart, speech of the tongue, and action of the limbs,” used “speech” and “action” to designate outward manifestations, and therefore needed to add conviction of the heart. By “conviction of the heart,” he must also include the actions of the heart that accompany its affirmation of the truth, such as love of Allah, fear of Allah, reliance upon Allah, and the like. For the actions of the heart have an even stronger claim to inclusion in faith than the actions of the limbs, by agreement of all groups.

Some jurists of the generation following the Successors did not agree to describe faith as decreasing, because they found increase mentioned in the Quran but did not find decrease mentioned. This is one of the two views reported from Mālik. The other report from him—which is the well-known position among his followers—agrees with the position of the rest: that faith increases and decreases.

Some avoided the terms “increase” and “decrease” in favour of speaking of differences in degree, saying: “I say that faith differs in degree and varies.” This is reported from Ibn al-Mubārak.

and his aim was to turn away from a disputed expression to a meaning whose truth was beyond doubt. Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān and his followers denied that faith varies in degree, that deeds form part of it, and that one may qualify one’s profession of faith. These belonged to the Murji’ah among the jurists. As for Ibrāhīm al-Nakha‘ī—the leading scholar of Kufa and teacher of Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān—and others like him, together with his predecessors among the companions of Ibn Mas‘ūd, such as ‘Alqamah and al-Aswad, they were among the staunchest opponents of the Murji’ah and would qualify their professions of faith. Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, however, departed from his predecessors; others followed him, and various groups among the people of Kufa and subsequent generations adopted this position.

The “early generations and the imams” strongly denounced these people, declared them innovators, and spoke sternly against them. Yet I know of none of them who declared them unbelievers. Rather, they agreed that these people were not to be declared unbelievers on this account. Ahmad and other imams expressly stated that these Murji’ah were not to be declared unbelievers. Anyone who attributes to Ahmad or another imam a declaration that these people were unbelievers, or places them among those innovators whose unbelief is disputed, has made a grave error.

What is reliably transmitted from Ahmad and other such imams is the declaration of unbelief concerning the Jahmiyyah, the Mushabbihah—those who liken Allah to His creation—and others like them. Ahmad did not declare the “Khawārij” unbelievers, nor the “Qadariyyah” who affirmed Allah’s knowledge while denying that He creates human actions and that His will encompasses all things. However, two positions have been reported from him concerning whether they are to be declared unbelievers. As for the “Murji’ah,” his position that they are not to be declared unbelievers is consistent. Indeed, he prayed behind the Jahmiyyah who propagated their doctrine, subjected people to tests concerning it, and inflicted severe punishments on those who would not agree with them. Ahmad and others like him did not declare them unbelievers. Rather, he recognized their faith and leadership, prayed for them, and held the same position regarding praying behind them, performing Hajj and going to war with them, and the prohibition of rebelling against them as he did regarding comparable rulers.

At the same time, he condemned the false doctrine they had introduced, which constituted grave unbelief, even if they themselves did not know that it was unbelief. He opposed it and strove against them to secure its rejection as far as he could. Thus, he combined obedience to Allah and His Messenger in upholding the Sunnah and the religion and condemning the innovations of the heretical Jahmiyyah with respect for the rights of the believers, both rulers and the wider community—even if they were ignorant innovators or unjust evildoers.

Those well-known figures, such as Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, Abū Hanīfah, and other jurists of Kufa, regarded verbal profession and belief in the heart as components of faith. This was also the position of Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb and others like him. Their position on this did not vary, nor is it reported that they said faith consists solely in the heart’s assent.

Rather, they attributed this view to “Jahm ibn Safwān,” reporting that he said: “Faith consists solely in the heart’s knowledge, even without verbal acknowledgment.” They condemned this so strongly that Wakī‘ ibn al-Jarrāh, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others pronounced a general judgment of unbelief upon those who held this view, for it is one of the doctrines of the Jahmiyyah.

And His words:

They said: Iblīs neither disbelieved any report nor denied the truth, for Allah commanded him without a messenger. Rather, he disobeyed and acted arrogantly. Thus, he was an unbeliever without inwardly disbelieving. This matter is examined in detail elsewhere.

After these views, the doctrine of the Karrāmiyyah arose: faith consists in verbal profession without the heart’s assent. Yet they also held that such a person would be punished in the Hereafter and remain in the Fire forever.

Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Sālihī said that faith consists solely in the heart’s assent and knowledge, but necessarily entails certain things: if these are absent, this indicates that the heart’s assent is absent. Any outward statement or action that the revealed law identifies as unbelief is so designated because it indicates the absence of the heart’s assent and knowledge. Unbelief consists only in that one characteristic, and faith consists only in the assent and knowledge within the heart.

This is the better-known of the two positions attributed to Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī. His followers, such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr, Abū al-Ma‘ālī, and others like them, adopted it. For this reason, writers on doctrinal schools classified them among the Murji’ah. The other position reported from him agrees with that of the early generations and the scholars of hadith: faith consists in speech and action. A group of his followers adopted this position.

Nevertheless, he and the majority of his followers agreed with the scholars of hadith concerning qualifying one’s profession of faith by saying, “if Allah wills.” In his view, unqualified faith is the faith in which one ultimately dies, and this is what that qualification refers to;

He also forbade declaring without qualification that faith is created or uncreated, and wrote on this subject a treatise known among the people of the Sunnah in Kitāb al-Maqālāt (Book of Doctrinal Views). He stated that he upheld their position.

A group of later followers of Abū Hanīfah—such as Abū Mansūr al-Māturīdī and others like him—adopted a fundamentally similar position. They said that faith consists in what is within the heart, while outward profession is a condition for the application of worldly rulings. Yet these scholars endorse qualifying one’s profession of faith by saying “if Allah wills,” and related matters, as is known from their principles.

The underlying disagreement over faith among these groups—the Khawārij, Murji’ah, Mu‘tazilah, Jahmiyyah, and others—stems from their treating faith as a single entity: if any part of it disappears, all of it disappears; and if any part is present, all of it is present. Thus, they did not accept that some of it could disappear while some remained, as indicated by the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Whoever has a grain’s weight of faith in his heart will come out of the Fire.”

The Khawārij and Mu‘tazilah then said that all acts of obedience form part of faith. If some of these are lost, part of faith is lost, and consequently all the rest is lost. They therefore ruled that someone who commits a major sin has no faith whatsoever.

The Murji’ah and Jahmiyyah said that faith is only a single, indivisible thing: either the heart’s assent alone, as the Jahmiyyah hold, or the assent of both heart and tongue, as the Murji’ah hold. They argued that if deeds were included in faith, they would become part of it; if those deeds were lost, part of faith would be lost. This would necessarily mean excluding the person who commits a major sin from faith, which is the position of the Mu‘tazilah and Khawārij. Yet faith may have things that necessarily accompany it and signs that indicate it

 وَهَذَا قَوْل الْخَوَارِجِ وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ قَالُوا:
 وَلِأَنَّهُ يَلْزَمُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّجُلُ مُؤْمِنًا بِمَا فِيهِ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ كَافِرًا بِمَا فِيهِ مِنْ الْكُفْرِ فَيَقُومُ بِهِ كُفْرٌ وَإِيمَانٌ وَادَّعَوْا أَنَّ هَذَا خِلَافُ الْإِجْمَاعِ وَلِهَذِهِ الشُّبْهَةِ - وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ - امْتَنَعَ مَنْ امْتَنَعَ مِنْ أَئِمَّةِ الْفُقَهَاءِ أَنْ يَقُولَ بِنَقْصِهِ؛
 كَأَنَّهُ ظَنَّ:
 إذَا قَالَ ذَلِكَ يَلْزَمُ ذَهَابَهُ كُلَّهُ؛ بِخِلَافِ مَا إذَا زَادَ.
translated_text:
so that their absence is taken as evidence of its absence.

Each of the two groups regarded the early generations, the community, and the scholars of hadith as inconsistent because they said, “Faith consists of words and deeds,” yet also maintained that it does not disappear when some deeds are absent. Indeed, Ibn al-Khatīb and others like him considered al-Shāfi‘ī inconsistent on this point. Al-Shāfi‘ī was one of the leading scholars of the Sunnah, and his statements refuting the Murji’ah are well known. In the Book of Purification in al-Umm, he recorded the consensus of the Companions, their successors, and the generation following them upon the position of Ahl al-Sunnah. When Ibn al-Khatīb wrote a work on this subject—himself holding the position of Jahm and al-Sālihī concerning faith—he found al-Shāfi‘ī’s statement problematic and considered it contradictory.

The crux of their specious argument is that a composite entity ceases to exist when some of its constituent parts are removed. Take ten, for example: if part of it is removed, it is no longer ten. The same applies to physical compounds such as sakanjabīn: if either of its two ingredients is removed, it ceases to be sakanjabīn. They argued that if faith consists of outward and inward words and deeds, it must cease to exist when some of these are absent. This is the position of the Khawārij and Mu‘tazilah.

They further argued: “It would also follow that a person could be a believer by virtue of the faith within him and a disbeliever by virtue of the disbelief within him, so that both disbelief and faith would coexist in him.” They claimed that this was contrary to consensus.

It was because of this specious argument—and Allah knows best—that some leading jurists declined to say that faith decreases. It is as though they thought that affirming its decrease would necessarily imply its complete disappearance, whereas affirming its increase would not.

translated_text:
Furthermore, “this specious argument” is the very argument advanced by those who denied that obedience and disobedience could coexist in one person: obedience is part of faith, and disobedience is part of disbelief, so faith and disbelief cannot coexist in him. They said that a person can only be wholly a believer or wholly a disbeliever. They then extended their judgment concerning a single individual to a single deed, saying: “A single deed cannot be loved in one respect and disliked in another.” Abū Hāshim took this to an extreme, extending it to things united by kind. He said: “Within the general category of prostration, bowing, or any other action, some forms cannot constitute obedience while others constitute disobedience, because a single essence cannot be characterized by two different attributes. Rather, obedience and disobedience pertain to the actions of the heart—that is, the intention of the person prostrating—not to his outward action.” People strongly condemned this view of his, explaining how it contradicted consensus and denied self-evident truths established by revelation and reason, thereby demonstrating its invalidity.

The thinking of these people goes no further than contemplating an absolute, abstract essence conceived in their minds. Thus they say: “Faith considered in itself, and prostration considered in itself, cannot admit of degrees or differences,” and other such statements. Had they been rightly guided, they would have known that things existing outside the mind are distinguished by their particular characteristics, and that an absolute, abstract essence exists only in the mind. They would also have known that when people speak of differences and degrees, they are speaking of differences and degrees among existing things, not of degrees within something absolute and abstract in the mind that has no external existence. as conceived by the mind, then it admits of neither differences nor degrees. Yet this exists only in minds, not in external reality. Many who discuss the principles of jurisprudence have fallen into a similar error, denying that intellect, obligation, or prohibition admit of degrees. This denial is the position of Judge Abū Bakr, Ibn ‘Aqīl, and others like them. The majority, however, hold the opposite view, which is the position of Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī, Abū Muhammad al-Barbahārī, Judge Abū Ya‘lā, Abū al-Khattāb, and others. A similar error befell the logicians and philosophers, and those speculative theologians and proponents of union who followed them, in affirming the oneness and unity of the Necessary Existent. It ultimately led them to conclusions that entail sheer negation, as we have explained elsewhere.

The Greek logicians are inconsistent on this matter: one of them asserts a proposition and also asserts its contradictory, as detailed in the relevant discussion. Here we shall address what pertains to the present subject. We say—and there is no power nor strength except through Allah—that the discussion concerns “two aspects”:

First: Does the absence of one branch of faith necessarily entail the absence of the others?

Second: Does the presence of one necessarily entail the presence of the others?

translated_text:
As for the “first” aspect, when a reality comprises several elements—whether concrete entities or accidents—the loss of some of those elements may or may not entail the loss of the rest. The loss of some elements gathered together does not necessarily entail the loss of the others. Whether this whole is called composite, compound, or something else, the loss of some of its parts does not necessarily entail the loss of the rest.

Their examples of ten and oxymel (a honey-and-vinegar mixture) bear this out. If one is removed from ten, the remaining nine need not disappear; the nine may remain. Likewise, if one of a compound’s two components is lost, the other need not disappear. The most they can say, however, is that the combined form has ceased to exist, its configuration as a whole has disappeared, and it has lost the name it deserved by virtue of that combination and composition—just as the names “ten” and “oxymel” no longer apply.

The response is this: no reasonable person disputes that this composite whole no longer retains its original composition. Nor does any reasonable person claim that, when some elements of faith, prayer, Hajj, or other acts of worship comprising several elements are lost, that composite whole remains just as it was before those elements were lost. Likewise, the terms city, house, village, mosque, and similar expressions apply to an assembled whole; many of its parts may subsequently be lost, yet the name remains.

The same applies to the names of animals and plants. The term tree, for example, applies to the whole tree, including its branches and other parts. Since composite wholes are of two kinds—indeed, most belong to this kind—their claim that losing a part necessarily entails losing the name is unsound if the name can still apply to the remaining part. Clearly, the term “faith” belongs to this category, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no deity worthy of worship but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

It is also clear that when removing harmful things and similar acts are absent, the term “faith” does not cease to apply. It is authentically reported from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the two Sahīh collections that he said:

“Whoever has a grain’s weight of faith in his heart will come out of the Fire.”

He thus stated that faith is divisible, that some of it remains, and that this remaining portion is faith. It is therefore clear that some faith may be lost while some remains. This refutes their unsound premises and shows that the term “faith” is like the terms “Quran,” “prayer,” “Hajj,” and the like.

Hajj and similar acts include elements whose omission leaves Hajj short of its obligatory completeness without invalidating it, such as stoning the pillars, spending the night at Minā, and similar acts. They also include elements whose omission detracts from their recommended completeness, such as raising one’s voice in the pilgrimage proclamation, walking briskly with short steps, and baring the right shoulder during the first circumambulation. You have thus seen that the parts of a thing differ in their rulings, both under religious law and in the natural order. If an objector says, “This part belongs to its essence, while that part lies outside its essence,” he is asked, “What do you mean by ‘essence’?” If he says, “I mean that whose loss renders its possessor a disbeliever,” he is told: “In this respect, faith does not have a single essence—like the essence of what the term ‘Muslim’ denotes—for all legally accountable people at all times, as is the case with blackness and whiteness. Rather, faith and disbelief vary according to the accountable individual, whether the obligation has been communicated to him, whether the injunction imposing that obligation has ceased to apply, and so forth.”

Likewise, faith and what is obligatory for another person, considered without qualification, are not the same as the faith obligatory for him at every particular time. When Allah sent Muhammad as a messenger to creation, people were obliged to believe what he reported and obey what he commanded. At that time, he had not commanded them to perform the five daily prayers, fast the month of Ramadan, or make the pilgrimage to the House. Nor had he forbidden them wine, usury, and similar things, and most of the Quran had not yet been revealed. Whoever then believed him concerning what had been revealed of the Quran and acknowledged what he had commanded of the two testimonies of faith and their attendant requirements was, at that time, a believer whose faith was complete in all that was required of him. Yet, had he come with that same faith after the Hijrah, it would not have been accepted from him; had he confined himself to it, he would have been a disbeliever.

Imam Ahmad said: “Faith was incomplete at the outset, then continued to increase until it became complete.” For this reason,

translated_text:
Allah Most High said in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favor upon you.”

Furthermore, even after the Quran had been revealed and the religion perfected, if only part of the religion reached a person, he was required to believe in everything the Messenger brought in general, and in whatever had reached him from the Messenger in detail. As for what had not reached him and which he had no means of knowing, he was required to know it in detail only when it reached him.

Likewise, if a person believed firmly in the Messenger and died before the time for prayer began, or before any deeds became obligatory upon him, he died with complete faith in all that was required of him. Once the time for prayer begins, however, he must pray: something has now become obligatory upon him that was not obligatory before. Similarly, someone capable of performing the pilgrimage and engaging in jihad is required to have detailed belief and act accordingly in ways not required of someone else.

Thus, the requirements of faith vary according to the stage reached in the descent of revelation from heaven and according to whether or not its message has reached the legally accountable individual. These are among the factors that cause assent itself to vary. Its character also differs according to ability, inability, and other factors that give rise to obligation; these likewise cause the deeds required to differ. Clearly, what is obligatory upon each of these individuals is not identical to what is obligatory upon another.

If, then, the very content of faith required under a single revealed law varies and admits of degrees—even though all these forms share a common core, such as acknowledging the Creator, devoting religion sincerely to Him alone, and acknowledging His messengers and the Last Day in general—it is clear that when someone fulfills some of what is obligatory upon him but not the rest, his fulfillment of faith is partial, just as other obligations may be partially fulfilled.

It remains to be said:

The remaining part may or may not be a prerequisite for the part fulfilled. An example of its being a prerequisite is someone who believes in part of the Scripture and disbelieves in another part, or believes in some messengers and disbelieves in others. As Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, saying, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ and wish to adopt a way in between—”

“They are truly the disbelievers, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.”

The omitted part, however, may not be a prerequisite for either the existence or the acceptance of the other part. In that case, faith and hypocrisy may coexist within a person, as may some branches of faith and a branch of disbelief. Thus, it is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There are four traits which, if all are present in a person, make him a pure hypocrite. Whoever possesses one of them possesses a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when entrusted, he betrays the trust; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he behaves wickedly.”

It is also reported in the Sahīh that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever dies without having fought in battle or even contemplated doing so dies with a branch of hypocrisy.”

It is also established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Abū Dharr:

“You are a man who has a trait of pre-Islamic ignorance.”

It is also reported in the Sahīh that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There are four practices of pre-Islamic ignorance among my community that they will not abandon: boasting of ancestral standing, disparaging lineages, wailing over the dead, and seeking rain through the stars.”

It is also reported in the two Sahīh collections that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Abusing a Muslim is sinful disobedience

and fighting him is disbelief.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Two practices among people constitute disbelief on their part: disparaging lineage and wailing over the dead.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not disown your fathers, for disowning your fathers is disbelief on your part.”

This is also part of the Quran whose recitation was abrogated: “Do not disown your fathers, for disowning your fathers is disbelief on your part.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Dharr reported hearing the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“No man knowingly claims someone other than his own father as his father without committing disbelief. Whoever claims what is not his is not one of us, and let him take his seat in the Fire. Whoever accuses a man of disbelief or calls him ‘enemy of Allah’ when he is not such will have that accusation return upon himself.”

Al-Bukhārī’s wording is:

“No man knowingly claims someone other than his own father as his father without disbelieving in Allah. Whoever claims to belong to a people to whom he does not belong, let him take his seat in the Fire.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Jarīr and Ibn ʿUmar reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said during the Farewell Pilgrimage:

“Do not revert after me to being disbelievers, striking one another’s necks.”

Al-Bukhārī also narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbās. In al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If a man says to his brother, ‘You disbeliever,’ one of the two has incurred it.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Zayd ibn Khālid said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led us in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiyah after rain had fallen during the night. When he finished, he turned to the people and asked, ‘Do you know what your Lord said tonight?’ They replied, ‘Allah and His Messenger know best.’ He said, ‘He said: “This morning, among

My servants are those who believe in Me and those who disbelieve. Whoever says, ‘We were given rain by Allah’s grace and mercy,’ believes in Me and disbelieves in the star. But whoever says, ‘We were given rain through such-and-such a star,’ disbelieves in Me and believes in the star.”’”

In Sahīh Muslim, it is reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Have you not considered what your Lord has said? He said: ‘Whenever I bestow a blessing upon My servants, some of them disbelieve on account of it, saying, “It was through this star or those stars.”’”

There are other similar examples in the hadiths. Regarding the statements of Allah Most High, “Those who do not judge by what Allah has revealed—it is they who are disbelievers,” “it is they who are defiantly disobedient,” and “wrongdoers,” Ibn ʿAbbās and several other early scholars said: “A lesser form of disbelief, a lesser form of defiance, and a lesser form of wrongdoing.” Ahmad, al-Bukhārī, and others have mentioned this.

The second principle:

The branches of faith may entail one another when faith is strong, but not when it is weak. When the heart’s belief, knowledge, and love of Allah and His Messenger grow strong, this necessarily produces hatred of Allah’s enemies. As Allah Most High says:

“Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

He also says:

“You will not find people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their clan. Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

Yet a person may feel affection for them

It was because of this suspicion that “ʿUmar called Hātib a hypocrite, saying, ‘Let me, O Messenger of Allah, strike off this hypocrite’s head.’ He replied, ‘He was present at Badr.’” Thus, ʿUmar was acting on an interpretation when he called him a hypocrite, because of the suspicious act he had committed. The same applies to Usayd ibn Hudayr’s words to Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah: “By Allah’s life, you have spoken falsely! We will certainly kill him. You are nothing but a hypocrite arguing on behalf of the hypocrites.”

The same applies to the Companion who said of Mālik ibn al-Dukhshum, “He is a hypocrite,” even if he said this because he saw in him a degree of association with, and affection for, the hypocrites. Thus, those accused of hypocrisy were not all of one kind. Among them were outright hypocrites; others possessed both faith and hypocrisy; and others were predominantly believers but had a branch of hypocrisy within them. Many of their sins were assessed in light of how manifest faith had become. When faith grew strong, and its presence and strength became manifest in the year of Tabūk, they came to be reproached for hypocrisy over things for which they had not previously been reproached;

Hypocrisy, like disbelief, has lesser forms. Hence it is often said that there is disbelief that takes a person outside Islam and disbelief that does not, and major hypocrisy and minor hypocrisy, just as associating partners with Allah is said to be of two kinds: minor and major.

Hence it has been said that a sinful member of the Muslim community may be called a believer in one respect and denied that designation in another. This makes clear that a man may be a Muslim without being a believer or an outright hypocrite. Rather, he may possess the foundation of faith without fulfilling its obligatory requirements. For this reason, Ahmad and other leading scholars rejected the interpretation of the Prophet’s words, “is not one of us,” as meaning “is not like us” or “is not among the best of us.” Ahmad said, “This is the interpretation of the Murji’ah.” They argued that, on this interpretation, if someone did not commit this major sin, he would be like the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Likewise, the interpretation of the Khawārij and Mu‘tazilah—that such a person loses faith altogether and deserves to remain eternally in the Fire—is an objectionable interpretation, as explained earlier. Neither interpretation is correct.

This is further clarified by the well-known fact that knowing what is loved entails loving it, knowing what is revered entails revering it, and knowing what is feared entails fearing it. Thus, knowledge of Allah and affirmation of Him and His most beautiful names and most exalted attributes necessarily give rise to love, reverence, and awe of Him in the heart. This, in turn, necessarily gives rise to the desire to obey Him and an aversion to disobeying Him.

People have disputed at length whether an intention unaccompanied by action incurs punishment. Those who say that it does not cite the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

They also cite the hadith recorded in the two Sahīh collections from Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If a servant contemplates committing an evil deed, it is not recorded against him. If he commits it, it is recorded against him as a single evil deed. Another version states:

“If he refrains from it, record it for him as a good deed, for he refrained from it only for My sake.”

Those who say that it does incur punishment cite the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recorded in the Sahīh:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire.” He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, we understand the case of the killer, but what of the one killed?” He replied, “He intended to kill his opponent.”

They also cite the hadith narrated and graded authentic by al-Tirmidhī, from Abū Kabshah al-Anmārī, reporting from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning two men: one has been given knowledge and wealth and spends it in obedience to Allah; the other has been given knowledge but no wealth, and says, “If I had wealth like so-and-so, I would use it as he does.” The Prophet said, “They are equal in reward.” Another man has been given wealth by Allah but no knowledge, and spends it in disobedience to Allah; and another has been given neither knowledge nor wealth by Allah, and says, “If I had wealth like so-and-so, I would use it as he does.” The Prophet said, “They are equal in sin.”

 فَرْقٌ بَيْنَ الْهَمِّ وَالْإِرَادَةِ 
" فَالْهَمُّ "
 قَدْ لَا يَقْتَرِنُ بِهِ شَيْءٌ مِنْ الْأَعْمَالِ الظَّاهِرَةِ فَهَذَا لَا عُقُوبَةَ فِيهِ بِحَالِ بَلْ إنْ تَرَكَهُ لِلَّهِ كَمَا تَرَكَ يُوسُفُ هَمَّهُ أُثِيبَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ كَمَا أُثِيبَ يُوسُفُ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ أَحْمَد: الْهَمُّ هَمَّانِ: هَمُّ خَطِرَاتٍ، وَهَمُّ إصْرَارٍ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الَّذِي دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ أَنَّ يُوسُفَ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ فِي هَذِهِ الْقَضِيَّةِ ذَنَبٌ أَصْلًا بَلْ صَرَفَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ السُّوءَ وَالْفَحْشَاءَ إنَّهُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ؛ مَعَ مَا حَصَلَ مِنْ الْمُرَاوَدَةِ وَالْكَذِبِ وَالِاسْتِعَانَةِ عَلَيْهِ بِالنِّسْوَةِ وَحَبْسِهِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَسْبَابِ الَّتِي لَا يَكَادُ بَشَرٌ يَصْبِرُ مَعَهَا عَنْ الْفَاحِشَةِ وَلَكِنَّ يُوسُفَ اتَّقَى اللَّهَ وَصَبَرَ فَأَثَابَهُ اللَّهُ بِرَحْمَتِهِ فِي الدُّنْيَا. 
{وَلَأَجْرُ الْآخِرَةِ خَيْرٌ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَكَانُوا يَتَّقُونَ}
. وَأَمَّا 
" الْإِرَادَةُ الْجَازِمَةُ "
 فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَقْتَرِنَ بِهَا مَعَ الْقُدْرَةِ فِعْلُ الْمَقْدُورِ وَلَوْ بِنَظْرَةِ أَوْ حَرَكَةِ رَأْسٍ أَوْ لَفْظَةٍ أَوْ خُطْوَةٍ أَوْ تَحْرِيكِ بَدَنٍ؛ وَبِهَذَا يَظْهَرُ مَعْنَى قَوْلِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إذَا الْتَقَى الْمُسْلِمَانِ بِسَيْفَيْهِمَا فَالْقَاتِلُ وَالْمَقْتُولُ فِي النَّارِ}
.
 فَإِنَّ الْمَقْتُولَ أَرَادَ قَتْلَ صَاحِبِهِ فَعَمِلَ مَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ الْقِتَالِ وَعَجَزَ عَنْ حُصُولِ الْمُرَادِ وَكَذَلِكَ الَّذِي قَالَ:
 لَوْ أَنَّ لِي مِثْلَ مَا لِفُلَانِ لَعَمِلْت فِيهِ مِثْلَ مَا يَعْمَلُ فُلَانٌ فَإِنَّهُ أَرَادَ فِعْلَ مَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ وَهُوَ الْكَلَامُ وَلَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ 
(*)
 وَلِهَذَا كَانَ مَنْ دَعَا إلَى ضَلَالَةٍ كَانَ عَلَيْهِ مِثْلُ أَوْزَارِ مَنْ اتَّبَعَهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَنْقُصَ مِنْ أَوْزَارِهِمْ شَيْءٌ لِأَنَّهُ أَرَادَ ضَلَالَهُمْ فَفَعَلَ مَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ دُعَائِهِمْ إذْ لَا يَقْدِرُ إلَّا عَلَى ذَلِكَ.
original_footnote:
(*) قال الشيخ ناصر بن حمد الفهد (ص ٦٤):
ويظهر وقوع سقط، وأن صواب العبارة (ولم يقدر على غير ذلك) والله تعالى أعلم.
translated_text:
The distinction to be made here is this: there is a difference between contemplating a deed and intending it.

“Contemplation” may be unaccompanied by any outward action; in that case, it incurs no punishment whatsoever. Indeed, if a person abandons it for Allah’s sake, as Joseph abandoned what he had contemplated, he is rewarded for doing so, just as Joseph was rewarded. Hence Ahmad said, “Contemplation is of two kinds: passing thoughts and persistent resolve.”

Thus, the Quran indicates that Joseph committed no sin whatsoever in this affair. Rather, Allah turned evil and indecency away from him, for he was one of His chosen servants. This was despite the attempts to seduce him, the lies, the enlistment of the women against him, his imprisonment, and the other circumstances under which scarcely any human being could patiently refrain from sexual immorality. Yet Joseph feared Allah and remained patient, so Allah, in His mercy, rewarded him in this world.

“And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of Allah.”

As for “firm intention,” when a person has the ability to act, it must be accompanied by whatever action lies within his power—even a glance, a movement of the head, a word, a step, or a bodily movement. This clarifies the meaning of the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire.”

The one killed intended to kill his opponent and fought as best he could, but was unable to achieve his aim. The same applies to the man who said, “If I had wealth like so-and-so, I would use it as he does.” He intended to do what lay within his power, namely speaking, but was unable to do that (*).

Likewise, whoever calls others to misguidance bears a burden of sin equal to that of those who follow him, without their burdens being diminished in the least. This is because he intended their misguidance and did what lay within his power by calling them to it, since that alone was within his power.
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (p. 64):
There appears to be an omission; the correct wording would be: “and he was unable to do anything beyond that.” And Allah Most High knows best.

translated_text:
Once this relationship between “intention and action” is clear, the heart’s affirmation and knowledge entail action of the heart, just as sensory perception entails voluntary movement. For the soul has two faculties: the faculty of perceiving what is congenial or adverse, sensing it, acting upon it, and affirming it; and the faculty of loving what is congenial, hating what is adverse, and responding to perception through fear, hope, allegiance, and enmity. Perceiving what is congenial brings pleasure, joy, and happiness, while perceiving what is adverse brings pain and sorrow. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every child is born upon the natural disposition. Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to an intact offspring. Do you see any among them that is mutilated?”

Hearts are thus naturally disposed to acknowledge Allah, believing in Him and submitting to Him. Yet things arise that corrupt them. Knowing the truth entails loving it, and knowing falsehood entails hating it, because the natural disposition includes love of truth and hatred of falsehood. Yet things may arise that corrupt it: either doubts that prevent it from affirming the truth, or desires that prevent it from following it. Hence Allah has commanded us to say in prayer:

“Guide us to the straight path.”

“The path of those You have blessed—not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Jews have incurred Allah’s anger, and the Christians have gone astray.”

This is because the Jews recognize the truth as they recognize their own sons, yet do not follow it because of their arrogance and envy, which give rise to hatred of the truth and hostility towards it. The Christians practise worship, and in their hearts are compassion and mercy; they also invented monasticism. Yet this is without knowledge, so they are astray. The former have knowledge without a sound intention, while the latter

intend good without knowing what it is. Added to this are conjecture and the pursuit of desires, so that, in reality, neither beneficial knowledge nor beneficial intention remains. Rather, their condition is as Allah Most High said of the polytheists among the People of the Book:

“They will say, ‘Had we only listened or used our reason, we would not have been among the inhabitants of the Blaze.’”

Allah Most High also said:

“We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear. They are like cattle—indeed, they are further astray. It is they who are heedless.”

Thus, faith in the heart does not constitute faith through mere affirmation unaccompanied by the heart’s action and what it entails, such as love of Allah and His Messenger. Nor does mere conjecture and desire constitute faith. Rather, the very foundation of faith requires both the heart’s affirmation and the heart’s action. The word īmān (faith) is not synonymous with tasdīq (affirmation), as some people suppose.

For affirmation may be applied to any report. Someone who states something commonly known, such as “One is half of two” or “The sky is above the earth,” may be answered with “You have spoken the truth” and “We affirm that.” But one does not say, using the word for faith, “We believe you” or “We believe in this” unless what is reported concerns something unseen. Thus, regarding the person reporting it, one says, “We believe him,” and regarding what is reported, “We believe in it.” As Joseph’s brothers said:

“But you will not believe us.”

That is, you will not accept and affirm what we say, because they were reporting something he had not witnessed. Other examples include Allah Most High’s words:

“Should we believe you when the lowliest have followed you?”

And His words:

“He believes in Allah and believes the believers.”

And His words:

“Should we believe two human beings like ourselves, while their people serve us?”

And His words:

“If you do not believe me, then leave me alone.”

“Yet none believed Moses except some of the offspring of his people.”

That is, they accepted his word.

وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ الْإِيمَانَ يُفَارِقُ التَّصْدِيقَ أَيْ:
 لَفْظًا وَمَعْنًى؛
 فَإِنَّهُ أَيْضًا يُقَالُ:
 صَدَّقْته فَيَتَعَدَّى بِنَفْسِهِ إلَى الْمُصَدَّقِ وَلَا يُقَالُ أَمِنْته إلَّا مِنْ الْأَمَانِ الَّذِي هُوَ ضِدُّ الْإِخَافَةِ بَلْ آمَنْت لَهُ وَإِذَا سَاغَ أَنْ يُقَالَ: مَا أَنْتَ بِمُصَدِّقِ لِفُلَانِ كَمَا يُقَالُ: هَلْ أَنْتَ مُصَدِّقٌ لَهُ.
 لِأَنَّ الْفِعْلَ الْمُتَعَدِّيَ بِنَفْسِهِ إذَا قُدِّمَ مَفْعُولُهُ عَلَيْهِ أَوْ كَانَ الْعَامِلُ اسْمَ فَاعِلٍ وَنَحْوِهِ مِمَّا يَضْعُفُ عَنْ الْفِعْلِ فَقَدْ يُعَدُّونَهُ بِاللَّامِ تَقْوِيَةً لَهُ كَمَا يُقَالُ:

" الْفَرْقُ الثَّانِي "
: مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ أَنَّ الْإِيمَانَ لَا يُسْتَعْمَلُ فِي جَمِيعِ الْأَخْبَارِ بَلْ فِي الْإِخْبَارِ عَنْ الْأُمُورِ الْغَائِبَةِ وَنَحْوِهَا مِمَّا يَدْخُلُهَا الرَّيْبُ. فَإِذَا أَقَرَّ بِهَا الْمُسْتَمِعُ قِيلَ آمَنَ بِخِلَافِ لَفْظِ التَّصْدِيقِ فَإِنَّهُ عَامٌّ مُتَنَاوِلٌ لِجَمِيعِ الْأَخْبَارِ. وَأَمَّا 
" الْمَعْنَى "
: فَإِنَّ الْإِيمَانَ مَأْخُوذٌ مِنْ الْأَمْنِ الَّذِي هُوَ الطُّمَأْنِينَةُ؛
 كَمَا أَنَّ لَفْظَ الْإِقْرَارِ:
 مَأْخُوذٌ مِنْ قريقر وَهُوَ قَرِيبٌ مِنْ آمَنَ يَأْمَنُ؛ لَكِنَّ الصَّادِقَ يُطْمَأَنُّ إلَى خَبَرِهِ؛ وَالْكَاذِبَ بِخِلَافِ ذَلِكَ كَمَا يُقَالُ الصِّدْقُ طُمَأْنِينَةٌ وَالْكَذِبُ رِيبَةٌ؛
 فَالْمُؤْمِنُ دَخَلَ فِي الْأَمْنِ كَمَا أَنَّ الْمُقِرَّ دَخَلَ فِي الْإِقْرَارِ وَلَفْظُ الْإِقْرَارِ يَتَضَمَّنُ الِالْتِزَامَ ثُمَّ إنَّهُ يَكُونُ عَلَى وَجْهَيْنِ:
translated_text:
And this is because īmān (faith) differs from tasdīq (affirmation) in both wording and meaning. One says saddaqtuhu (“I affirm him”), so the verb takes the person affirmed as its direct object. But amintuhu is used only in connection with security, the opposite of causing fear; instead, one says āmantu lahu (“I believe him”).

If one may say mā anta bi-musaddiqin li-fulān (“You do not affirm so-and-so”), just as one says hal anta musaddiqun lahu (“Do you affirm him?”), this is because a verb that normally takes a direct object may take the preposition lām to reinforce its grammatical operation when its object precedes it, or when the governing word is an active participle or another form whose grammatical operation is weaker than that of a verb. Thus, one says: ‘araftu hādhā (“I knew this”) and anā bihi ‘ārif (“I know it”); darabtu hādhā (“I struck this”) and anā lahu dārib (“I strike it”); and samma‘tu hādhā wa-ra’aytuhu (“I made this heard and saw it”) and anā lahu sāmi‘ wa-rā’in (“I hear and see it”). Likewise, one says saddaqtuhu (“I affirm him”) and anā lahu musaddiq (“I affirm him”), but not saddaqtu lahu bihi (“I affirmed it to him”).

This differs from āmana: when affirmation is intended, one does not say āmantuhu, as one says aqrartu lahu (“I acknowledged it to him”). In this usage, one says āmantu lahu (“I believe him”), just as one says aqrartu lahu (“I acknowledged it to him”). This, then, is a difference in wording.

The “second difference” is what was mentioned earlier: the word īmān is not used for every report, but for reports about unseen matters and similar things concerning which doubt may arise. When the listener acknowledges them, he is said to have believed. By contrast, the word tasdīq is general and encompasses all reports.

As for “meaning,” īmān derives from amn (security), which is a state of reassurance, just as iqrār (acknowledgment) derives from qarra–yaqirru (to settle), which is close in meaning to being secure. A truthful person’s report inspires reassurance, whereas a liar’s does the opposite. As the saying goes, “Truthfulness brings reassurance, while lying brings doubt.” Thus, the believer enters a state of security, just as the one who acknowledges enters a state of acknowledgment. The word iqrār also entails commitment, and it takes two forms:

When a man is given a report that does not involve reassurance concerning the one reporting it, he is not said to “believe him,” unlike a report that does involve such reassurance. A person’s report may entail the listener’s obedience to him, or it may entail nothing beyond reassurance concerning his truthfulness. When it entails the listener’s obedience, the listener does not believe the speaker unless he commits himself to obeying him as well as affirming his truthfulness.

Indeed, the term “disbelief”—the opposite of faith—has been used for the very refusal to obey and submit. By the same reasoning, the term “faith,” like the term “acknowledgment,” may be used for the very commitment to obey and submit. Allah commanded Iblīs to prostrate before Adam, but he refused, acted arrogantly, and was among the disbelievers.

a declaration that the person reporting is truthful, while rejection as false is a declaration that he is lying. A man who is lying may sometimes be affirmed as truthful, while a truthful man may at other times be declared a liar. Affirmation and rejection as false are thus two kinds of report: both are reports about reports. As for realities that exist in their own right and may be known independently of any report, the terms “affirmation” and “rejection as false” are scarcely used of them unless someone reporting them is presupposed. This is unlike faith, acknowledgment, denial, repudiation, and similar terms, which apply both to realities and to reports about those realities.

Furthermore, beings may be loved or hated, befriended or opposed, obeyed or disobeyed; one may humble oneself before them or arrogantly refuse to do so. In relation to these beings, such meanings are specifically conveyed by the terms “faith,” “disbelief,” and the like. By contrast, terms such as “affirmation” and “truthfulness” apply to what is directed towards those beings, such as love and hatred. Thus one speaks of “true love” and “true hatred.” Just as truth and falsehood, when realities are affirmed or denied, pertain to the report affirming or denying them rather than directly to the reality itself, so too, in love, hatred, and the like, they pertain to the love or hatred rather than directly to the reality itself. This differs from the terms “faith” and “disbelief,” which apply directly to beings, without the mediation of acknowledgment or denial, love or hatred, reassurance or aversion.

This is borne out by the well-known transmitted supplication recited when touching the Black Stone:

“O Allah, with faith in You, affirmation of Your Book, fidelity to Your covenant, and adherence to the Sunnah of Your Prophet Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

It says “with faith in You,” not “affirmation of You,” whereas it says “affirmation of Your Book.” And the Most High said of

Mary:

“And she affirmed the words of her Lord and His Books.”

Thus He made affirmation pertain to words and books. Another example is the hadith in the Sahīh collection, in which the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Allah has given His guarantee to whoever goes out in His cause, motivated solely by faith in Me and affirmation of My words.”

Another version reads, “faith in Me and affirmation of My messengers”; and another, “motivated solely by striving in Allah’s cause and affirmation of His words.” In all these versions, the wording of affirmation pertains to words and messengers. Likewise, the hadith in the Sahīh collection states:

“The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—mentioned lofty stations in Paradise. He was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, those are stations that none but the prophets can attain.’ He replied, ‘On the contrary! By Him in whose hand is my soul, men who have faith in Allah and affirm the messengers can attain them.’”

One does not now find among the familiar usages in the speech of the early generations such expressions as “I have affirmed Allah,” “So-and-so affirms Allah,” “He affirmed Allah,” and the like, as one finds “So-and-so has faith,” “He has faith in Allah,” “with faith in Allah,” “We have faith in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers,” “We have faith in Allah alone,” and similar expressions. The Quran, hadith, and the speech of both the learned and ordinary people abound in such expressions as “faith in Allah,” “He has faith in Allah,” “We have faith in Allah,” and “O you who have faith.” Yet I know of no instance of “affirmation of Allah,” “They affirmed Allah,” “O you who have affirmed Allah,” or the like—unless there is something that does not come to mind at this moment, though I do not think there is.

The word “faith” is also used in relation to a report, as in:

“Each has faith in Allah,”

meaning that each acknowledges Him. The Messenger is believed insofar as he conveys a report, and one has faith in him insofar as his messengership is among the things he has reported, just as one has faith in Allah, His angels, and His Books. Thus “faith” entails acknowledgment of what he has reported

At other times, it is considered in terms of failing to acknowledge what he has reported. Fundamental to this is what he has reported about Allah and His names. Thus, denying matters in this category is graver than denying other matters, even though the Messenger has reported both.

Merely believing his report and knowing that what he has reported is true does not constitute faith if it is accompanied by neither inward nor outward obedience to his command, nor love or reverence for Allah. The disbelief of Iblīs, Pharaoh, the Jews, and others like them did not originate in a lack of belief or knowledge. No one conveyed a report to Iblīs; rather, Allah commanded him to prostrate before Adam, but he refused, acted arrogantly, and became one of the disbelievers. His disbelief consisted in refusal, arrogance, and what followed from them—not in disbelieving a report.

Likewise, Pharaoh and his people rejected the signs out of injustice and arrogance, though inwardly they were certain of them. Moses said to him:

“You know well that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent down these signs.”

The first is that arrogance, refusal, envy, and similar things that constitute disbelief necessarily entail the absence of the knowledge and affirmation that constitute faith. This is the basis of the position of Jahm, al-Sālihī, al-Ashʿarī—according to the view widely attributed to him—and most of his followers, such as Judge Abū Bakr and those who follow him. They regard inward and outward deeds as necessary consequences of faith, rather than constituents of faith itself, and regard whatever is indispensable to faith as an inseparable consequence of affirmation. On this view, inward affirmation cannot coexist with disbelief under any circumstances.

Alternatively, it may be said that the heart can possess knowledge and affirmation of the truth, while the envy, arrogance, and similar traits within it prevent its surrender, submission, and love. This is not comparable to the relationship between will and action, for will, when coupled with ability, necessarily brings about what is intended. Knowledge and affirmation of the truth, however, even when accompanied by the ability to act, do not necessarily produce that action. There must also be a desire for the truth and love for it.

Thus, if someone says, “Complete ability, without firm resolve, necessarily brings about the intended outcome that lies within one’s power and ensures its occurrence,” he is mistaken. Will is also indispensable.

This makes clear the error of those philosophers who say that Allah’s knowledge of created things alone necessarily brings them into existence. Likewise, people judge mistaken anyone who says that merely willing possible things, without the power to bring them about, necessarily brings them into existence. They likewise judge mistaken anyone who says that power alone suffices. Rather, knowledge, power, and will are all indispensable for bringing into existence what is within one’s power and intended. Will necessarily entails conceiving of what is intended and knowing it.

As for knowledge, will, power, and similar attributes, although it may be said that they necessarily accompany one another in a living being, or that life necessarily entails these attributes, or that some attributes depend upon others, there is no doubt that not everything known is willed

Rather, knowledge is indispensable, as is something else whereby one becomes the lover and the other the beloved.

Thus, the claim that mere knowledge and affirmation within a person constitute faith and necessarily produce deeds of the heart—so that their absence indicates the absence of knowledge—is comparable to saying that Allah’s mere knowledge of the order of the world necessarily brings it into existence, without any will on His part. It also resembles the philosophers’ claim that the soul’s happiness consists merely in knowing realities, without coupling this with love for Allah Most High and worship of Him, without which happiness cannot be complete. It is likewise comparable to saying that the perfection of the body or soul consists in love without any accompanying voluntary movement, or that pleasure consists merely in perception and awareness.

All rational people agree that this is mistaken. Rather, one must perceive something agreeable; and this agreeableness requires love on the part of the perceiver for what is perceived. That love, harmony, and agreeableness are not identical with perceiving the object and being aware of it.

Many philosophers, physicians, and their followers have said that “pleasure” is the perception of what is agreeable. Yet their account falls short. Rather, pleasure is a state that follows the perception of what is agreeable. Consider someone who loves and craves something sweet, then perceives it through tasting and eating. Pleasure is not merely the tasting itself, but something he experiences within himself that accompanies the tasting.

Thus, two things are required “initially,” and two “subsequently.” “Initially,” there must be awareness of the beloved object and love for it. What one has no awareness of cannot conceivably be desired; and what one is aware of, but has no love for within oneself, is not desired. Then, when

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the transmitted supplication:

“O Allah, I ask You for the pleasure of looking upon Your Face and the longing to meet You, without harmful affliction or a trial that leads astray.”

And in the authentic hadith:

“When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will announce, ‘O people of Paradise, Allah has made you a promise that He wishes to fulfil for you.’ They will say, ‘What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise, and protected us from the Fire?’ He said: ‘Then He will lift the veil, and they will look upon Him. Nothing He has given them will be dearer to them than looking upon Him.’”

Narrated by Muslim and others. Pleasure thus accompanies looking upon Him. Nothing is dearer to them than looking upon Him because of the pleasure that accompanies it—not because looking itself is pleasure.

In sum, faith in the heart must include believing in Allah and His Messenger and loving Allah and His Messenger. Mere belief accompanied by hatred of Allah and His Messenger and hostility towards Allah and His Messenger is not faith, by the consensus of the Muslims. Mere belief and knowledge do not necessarily entail love unless the heart is free of obstacles such as envy and pride, for the soul is naturally disposed to love the truth, which accords with its nature. Nothing is dearer to sound hearts than Allah. This is pure monotheism, the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, whom Allah took as an intimate friend.

Allah Most High said:

“On the Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit, except to one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.”

Thus, mere

knowledge does not necessarily produce love for its object unless the soul possesses another faculty attuned to that object—and this faculty does exist in the soul. Each of these two faculties strengthens the other: knowledge strengthens action, and action strengthens knowledge. Whoever knows Allah and has a sound heart loves Him. The more he knows Him, the more he loves Him; and the more he loves Him, the more he remembers Him and knows His names and attributes. Strong love leads to frequent remembrance of the beloved, just as hatred leads one to avoid mentioning the one one hates. Whoever is hostile to Allah and His Messenger and sets himself against Allah and His Messenger is thereby led to refrain from speaking well of Allah and His Messenger and from mentioning what inspires love. His knowledge of Him consequently weakens, until he may even forget Him.

As Allah Most High said:

“And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves.”

And Allah Most High said:

“And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his own desires, and whose conduct is beyond all bounds.”

Belief and knowledge may nevertheless coexist with hatred and hostility, but they are weak belief and weak knowledge. Were it not for that hatred and hostility, however, this would produce enough love for Allah and His Messenger to make the person a believer. Thus, complete knowledge is a condition of faith. Hence, the correct view is that ignorance of some of Allah’s names and attributes does not make a person a disbeliever, provided that he acknowledges what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, and nothing has reached him that would require him to know what he is ignorant of in such a way that his failure to know it would constitute disbelief. An example is the hadith of the man who instructed his family to burn him and then scatter his ashes. Indeed, those who know Allah differ in their knowledge of Him. This is why someone who does not act upon his knowledge is described as ignorant and lacking knowledge.

Allah Most High said:

“Allah only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon afterwards.”

translated_text:
“I asked the Companions of Muhammad about this verse, and they told me: ‘Everyone who disobeys Allah is ignorant, and everyone who repents before death has repented soon afterwards.’”

Another example is the statement of Ibn Masʿūd: “To fear Allah is knowledge enough, and to be deluded about Allah is ignorance enough.” Al-Shaʿbī was once addressed as “O scholar!” He replied: “The scholar is one who fears Allah.” Allah Most High has said:

“Of all His servants, only those with knowledge fear Allah.”

Abū Hayyān al-Taymī said: “Scholars are of three kinds: one who knows Allah and His commands; one who knows Allah but does not know His commands; and one who knows His commands but does not know Allah. The one who knows Allah is he who fears Him, and the one who knows Allah’s commands is he who knows His limits and prescribed duties.”

Allah Most High has said:

“Of all His servants, only those with knowledge fear Allah.”

This indicates that everyone who fears Allah possesses knowledge, which is true. It does not indicate that everyone who possesses knowledge fears Him. However, since knowledge of Him necessarily produces fear when nothing counteracts it, the absence of that fear indicates weakness in the underlying knowledge: were that knowledge strong, it would overcome whatever counteracts it.

Likewise, the word “intellect” may refer to the innate faculty through which one acquires knowledge, to various kinds of knowledge, or to acting as that knowledge requires. Similarly, the word “ignorance” may express either the absence of knowledge or the failure to act as knowledge requires. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When one of you is fasting, let him neither speak obscenely nor behave foolishly. If someone insults him or fights him, let him say: ‘I am a man who is fasting.’”

Here, ignorance means wrongful speech, akin to compound ignorance. Another example is the poet’s saying:

Let no one act foolishly toward us—
Or we shall outdo the foolish in their folly.

It is in this sense that jāhiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) received its name: it involves either a lack of knowledge or a failure to act upon it. Another example is the Prophet’s saying to Abū Dharr, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he exchanged insults with a man and taunted him about his mother: “You are a man who still has a trait of pre-Islamic ignorance.” Allah Most High has also said:

“When those who disbelieved harboured pride in their hearts—the pride of the Age of Ignorance.”

Anger and pride drive a person to do what harms him and abandon what benefits him. This is ignorance in the sense of acting contrary to knowledge: a person may go so far as to do what he knows will harm him and abandon what he knows will benefit him, because of the hatred and hostility he harbours towards certain people and actions. In this state, he is not entirely devoid of knowledge and assent to the truth. Rather, because of the hatred and envy within him, their demands overpower the dictates of knowledge. The absence of the effects and conduct that knowledge should produce thus indicates its weakness.

Yet this effect and outcome do not arise from knowledge alone, but from knowledge together with the soul’s love of what benefits it and hatred of what harms it. If the soul contracts a disease that corrupts it, it comes to love what harms it and hate what benefits it. It then becomes like a sick person who consumes something harmful because he craves it, despite knowing that it harms him.

I say: This is the meaning of the report attributed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah loves penetrating insight when doubts arise, and He loves sound reason when desires assail.”

Al-Bayhaqī related it as a mursal report (one attributed directly to the Prophet by a Successor). Allah Most High has said:

“And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, men of strength and insight.”

He thus described them as possessing strength in action and insight in knowledge. The foundation of strength is strength of heart, which gives rise to love of good and hatred of evil. The believer’s strength lies in his heart and his weakness in his body, whereas the hypocrite’s strength lies in his body and his weakness in his heart. Thus, faith must

Perfect love, when accompanied by ability, necessarily entails bodily activity in the form of outward speech and action, as explained above. Whoever regards knowledge and affirmation alone as necessarily producing everything encompassed by the term faith, and everything called faith, is mistaken. Rather, both knowledge and love are essential.

Knowledge is a prerequisite for loving the beloved, just as life is a prerequisite for knowledge. Yet knowing something and affirming its existence do not necessarily entail loving it, unless there is something within the lover that draws him to what he knows and gives him reason to love it. Thus, a person affirms the existence of many things and knows them while hating them. For example, he affirms the existence of devils and disbelievers while hating them. Merely affirming something’s existence does not entail loving it.

Allah, glorified is He, however, deserves in Himself to be loved and worshipped, and His Messenger deserves to be loved for His sake. Hearts possess an innate disposition that calls for loving and obeying Him, just as they possess a disposition that calls for knowing Him and affirming belief in Him. Whoever affirms belief in Him and His Messenger but does not love Him and His Messenger is not a believer until, alongside that affirmation, he also possesses love for Him and His Messenger.

When affirmation of belief in Him and love for Him are established in the heart, the body must necessarily respond with the outward words and deeds that they entail. The words and deeds manifested by the body are the necessary consequence of what is in the heart, its evidence and its effect. Likewise, the body’s words and deeds also influence what is in the heart. Each thus influences the other, but the heart is the root, and the body its branch. The branch draws sustenance from its root, while the root is strengthened and made firm by its branch. This is like the tree used as a parable for the declaration of faith. He says:

exalted is He:

“Allah sets forth a parable: a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firmly established and whose branches reach into the sky. It yields its fruit at all times by its Lord’s permission.”

This is the declaration of Allah’s oneness. The stronger, more deeply rooted, and better watered a tree’s root becomes, the stronger its branches become. Likewise, when its branches are nourished by rain and wind, this affects its root. The same applies to “faith” in the heart and “Islam” as outwardly manifested. Since outward words and deeds both necessarily follow from and necessarily imply inward words and deeds, the former serve as evidence of the latter, as in His saying, exalted is He:

“You will not find people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kinsfolk. Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Him.”

He thus states that those who believe in Allah and the Last Day will not be found showing affection for the enemies of Allah and His Messenger. Rather, faith itself is incompatible with affection for them. If such affection arises, it indicates a deficiency in faith. Likewise, He says:

“You see many of them taking the disbelievers as allies. Evil indeed is what their souls have sent ahead for them: Allah is angry with them, and they will abide in the punishment forever.”

“Had they believed in Allah, the Prophet, and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

Likewise, He says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He, exalted is He, thus states that these are the ones who are truthful when they say, “We believe.” This indicates that, among those who say, “We believe,” some are truthful and others are lying. The one who lies has hypocrisy in proportion to his lying.

Allah, exalted is He, says concerning the hypocrites:

“Among the people are those who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ yet they are not believers.”

—through to His saying—

“They will have a painful punishment because they used to lie.”

There are two well-known readings of yakdhibūn (“they lie”). A hadith states:

“The foundation upon which hypocrisy is built is lying.”

Allah, exalted is He, says:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.’ Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars.”

He, exalted is He, also says:

“Among them are those who pledged to Allah, ‘If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and be among the righteous.’ But when He gave them of His bounty, they became miserly with it and turned away in aversion. So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they broke their promise to Allah and because they used to lie.”

He also says:

“Among them are those who criticize you concerning the charitable alms.”

There are many similar passages.

In short, no one who reflects on what he is saying can doubt that a man does not become a believer merely through assent in his heart while hating Allah and His Messenger, arrogantly refusing to worship Him, and showing hostility towards Him and His Messenger. For this reason, the great majority of the Murji’ah held that the actions of the heart are included in faith, as reported by writers on sectarian doctrines. Among them is al-Ash‘arī, who said in his book, Maqālāt (Doctrinal Views):

" الْفِرْقَةُ الْعَاشِرَةُ "
: مِنْ الْمُرْجِئَةِ أَصْحَابُ أَبِي مُعَاذٍ التومني يَزْعُمُونَ: أَنَّ الْإِيمَانَ تَرْكُ مَا عَظُمَ مِنْ الْكَبَائِرِ وَهُوَ اسْمٌ لِخِصَالِ إذَا تَرَكَهَا أَوْ تَرَكَ خَصْلَةً مِنْهَا كَانَ كَافِرًا فَتِلْكَ الْخَصْلَةُ الَّتِي يَكْفُرُ بِتَرْكِهَا إيمَانٌ وَكُلُّ طَاعَةٍ إذَا تَرَكَهَا التَّارِكُ لَمْ يُجْمِعْ الْمُسْلِمُونَ عَلَى تَكْفِيرِهِ فَتِلْكَ الطَّاعَةُ شَرِيعَةٌ مِنْ شَرَائِعِ الْإِيمَانِ تَارِكُهَا إنْ كَانَتْ فَرِيضَةً يُوصَفُ بِالْفِسْقِ فَيُقَالُ لَهُ إنَّهُ يَفْسُقُ وَلَا يُسَمَّى بِالْفِسْقِ وَلَا يُقَالُ فَاسِقٌ وَلَيْسَتْ تَخْرُجُ الْكَبَائِرُ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ إذَا لَمْ تَكُنْ كُفْرًا وَتَارِكُ الْفَرَائِضِ مِثْلَ الصَّلَاةِ وَالصِّيَامِ وَالْحَجِّ عَلَى الْجُحُودِ بِهَا وَالرَّدِّ لَهَا وَالِاسْتِخْفَافِ بِهَا كَافِرٌ بِاَللَّهِ وَإِنَّمَا كَفَرَ لِلِاسْتِخْفَافِ وَالرَّدِّ وَالْجُحُودِ،
 وَإِنْ تَرَكَهَا غَيْرَ مُسْتَحِلٍّ لِتَرْكِهَا مُتَشَاغِلًا مُسَوِّفًا يَقُولُ:
 السَّاعَةَ أُصَلِّي وَإِذَا فَرَغْت مِنْ لَهْوِي وَعَمَلِي فَلَيْسَ بِكَافِرِ وَإِنْ كَانَ يُصَلِّي يَوْمًا وَوَقْتًا مِنْ الْأَوْقَاتِ. وَلَكِنْ نُفَسِّقُهُ.
 وَكَانَ أَبُو مُعَاذٍ يَقُولُ:
 مَنْ قَتَلَ نَبِيًّا أَوْ لَطَمَهُ كَفَرَ وَلَيْسَ مِنْ أَجْلِ اللَّطْمَةِ كَفَرَ وَلَكِنْ مِنْ أَجْلِ الِاسْتِخْفَافِ وَالْعَدَاوَةِ وَالْبُغْضِ لَهُ.
