The ninth group of the Murjiʾah consists of those who affiliate themselves with Abū Hanīfah and his followers. They claim that faith consists of knowing Allah and the Messenger, and acknowledging what has come from Allah in general, without detailed specification.

The tenth group of the Murjiʾah consists of the followers of Abū Muʿādh al-Tūmanī. They claim that faith consists of avoiding the gravest major sins. It is a designation for qualities whose abandonment, whether altogether or individually, renders a person a disbeliever. Thus, any quality whose abandonment constitutes disbelief is faith. As for any act of obedience whose omission is not unanimously held by Muslims to constitute disbelief, it is one of the ordinances of faith. If that act is obligatory, the person who abandons it is described as committing sinful conduct: one says that he acts sinfully, but does not label him a sinner. Major sins do not exclude a person from faith, provided they do not constitute disbelief.

Whoever abandons obligations such as prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage out of denial, rejection, or contempt for them is a disbeliever in Allah. His disbelief is due to that contempt, rejection, and denial. But if he abandons them without considering their abandonment lawful, being distracted and procrastinating, saying, “I will pray shortly, when I have finished my amusement and my work,” he is not a disbeliever, even if he prays on a given day and at one of the prayer times. Nevertheless, we deem him guilty of sinful conduct.

Abū Muʿādh used to say: “Whoever kills or slaps a prophet becomes a disbeliever. His disbelief is not because of the slap itself, but because of his contempt, hostility, and hatred toward him.”

translated_text:
The eleventh group of the Murjiʾah consists of the followers of Bishr al-Marīsī. They say that faith is assent, because faith in the linguistic sense means assent, and whatever is not assent is not faith. Bishr claims that assent involves both the heart and the tongue. Ibn al-Rāwandī also held this view. Ibn al-Rāwandī claimed that disbelief consists of denial, rejection, concealment, and covering; nothing can constitute disbelief unless it is disbelief in the linguistic sense, and nothing can constitute faith unless it is faith in the linguistic sense. He claimed that prostrating to the sun is not disbelief, nor is prostrating to anything other than Allah disbelief. Rather, it is a sign of disbelief, because Allah has made clear that only a disbeliever prostrates to the sun.

He said: “The twelfth group of the Murjiʾah is the Karrāmiyyah, the followers of Muhammad ibn Karrām. They claim that faith consists of acknowledgement and assent with the tongue, without the heart. They deny that knowledge in the heart, or anything other than verbal assent, constitutes faith.”

Most of these views that al-Ashʿarī reported from the Murjiʾah imply that, according to them, faith necessarily includes some actions of the heart. Only a small minority disputed this, such as Jahm and al-Sālihī.

In al-Maqālāt, he also presented a summary of the position of the adherents of hadith and the people of the Sunnah. He said:

“In summary, the adherents of hadith and the people of the Sunnah affirm Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, what has come from Allah, and what trustworthy narrators have transmitted from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They reject none of this. They affirm that Allah is one God, unique, the Self-Sufficient, who has taken no consort

‘The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.’

They affirm that He has two hands, without specifying how, as He said:

‘Whom I created with My two hands.’

And as He said:

‘Rather, both His hands are outstretched.’

They affirm that He has two eyes, as He said:

‘Sailing under Our eyes.’

And that He has a face, as He said:

They affirm that Allah’s names must not be described as other than Allah, as the Muʿtazilah and the Khawārij have claimed.”

He went on to say:

“They say that the Quran is the speech of Allah, uncreated, and that discourse concerning suspension of judgment and the utterance is an innovation. Whoever advocates suspension of judgment or a position concerning the utterance is, in their view, an innovator. One must neither say that uttering the Quran is created nor that it is uncreated.”

He went on to say:

“They do not declare anyone among those who face the qiblah to be a disbeliever because of a sin he commits, such as fornication, theft, or similar major sins. They remain believers by virtue of the faith they possess, even if they commit major sins.

“In their view, faith consists of believing in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and divine decree—its good and its evil, its sweetness and its bitterness—and believing that whatever missed them could never have befallen them, and whatever befell them could never have missed them. Islam is to testify that there is no god but Allah, as stated in the hadith. In their view, Islam is distinct from faith.”

He went on to say:

“They affirm that faith consists of speech and action, that it increases and decreases, and they do not say that it is created or that it is uncreated.”

This is his position in this book, in which he agreed with Ahl al-Sunnah and the adherents of hadith, contrary to the position he defended in al-Mūjaz. The point here is that most groups within the Muslim community include acts of the heart within faith. Even most groups among the Murjiʾah affirm this. As for the Muʿtazilah, the Khawārij, Ahl al-Sunnah, and the adherents of hadith, their position on this is well known. Only those Murjiʾah who followed Jahm ibn Safwān disputed it. This position is anomalous, just as the position of the Karrāmiyyah, who say that faith consists merely of verbal profession, is also anomalous.

This, too, deserves careful attention. Many who discuss “the question of faith”—whether deeds are included in it and whether it consists of speech and action—suppose that the disagreement concerns only bodily deeds, and that “speech” means verbal profession. This is mistaken. By Muslim consensus, mere verbal profession without inward belief does not constitute faith. Nor, according to Muslims generally, does inward assent alone constitute faith, apart from certain outliers among the followers of Jahm and al-Sālihī. Their position involves greater intellectual sophistry and more serious conflict with religious rulings than Ibn Karrām’s position does, except in the case of certain outliers among Ibn Karrām’s followers.

Likewise, the heart’s assent, when unaccompanied by love or reverence for Allah, but instead accompanied by hatred and hostility towards Allah and His messengers, is not faith by Muslim consensus.

Ibn Karrām’s position differs in designation, not in judgment. Although he calls the hypocrites believers, he says that they will remain in the Fire eternally. Thus, he differs from the Muslim community in designation, not in judgment, whereas the followers of Jahm differ in both designation and judgment.

Section

Once it is understood that faith is rooted in the heart, the term “faith” sometimes refers to the heart’s inward affirmations and acts, such as assent, love, reverence, and the like. Outward words and deeds are then its necessary consequences, effects, and signs. At other times, it refers to what is in both the heart and the body, thus including what faith entails and requires within the meaning of the term. This makes clear that outward deeds are called Islam, and that they sometimes fall within the meaning of faith and sometimes do not.

This is because the meaning of a single term varies according to whether it is used alone or alongside another term. Used alone, it may encompass two meanings; when paired with another term, it may denote only one of them. For example, when either “the poor” or “the needy” is used alone, it includes the other; when the two are mentioned together, each denotes a distinct category. Likewise, when “what is right” and “what is wrong” are used without qualification, as in the words of the Most High:

“He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong,”

this includes immorality and transgression. But when “what is wrong” is mentioned alongside either one of these, as in His words:

“Indeed, prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing,”

or alongside both, as in the words of the Most High:

“And He forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and transgression,”

When the term “faith” is used alone, it may encompass both, as in the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘None has the right to be worshipped but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road.”

In this case, Islam falls within the meaning of faith and forms part of it. Thus, “faith” is said to encompass all inward and outward acts of obedience. Another example is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, to the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays:

“I command you to have faith in Allah. Do you know what faith in Allah is? To testify that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to establish prayer, to give zakah, to fast Ramadan, and to pay one-fifth of the spoils.”

This was recorded in the two Sahīh collections. Here he explained faith in the same terms with which he explained Islam, because by the two testimonies he meant bearing witness to them both inwardly and outwardly. He was addressing the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays, who were among the best of people. They were the first to hold Friday prayer in their own locality after the people of Medina, as Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“The first Friday prayer held in Islam after the Friday prayer in Medina was at Jawāthā, a village in Bahrain.”

They said:

When, however, faith is mentioned alongside Islam, faith is in the heart, while Islam is outward, as reported in al-Musnad from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Islam is outward, and faith is in the heart. Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death, and to believe in divine decree, both its good and its evil.”

Whenever a person attains this faith, it necessarily follows that he also attains Islam: the two testimonies of faith, prayer, zakah, fasting, and Hajj. His belief in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers entails surrender and submission to Allah. It is impossible for acknowledgment, love, and submission to exist inwardly without being expressed outwardly when one is able to do so, just as firm resolve, coupled with the ability to act, cannot exist without the intended act taking place.

From this, you can understand that someone whose heart has firm faith cannot fail to utter the two testimonies when able to do so. Failure to utter them despite having the ability necessarily entails the absence of complete faith in the heart. This reveals the error of Jahm and his followers in claiming that mere faith, without outward faith, benefits a person in the Hereafter. This is impossible, for complete faith cannot exist in the heart without its necessary consequences appearing outwardly, according to one’s ability. It is impossible for someone to love another with firm love, be able to maintain ties with him, and yet make no outward move toward doing so.

Had it stemmed from faith in his heart, he would necessarily have uttered the two testimonies. The very motive that led him to support the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him—family loyalty—also led him to refuse to utter the two testimonies, unlike Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and others like him. Allah Most High says:

“But the most righteous will be kept away from it—the one who gives his wealth to purify himself, not to repay anyone for a favor, but only seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High. And he will surely be pleased.”

Errors in these matters arise in several ways:

(First) The belief that knowledge and assent necessarily entail everything that faith requires.

(Second) The assumption that people do not differ in what is within their hearts.

(Third) The assumption that acceptable faith can exist in the heart without outward speech and outward action.

(Fourth) The assumption that there is nothing in the heart but assent, and nothing outward but the actions of the limbs. The correct understanding is that the heart has actions alongside assent, while what is outward comprises both speech and action; both necessarily entail what is inward.

The Murjiʾah excluded outward action from faith. Those among them who also intended to exclude the actions of the heart, treating them as nothing more than assent, are plainly astray. As for those who intended to exclude outward action, they are told: outward action necessarily accompanies inward action and cannot be separated from it; the absence of what is outward is evidence of the absence of what is inward.

Thus, the remaining dispute concerns whether outward action is part of what the term “faith” denotes, conveyed by inclusion within its meaning, or a necessary concomitant of what it denotes.

The precise answer is that outward action is sometimes included within the term and sometimes necessarily accompanies what it denotes, depending on whether the term is used alone or alongside another term. When faith is mentioned alongside Islam, what “Islam” denotes falls outside the meaning of “faith,” as in the hadith of Gabriel, although it necessarily accompanies it. Likewise, when faith is mentioned alongside deeds, as in His words:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds,”

one may say that deeds are not included within the term “faith,” although they necessarily accompany it. Alternatively, one may say that they are included, and that their separate mention joins the particular to the general. In either case, deeds give practical expression to what faith denotes and confirm it. For this reason, a group of scholars—including Shaykh Abū Ismā'īl al-Ansārī? and others—said: Faith consists entirely of affirmation: the heart affirms what the messengers brought, the tongue confirms what is in the heart, and deeds confirm speech, as when one says, “His deeds confirmed his words.” Another example is the Prophet’s saying, peace and blessings be upon him:

“The eyes commit fornication, and their fornication is looking; the ears commit fornication, and their fornication is listening; the hand commits fornication, and its fornication is grasping; the foot commits fornication, and its fornication is walking. The heart wishes and desires, and the private parts confirm this or belie it.”

Affirmation applies both to reports and to intent. Thus, one says, “So-and-so is sincere in his resolve,” “sincere in his love,” and “They launched a resolute charge.”

is among the gravest errors. People are not equal in affirmation, love, reverent fear, or knowledge; rather, they differ in degree in many respects.

Moreover, their exclusion of deeds suggests that they have also excluded deeds of the heart, and this is unquestionably false. Someone who affirms the Messenger’s truthfulness yet hates him and opposes him in heart and deed is unquestionably a disbeliever, as is self-evident. If, however, they include deeds of the heart within faith, they are still mistaken, since faith cannot exist in the heart without any bodily action.

The purpose here is not to enumerate every particular act. Rather, consider someone who believes in Allah and His Messenger in his heart: if he sees the Messenger and his enemies fighting him, and can watch them and urge others to support the Messenger without suffering harm, can it ordinarily be conceived that he would make no move whatsoever to support the Messenger? It is well known that this is impossible. Thus, jihad that is incumbent upon a person, according to his ability, is part of faith, and its absence is evidence that the reality of faith is absent. Indeed, it is authentically reported from him:

“Whoever dies without having fought or contemplated fighting dies with a trait of hypocrisy.”

This hadith indicates that a person may possess some traits of hypocrisy alongside the faith he has. Also relevant are the words of Allah Most High:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful.”

Furthermore, it is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue; and if he cannot, then with his heart. That is the weakest level of faith.” In another narration: “Beyond that there is not a mustard seed’s weight of faith.”

This makes clear that if the heart has no hatred for the evils that Allah hates, it is devoid of faith. Hatred and love are deeds of the heart. It is well known that Iblīs and those like him know that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden these things, yet they do not hate them. Rather, they call others to what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

Furthermore, those who follow the view of Jahm and al-Sālihī have explicitly stated that reviling Allah and His Messenger, professing the Trinity, and uttering any words of disbelief do not constitute inward disbelief, but are merely outward evidence of disbelief. They hold that someone who reviles and insults in this way may nevertheless inwardly know Allah, affirm His oneness, and believe in Him. When they are confronted with proof from a scriptural text or scholarly consensus that such a person is a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly, they say: “This implies that such conduct necessarily entails inward denial, and that faith necessarily excludes it.”

They should be told: We have two established facts. (The first) is necessarily known from the religion, and (the second) is necessarily known from reflection on our own selves. translated_text:
a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly, and that anyone who says, “Such a person may inwardly be a believer in Allah and be a disbeliever only outwardly,” has made a claim whose falsity is necessarily known from the religion.

Allah has mentioned the disbelievers’ statements in the Quran and, on account of them, declared them disbelievers deserving of the threatened punishment. If their statements of disbelief were merely like witnesses’ testimony against them, or like an admission in which the person making it is mistaken, Allah would not have deemed them deserving of the threatened punishment on the basis of testimony that might be true or false. Rather, He would have punished them only on condition that the testimony was true. Examples include His words, Most High:

“Those who say, ‘Allah is the third of three,’ have certainly disbelieved.”

“Those who say, ‘Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,’ have certainly disbelieved.”

And there are other such passages.

As for the second established fact: if a person believes in his heart that the Messenger is truthful and that he is Allah’s Messenger, and loves and reveres him, it is impossible for him, while in that state, to curse and revile him. Such conduct is inconceivable without some measure of disregard for him and his sanctity. It is therefore clear that merely believing him to be truthful does not constitute faith unless accompanied by love and reverence for him in the heart.

Furthermore, Allah, glorified is He, says:

“Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in jibt and tāghūt?”

And He says:

“Whoever rejects tāghūt and believes in Allah has grasped the firmest handhold.”

This makes clear that tāghūt can be believed in or rejected. It is well known that believers and disbelievers alike may affirm its existence and the attributes it possesses. Both believers and disbelievers know the nature of idols, Satan, and magic.

Allah, Most High, has said concerning magic:

“Until they both say, ‘We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.’ Yet they learn

from them that by which they cause division between a man and his wife,” up to His words:

“And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter.”

Those who followed what the devils recited during Solomon’s reign and cast Allah’s Book behind their backs as though they did not know, know that they will have no share in the Hereafter; yet they disbelieve nonetheless.

Likewise, if someone who believes in jibt and tāghūt knows how magic causes division between a man and his wife and other such effects of jibt, and knows the nature of Satan and the idols and the trials they bring about, that knowledge does not constitute his belief in them. It is well known that no one believed that they create things, do whatever they will, or possess other attributes exclusive to lordship. Rather, people believed that worshipping them would secure some of the things they sought. Thus, devils would speak to them from within the idols and inform them of certain matters. Similar things occur in these times with the idols worshipped by the people of India and China, the Turks, and others.

Their disbelief on account of these idols consisted in submitting to them, supplicating to them, worshipping them, taking them as intermediaries, and the like—not simply acknowledging the effects that occur in connection with such practices. A knowledgeable believer knows of these effects and acknowledges their existence, but he also knows the harm that follows in this world and the Hereafter, and therefore hates such practices. A disbeliever may also know that this harm exists, but his love of the present life drives him to disbelief.

This is made clear by His words:

“Those who disbelieve in Allah after having believed—not those who are compelled while their hearts remain firm in faith, but those who open their hearts to disbelief—will incur Allah’s wrath and have a tremendous punishment.”

“That is because they preferred the life of this world to the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.”

“Those are the ones whose hearts, hearing, and sight Allah has sealed, and it is they who are heedless.”

“Without doubt, they will be the losers in the Hereafter.”

Allah Most High mentions those who disbelieve in Him after having believed and the punishment He threatens them with in the Hereafter. He then says:

“That is because they preferred the life of this world to the Hereafter.”

He thus makes clear that this is why they deserved the threatened punishment. It is well known that affirmation and denial, knowledge and ignorance, belong to a different category from love and hatred. These people say that they deserved the threatened punishment only because affirmation and faith had departed from their hearts, even if this departure may have resulted from preferring the present life to the Hereafter. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted is He, identifies this preference for the present life over the Hereafter as the fundamental cause of their loss. Such a preference may coexist with knowing and affirming that disbelief brings harm in the Hereafter and that one will have no share therein.

Furthermore, He, glorified is He, exempted those compelled from being counted among the disbelievers. If disbelief could only consist in the heart’s denial and ignorance, He would not have made an exception for those compelled, since it is impossible to compel the heart to deny or be ignorant. It is therefore clear that uttering words of disbelief constitutes disbelief, except under compulsion.

As for His words, Most High:

“But those who open their hearts to disbelief”—

that is, because they prefer the present life to the Hereafter. The Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also illustrate this:

“A man will be a believer in the morning and a disbeliever by evening, and a believer in the evening and a disbeliever by morning, selling his religion for some worldly gain.”

The verse was revealed concerning ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir, Bilāl ibn Rabāh, and others like them among the believers

translated_text:
who were oppressed, when the polytheists compelled them to revile the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and utter similar words of disbelief. Some complied verbally, like ‘Ammār, while others endured the ordeal, like Bilāl. None of them was compelled to change his inner convictions; rather, they were compelled to speak. Whoever uttered such words without coercion did so only with his heart open to them.

Furthermore, “A group of Jews came to the Prophet and said, ‘We testify that you are indeed a messenger.’ They did not thereby become Muslims, because they said this merely to report what they held within themselves—that is, ‘We know and are certain that you are the Messenger of Allah.’ He said, ‘Why, then, do you not follow me?’ They replied, ‘We fear the Jews.’”

Thus, mere knowledge and reporting that knowledge do not constitute faith. One must profess faith as a declaration entailing commitment and submission, while also expressing one’s inner conviction. The hypocrites made a false assertion and were therefore disbelievers inwardly. These people uttered it without commitment or submission and were therefore disbelievers both outwardly and inwardly.

Likewise, it is widely reported that Abū Tālib knew that Muhammad was a prophet. The following verse is attributed to him:

“I know indeed that Muhammad’s religion
Is among the finest religions of mankind.”

Yet he refused to acknowledge Allah’s oneness and Muhammad’s prophethood out of love for his forefathers’ religion and aversion to being reproached by his people. His inward knowledge was not accompanied by the love and submission that exclude their opposites—love of falsehood and aversion to the truth—and so he was not a believer.

translated_text:
As for Iblīs, Pharaoh, the Jews, and others like them, the disbelief, desire for supremacy, and envy within them prevented them from loving Allah and worshipping Him in their hearts, without which faith cannot be complete. Their hearts harboured such aversion to Allah’s pleasure and pursuit of what angered Him as constituted disbelief, against which knowledge was of no avail.

Section

Faith varies in degree, increasing and decreasing, in several respects:

(The first)

Outward deeds: people differ in these, and their deeds increase and decrease. There is agreement that these admit of increase and decrease; the disagreement concerns whether they fall within the meaning of faith. Those who deny their inclusion say that they are the fruits of faith and what it entails, and are therefore included in it figuratively on that account. This is what they mean by faith increasing and decreasing: its fruits increase and decrease.

The response is that, as explained above, these deeds are necessary consequences of faith and are entailed by it. It is impossible for complete faith to exist in the heart without any outward speech or action. As for whether deeds are a necessary consequence of faith or a part of it, this varies according to whether the term “faith” is used on its own or alongside the terms “Islam” and “deeds,” as explained above. As for their claim that the increase concerns outward deeds, not what gives rise to and entails them, this is mistaken,

for if the effects and consequences of things differ in degree, this entails that the things themselves differ in degree. Otherwise, identical determining causes would necessarily produce identical effects and consequences. Thus, differences in people’s outward deeds entail differences in what gives rise to and necessitates those deeds. This makes clear:

(The second)

The second respect in which faith increases and decreases is the increase and decrease of the deeds of the heart. Every believer knows from direct experience that people differ in their love for Allah and His Messenger, their fear of Allah, their turning to Him, their reliance upon Him, and their sincerity towards Him. They also differ in how free their hearts are from showing off, arrogance, self-admiration, and similar traits, and in their compassion for others, their sincere concern for them, and other qualities of faith.

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever possesses three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else; that he loves a person only for Allah’s sake; and that he hates to return to disbelief after Allah has saved him from it as much as he hates to be cast into the Fire.”

Allah Most High says:

“Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, and your clan”

up to His words:

“are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait.”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“By Allah, I fear Allah more than any of you and know His prescribed limits best.”

He also said:

“None of you believes until I am dearer to him than his child, his father, and all people.”

“ʿUmar said to him, ‘O Messenger of Allah, you are dearer to me than everything except myself.’ He replied, ‘No, ʿUmar—not until I am dearer to you than your own self.’ ʿUmar said, ‘Then you are indeed dearer to me than my own self.’ He replied, ‘Now, ʿUmar.’”

translated_text:
These hadiths and others like them are found in the authentic collections, and they show that love and reverent fear vary in degree. Allah Most High says:

“Those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

This is something a person experiences within himself: he may love the same thing more at one time than at another, and fear it more at one time than at another. Hence, people of knowledge are among those who most emphatically affirm that faith increases and decreases, because they experience this within themselves. Another example is His saying, Most High:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but it increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

What increased in them was tranquility and calm. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The believers most complete in faith are those with the best character.”

(The third respect)

The assent and knowledge within the heart vary in degree according to whether they are general or detailed. The assent of someone who believes the Messenger in general, without knowing the details of what he conveyed, is not like that of someone who knows what he conveyed about Allah, His names and attributes, Paradise, Hell, and the nations, and believes him concerning all of this. Nor is someone who commits himself to obeying him in general, but dies before learning the details of what he commanded, like someone who lives long enough to learn those details and obey him in them.

(The fourth respect)

Knowledge and assent themselves vary in degree, just as the other attributes of a living being—ability, will, hearing, sight, and speech—vary in degree. Indeed, so do all accidental properties, such as motion, blackness, whiteness, and the like. If the ability to do something varies in degree, then reporting about it likewise varies in degree. Likewise, they differ in their perception of the same sound. Two people may utter the same word yet differ in how they pronounce it. They may likewise differ in their perception of the smell or taste of the same thing.

There is no attribute of a living being, no form of its perception or movement—indeed, no attribute even of things other than living beings—that does not admit differences of degree beyond human reckoning. Thus, it may be said: no created being knows anything in every respect as Allah knows it. Rather, Allah’s knowledge of a thing is more perfect than anyone else’s knowledge of it, however the matter is conceived. The difference between these two kinds of knowledge is not merely that one has a beginning while the other is eternal; they differ in other respects as well.

A person experiences within himself varying degrees of knowledge of the same object, just as he experiences varying degrees in hearing the same sound, seeing the same object, exercising his ability to do the same thing, loving what he loves, hating what he hates, being pleased with what pleases him, being displeased with what displeases him, willing what he wills, and disliking what he dislikes. Whoever denies differences of degree in these realities is a sophist.

(The fifth respect)

Someone whose assent and love rest on evidence that produces certainty and exposes the falsity of an intervening doubt is not on the same footing as someone whose assent rests on lesser grounds. No reasonable person doubts that knowledge attained through numerous strong proofs, recognition of the falsity of opposing doubts, and demonstration of the invalidity of the arguments advanced in their support is unlike knowledge obtained from a single proof without awareness of the doubts raised against it. For the stronger and more numerous a thing’s causes become, and the more its obstacles are removed and disappear, the more this ensures its perfection, strength, and completeness.

(The sixth respect)

These matters differ in degree according to their persistence and stability, and according to how consistently they are remembered and kept in mind, just as hatred arises through heedlessness of something and turning away from it. Knowledge, assent, love, reverence, and other such things within the heart are attributes, accidents, and states that endure and arise as their causes endure and arise. Although knowledge resides in the heart, heedlessness prevents it from being actively present. Someone who knows something but is heedless of it is at a lower level than someone who keeps it in mind.

ʿUmayr ibn Habīb al-Khatmī, one of the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Faith increases and decreases.” They asked, “How does it increase and decrease?” He replied, “When we praise Allah, remember Him, and glorify Him, that is its increase. When we become heedless, forget, and neglect our duties, that is its decrease.”

(The seventh respect)

It may be said that nothing within a human being admits greater differences and disparities of degree than faith. Whatever attributes or actions are affirmed despite their differences of degree, faith admits even greater differences. For example, a person knows from his own experience that the love within his heart varies in degree, whether it is love for his child or his wife

or his position of authority, his homeland, his friend, a physical form, his horses, his garden, his gold, his silver, or any of his other possessions. Love begins with attachment, because the heart becomes attached to the beloved; then comes yearning, as the heart pours itself out toward the beloved; then consuming passion, which clings to the heart as a creditor clings to his debtor. It then becomes ardent love, until it reaches enslavement—meaning servitude; Taym Allāh means “servant of Allah.” The heart thus becomes a slave to the beloved, obedient and unable to depart from the beloved’s command. Many who are infatuated with physical forms have reached conditions well known to people: some have been driven to kill themselves and their beloved, or to disbelief and apostasy from Islam. Others have been driven to madness and the loss of reason, to abandoning such greatly cherished things as family, wealth, and authority, or to disease in their bodies and teeth.

For every perfection in created beings is an effect of His perfection; every perfection established for a created being is more fittingly attributed to the Creator; and every imperfection from which a created being is free is even more fittingly denied of the Creator. This holds according to the approach and terminology of every school.

Thus, one says, “The perfection of an effect derives from the perfection of its cause,” while another says, “The perfection of what is made and created derives from the perfection of its Maker and Creator.”

In the hadith narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad and by Ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh, Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No servant is afflicted by worry or sorrow and says, ‘O Allah, I am Your servant, the son of Your maidservant. My forelock is in Your hand. They asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, should we not learn these words?’ He replied, ‘Yes indeed. Whoever hears them should learn them.’”

In this hadith, he states that Allah has names which He has kept exclusively with Himself in His knowledge of the unseen. Allah’s names encompass His attributes; they are not mere proper names. Rather, His names—such as the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the Most Merciful, the All-Wise, and others—each indicate meanings of His attributes that the other names do not indicate, while all share in denoting His Essence. whomever He wills among His servants, it follows that people differ more greatly in their knowledge of Him than in their knowledge of anything else they know.

This makes clear to you that those speculative theologians and rational thinkers who claim to have known Allah fully—such that none of His attributes remains unknown to them, and that whatever they do not know and have no evidence to establish is therefore nonexistent in reality—are mistaken, in error, innovators, and astray. Their argument is untenable. For the absence of conclusive or presumptive evidence for something is evidence of its nonexistence, unless it is known that its existence necessarily entails that evidence.

An example is something which, had it existed, people would have had ample interest and motivation to report. Such reporting would then be a necessary consequence of its existence, so the absence of that necessary consequence would establish the absence of what entails it. Thus, we know that if there were a great city like Baghdad or Cairo between Syria and the Hijaz, people would report its existence. If only one, two, or three people reported it, we would know that they were lying.

Likewise, we know that if anyone had claimed prophethood during the lifetime of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as Musaylima, al-ʿAnsī, Tulayha, and Sajāh did, people would have reported his claim just as they reported theirs. Had anyone attempted to rival the Quran and produced something people thought comparable to it, that too would have been transmitted, just as the ‘Quran’ of Musaylima the Liar was transmitted, as were al-Fusūl wa-l-Ghāyāt by Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī and other compositions by those who attempted to rival it—even when these were absurdities that no rational person would consider comparable to it.

Accordingly, ordinary human habits and inclinations would provide an even stronger impetus and greater eagerness to transmit something displaying an apparent resemblance and equivalence to it, whether people loved it or hated it. This is something inherent in human nature.

كَمَا نَقَلُوا قُنُوتَهُ الْعَارِضَ الَّذِي دَعَا فِيهِ لِقَوْمِ وَعَلَى قَوْمٍ وَكَانَ نَقْلُهُمْ لِذَلِكَ أَوْكَدَ - وَكَمَا يُعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ لَمَّا صَلَّى بِعَرَفَةَ وَمُزْدَلِفَةَ قَصْرًا وَجَمْعًا لَوْ أَمَرَ أَحَدًا خَلْفَهُ أَنْ يُتِمَّ صَلَاتَهُ أَوْ أَنْ لَا يَجْمَعَ مَعَهُ لَنَقَلَ النَّاسُ ذَلِكَ كَمَا نَقَلُوا مَا هُوَ دُونَ ذَلِكَ.
translated_text:
Likewise, it is known that if ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib had sought the caliphate during the reigns of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān and fought for it, people would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted what happened after them. Similarly, had the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed ʿAlī to lead the people in prayer, they would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted his instruction to Abū Bakr and Abū Bakr’s leading the people in prayer. Had he designated ʿAlī as his successor to the caliphate, they would have transmitted that, just as they transmitted matters of lesser importance.

Indeed, it is likewise known that he and his Companions did not gather to listen to frame drums or handclapping, nor for dancing and pipe-playing. Likewise, he and they did not gather after the prayers to supplicate, raise their hands, and so forth; had he done so, they would have transmitted it. Similarly, it is known that he did not perform the noon, afternoon, and night prayers as four units while travelling. Had he sometimes prayed four units while travelling, people would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted his combining two prayers on some occasions.

Likewise, it is known that he did not perform the obligatory prayers alone, but rather performed them in congregation. Similarly, he and his Companions did not carry earth with them while travelling for dry ablution, offer funeral prayers every night for Muslims who died, or intend a devotional retreat whenever they entered a mosque to pray. Likewise, it is known that he did not offer a funeral prayer in absentia for anyone other than al-Najāshī.

Similarly, it is known that had he regularly recited an audible, prescribed qunūt supplication in the dawn prayer or any other prayer, people would have transmitted this—just as they transmitted his occasional qunūt, in which he supplicated for some people and against others. They would have had even stronger reason to transmit such a regular practice.

Likewise, when he shortened and combined the prayers at ʿArafah and Muzdalifah, had he instructed anyone praying behind him to complete his prayer in full or not to combine the prayers with him, people would have transmitted this, just as they transmitted matters of lesser importance.

Likewise, it is known that he did not command women in his time who were menstruating for the first time to perform a ritual bath after one day and one night had elapsed; that he did not command his Companions to wash off semen that came into contact with their bodies or clothes; and that he did not prescribe any particular wording for marriage, sale, lease, or any other contract. When he performed the Farewell Pilgrimage, he did not perform an ʿumrah immediately afterward. When he departed from Minā for Mecca on the Day of Sacrifice, he did not first perform circumambulation and saʿy, then circumambulate a second time. There are many other such examples, too numerous to mention. Anyone who carefully examines the two Sahīh collections and other similarly authoritative works, and acquaints himself with the statements of the Companions, the Successors, and the esteemed imams who followed their path—in earlier and later times—will recognize the soundness of what we have presented in this discussion.

And (the point here) is that if the existence of what is indicated necessarily entails the existence of evidence for it, then the absence of that evidence is evidence of its nonexistence. But if it can exist while we remain unaware of the evidence establishing it, then our lack of knowledge of evidence for its existence is not evidence of its nonexistence. Thus, if we have no evidence indicating some of Allah’s names and attributes, this does not necessarily entail their nonexistence. Neither revelation nor reason indicates that we must know every name and attribute that belongs to Him, exalted is He. Indeed, the best of creation and the most knowledgeable of them about Allah said in an authentic hadith:

“I cannot enumerate Your praises; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

And in the authentic hadith concerning intercession:

“I shall fall down in prostration and praise my Lord with praises He will inspire me to utter, which I cannot now enumerate.”

If the best of creation cannot enumerate His praises, and does not now know the praises with which he will praise Him when prostrating to intercede, how could anyone else know all the praises of Allah

translated_text:
and the praise offered to Him? All His most beautiful names form part of His praise and of what is said in praise of Him. Since this is so, the more thoroughly a person knows His names and attributes, the more thoroughly he knows Allah.

Indeed, the more a person knows the names and attributes of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the more he knows the Prophet. Someone who knows that he is a prophet is not like someone who knows that he is a messenger; someone who knows that he is a messenger is not like someone who knows that he is the last of the messengers; and someone who knows that he is the last of the messengers is not like someone who knows that he is the foremost of Adam’s descendants. Nor is someone who knows this like someone who knows the distinctions Allah has granted him: intercession, the Pool, the Praiseworthy Station, the religion, and his other virtues, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Not everyone who is unaware of one of his distinctive qualities is thereby a disbeliever. Indeed, many believers have never heard of many of his virtues and distinctive qualities. Likewise, not everyone who is unaware of some of Allah’s names and attributes is thereby a disbeliever, for many believers have never heard much of what His Messenger said in describing Him and reporting about Him.

These considerations and others like them demonstrate the varying degrees of faith within the heart. As for the differences between people in their outward words and deeds, these are plain to everyone. And Allah knows best.

Section

Once this is clear, and it is understood that faith in the heart—affirmation, love, and other such qualities—necessarily entails outward words and deeds, just as complete resolve, together with the ability to act, necessarily brings about what is intended, and that the faith required in the heart cannot exist without its necessary consequences becoming manifest, the “intellectual doubts” concerning this issue are dispelled. All that remains is a “verbal dispute”: are the necessary consequences of inward faith part of faith itself, included within its meaning, so that the term “faith” encompasses them through inclusion and its general scope? Or do they necessarily follow from faith as its effect and fruit, so that the term “faith” signifies them by necessary implication?

The “truth of the matter” is that the term “faith” is sometimes used in one sense and sometimes in the other, as explained previously. When faith is mentioned together with Islam or deeds, it denotes only what is inward. When mentioned on its own, however, it may encompass both the inward and the outward. In this way, the scriptural texts are reconciled.

Thus, in the statement:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is none worthy of worship but Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road. Modesty is a branch of faith.”

The term “faith” is mentioned on its own, so it includes both the inward and the outward. As for his statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith of Gabriel:

“Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day.”

He mentioned this alongside his statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Islam is to testify that there is none worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of

Allah, establish prayer, pay zakah, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House.” Thus, when he mentioned it separately from the term “Islam,” he described what the term encompasses in that hadith, where it stands alone without being paired with another term. In this hadith, however, it is paired with the term “Islam.” In the statement of the Most High:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him,”

Islam includes what is inward. If someone performed the outward deeds without the inward reality, he would not have embraced the religion that, in Allah’s sight, is Islam. But when Islam is mentioned alongside faith, as in the statement of the Most High:

“The Bedouins say, ‘We believe.’ Say, ‘You have not believed; rather, say, “We have submitted,”’”

and His statements:

“So We brought out whoever was there of the believers.”

“But We found there only one household of Muslims.”

And the statement of the Most High:

“Indeed, Muslim men and Muslim women, believing men and believing women,”

Islam may denote outward deeds, as in the hadith of Anas in al-Musnad, reporting that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Islam is outward, while faith is in the heart.”

Whoever understands that a term’s meaning varies according to whether it stands alone or is paired with another—as with the terms “poor,” “needy,” “right,” “wrong,” “transgression,” and other terms, and as is also the case in the languages of all peoples, Arab and non-Arab—will have his doubts concerning this subject dispelled. And Allah knows best.

If someone says, “The term ‘faith’ encompasses deeds only figuratively,” the response is:

First, this claim is no better founded than the claim that deeds are excluded from it only figuratively. Indeed, the latter claim is stronger, because deeds are excluded from its meaning only when it is mentioned alongside the terms “Islam” and “deeds.” Deeds are included in its meaning when it stands alone, as in the statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “Faith has seventy-odd branches

Second, he should be told: There is no disagreement that outward deeds are an offshoot of the inward state, necessitate it, and are entailed by it. But are they included in what the term denotes and constitute part of it, or are they a necessary accompaniment to it, like an extrinsic condition or a consequent effect?

It is well known that religious and legal terms, such as “prayer,” “zakah,” “pilgrimage,” and the like, denote—by agreement of the jurists—the entirety of prayer and pilgrimage as prescribed by Islamic law. Some maintain that such a term denotes only what it ordinarily denotes in the language, and that whatever the Lawgiver has added is merely an additional legal requirement and a condition, rather than part of what the term denotes. This was the position of al-Qādī Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, and those who agreed with them: Islamic law introduced additional legal requirements, making them conditions relating to intention, deeds, and supplication, without including them in what the terms “pilgrimage,” “fasting,” and “prayer” denote. Their view is regarded as the weaker one by the jurists and the great majority of those associated with religious learning. Hence, the majority of the followers of the four imams oppose this view.

Thus, if someone says that the term “faith” denotes nothing more than assent, while its being assent to Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers, and its necessarily entailing love for Allah and His Messenger and the like, are conditions of the legal ruling rather than part of what the term denotes—then this view, if not weaker than the preceding one, is no less weak. The same applies to someone who says, “Outward deeds

are necessary accompaniments of the inward state and are not included in what the term denotes when used without qualification”—his view resembles theirs. When the Lawgiver couples deeds with faith, this is like coupling pilgrimage with acts that complete it, as when one says, “Whoever performs pilgrimage to the House, circumambulates it, walks between Safā and Marwah, stands at ʿArafah, and stones the pillars”; or, “Whoever prays, reciting, bowing, and prostrating.” Likewise, he said, “Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and in hope of reward.” It is well known that this would not be fasting as prescribed by Islamic law unless it were done out of faith and in hope of reward.

He also said:

“Whoever performs pilgrimage to this House, neither engaging in sexual intercourse nor committing sins, returns free of sins as on the day his mother gave birth to him.”

It is well known that sexual intercourse invalidates the pilgrimage, while sin diminishes its reward. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever offers our prayer, faces our direction of prayer, and eats what we slaughter.”

A person is not considered to be praying unless he faces our direction of prayer during it. Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has prescribed five prayers for His servant each day and night. Whoever observes them diligently has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise. Whoever does not observe them diligently has no covenant with Allah: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will forgive him.”

He thus mentioned the person who observes them diligently. It is well known that a person does not perform them in the manner commanded unless he observes them diligently. Yet he explained that the warning of punishment is subject to this condition. Thus, failure to observe them diligently does not necessarily mean that he does not perform them after their appointed time, though he would not thereby be observing them diligently.

For observing them diligently necessarily entails performing them, as Allah said:

“Guard strictly the prayers, especially the middle prayer.”

This was revealed when the afternoon prayer was delayed in the year of the Battle of the Trench. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah fill their bellies and their graves with fire, just as they kept us from the middle prayer until the sun had set.”

translated_text:
And this makes it clear that citing this as evidence that one who abandons prayer does not become a disbeliever is a weak argument. Rather, it indicates that one who fails to observe the prayers diligently does not become a disbeliever. Thus, if he performs a prayer after its prescribed time, he does not become a disbeliever. Hence the report concerning rulers who delay the prayer beyond its prescribed time:

“It was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, should we not fight them?’ He replied, ‘No, so long as they pray.’”

Likewise, when Ibn Masʿūd was asked about Allah’s words, “They neglected prayer,” he said, “This means delaying it beyond its prescribed time.” He was told, “We thought it meant abandoning it.” He replied, “Had they abandoned it, they would have been disbelievers.”

The point is that an “unqualified term” may encompass many things, even though they may also be mentioned separately.

To someone who says, “Outward deeds are included in the term ‘faith’ only figuratively,” the response is: “Your disagreement is merely verbal. For if you concede that these deeds are necessary accompaniments and consequences of the obligatory faith within the heart, then the absence of a necessary accompaniment entails the absence of that which necessitates it. Thus, the absence of these outward deeds necessarily entails the absence of inward faith. If you acknowledge this, the disagreement is merely verbal.”

But if you assert what Jahm and his followers actually maintain—that the full measure of obligatory faith can remain firmly established in the heart while a person outwardly manifests disbelief and abandons all outward obligations—you are told: “This contradicts your statement that outward deeds necessarily accompany inward faith and are entailed by it.” Indeed, you are told: “What your position really amounts to is that outward deeds sometimes accompany inward faith and are sometimes absent from it. They are therefore neither its necessary accompaniment nor something it entails or causes. Rather, they are an indicator: when present, they indicate the presence of inward faith, but when absent, their absence does not indicate its absence. This is what your position really amounts to.”

translated_text:
And this is as unsound rationally as it is according to revealed law. Such outward conduct is not conclusive evidence, since it also appears in a hypocrite. It serves as evidence only in certain matters pertaining to worldly life, just as words indicate meanings. This is what your position really amounts to. You are therefore told:

It would follow that outward deeds are neither a fruit of inward faith nor a necessary consequence of it or something it entails. For if inward faith itself were what necessitates this outward conduct, its existence would not depend on anything else. An effect that necessarily results from something does not depend on anything else; rather, the existence of the cause necessarily entails the existence of its effect. Thus, if outward conduct were a necessary consequence of inward faith, it would not depend on anything else: whenever the necessitating cause existed, its necessary consequence would exist.

But if outward conduct sometimes accompanies inward faith and is sometimes absent, it could result from that other factor, or it could depend on both together. That other factor would either operate independently of faith or jointly with it. At best, outward conduct would depend on both together: that other factor and faith.

Indeed, outward conduct is known to exist without faith, as in the deeds of a hypocrite. In that case, outward deeds neither necessarily imply faith nor necessarily accompany it. Rather, they sometimes coexist with faith and sometimes with its opposite. Faith would therefore be neither their cause nor what necessitates or entails them. This would invalidate their being evidence of faith, because evidence must necessarily imply what it indicates. And this is indeed true: merely uttering the two testimonies of faith does not necessarily imply the faith that benefits a person before Allah.

“O you who believe, when believing women come to you as emigrants, examine them. Allah knows best their faith. If you find them to be believers, do not send them back to the disbelievers.”

This shows that merely displaying Islam is not evidence of inward faith. Were it otherwise, the emigrant women who came as Muslims would not have needed to be examined. It also shows that examination and testing reveal a person’s inward state, so that it becomes known whether he is a believer or not. Thus, in the hadith traced back to the Prophet:

“If you see a man regularly attending the mosque, testify to his faith, for Allah says: ‘The mosques of Allah are maintained only by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah’—to the end of the verse.”

If it is said: “Outward deeds sometimes result from faith and sometimes from something else. Uttering the two testimonies of faith, for example, sometimes results from faith in the heart and sometimes amounts to dissimulation, as with the faith professed by the hypocrites. Allah Most High says: ‘Among the people are those who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not believers.’ When we call these deeds a fruit of faith, we mean when they proceed from faith in the heart, not from hypocrisy.”

The response is: If they proceed from faith, then either faith itself necessitates them, or they depend on something else. If faith itself necessitates them, this establishes that they necessarily accompany faith in the heart as an effect inseparable from it. This is precisely the point to be established. If, however, they depend on something else, faith would be part of the cause; this would make them a fruit and effect of the other part, since in reality they are an effect and fruit of both together. It thus becomes clear that righteous outward deeds cannot be a fruit of inward faith and an effect

of it unless faith necessitates and entails them. In that case, the consequence necessarily accompanies what necessitates it, and the effect necessarily accompanies its cause. Any deficiency in obligatory outward deeds is therefore due to a deficiency in the faith within the heart. It is inconceivable that the required faith within the heart should be complete while obligatory outward deeds are absent. Rather, completeness in the former necessarily entails completeness in the latter, just as deficiency in the latter entails deficiency in the former. To suppose complete faith within the heart without outward words and deeds is like supposing a fully realized consequence without what necessitates it, or a complete cause without its effect. This is impossible.

This and other considerations demonstrate the falsity of the position of Jahm, al-Sālihī, and those who followed them concerning “faith,” such as al-Ashʿarī in the better-known of his two positions, most of his followers, and a group of later followers of Abū Hanīfah, such as al-Māturīdī and others like him. They regarded faith as mere assent within the heart, in which all people are equal: it is either absent or present and admits of no division. They held that faith can exist in its entirety within the heart even while a person willingly, without coercion, utters words of disbelief and reviles Allah and His Messenger; and that whenever outward statements establish that their speaker is a disbeliever, this is because those statements necessarily imply the absence of that assent within the heart—in deeds … (1) They also held that righteous outward deeds do not necessarily accompany inward faith within the heart; rather, faith within the heart can be complete without them.

This position is erroneous in several respects:

First: They excluded the love of Allah, fear of Him, and similar things that reside within the heart

Second: They held that those known to be disbelievers—such as Iblīs, Pharaoh, the Jews, Abū Tālib, and others—were disbelievers only because their conduct necessarily implied a lack of inward assent. This flies in the face of reason and direct observation. Likewise, they held that hating and envying the Messenger out of aversion to his religion necessarily implies not knowing that he is truthful, and made other similar claims.

(Third): They held that uttering words of disbelief—such as reviling Allah and His Messenger, professing the Trinity, and the like—may coexist with the reality of faith within the heart, and that someone who does this may truly be a believer in Allah’s sight, destined for bliss in the Hereafter. The falsity of this is necessarily known from the religion of Islam.

(Fourth): They held that someone who never professes faith, despite being able to do so, and never performs any outward act of obedience to Allah, despite being obliged and able to do so, may nevertheless be a believer in Allah whose faith is complete, destined for bliss in the Hereafter. These outrageous positions are peculiar to the Jahmiyyah, as distinct from the Murji’ah among the jurists and others.

(Fifth): This objection applies both to them and to the Murji’ah: they said that a person may be a believer whose faith is complete, equal to the faith of the prophets and the utterly truthful, even if he does no good—neither praying, maintaining ties of kinship, nor speaking truthfully—and commits every major sin without exception. in their view, a man who lies whenever he speaks, breaks his promises, and betrays whatever is entrusted to him—persistently lying, betraying trusts, and breaking covenants, never prostrating once to Allah, never doing anyone a single kindness, never fulfilling a trust, and committing every lie, injustice, and indecency within his power—is nevertheless a believer whose faith is complete, equal to the faith of the prophets.

This consequence follows for everyone who does not hold that outward deeds are necessary consequences of inward faith. Once someone affirms that they are its necessary consequences, and that inward faith necessarily entails outward righteous deeds, whether those deeds are necessary consequences of what is denoted by faith or are part of it becomes (a merely verbal dispute, as explained earlier).

(Sixth): Their position entails that someone who willingly prostrates to the cross and idols, deliberately throws a copy of the Quran into a latrine, kills a person unjustly, kills everyone he sees praying, sheds the blood of everyone he sees performing pilgrimage to the House, and does to the Muslims what the Qarmatians did, may nevertheless be a believer and an ally of Allah, with faith equal to that of the prophets and the utterly truthful. For inward faith is either incompatible with these acts or it is not. If it is not incompatible with them, they can coexist with it; thus, they can occur only in the absence of inward faith. If, however, these acts are incompatible with inward faith, refraining from them is something faith necessarily entails, requires, and brings about. Thus, only someone who refrains from these acts can possess the required inward faith. Whoever does not refrain from them thereby demonstrates the corruption of his inward faith. translated_text:
in outward conduct are necessary consequences of inward faith, then they are entailed and required by it. It is evident that they grow stronger as it grows stronger, increase as it increases, and decrease as it decreases. For an effect increases only when that which necessitates and produces it increases, and decreases only when that decreases. Thus, if outward action is held to be entailed and required by inward faith, its increase must result from an increase in inward faith and therefore indicate that increase. Likewise, its decrease must result from a decrease in inward faith and therefore indicate that decrease. This is precisely the point to be established.

When the believer reflects rationally on all these matters, it becomes clear to him that the position of the early generations is the true position, from which there can be no departure. Whoever opposes them is committed to untenable consequences whose invalidity is evident from plain reason and sound transmitted evidence, just as with all other positions that contradict those of the early generations and the leading scholars. And Allah knows best.

The assertion of Jahm and those who agree with him—that faith is merely knowledge and assent, and that through this alone a person deserves reward and felicity—resembles the assertion of certain Peripatetic philosophers and their followers that human felicity consists merely in knowing existence as it truly is. Just as the positions of the Jahmiyyah and these philosophers closely resemble one another on “questions of the divine names and attributes” and “questions of compulsion and divine decree,” so too do their positions on “questions of faith.”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained some of its flaws. For example, knowledge is only one of the soul’s two faculties. The soul has “two faculties”: the faculty of knowledge and assent, and the faculty of will and action, just as an animal has “two faculties”: the faculty of sensation and the faculty of voluntary movement.

translated_text:
A person does not become upright merely by knowing the truth without loving it, desiring it, and following it. Likewise, his felicity does not consist in knowing Allah and acknowledging what He deserves without loving, worshipping, and obeying Him. Rather, the person most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection will be a scholar whose knowledge Allah did not make beneficial to him. When a person knows the truth but hates it and opposes it, he deserves a measure of Allah’s wrath and punishment that someone unlike him does not deserve. Similarly, someone who intends and seeks the truth—but is ignorant of what he seeks and the path to it—is affected by misguidance and deserves a measure of the curse—which means being far removed from Allah’s mercy—that someone unlike him does not deserve.

For this reason, Allah has commanded us to say:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred Your wrath, nor of those who have gone astray.”

“Those who have incurred wrath” knew the truth but neither loved nor followed it. “Those who have gone astray” sought the truth, but were ignorant and misguided concerning both the truth and the path to it. The former resembles a wicked scholar, and the latter an ignorant worshipper. The former is the condition of the Jews, who have incurred wrath; the latter is the condition of the Christians, who have gone astray. As is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he said:

“The Jews have incurred wrath, and the Christians have gone astray.”

The “philosophers” are in a worse condition than the Jews and Christians, for they combine the ignorance and misguidance of the latter with the wickedness and wrongdoing of the former. Thus, they possess a degree of ignorance and wrongdoing found in neither the Jews nor the Christians. They locate felicity merely in knowing realities, so that a person becomes an intelligible world corresponding to the existing world. Yet they acquired no knowledge of Allah

and His names, attributes, angels, books, messengers, creation, and command, except for a scant amount. Their ignorance thus exceeded their knowledge, and their misguidance outweighed their guidance. They vacillated between simple and compound ignorance.

Their discussions of natural philosophy and mathematics do not bring the soul to perfection and soundness. This is attained only through knowledge of divine matters, yet their discourse on these matters is like:

“The flesh of a lean camel atop a rugged mountain: neither is the mountain easy to climb, nor is the flesh fat enough to be worth carrying away.”

Their discourse on the “Necessary Existent” contains a little truth amid much falsehood and error. The same applies to their discourse on the “intellects” and “souls,” which their followers among religious communities claim are the angels described by the messengers. This is not so. Rather, their claim that these are the angels is akin to their claim that the “Necessary Existent” is absolute existence subject to the condition of absoluteness, despite their acknowledgment that what is absolute under this condition exists only in the mind. Likewise, upon examination, their discourse on intellects and souls reduces to entities posited in the mind that have no reality in the external world.

Moreover, their discourse contains notions—associating partners with Allah; affirming a lord who originates the entire universe apart from itself, though it is itself an effect of Him; and affirming a lord who originates everything beneath the lunar sphere and is an effect of the lord above it, that lord in turn being an effect of a lord above it—that are far, far more abhorrent than the Christians’ claim that the Messiah is the son of Allah, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Their early authorities had nothing whatsoever to say about prophethood. Their later thinkers are bewildered concerning it. Some deny it, as did Ibn Zakariyyā al-Rāzī and others like him, despite maintaining that the world came into existence.

translated_text:
They affirmed five eternal principles and adopted some of the worst and most corrupt doctrines. Others affirm prophethood while maintaining that the world is eternal, such as Ibn Sīnā and those like him. Yet they place the prophet on the level of a just king, treating prophethood in its entirety as the same kind of unveiling, influence, and imaginative experience that some righteous people attain. They identify “three things” as the prophet’s distinctive qualities: the faculty of sound intuition, which they call the sacred faculty; the faculty of exerting influence upon the world; and the sensory faculty through which he hears and sees intelligible realities represented within his own imagination. Thus, according to them, Allah’s speech consists of the sounds within his soul, and His angels are the forms and lights within their souls. These qualities are attained by most people who practise spiritual discipline and purification; hence, in their view, prophethood can be acquired.

Consequently, all who followed their path—such as al-Suhrawardī, who was put to death, Ibn Sabʿīn al-Maghribī, and others like them—sought prophethood and hoped to be told, “Arise and warn.” One says, “I shall not die until I am told: ‘Arise and warn.’” The other takes up residence in Mecca and makes his way to the Cave of Hirāʾ, seeking revelation to descend upon him there just as it descended upon the one who, like himself, was wrapped and cloaked. Each of these two, and others like them, pursues his aim through various forms of sīmiyā, which is a kind of magic, imagining that the prophets’ miracles were a form of sīmiyā magic.

Those unable to seek or claim prophethood—because they knew the saying of the truthful and trustworthy Prophet:

“There is no prophet after me,”

or for some other reason—such as Ibn ʿArabī and those like him, sought what they considered higher than prophethood. They maintained that the Seal of the Friends of Allah is greater than the Seal of the Prophets, and that a friend of Allah receives directly from Allah without an intermediary

whereas the prophet receives through the intermediary of an angel. This was founded on a principle held by the philosophers he followed. According to them, angels are the luminous, imaginary forms that take shape within the soul of a prophet or a friend of Allah. Thus, “angels,” in their view, are what he imagines within himself. The “prophet,” according to them, receives through this act of imagining, whereas the “friend of Allah” receives intellectual knowledge without it. There is no doubt that someone who receives knowledge without imagining is more perfect than someone who receives it through imagining.

Having adopted these would-be philosophers’ conception of prophethood, they began to say that friendship with Allah is greater than prophethood, just as many philosophers say that the philosopher is greater than the prophet. This is the position of al-Fārābī, Mubashshir ibn Fātik, and others. They say that prophethood is the highest attainment in the eyes of the masses, but not in those of the elite. They also say that the prophet’s distinctive quality is his skill in evoking images and forming them in his own imagination.

Then came those who cast philosophy in the mould of friendship with Allah, calling the practitioner of philosophy a friend of Allah. They took the philosophers’ ideas and presented them as spiritual unveiling and being addressed by Allah. They said that the friend of Allah is greater than the prophet because he receives abstract meanings from Allah without the intermediary of imagining anything within himself, whereas the prophet receives them through the forms and sounds he imagines within himself.

This falsehood did not satisfy them: they went so far as to claim that all the prophets and messengers draw their knowledge of Allah from the lamp-niche of the Seal of these friends of Allah—someone who is among the most ignorant of all creation concerning Allah and among those furthest removed from His religion. In their view, knowledge of Allah consists in knowing Him as “absolute existence” pervading all beings, so that the existence of every being is identical with the existence of the Necessary Existent. We have been told that Ibn ʿArabī and Shaykh Abū Hafs al-Suhrawardī disagreed over whether, when the Real manifests Himself to a servant, He can address him or not. Shaykh Abū Hafs al-Suhrawardī said: “Yes, that is possible.” Ibn ʿArabī said: “That is not possible.” I think each spoke in the other’s absence. Ibn ʿArabī was then told: “Al-Suhrawardī says such-and-such.” He replied: “Poor fellow! We were speaking of witnessing the Essence, while he is speaking of witnessing the attributes.”

Many followers of Sufism and spiritual discipline, and seekers of the path of spiritual realization and knowledge—despite believing that they follow the messengers and avoid innovations contrary to their teaching—repeat and revere these words, and esteem Ibn ʿArabī for saying such things. They do not know that he based these words on his corrupt foundation of heresy, which combines the negation of the divine attributes with the identification of Allah with creation. For, in his view, the Lord’s reality is abstract existence, having neither name nor attribute. He cannot be seen in this world or in the Hereafter, nor does He possess speech, knowledge, or any other attribute subsisting in Him. Rather, He is seen appearing in created beings and manifesting Himself in things that have been made. In his view, this is other than the existence of existing beings. He also likened it, at times, to a universal manifesting itself in its particulars, as a genus manifests itself in its species, and a species in the particular—just as animality appears in every animal and humanity in every human being.

concrete entities are accompanied by intelligible substances corresponding to the universals predicated of them. Thus, they suppose that within a particular human being there is an intelligible human, an intelligible animal, an intelligible rational being, an intelligible sentient being, and an intelligible body. This is the essence to which existence accrues, and that essence is shared by all particular individuals. Such discourse impresses those who have neither understood it nor reflected upon it. Once someone understands its true nature, however, it becomes clear to him that it resembles the speech of madmen more than that of rational people, for it contradicts both sense perception and reason.

Their error arose from conceiving “absolute universals” in their minds and then supposing that these existed in external reality. Their error here is the reverse of their error concerning the prophets: the prophets witnessed things outside themselves, yet these heretics claimed that those things were within their minds. These heretics, meanwhile, perceived “absolute universals” within their own minds and supposed that they existed externally, although they existed only in their minds. Thus, they placed what was in their minds in external reality, where it did not exist, and placed what the prophets reported within the prophets’ minds, although it existed externally. Hence, they denied the unseen realities reported by the prophets.

They then held that the existence of the Lord—the Creator of the worlds, distinct from all His creatures—is of the same kind as the existence of humanity in human beings and animality in animals, or something similar, such as existence inhering in subsistence—according to those who say that the nonexistent is a thing. They wanted to make Him something existing within created beings while remaining other than them. Accordingly, they drew analogies for Him, sometimes with universals, sometimes with matter and form, and sometimes with existence as distinct from subsistence. When they likened Him to perceptible things, they likened Him to light in glass or air in a tuft of wool.
