 إنَّمَا مَثَّلُوا بِهِ مِنْ الْمَادَّةِ مَعَ الصُّورَةِ وَالْكُلِّيَّاتِ مَعَ الْجُزْئِيَّاتِ وَالْوُجُودِ مَعَ الثُّبُوتِ: كُلُّ ذَلِكَ يَرْجِعُ عِنْدَ التَّحْقِيقِ إلَى شَيْءٍ وَاحِدٍ لَا شَيْئَيْنِ فَجَعَلُوا الْوَاحِدَ اثْنَيْنِ كَمَا جَعَلُوا الِاثْنَيْنِ وَاحِدًا فِي مِثْلِ صِفَاتِ اللَّهِ يَجْعَلُونَ الْعِلْمَ هُوَ الْعَالِمُ، وَالْعِلْمَ هُوَ الْمَعْلُومُ وَالْعِلْمَ هُوَ الْقُدْرَةُ، وَالْعِلْمَ هُوَ الْإِرَادَةُ وَأَنْوَاعُ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ الَّتِي إذَا تَدَبَّرَهَا الْعَاقِلُ تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ أَنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ مِنْ أَجْهَلِ النَّاسِ بِالْأُمُورِ الْإِلَهِيَّةِ، وَأَعْظَمِ النَّاسِ قَوْلًا لِلْبَاطِلِ؛ مَعَ مَا فِي نُفُوسِهِمْ وَنُفُوسِ أَتْبَاعِهِمْ مِنْ الدَّعَاوَى الْهَائِلَةِ الطَّوِيلَةِ الْعَرِيضَةِ كَمَا يَدَّعِي إخْوَانُهُمْ الْقَرَامِطَةُ الْبَاطِنِيَّةُ أَنَّهُمْ أَئِمَّةٌ مَعْصُومُونَ مِثْلُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَهُمْ مِنْ أَجْهَلِ النَّاسِ وَأَضَلِّهِمْ وَأَكْفَرِهِمْ. 
(الثَّانِي)
 : أَنَّهُمْ عَلَى كُلِّ تَقْدِيرٍ مِنْ هَذِهِ التَّقْدِيرَاتِ يَجْعَلُونَ وُجُودَهُ مَشْرُوطًا بِوُجُودِ غَيْرِهِ الَّذِي لَيْسَ هُوَ مُبْدِعًا لَهُ؛ فَإِنَّ وُجُودَ الْكُلِّيَّاتِ فِي الْخَارِجِ مَشْرُوطٌ بِالْجُزْئِيَّاتِ، وَوُجُودَ الْمَادَّةِ مَشْرُوطٌ بِالصُّورَةِ وَكَذَلِكَ بِالْعَكْسِ، وَوُجُودَ الْأَعْيَانِ مَشْرُوطٌ بِثُبُوتِهَا الْمُسْتَقِرِّ فِي الْعَدَمِ؛ فَيَلْزَمُهُمْ عَلَى كُلِّ تَقْدِيرٍ أَنْ يَكُونَ وَاجِبُ الْوُجُودِ مَشْرُوطًا بِمَا لَيْسَ هُوَ مِنْ مُبْدِعَاتِهِ، وَمَا كَانَ وُجُودُهُ مَوْقُوفًا عَلَى غَيْرِهِ الَّذِي لَيْسَ هُوَ مَصْنُوعًا لَهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ وَاجِبَ الْوُجُودِ بِنَفْسِهِ وَهَذَا بَيِّنٌ.
translated_text:
and thus they drew analogies for the Lord of the worlds, went astray, and could find no way forward.

They are misguided in these analogies in several respects:

First: Upon examination, everything they use in these analogies—matter together with form, universals together with particulars, and existence together with subsistence—amounts to one thing, not two. They have made one thing into two, just as they make two things into one in matters such as Allah’s attributes: they identify knowledge with the knower, knowledge with the known, knowledge with power, and knowledge with will. When a rational person reflects upon such claims, it becomes clear to him that these people are among the most ignorant concerning divine matters and among the greatest proponents of falsehood. Yet they and their followers entertain extravagant, sweeping claims about themselves, just as their brethren, the esotericist Qarmatians, claim to be infallible imams like the prophets, although they are among the most ignorant, misguided, and unbelieving of people.

(Second): On every one of these assumptions, they make His existence conditional upon the existence of something else that He did not originate. The existence of universals in external reality is conditional upon particulars; the existence of matter is conditional upon form, and vice versa; and the existence of concrete entities is conditional upon their subsistence, fixed in nonexistence. On every assumption, therefore, their position entails that the Necessary Existent is dependent upon something He did not originate. Whatever depends for its existence upon something else that it did not create cannot be necessarily existent in itself. This is clear.

الثَّالِثُ:
 أَنَّ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ يَعُودُ عِنْدَ التَّحْقِيقِ إلَى أَنْ يَكُونَ وُجُودُ الْخَالِقِ عَيْنَ وُجُودِ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ وَهُمْ يُصَرِّحُونَ بِذَلِكَ؛
 لَكِنْ يَدَّعُونَ الْمُغَايَرَةَ بَيْنَ الْوُجُودِ وَالثُّبُوتِ:
 أَوْ بَيْنَ الْوُجُودِ وَالْمَاهِيَّةِ: وَبَيْنَ الْكُلِّ وَالْجُزْءِ، وَهُوَ الْمُغَايَرَةُ بَيْنَ الْمُطْلَقِ وَالْمُعَيَّنِ؛

 بِالْحُلُولِ. تَارَةً يَجْعَلُونَ الْخَالِقَ حَالًّا فِي الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ، وَتَارَةً مَحَلًّا لَهَا وَإِذَا حَقَّقَ الْأَمْرُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِعَدَمِ الْمُغَايَرَةِ كَانَ حَقِيقَةُ قَوْلِهِمْ أَنَّ الْخَالِقَ هُوَ نَفْسُ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ فَلَا خَالِقَ وَلَا مَخْلُوقَ وَإِنَّمَا الْعَالَمُ وَاجِبُ الْوُجُودِ بِنَفْسِهِ.
الرَّابِعُ:

" التَّوْحِيدِ "

 ثُمَّ هُمْ عِنْدَ التَّحْقِيقِ يَجْعَلُونَهُ عَيْنَ الْأَجْسَامِ الْكَائِنَةِ الْفَاسِدَةِ الْمُسْتَقْذَرَةِ وَيَصِفُونَهُ بِكُلِّ نَقْصٍ كَمَا صَرَّحُوا بِذَلِكَ قَالُوا:
 أَلَا تَرَى الْحَقَّ يَظْهَرُ بِصِفَاتِ الْمُحْدَثَاتِ؟ وَأَخْبَرَ بِذَلِكَ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ وَبِصِفَاتِ النَّقْصِ؛ وَبِصِفَاتِ الذَّمِّ،
 وَقَالُوا:
 الْعَلِيُّ لِذَاتِهِ هُوَ الَّذِي يَكُونُ لَهُ الْكَمَالُ الَّذِي يَسْتَغْرِقُ بِهِ جَمِيعَ الْأُمُورِ الْوُجُودِيَّةِ وَالنِّسَبِ الْعَدَمِيَّةِ سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ مَحْمُودَةً عُرْفًا وَعَقْلًا وَشَرْعًا؛ أَوْ مَذْمُومَةً عُرْفًا وَعَقْلًا وَشَرْعًا، وَلَيْسَ ذَلِكَ إلَّا لِمُسَمَّى اللَّهِ خَاصَّةً فَهُوَ مُتَّصِفٌ عِنْدَهُمْ بِكُلِّ صِفَةٍ مَذْمُومَةٍ كَمَا هُوَ مُتَّصِفٌ بِكُلِّ صِفَةٍ مَحْمُودَةٍ وَقَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى هَؤُلَاءِ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ فَإِنَّ أَمْرَهُمْ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ أَنْ يُبْسَطَ هُنَا. وَلَكِنَّ الْمَقْصُودَ التَّنْبِيهُ عَلَى تَشَابُهِ رُؤُوسِ الضَّلَالِ حَتَّى إذَا فَهِمَ الْمُؤْمِنُ
translated_text:
Third: Upon examination, this argument amounts to identifying the Creator’s existence with the very existence of created beings. They state this explicitly, yet claim a distinction between existence and subsistence, or between existence and essence, and between the whole and the part—which is the distinction between the absolute and the particular. Hence their doctrine of indwelling: sometimes they make the Creator dwell within created beings, and sometimes they make Him that within which created beings dwell. When the matter is rigorously examined and it is established against them that there is no distinction, their position amounts to saying that the Creator is the very same as created beings. There is then neither Creator nor creation; rather, the world is necessarily existent in itself.

Fourth: They profess what they claim to be “divine oneness,” declaring Him free of multiplicity in His necessary attributes and His names, of temporal events inhering in Him, and of being a body or a substance. Yet, upon examination, they identify Him with the very repulsive bodies that come into being and pass away, and ascribe every deficiency to Him. They have explicitly stated this, saying:

“Do you not see that the Real manifests Himself with the attributes of originated things? He has spoken of Himself in these terms, and with attributes of deficiency and blame.”

They also say:

“He who is Most High in Himself is the one whose perfection encompasses all existential realities and privative relations, whether praiseworthy according to custom, reason, and revealed law, or blameworthy according to custom, reason, and revealed law. This belongs exclusively to the One named Allah.”

Thus, according to them, He possesses every blameworthy attribute just as He possesses every praiseworthy attribute. These people have been discussed at length elsewhere, for their case is too extensive to expound here. " سُلْطَانَ الْأَقْطَابِ "
؛ وَكَانَ عِنْدَهُ مِنْ التَّعْظِيمِ لِابْنِ عَرَبِيٍّ وَابْنِ حموية؛ وَالْغُلُوُّ فِيهِمَا أَمْرٌ عَظِيمٌ فَبَيَّنَتْ لَهُ كَثِيرًا مِمَّا يَشْتَمِلُ عَلَيْهِ كَلَامُهُمَا مِنْ الْفَسَادِ وَالْإِلْحَادِ وَالْأَحَادِيثِ الْمَكْذُوبَةِ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَجَرَى فِي ذَلِكَ فُصُولٌ؛ لِمَا كَانَ عِنْدَهُ مِنْ التَّعْظِيمِ مَعَ عَدَمِ فَهْمِ حَقِيقَةِ أَقْوَالِهِمَا وَمَا تَضَمَّنَتْهُ مِنْ الضَّلَالَاتِ. وَكَانَ مِمَّنْ حَدَّثَنِي عَنْ شَيْخِهِ الطاووسي الَّذِي كَانَ بهمدان عَنْ سَعْدِ الدِّينِ
translated_text:
the teaching of one of them, this helps him understand that of another, guard himself against them, and expose their misguidance, given the many errors they have spread in the world.

For Ibn ‘Arabī, according to his claim, the self-disclosure of the Essence is nothing more than an absolute witnessing, which is the existence of existing things, abstracted and unqualified, without name or attribute. It is well known that anyone who conceives of this cannot be addressed by it. Hence his claim that no address occurs when the Essence discloses itself.

Abū Hafs al-Suhrawardī, however, was more knowledgeable about the Sunnah, more faithful to it, and better than him. He had encountered the hadiths stating that Allah reveals Himself to His servants and addresses them when He reveals Himself to them, and he believed this. Yet Ibn ‘Arabī was more renowned for his philosophy than al-Suhrawardī was for his adherence to the Sunnah. Thus, the followers of both held Ibn ‘Arabī in greater esteem, despite acknowledging that al-Suhrawardī followed the Sunnah more closely.

This was related to me by a visiting shaykh known as Husām al-Dīn, who followed the path of Ibn Hamawayh, whom his followers called “Sultan of the Spiritual Poles.” He held Ibn ‘Arabī and Ibn Hamawayh in immense reverence and went to great extremes in exalting them. I explained to him much of the corruption, heresy, and hadiths falsely attributed to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, contained in their writings. Lengthy discussions ensued on this subject because of his reverence for them, despite his failure to understand the true nature of their statements and the errors they contained.

He was also among those who related to me, from his shaykh al-Tāwūsī, who was in Hamadan, on the authority of Sa‘d al-Dīn

بْنِ حمويه أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 مُحْيِي الدِّينِ ابْنُ عَرَبِيٍّ بَحْرٌ لَا تُكَدِّرُهُ الدِّلَاءُ؛
 لَكِنَّ نُورَ الْمُتَابَعَةِ النَّبَوِيَّةِ عَلَى وَجْهِ الشَّيْخِ شِهَابِ الدِّينِ السهروردي شَيْءٌ آخَرُ فَقُلْت لَهُ:
 هَذَا كَمَا يُقَالُ: كَانَ هَؤُلَاءِ أُوتُوا مَنْ مُلْكِ الْكُفَّارِ مُلْكًا عَظِيمًا. لَكِنَّ نُورَ الْإِسْلَامِ الَّذِي عَلَى شِهَابِ غَازِيٍّ صَاحِبِ 
" ميافا رُقِّينَ "
 شَيْءٌ آخَرُ. فَإِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يُعَظِّمُونَ ابْنَ عَرَبِيٍّ؛ وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ الشَّيْخَ شِهَابَ الدِّينِ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُتَمَكِّنًا مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ السُّنَّةِ وَمُتَابَعَتِهَا وَتَحْقِيقِ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ الرُّسُلُ؛ كَتَمَكُّنِ ابْنِ عَرَبِيٍّ فِي طَرِيقِهِ الَّتِي سَلَكَهَا وَجَمَعَ فِيهَا بَيْنَ الْفَلْسَفَةِ وَالتَّصَوُّفِ.
 وَهَؤُلَاءِ إنَّمَا يَقْطَعُ دَابِرَهُمْ الْمُبَايَنَةُ بَيْنَ الْخَالِقِ وَالْمَخْلُوقِ وَإِثْبَاتُ تَعَيُّنِهِ مُنْفَصِلًا عَنْ الْمَخْلُوقِ تُرْفَعُ إلَيْهِ الْأَيْدِي بِالدُّعَاءِ وَإِلَيْهِ كَانَ مِعْرَاجُ خَاتَمِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ السهروردي فِي عَقِيدَتِهِ الْمَشْهُورَةِ قَوْلَهُ:
 
" بِلَا إشَارَةٍ وَلَا تَعْيِينٍ "

ibn Hamawayh that he said:

“Muhyī al-Dīn Ibn ‘Arabī is an ocean that buckets cannot muddy. Yet the light of following the Prophet upon the face of Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn al-Suhrawardī is another matter.”

I said to him: “This is like saying: ‘These men were granted immense dominion of the kind possessed by unbelievers. Yet the light of Islam upon Shihāb Ghāzī, the ruler of Mayyāfāriqīn, is another matter.’”

They held Ibn ‘Arabī in such esteem because Shaykh Shihāb al-Dīn was not as accomplished in knowing and following the Sunnah, and ascertaining the truth brought by the messengers, as Ibn ‘Arabī was in the path he pursued, in which he combined philosophy and Sufism.

These people can only be cut off at the root by affirming the distinction between the Creator and creation, and affirming His distinct identity, separate from creation: hands are raised to Him in supplication, and to Him the Seal of the Prophets ascended. Al-Suhrawardī stated in his well-known creed:

“Without pointing to Him or identifying Him distinctly.”

This was precisely what these people used to gain the upper hand over him. For once pointing to Him and identifying Him distinctly are denied, nothing remains but sheer nonexistence and negation of the divine, or heresy, the oneness of all existence, and divine indwelling.

Ibn Sab‘īn and other heretics like him say:

“No pointing, no distinct identification;
The very thing you see is an essence unseen,
And an essence unseen is the very thing you see.”

In their formulas of remembrance, they say, “There is nothing but Allah,” instead of the Muslims’ declaration, “There is no god but Allah,” because they believe that He is the existence of everything that exists, and thus nothing exists but Him.

Muslims, however, know that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything; that He is neither created things, nor a part of them, nor an attribute of them, but is separate from them. They affirm that He is the God who deserves worship to the exclusion of all other

And he says:

In this they resemble the Peripatetic philosophers, who locate human perfection in knowledge. For them, the “highest science” and “first philosophy” consist in studying being and its concomitants. They make the Necessary Existent absolute existence, subject to the condition of absoluteness. The former, however, change the terminology, expressing philosophical and Greek heresies in Islamic, Quranic language. All this has been established and discussed at length elsewhere.

Section

The hadith begins with his question about “Islam.” He answered him:

“Islam is that you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform the pilgrimage to the House.”

These are the five mentioned in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Islam is built upon five: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving zakat, fasting Ramadan, and performing the pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to make the journey.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said this after Allah had made the pilgrimage obligatory; hence he mentioned all five. Most hadiths do not mention the pilgrimage. In the hadith concerning the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, he said:

“I command you to believe in Allah alone. Do you know what believing in Allah alone means? Testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving zakat, fasting Ramadan, and giving one-fifth of the spoils.”

translated_text:
The hadith concerning the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays is among the best-known and most authentic hadiths. Some versions in al-Bukhārī do not mention fasting, but it is mentioned in many of his versions and in Muslim’s collection. It is also mentioned in the hadith of Abū Saʿīd recounting the visit of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, which Muslim narrated from him in his Sahīh. Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim narrated the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, which states that he commanded them to give one-fifth of the spoils. The obligation to pay this fifth was not instituted until the Battle of Badr, whereas fasting Ramadan had been made obligatory before that.

The delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays was among the finest delegations to visit the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Their visit took place before the pilgrimage became obligatory. It has been said that they came in the Year of Delegations, the ninth year, but the correct view is that they came earlier. They said, “Between us and you is this group of unbelievers from Mudar”—meaning the people of Najd—“and we can only reach you during a sacred month.” By the ninth year, however, the Arabs had been subdued and had abandoned warfare. They were either Muslims or apprehensive parties to treaties, after Allah had granted the conquest of Mecca and the Muslims had defeated Hawāzin at Hunayn. They had merely been waiting for the conquest of Mecca before embracing Islam.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, to lead the pilgrimage in the ninth year. He then sent ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, after him to give effect to the treaties between the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Arabs. However, he granted them a respite of four months from the time of Abū Bakr’s pilgrimage, which took place in Dhū al-Qaʿdah.

Allah Most High said:

“Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists”—to the end of the verse.

These four months for which they granted a respite are the four sacred months.

Both versions are found in the two Sahīh collections, but al-Bukhārī did not mention pilgrimage in the first; instead, he mentioned fasting. The first account is more complete, and people treat the two reports as a single hadith. It seems—and Allah knows best—that al-Bukhārī regarded the mention of pilgrimage in it as an error. For Saʿd ibn Abī Bakr belong to Hawāzin, who are related to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through marriage. The battle of Hunayn was fought against Hawāzin after the conquest of Mecca, and they all embraced Islam after the battle. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, returned the women and children to them after distributing them among the troops and securing the troops’ willing consent to this. This visit could therefore only have taken place before the conquest of Mecca, when pilgrimage had not yet been made obligatory.

The hadith of Talhah ibn ʿUbayd Allah mentions only prayer, zakah and fasting. It has been said that this is the hadith of Dimām. It appears in the two Sahīh collections, where Talhah ibn ʿUbayd Allah said:

“A man from Najd, with dishevelled hair, came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. We could hear the sound of his voice but could not understand what he was saying until he drew near to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He was asking about Islam. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Five prayers each day and night.’

“He asked, ‘Must I do anything beyond that?’

“He replied, ‘No, unless you choose to do more voluntarily.’

“Talhah continued: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned zakah to him. He asked, ‘Must I give anything beyond that?’ He replied, ‘No, unless you choose to give voluntarily.’ The man then turned to leave, saying, ‘By Allah, I shall neither add to this nor subtract from it.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘He will succeed if he is truthful.’”

I perform the prescribed prayers, fast Ramadan, regard what is lawful as lawful and what is forbidden as forbidden, and do nothing beyond that, will I enter Paradise?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ The man said, ‘By Allah, I shall do nothing beyond that.’” Another version reads: “Al-Nuʿmān ibn Qawqal came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

This hadith of al-Nuʿmān dates from an early period, for al-Nuʿmān ibn Qawqal was killed before the conquest of Mecca by a member of Banū Saʿd ibn al-ʿĀs, as established in the Sahīh. These hadiths were thus given in answer to people’s questions, whereas the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar was an unsolicited statement.

The hadiths concerning calling people to Islam and fighting mention prayer and zakah, as in the report in the two Sahīh collections from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, who said that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been commanded to fight people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish prayer, and pay zakah. If they do so, their lives and property are protected from me, except as required by Islam, and their reckoning rests with Allah.”

The two compilers also included it in their Sahīh collections on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, and Muslim narrated it from Jābir, with the wording:

“I have been commanded to fight people until they testify that there is no god but Allah. If they say this, their lives and property are protected from me, except as required by that testimony.”

Abū Bakr said: “By Allah, I shall fight those who distinguish between prayer and zakah, for zakah is a right due on wealth.”

It was part of Abū Bakr’s understanding of the religion that he understood from this abridged hadith that fighting to enforce zakah was fighting to enforce a right due on wealth. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, clarified what he meant in the fuller wording narrated by Ibn ʿUmar.

The Quran explicitly accords with the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, as Allah Most High says:

“But if they repent, establish prayer, and pay zakah, then let them go their way.”

And in the hadith concerning Muʿādh, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent him to Yemen, he mentioned only prayer and zakah. The fact that some hadiths mention certain pillars but not others has puzzled some people. Some have explained this by saying that certain narrators abridged the hadiths they transmitted. But this is not so, for such an explanation impugns the narrators and accuses them of lying. What this explanation describes applies only to different accounts of the same hadith: for example, the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, in which some narrators mentioned fasting while others did not; the hadith of Dimām, in which some mentioned all five while others did not; and the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Qawqal, in which some mentioned fasting while others did not. In such cases, we know that one of the two narrators either omitted part of the report or mistakenly added something.

With two separate hadiths, however, the matter is different, especially since the reports establishing that the answers differed have been transmitted through so many channels as to yield certainty. They also contain conclusive evidence that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said one thing on one occasion and another on another occasion. The Quran confirms this, for in some verses Allah made brotherhood in faith conditional only upon prayer and zakah, as in His words, Most High:

“But if they repent, establish prayer, and pay zakah, then they are your brothers in religion.”

Likewise, He made the cessation of fighting conditional upon this in His words, Most High:

“But if they repent, establish prayer, and pay zakah, then let them go their way.”

The hadith of Ibn ʿUmar in the two Sahīh collections, which agrees with this verse, has already been cited.

Furthermore, in the hadith of the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays, he mentioned the fifth of the spoils because they were a community capable of defending itself and engaged in fighting.

and such a matter would not be mentioned in answer to someone asking about his personal obligations. There are, however, two answers to this:

The first is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, answered according to the obligations that had been revealed. The first thing Allah made obligatory was the two testimonies of faith, followed by prayer. He commanded prayer at the very beginning of revelation. Indeed, it is established in the Sahīh collection that the first revelation he received was:

“Recite in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging substance,”

down to His words:

“Taught man that which he knew not.”

Then, after that, it was revealed to him:

“O you wrapped in your cloak, arise and warn.”

This address commissioned him as a messenger to humankind, and that commissioning followed his receiving revelation, for the earlier address contained no such commission. The end of Surah Iqraʾ reads:

“Prostrate and draw near.”

Thus, the beginning of the surah commands recitation, while its end commands prostration. Prayer consists of words and actions: its finest words are Quranic recitation, and its finest action is prostration. Recitation is the first of its utterances intended in their own right, and what follows is subordinate to it.

It has been reported that when prayer was first made obligatory, it consisted of two units in the morning and two in the evening. Then the five daily prayers were made obligatory on the night of the Ascension, each consisting of two units. When he emigrated, the prayer offered while travelling was left unchanged, while additional units were added to the prayer offered while resident.

Prayer was brought to completion gradually. At first, they would speak during prayer, and it contained no tashahhud (the testimony of faith recited while seated). They were then commanded to recite the tashahhud and forbidden to speak. Likewise, they had no call to prayer in Mecca; it was instituted only in Medina after the migration. The Friday prayer, the Eid prayer, the eclipse prayer, the prayer for rain, the night prayers of Ramadan, and other such prayers were likewise instituted only in Medina after the migration.

They were also commanded in Mecca to give zakat and to do good, but the prescribed dues and minimum thresholds of zakat were instituted only in Medina. As for “fasting the month of Ramadan,” it was made obligatory only in the second year after the Hijrah, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, lived through nine Ramadans.

As for “Hajj,” people differed over when it became obligatory. One group said that it was made obligatory in the sixth year after the Hijrah—the year in which, by common agreement, al-Hudaybiyah took place. They said: “This verse indicates that both Hajj and umrah are obligatory, because the command to complete an act entails the command both to begin it and to complete it.”

The majority, however, said that Hajj became obligatory only later. Some said in the ninth year, others in the tenth; this is the correct view. For the verse establishing its obligation is His saying, Most High:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people.”

This verse occurs in Surah Āl ‘Imrān, in the course of His address to the People of the Book. The opening of Āl ‘Imrān, together with its passages addressing the People of the Book, was revealed when the Christian delegation from Najrān came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and debated with him concerning the Messiah.

They were the first of the People of the Book to pay the jizyah. The delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. According to the correct view, their arrival preceded the conquest of Mecca, as we have explained. They said: “O Messenger of Allah, between us and you lies this tribe of unbelievers from Mudar.” They meant the people of Najd—Tamīm, Asad, and Ghatafān—because they lay between al-Bahrayn and Medina. ‘Abd al-Qays belong to Rabī‘ah, not Mudar. Once Mecca was conquered, this fear disappeared. When the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays came to him, he commanded them to observe prayer, pay zakat, fast Ramadan, and pay one-fifth of the spoils of war; he did not command them to perform Hajj.

As for the hadith of Dimām, we have already noted that al-Bukhārī did not mention Hajj in it, just as he did not mention it in the hadiths of Talhah, Abū Hurayrah, and others, despite their assertion: “These hadiths relate to the account of Dimām.” This is possible, although the date of this Dimām’s arrival is not certain.

As for His saying:

“And complete Hajj and umrah for Allah.”

This verse contains only the command to complete them, which makes their completion obligatory upon anyone who has begun them. This command was revealed when they entered the state of consecration for umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah and were then prevented from proceeding. They were commanded to complete it, and He explained to them the ruling concerning being prevented from completing the rites. At that time, neither umrah nor Hajj had yet become obligatory upon them.

A person can refrain from intending to fast and can eat secretly, just as he can conceal his state of minor or major ritual impurity. He therefore made this conditional upon prayer and zakat, rather than fasting, even though fasting is obligatory. He sent Mu‘ādh to Yemen toward the end of his mission, after fasting had been made obligatory—indeed, after the conquest of Mecca, after Tabūk, and after Hajj and jizyah had been made obligatory. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died while Mu‘ādh was in Yemen, and Mu‘ādh returned to Medina only after his death. He did not mention fasting in this hadith because it is subsidiary and inward. Nor did he mention Hajj, because its obligation applies to particular people rather than everyone, and it is obligatory only once in a lifetime.

For this reason, the scholars differed over declaring someone a disbeliever for abandoning any of these “four obligations” while acknowledging that they are obligatory. As for the “two testimonies of faith,” anyone who does not pronounce them despite being able to do so is a disbeliever by the agreement of the Muslims. According to the early generations of this community, its imams, and the great majority of its scholars, he is a disbeliever both inwardly and outwardly.

A group among the Murji’ah—the Jahmī Murji’ah, such as Jahm, al-Sālihī, and their followers—held that if he assents in his heart, he is a disbeliever outwardly but not inwardly. The basis of this view has already been pointed out. It is an innovated view in Islam that none of the imams held. It has already been explained that inward faith necessarily entails outward profession—and indeed, more than that—and that inward faith, consisting of assent, love, and submission, cannot exist without outward profession.

As for those against whom the proof has not been established—for example, someone who has only recently embraced Islam, or who grew up in a remote desert region where the laws of Islam had not reached him, or someone in similar circumstances—or those who mistakenly believe that people who believe and do righteous deeds are exempt from the prohibition of intoxicating drink, as did those whom ‘Umar called upon to repent: such people are called upon to repent, and the proof is established against them. If they persist, they then become disbelievers; they are not judged to be disbelievers before that. Likewise, the Companions did not judge Qudāmah ibn Maz‘ūn and his companions to be disbelievers when they fell into their mistaken interpretation.

As for someone who abandons any of these four pillars while acknowledging its obligation, the scholars hold several views on declaring him a disbeliever, all of which are reported from Ahmad:

The first is that he becomes a disbeliever by abandoning any one of the four, even Hajj. Although the scholars differ over whether Hajj may be deferred, whenever he resolves to abandon it altogether, he becomes a disbeliever. This is the view of a group among the early generations and one of the positions reported from Ahmad, which Abū Bakr adopted.

The second is that he does not become a disbeliever by abandoning any of these duties so long as he acknowledges its obligation. This is the well-known position among many jurists belonging to the schools of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, and al-Shāfi‘ī. It is also one of the positions reported from Ahmad, adopted by Ibn Battah and others.

The third is that he becomes a disbeliever only by abandoning prayer. This is the third position reported from Ahmad, and the view of many of the early generations, a group of Mālik’s and al-Shāfi‘ī’s followers, and a group of Ahmad’s followers.

The fourth is that only abandoning prayer or zakat renders him a disbeliever.

The fifth is that abandoning prayer renders him a disbeliever, as does withholding zakat if he fights the ruler over it, but not abandoning fasting or Hajj.

This issue has two aspects: the first concerns establishing outward disbelief, and the second concerns establishing inward disbelief.

As for the second aspect, it rests upon the question of faith consisting of speech and action, as discussed above. It is impossible for a man to have firmly established faith in his heart that Allah has obligated him to pray, pay zakat, fast, and perform Hajj, yet live his entire life without making a single prostration to Allah, fasting any part of Ramadan, paying any zakat for Allah’s sake, or performing Hajj to His House. This is impossible. Such conduct can only arise from hypocrisy and heresy in the heart, not from genuine faith.

For this reason, it is only the disbelievers whom He, glorified be He, describes as refusing to prostrate, as in His words:

“On the Day when the Shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostrate, but will be unable to do so.”

“Their eyes downcast, humiliation will overwhelm them, although they used to be called to prostrate while they were sound.”

It is established in the two Sahīh collections and elsewhere, in the lengthy hadith about Allah’s manifestation narrated by Abū Hurayrah, Abū Sa‘īd, and others:

“When He, Most High, manifests Himself to His servants on the Day of Resurrection, the believers will prostrate before Him. But anyone who used to prostrate in this world for show and reputation will be left with a back as rigid as a slab, unable to prostrate.”

If this is the condition of someone who prostrated for show, what, then, of someone who never prostrated at all? It is also established in the Sahīh:

“The Fire consumes every part of the son of Adam except the places of prostration, for Allah has forbidden the Fire to consume them.”

Thus, it is known that the Fire will consume the entirety of anyone who did not prostrate to Allah. Likewise, it is established in the Sahīh:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will recognize his community on the Day of Resurrection by their radiant faces, hands, and feet, bearing the traces of ablution.”

This indicates that anyone without this radiance will not be recognized by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and so will not belong to his community.

And His words, Most High:

“Eat and enjoy yourselves for a little while; indeed, you are criminals. Woe that Day to those who deny the truth! And when they are told, ‘Bow down,’ they do not bow down. Woe that Day to those who deny the truth!”

And His words, Most High:

“What is the matter with them that they do not believe, and when the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate? Rather, those who disbelieve deny the truth. And Allah knows best what they keep hidden.”

Likewise, His words, Most High:

“He neither affirmed the truth nor prayed, but denied and turned away.”

Likewise, His words, Most High:

“‘What brought you into Saqar?’ They will say, ‘We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor. We used to indulge in vain discourse with those who did so, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment, until death came to us.’”

Thus, He describes him as abandoning prayer just as He describes him as failing to affirm the truth. He also describes him as denying and turning away. The one who “turns away” is the disobedient person who refuses to obey, as He says,

Most High:

“You will be called to face a people of great military might, whom you will fight unless they submit. If you obey, Allah will grant you a good reward; but if you turn away as you did before, He will punish you with a painful punishment.”

Likewise, He describes the people of Saqar as not having been among those who prayed. He also pairs denial with turning away in His words:

“Have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays? Have you considered whether he is rightly guided, or enjoins righteousness? Have you considered whether he denies the truth and turns away? Does he not know that Allah sees? No! If he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock—a lying, sinful forelock.”

Furthermore, in the Quran, He makes brotherhood in religion conditional upon actually establishing prayer and giving zakah, just as He makes it conditional upon repentance from disbelief. When these conditions are absent, brotherhood is absent.

It is also established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The covenant between us and them is prayer; whoever abandons it has disbelieved.”

And in the Musnad:

“Whoever deliberately abandons prayer has forfeited the covenant of protection.”

Moreover, prayer is the distinguishing mark of the Muslims. Hence they are referred to by it: people say, “Those who pray have differed,” and, “Those who face the direction of prayer have differed.” Writers on Muslim doctrines speak of “The Doctrines of the Muslims and the Disagreements among Those Who Pray.” And in the Sahīh:

“Whoever prays as we pray, faces our direction of prayer, and eats the animals we slaughter is a Muslim, entitled to the same rights as us and bound by the same duties.”

There are many similar texts in the Quran and Sunnah. As for those who do not regard abandoning prayer and similar duties as disbelief, they have no argument that is not

applicable to one who denies its obligation just as it is to one who abandons it. Whatever answer they give concerning the former also serves as an answer to them concerning the latter. Moreover, the texts connect disbelief with turning away, as explained above. This resembles their appeal to the general statements invoked by the Murji’ah, such as his saying:

“Whoever testifies that there is no god but Allah, that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and that Jesus is Allah’s servant and Messenger, His word which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him … Allah will admit him to Paradise.”

They invoke other similar texts as well. The strongest evidence they rely upon is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has prescribed five prayers for His servants each day and night. Whoever observes them faithfully has a covenant with Allah that He will admit him to Paradise. Whoever does not observe them faithfully has no covenant with Allah: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will admit him to Paradise.”

They say: “He thus leaves the one who does not observe them faithfully subject to Allah’s will, whereas a disbeliever is not subject to His will.”

Yet this provides no evidence for their position. The promise is conditional upon observing the prayers faithfully, which means performing them at their appointed times as commanded. As the Most High says:

“Observe the prayers faithfully, especially the middle prayer.”

Failure to observe them faithfully can occur even when they are performed, if they are performed after their appointed time. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, delayed the afternoon prayer on the Day of the Trench, whereupon Allah revealed the verse commanding faithful observance of that prayer and the other prayers.

The Most High also says:

“But they were succeeded by generations who neglected prayer and followed their desires; they will meet with doom.”

Ibn Mas‘ūd and others were asked, “What does neglecting prayer mean?” He replied, “Delaying it beyond its appointed time.” They said, “We thought it meant nothing other than abandoning it.” He replied, “Had they abandoned it, they would have been disbelievers.”

Likewise, His words:

“So woe to those who pray, yet are heedless of their prayer.”

He censured them despite their praying, because they neglected its obligatory requirements: performing it at its appointed time and completing its obligatory acts. As established in Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! That is the hypocrite’s prayer! He watches the sun until, when it is between Satan’s two horns, he rises and pecks out four rak‘ahs, remembering Allah only a little during them.”

He described this as the hypocrites’ prayer because the person delayed it beyond its appointed time and pecked through it. It is also established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned rulers who would come after him and commit objectionable deeds. They asked, “Messenger of Allah, should we not fight them?” He replied, “No, so long as they pray.”

It is also established that he said:

“There will be rulers who delay prayer beyond its appointed time. Perform the prayer at its appointed time, then let your prayer with them be voluntary.”

Thus, he forbade fighting them so long as they prayed, indicating that if they did not pray, they were to be fought. He also explained that they would delay prayer beyond its appointed time. This constitutes a failure to observe it faithfully, not its abandonment.

Once the distinction between these two matters is understood, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, placed only those who failed to observe the prayers faithfully under Allah’s will, not those who abandoned them. The very reference to faithful observance implies that they prayed but failed to observe the prayers faithfully; it does not include those who failed to observe them faithfully. For if it did include such a case, they would undoubtedly be put to death as disbelievers and apostates.

It is inconceivable in ordinary circumstances that a man who believes in his heart, acknowledges that Allah has made prayer obligatory upon him, and is committed to the law of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and what he brought, would refuse the ruler’s command to pray until he is put to death, yet still be a believer inwardly. Such a man can only be a disbeliever. Even if he were to say, “I acknowledge that it is obligatory, but I do not perform it,”

such a statement, given his conduct, would be a lie on his part. It would be like someone throwing a copy of the Quran into a latrine while saying, “I testify that its contents are Allah’s words,” or setting about killing a prophet while saying, “I testify that he is Allah’s Messenger,” or committing similar acts incompatible with faith in the heart. If someone acting in this way says, “I am a believer in my heart,” his outward declaration is a lie.

This point deserves careful reflection. Whoever understands the connection between the outward and the inward will have his doubts concerning this matter dispelled. He will recognize that any jurist who says that someone who acknowledges the obligation of prayer but refuses to perform it should not be put to death—or should be put to death while remaining a Muslim—has been affected by the same misconception that affected the Murji’ah and the Jahmiyyah, and those who hold that firm resolve, together with full ability, may produce no action at all. Thus, those jurists who opposed putting such a person to death based their position on their view concerning “the question of faith”: that deeds are not part of faith.

It has already been explained that deeds, as a category, necessarily accompany faith in the heart, and that complete faith in the heart without any outward deeds is impossible, whether outward deeds are regarded as a necessary consequence of faith or as part of faith, as explained earlier. Accordingly, when a servant performs some of what he has been commanded to do and leaves some undone, he possesses faith in proportion to what he has done. Faith increases and decreases, and faith and hypocrisy may coexist in a servant.

As is established from him in the Sahīh, he said:

“Four traits, whoever possesses them all is a pure hypocrite; whoever possesses one of them has a trait of hypocrisy until he abandons it: when he speaks, he lies; when he is entrusted with something, he betrays the trust; when he makes a covenant, he breaks it; and when he disputes, he transgresses all bounds.”

translated_text:
This dispels the confusion concerning this matter. Many people—indeed, most people in many towns—neither regularly observe the five daily prayers nor abandon them altogether. Rather, they sometimes pray and sometimes neglect prayer. Such people possess both faith and hypocrisy, and the outward legal rulings of Islam apply to them regarding inheritance and similar matters. If these rulings apply to an outright hypocrite—such as Ibn Ubayy and other hypocrites like him—then they apply to these people with still greater reason.

Clarifying “this point” helps dispel the confusion. Many jurists suppose that anyone described as an unbeliever must be subject to the rulings governing someone who has openly apostatized: he may neither inherit nor be inherited from, nor enter into marriage with Muslims. They have even applied these rulings to adherents of innovation whom they declared unbelievers on the basis of interpretation. Yet this is not the case. It is established that people fell into “three categories”: a believer; an unbeliever who openly professed unbelief; and a hypocrite who outwardly professed Islam while concealing unbelief.

Among the hypocrites were some whom people recognized through signs and indications—indeed, some whose hypocrisy they did not doubt, and whose hypocrisy the Quran had revealed, such as Ibn Ubayy and others like him. Nevertheless, when these people died, their Muslim heirs inherited from them; and when a relative of theirs died, they were given their share of the inheritance. Their lives remained protected unless one of them became liable to punishment under the revealed law.

When the Harūriyyah rose against ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, and separated themselves from the Muslim community, he told them:

“You have the right that we neither bar you from the mosques nor withhold your share of the public revenues (fay’).”

But when they deemed it lawful to kill Muslims and seize their property, he fought them at the command of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace;

for he said:

“One of you would consider his own prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

Thus, fighting the Harūriyyah was established by the Sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the agreement of his Companions. Fighting them was not a battle of civil strife like the fighting that occurred between two great groups of Muslims. Rather, it is established in an authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to his son al-Hasan:

“This son of mine is a leader, and through him Allah will reconcile two great groups of Muslims.”

He also said in an authentic hadith:

“A renegade faction will break away at a time of division among the Muslims, and the nearer of the two groups to the truth will kill them.”

This indicates that al-Hasan’s decision to refrain from fighting was either obligatory or recommended, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have praised him for abandoning something obligatory or recommended. The other hadith indicates that those who fought the Khawārij—namely, ‘Alī and his companions—were nearer to the truth than Mu‘āwiyah and his companions. It also indicates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded fighting the Khawārij. Fighting them was not like the fighting at the Battle of the Camel and at Siffīn, for which there was no command from the Prophet.

The point is that ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and others among his companions did not declare them unbelievers, nor did they fight them until the Khawārij initiated hostilities against them. Scholars have differed over declaring the adherents of religious innovations and deviant inclinations unbelievers and over their remaining eternally in the Fire. “Two views” on this matter have been reported from every one of the imams

Some of their followers came to present this disagreement as applying to all adherents of religious innovation and to their remaining eternally in the Fire, even going so far as to maintain that every particular individual they considered an innovator would remain there forever. This involves countless errors. At the opposite extreme, others came to think that no adherent of deviant inclinations could be declared an unbeliever, even if they espoused heresy and the doctrines of those who deny the divine attributes and those who teach union between Creator and creation.

The correct understanding of this matter is as follows:

A statement may constitute unbelief—as with the doctrines of the Jahmiyyah, who said that Allah does not speak and will not be seen in the Hereafter—yet some people may not realize that it constitutes unbelief. A general declaration is made that whoever utters it is an unbeliever, as the early generations said:

“Whoever says, ‘The Quran is created,’ is an unbeliever, and whoever says, ‘Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter,’ is an unbeliever.”

Yet a particular individual is not judged an unbeliever until the proof has been established against him, as explained earlier. This is like someone who, on the basis of an interpretation, denies the obligation of prayer and zakat or considers wine and illicit sexual intercourse lawful. These rulings are far more widely known among Muslims than the doctrinal matters just mentioned. If someone whose interpretation of those rulings is mistaken is not judged an unbeliever until the matter has been explained to him and he has been called upon to repent—as the Companions did with the group who considered wine lawful—then this applies all the more to other matters.

This is also the basis for understanding the authentic hadith about the man who said:

“When I die, burn me, then grind me to powder in the sea. By Allah, if Allah has power over me, He will punish me as He has punished no one in all creation.”

Allah forgave this man despite his doubt about Allah’s power and His restoring him to life if they burned him. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
If it is asked:

“Allah has commanded striving against the unbelievers and the hypocrites in two verses of the Quran. If the hypocrite is outwardly subject to the rulings of Islam, how can one strive against him?”

The answer is that whatever faith or hypocrisy becomes firmly established in the heart must manifest its effects in speech and action. As one of the early generations said:

“No one conceals anything within himself without Allah revealing it in his facial expressions and slips of the tongue.”

Allah Most High says concerning the hypocrites:

“If We willed, We could show them to you, and you would recognize them by their marks; but you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech.”

Thus, if a hypocrite openly neglects obligations or commits prohibited acts in a manner that warrants punishment, he is punished for his outward conduct. He is not punished for what is known of his inward state without outward evidence. Hence, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knew those hypocrites whom Allah had identified to him. They would swear oaths to him while lying, yet he accepted their outward professions and entrusted their inner secrets to Allah.

The very foundation upon which hypocrisy rests is that the hypocrite’s private and public selves, his outward and inward states, necessarily differ. This is why Allah describes them in His Book as liars, just as He describes the believers as truthful. Allah Most High says:

“They will suffer a painful punishment because they used to lie.”

And He says:

“Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars.”

There are many similar passages. Allah Most High also says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truly sincere.”

And He says:

“Righteousness is not that you turn your faces towards the east or the west”—up to His words—“It is they who have been truthful, and it is they who are mindful of Allah.”

In brief, the fundamental principle underlying these issues is to understand that unbelief is of two kinds: overt unbelief

translated_text:
and the unbelief of hypocrisy. In rulings pertaining to the Hereafter, the hypocrite has the same status as the unbelievers. In worldly rulings, however, the rulings applicable to Muslims may apply to the hypocrite.

It has become clear that religion necessarily involves both speech and action. It is impossible for someone to believe in Allah and His Messenger in his heart, or in both his heart and his speech, while performing no outward obligation whatsoever—neither prayer, nor zakat, nor fasting, nor any other obligatory duty. Performing such duties, but not because Allah has made them obligatory—for example, returning a trust, speaking truthfully, or acting justly in one’s allocations and judgments, without faith in Allah and His Messenger—does not bring a person out of unbelief. For the polytheists and the People of the Book also regard these things as obligatory. Thus, a person cannot be a believer in Allah and His Messenger while performing none of the duties uniquely enjoined by Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Anyone who maintains that the faith which is obligatory can be attained without performing any obligatory deeds is plainly mistaken, whether he regards performing those duties as a necessary consequence of faith or as part of it—this distinction is merely verbal. This is the innovation of irjāʾ, whose adherents the early generations and the imams denounced so vehemently, making the well-known stern pronouncements concerning it. Prayer is the greatest, most universal, foremost, and most exalted of these duties.

As for ihsān (excellence), it is explained in his words:

“Worship Allah as though you see Him; for even though you do not see Him, He sees you.”

It has been said that ihsān means sincerity. The precise view, however, is that ihsān encompasses sincerity and more: it combines perfect sincerity to Allah with the performance of good deeds that Allah loves. Allah Most High says:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.”

And Allah Most High says:

“And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while doing good and follows the religion of Abraham, inclining to truth? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

Among the principles discussed earlier, I explained that “Islam”—the religion of Allah with which He revealed His Books and sent His messengers—means that the servant submits to Allah, Lord of all worlds. He surrenders to Allah alone, without partner, and devotes himself exclusively to Him, worshipping Him and no other. This is made clear by the finest of words and the foundation of Islam: the testimony that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah.

Islam has two opposites: arrogance and associating partners with Allah. Thus, it is reported that “Noah, peace be upon him, enjoined his sons to declare, ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah’ and ‘Glory be to Allah,’ and forbade them arrogance and associating partners with Allah,” in a hadith I have cited elsewhere. Whoever is too arrogant to worship Allah does not worship Him and therefore does not surrender to Him. Whoever worships Him and also worships another associates a partner with Him and therefore is not exclusively devoted to Him; rather, his devotion is divided.

The word “Islam” encompasses submission and purity of devotion, which is sincerity. It is known that all the messengers were sent with Islam in its general sense, which encompasses these meanings. As Allah Most High says:

“The prophets who submitted to Allah judged by it.”

Moses said:

“If you believe in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you have submitted to Him.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while doing good will have his reward with

his Lord.”

And when his Lord said to Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, “Submit,” he replied:

“I have submitted to the Lord of all worlds.”

“Abraham enjoined this upon his sons, as did Jacob”—who likewise enjoined it upon his sons—“O my sons! Allah has chosen this religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims.”

Joseph said:

“Cause me to die as a Muslim.”

There are many similar passages.

It is known that Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, is the leader of the upright Muslim monotheists who came after him. Allah made him a model and a leader, and the messengers from among his descendants brought this same religion. The Jews and Christians then introduced innovations that took them outside the religion of Allah they had been commanded to follow: Islam in its general sense. This is why we have been commanded to say:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray.”

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The Jews have incurred Allah’s anger, and the Christians have gone astray.”

Each of these two communities departed from Islam and became predominantly characterized by one of its two opposites. Arrogance predominates among the Jews, while associating partners with Allah is less common among them. Among the Christians, associating partners with Allah predominates, while arrogance is less common.

Allah has explained this in His Book, saying concerning the Jews:

“And when We took the covenant from the Children of Israel: ‘Worship none but Allah.’”

This is the foundation of Islam. The passage continues up to His words:

“And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear signs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant, rejecting some and killing others?”

This interrogative wording expresses condemnation of their conduct and blame for it. They are blamed only for what they actually did. Thus, it is clear that whenever a messenger came to them with something contrary to the desires of

their souls, they grew arrogant, killing some prophets and rejecting others. Such is the condition of an arrogant person who refuses to accept whatever does not accord with his desires. In an authentic hadith, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained arrogance as rejecting the truth and looking down on people. In Sahīh Muslim, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“No one with an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will enter the Fire, and no one with an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise.”

A man asked, “O Messenger of Allah, a man likes his clothes and shoes to look good. Is that arrogance?”

He replied, “No. Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Rather, arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down on people.”

Rejecting the truth means denying and repudiating it; looking down on people means despising and belittling them. Allah likewise mentions “arrogance” in the passage beginning with His words:

“And We inscribed for him on the Tablets something of all things,”

and continuing to His words:

“I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth without right. Even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. If they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as their way; but if they see the way of error, they will take it as their way.”

Such is the condition of someone who does not act upon his knowledge but instead follows his desires: he is one who goes astray. As Allah says:

“Relate to them the account of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but who cast them off. Satan then pursued him, and he became one of those who went astray. Had We willed, We would have elevated him through them, but he clung to earthly life and followed his desires.”

And so the verse continues. This is the likeness of corrupt scholars. Concerning Moses’s return to them, Allah said:

“When Moses’s anger subsided, he took up the Tablets, and in their inscription were guidance and mercy for those who stand in awe of their Lord.”

Those who stand in awe of their Lord are the opposite of those who follow their desires. As Allah Most High says:

“But as for the one who feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from desire, Paradise will indeed be his refuge.”

 فَإِنَّ الْعِلْمَ حَرْبٌ لِلْمُتَعَالِي كَمَا أَنَّ السَّيْلَ حَرْبٌ لِلْمَكَانِ الْعَالِي وَاَلَّذِينَ يَرْهَبُونَ رَبَّهُمْ عَمِلُوا بِمَا عَلِمُوهُ فَأَتَاهُمْ اللَّهُ عِلْمًا وَرَحْمَةً إذْ مَنْ عَمِلَ بِمَا عَلِمَ أَوْرَثَهُ اللَّهُ عِلْمَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ وَلِهَذَا لَمَّا وَصَفَ اللَّهُ النَّصَارَى:

translated_text:
Thus, those arrogant people who follow their desires are turned away from Allah’s signs: they neither know nor understand. Because they arrogantly abandoned acting upon what they knew and followed their desires, they were punished by being deprived of understanding and knowledge. For knowledge is an enemy to the haughty, just as flowing water is an enemy to high ground.

Those who stand in awe of their Lord acted upon what they knew, so Allah granted them knowledge and mercy. Whoever acts upon what he knows, Allah grants him knowledge of what he did not know. Thus, when Allah said of the Christians, “because among them are priests and monks”—the term ruhbān (monks) derives from rahbana (monasticism)—“and because they are not arrogant,” it was these qualities that made them nearer in affection to the believers. As He said:

“You will surely find the most hostile people toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate partners with Allah; and you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to the believers to be those who say, ‘We are Christians.’ That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant.”

Since they possessed awe and were free of arrogance, they were closer to guidance. He therefore said concerning those among them who became Muslims:

“When they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they recognize. They say, ‘Our Lord, we believe, so record us among the witnesses.’”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “With Muhammad and his community.” They are the community who bear witness. For Christians have religious resolve and worship, but lack knowledge and testimony. Thus, if the Jews are worse than them in being more arrogant, less in awe, and more hard-hearted, the Christians are worse than the Jews in being further astray, more given to associating partners with Allah, and further from treating as forbidden what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.

Allah described them as associating partners with Him through practices they invented, just as He described the Jews as possessing the arrogance they desired. Allah Most High said:

“They have taken their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah

son of Mary. Yet they were commanded only to worship one God; there is no god but Him. Glory be to Him! He is far above what they associate with Him.” Allah Most High also said:

“And when Allah says, ‘O Jesus, son of Mary, did you tell people, “Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah”?’ He will say, ‘Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say.’”

Up to His words:

“Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord”—and the rest of the verse.

In several places in His Book, Allah mentions their claims that Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary, that Allah is the third of three, and that Allah has taken a child. He explains the enormity of their fabrication, their insult to Allah, and their “monstrous” claim, at which:

“The heavens almost rupture, the earth splits apart, and the mountains collapse in devastation.”

For this reason, in several places He calls upon them to worship only one God, as in His words:

“O People of the Scripture, do not go to extremes in your religion, and say nothing about Allah except the truth.”

Up to His words:

“And do not say, ‘Three.’ Desist—it is better for you. Allah is but one God. Glory be to Him! He is far above having a child.”

Up to His words:

“The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels brought near to Him. Whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant—He will gather them all to Himself.”

This is because those who associate a created being—human or otherwise—with Allah themselves become guilty of associating partners with Him, while the human or jinn whom they associate with Him becomes arrogant. As He said:

“There were men among mankind who sought refuge with men among the jinn, and they increased them in arrogance.”

Allah thus states that His servants do not arrogantly refuse to worship Him, even if those who associate partners with Him take them as His partners.

Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“They have certainly disbelieved who say, ‘Allah is the third of three.’ There is no god but one God.”

Up to His words:

“The Messiah, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. His mother was a woman of truth”—and the rest of the verse.

Allah Most High also said:

“They have certainly disbelieved who say, ‘Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary.’ Yet the Messiah said, ‘O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Whoever associates partners with Allah—Allah has forbidden

Paradise to him.’” He thus states that the Messiah commanded them to worship Allah alone and forbade them to associate himself or anyone else with Allah, as they did.

Since arrogance was the foundation of the Jews’ religion, He punished them with humiliation:

“Humiliation has been imposed upon them wherever they are found.”

And since associating partners with Allah, through multiplying the paths to Him, was the foundation of the Christians’ religion, He led them astray from Him. Each community was thus punished for its wrongdoing with the opposite of what it intended:

“And your Lord is never unjust to His servants.”

As stated in the hadith:

“The tyrannical and arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in the forms of tiny ants, trampled under people’s feet.”

Likewise, in the report from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, transmitted both as his own statement and as a saying traced back to the Prophet:

“Everyone has a bridle upon his head. If he humbles himself, he is told, ‘Rise; may Allah raise you.’ But if he raises his head, he is told, ‘Be brought low; may Allah bring you low.’”

He, glorified and exalted, said:

“Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Yes indeed! My revelations came to you, but you denied them, acted arrogantly, and were among the disbelievers.”

“On the Day of Resurrection, you will see those who lied about Allah with their faces blackened. Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the arrogant?”

“And Allah will save those who feared Him, granting them triumph.”

For this reason, they deserved wrath and abhorrence.

As for the Christians, when they embraced religious innovations, He led them astray from Allah’s path. They strayed from Allah’s path, led many others astray, and departed from the right way. They had introduced these innovations only to draw nearer to Him and worship Him through them; yet these innovations took them farther from Him, led them astray from Him, and caused them to worship others besides Him.

Reflect, then, on this. May Allah Most High guide us to His straight path—the path of those whom He has blessed, not of those who have incurred wrath or gone astray.

He described some Jews as associating partners with Him when He said:

“The Jews say, ‘Ezra is the son of Allah.’”

And when He said:

“Say, ‘Shall I inform you of those whose recompense with Allah is worse than that? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He is angry, some of whom He turned into apes and pigs, and those who worshipped false gods.’”

Thus, among the Jews were those who worshipped idols and human beings. For whoever arrogantly rejects the truth is afflicted with submission to falsehood, so that the arrogant person becomes one who associates partners with Allah. Allah thus mentioned that Pharaoh and his people, despite their arrogance and denial, associated partners with Him. He related the words of the believer from Pharaoh’s household:

“My people! Why do I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire? You call me to disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I call you to the Almighty, the All-Forgiving. Without doubt, what you call me to has no claim to worship in this world or in the Hereafter.”

He also said:

“Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs,” to the end of the verse.

Joseph, the truthful, said to them:

“My two fellow prisoners! Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the All-Subduing? You worship besides Him nothing but names that you and your forefathers have invented, for which Allah has sent down no authority. Judgment belongs to Allah alone. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.”

Allah Most High also said:

“The chiefs of Pharaoh’s people said, ‘Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?’ He said, ‘We will kill their sons and spare their women. We certainly hold mastery over them.’”

If it is asked: “How could Pharaoh’s people have associated partners with Allah, when Allah has told us concerning Pharaoh

that he denied the Creator, saying:

‘What is the Lord of all worlds?’

He also said:

‘I know of no god for you other than myself.’

And:

‘I am your supreme lord.’

Allah said of his people:

‘When Our signs came to them, clear to see, they said, “This is obvious magic.” They denied them out of injustice and arrogance, though inwardly they were certain of them.’

Yet only someone who acknowledges Allah can associate partners with Him; someone who denies Him has not associated partners with Him?”

The reply is: Allah mentions denial of the Creator only in connection with the Pharaoh of Moses’s time. As for those who lived in Joseph’s time, the Quran indicates that they acknowledged Allah while associating partners with Him. Thus, Joseph’s words to the king, the minister, and the people presupposed acknowledgement of the Creator’s existence, as when he said:

“Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the All-Subduing?”

“Return to your master and ask him about the women,” down to his words, “My Lord indeed knows their schemes.”

“And Allah does not guide the schemes of the treacherous,” down to his words:

“Indeed, the soul constantly urges evil, except when my Lord bestows His mercy. My Lord is indeed All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

The believer mentioned in Āl Hā Mīm also said:

“Joseph had already come to you before with clear proofs, yet you remained in doubt about what he brought you. Then, when he died, you said, ‘Allah will never send another messenger after him.’”

This implies that those to whom Joseph was sent acknowledged Allah.

Likewise, before Joseph’s brothers recognized him, while they thought he belonged to Pharaoh’s household, they addressed him in terms that presupposed acknowledgement of the Creator. For example, they said:

“By Allah, you certainly know that we did not come to spread corruption in the land, nor have we ever been thieves.”

He said to them:

“You are in a worse position, and Allah knows best what you allege.”

He also said:

“Allah forbid that we should seize anyone except the one with whom we found our property.”

And they said to him:

“O chief minister, hardship has afflicted us and our family, and we have brought goods of little value. Give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards those who give charity.”

The Pharaoh who lived in Joseph’s time greatly honoured his parents and household when they arrived, while knowing their religion. A survey of human history also supports this. Denial of the Creator has never been the prevailing belief of any nation. Rather, the religion of unbelievers outside the prophetic message was to associate partners with Allah. Only some people denied the Creator. Their scholars were among the polytheistic Sabian philosophers who venerated temples, heavenly bodies, and idols. All the transmitted accounts of their history and lives indicate this.

But the Pharaoh of Moses’s time:

“Made fools of his people, and they obeyed him.”

It was he—not the earlier Pharaohs—who told them:

“I know of no god for you other than myself.”

Then, afterwards, he told them:

“I am your supreme lord.”

“So Allah seized him in exemplary punishment for the last and the first.”

That is, punishment for the first statement and punishment for the last. Inwardly, Pharaoh knew that the Creator existed; he merely acted arrogantly, like Iblīs, and denied His existence. Hence Moses said to him:

“You certainly know that none but the Lord of the heavens and the earth has sent down these signs as clear proofs.”

When he denied the Creator, he continued worshipping the deities he already worshipped. Allah Most High did not describe him as associating partners with Him, but rather as denying the Creator and worshipping other deities. Those among them who deny the Creator are arrogant: they often worship deities, yet never worship Allah.

Such a person says, “This world is necessarily existent in itself, and some of its parts exert an influence upon others.” He also says that he has benefited only through worshipping heavenly bodies, idols, and the like. Thus, the underlying meaning of the doctrine of these advocates of union who claim affiliation with Islam is the doctrine of Pharaoh.

وَكُنْت أُبَيِّنُ أَنَّهُ مَذْهَبُهُمْ وَأُبَيِّنُ أَنَّهُ حَقِيقَةُ مَذْهَبِ فِرْعَوْنَ حَتَّى حَدَّثَنِي الثِّقَةُ:

I used to explain that this was their doctrine and that it was the true substance of Pharaoh’s doctrine, until a trustworthy man reported to me that one of their leaders in falsehood had said, “We follow Pharaoh’s doctrine.” Hence the immense veneration they show Pharaoh in their books.

They do not acknowledge a Maker who created the world, nor do they affirm a Lord who governs created beings. Rather, they make nature itself the Maker. Thus they permit the worship of anything, saying that whoever worships it has worshipped Allah. In their view, worshipping anything other than Allah is inconceivable: whatever is worshipped is Allah. These existing things, they believe, are His parts or attributes, like a human being’s parts or attributes. When these people worship existing things, therefore, they do not worship them to bring them nearer to Allah, but because, in their view, they are Allah, a locus of His manifestation, one of His parts, one of His attributes, or one of His particular determinations.

These people worship what Pharaoh and other polytheists worship. But Pharaoh does not say, “They are Allah,” nor, “They bring us nearer to Allah.” The polytheists say, “They are our intercessors and bring us nearer to Allah,” whereas these people say, “They are Allah,” as explained above. Those others are greater in unbelief insofar as they acknowledged that they worshipped something other than Allah or denied Him. These people, however, are more far-reaching in their error insofar as they permit the worship of anything, claiming that it is Allah and that the worshipper is the one worshipped—even if they intended only to worship Allah.

Given that those others were polytheists, as they have been described, whereas the Pharaoh of Moses’s time was the one who denied the Maker and worshipped other deities, without Allah describing him as a polytheist, it is clear that polytheists may love their deities as they love Allah, or may love them more than they love Allah. Hence they revile Allah when their deities are reviled, as the Most High says:

Pharaoh’s people may have turned away from Allah altogether after previously associating partners with Him, accepting Pharaoh’s declarations:

“I am your lord, the Most High,”

and:

“I know of no god for you other than myself.”

Thus, when the believer addressed them, he mentioned both matters, saying:

“You call me to disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge.”

He mentioned disbelief in Him, which may include denying His existence, and also mentioned associating partners with Him. His words thus encompassed both positions and both states.

It has therefore become clear that one way an arrogant person becomes a polytheist is by worshipping other deities while arrogantly refusing to worship Allah. Calling this polytheism, however, is analogous to doing so in the case of someone who arrogantly refuses to devote his worship exclusively to Allah. As the Most High says:

“Indeed, whenever it was said to them, ‘There is no god but Allah,’ they would grow arrogant and say, ‘Are we really to abandon our gods for a mad poet?’”

These people are both arrogant and polytheists; their arrogance consists in refusing to devote their worship exclusively to Allah. An arrogant person who does not outwardly acknowledge Allah, such as Pharaoh, is therefore greater in unbelief than they are. Iblīs, who commands and loves all of this and arrogantly refuses to worship and obey his Lord, is greater in unbelief than these people, even though he knows that Allah exists and knows His greatness—just as Pharaoh, too, knew that Allah exists.

Since religious innovations and sins constitute a branch of unbelief and derive from its branches, just as acts of obedience are all a branch of faith and derive from it, and since it is known that someone who knows the truth but does not follow it is wayward and resembles the Jews, whereas someone who worships Allah without knowledge or revealed law is misguided and resembles the Christians—as some of the early generations used to say:

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—also said:

Section

The term “Islam” is used in two ways: transitively, as in His words:

“Who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah while doing good?”

And His words:

“Say, ‘I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have those who follow me.’ And say to those who were given the Scripture and to the unlettered, ‘Have you submitted yourselves?’”

And the rest of the verse. Likewise, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said in his supplication before sleep:

“I have submitted myself to You.”

It is also used intransitively, as in His words:

“When his Lord said to him, ‘Submit,’ he said, ‘I have submitted to the Lord of all worlds.’”

And His words:

“To Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth.”

And His words concerning Bilqīs:

“I submit with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of all worlds.”

It encompasses two meanings: first, obedience and submission; second, directing that submission sincerely and exclusively to Allah, as in His words:

“Allah presents an example: a man shared by quarrelling partners, and a man belonging exclusively to one man.”

Its defining declaration is, “There is no god but Allah.” It has two senses.
