translated_text:
The first is the religion common to all the prophets: worshipping Allah alone, without partner. All the prophets were sent with this religion, as the texts of the Quran and Sunnah establish that their religion was one.

The second is the religion, law, and way specific to Muhammad—the revealed law, the path, and the reality. This has two levels:

The first consists of outward words and deeds: the five pillars. The second is that these outward expressions accord with the inward state. The two verses in Allah’s Book and the two hadiths from the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—use the first interpretation. In this sense, Islam is broader than faith: every believer is a Muslim, but not every Muslim is a believer.

The second interpretation is intended in His words:

“Indeed, the religion in the sight of Allah is Islam.”

And His words:

“And that is the upright religion.”

It is also intended in the Prophet’s words, “I command you to have faith in Allah,” which he explained through the practices of Islam. According to this interpretation, complete faith, religion, and Islam are equivalent. This is the only meaning understood by the Muʿtazilah.

A third meaning may also be intended: the perfection of Islam. This is expressed in his words:

“A Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe.”

He has thus made others safe—that is, safe from himself.

As for the term “faith,” it is said that its original meaning is assent—though it is not synonymous with assent. Rather, it must be assent concerning something unseen; assenting to a report about something directly witnessed is not faith. This is because the word derives from security, meaning reassurance. This applies only to the one conveying a report, about whom doubt may arise, whereas things directly witnessed admit no doubt, except on this basis—then it is either assent by the heart alone, as maintained by

translated_text:
the Jahmiyyah and those of the Ash‘ariyyah who follow them; or assent of both heart and tongue, as the Murji’ah maintain; or of the tongue alone, as the Karrāmiyyah maintain; or assent through the heart, speech, and deeds—for all of these fall within the meaning of assent according to the scholars of hadith, as Shaykh al-Islām and others explained (*).

It has also been said that faith is, rather, acknowledgment: assent applies only to a report, whereas acknowledgment applies to both a report and a command, as in His words:

“Do you acknowledge this and accept My covenant on that basis?” They said, “We acknowledge it.”

Moreover, qarra and āmana are close in meaning. Faith means entering into security, while acknowledgment means entering into acknowledgment. Accordingly, the spoken declaration is an acknowledgment, and acting upon it is also an acknowledgment.

In the Quran, faith is used in two senses, involving a foundation and an obligatory branch. The foundation is what lies in the heart, distinct from deeds. Hence the distinction between them in His words:

“Those who believe and do righteous deeds.”

The sense encompassing both occurs in His words:

“The believers are only…”

“Those who believe do not ask your permission.”

It also occurs in the hadith of “al-hayyā” and that of “the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays.”

Faith comprises an indispensable foundation; an obligatory element whose absence diminishes it in a manner that makes a person deserving of punishment; and a recommended element whose absence deprives a person of a higher rank. Thus, with respect to faith, people include those who wrong themselves, those who take a middle course, and those who are foremost. The same applies to Hajj, the body, a mosque, and other entities, deeds, and attributes.

Among its various components are those whose loss leaves it short of the highest perfection; those whose loss leaves it short of the required completeness, through neglecting obligations or committing prohibited acts; and those whose loss removes an essential pillar—namely, abandoning belief and speech, which the Murji’ah and Jahmiyyah claim alone constitute what is meant by faith. This resolves the misconceptions of the various sects.

Faith is rooted in the heart and perfected through outward deeds. Islam is the reverse: its foundation is outward, and its perfection lies in the heart.

He also said—may Allah have mercy on him:

Section

It is well known that the foundation of “faith” is faith in Allah and His Messenger. This is also the foundation of knowledge of Allah, as I explained at the beginning of this volume (*).

As for “faith in Allah,” humanity at large has generally acknowledged it, apart from fringe sects such as the Dahrī philosophers, the Ismā‘īliyyah, and others like them, or those who hypocritically profess it while outwardly claiming adherence to the religions. The differences among the adherents of religions concern His names, attributes, actions, rulings, the worship due to Him, and similar matters.

As for “faith in the Messenger,” this is the crucial matter, for faith in Allah is incomplete without faith in him, and neither salvation nor happiness can be attained without it, since he is the way to Allah, glorified be He. Hence the two pillars of Islam are:

“I bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.”

It is well known that faith is acknowledgment, not merely assent. Acknowledgment involves the heart’s affirmation, which is assent, and the heart’s action, which is submission—believing the Messenger

Hypocrisy frequently concerns one’s relationship with the Messenger, and this is the predominant form of hypocrisy that Allah mentions in the Quran concerning the hypocrites during his lifetime. Disbelief is the absence of faith, whether accompanied by denial, arrogance, refusal, or aversion. Whoever lacks affirmation and submission in his heart is therefore a disbeliever.

There are, then, “two kinds of hypocrisy”: hypocrisy among people of learning and speculative theology, and hypocrisy among people of religious practice and worship.

As for outright hypocrisy, whose perpetrator is unquestionably a disbeliever, it consists in not considering it obligatory to believe what the Messenger reports or to obey what he commands, even while believing that the Messenger possesses great knowledge and excellence in practice, and that believing and obeying him is permissible. Such a person nevertheless says that differences between religions do not matter so long as the One worshipped is the same. He holds that salvation and happiness can be attained both by following the Messenger and without following him—through philosophy and Sabianism, or through Judaism and Christianity. This is the position of the Sabian philosophers on this question and on others. For even if they believe and obey him, they do not consider this obligatory for everyone on earth, such that whoever fails to believe and obey him will be punished. Rather, they regard it as comparable to adhering to an imam’s school, following a shaykh’s path, or obeying a king. This is the religion of the Tatars and those who join them.

As for the lesser degree of hypocrisy, it consists in seeking knowledge of Allah independently of what the Messenger reports, or seeking to act for Allah independently of what he commands. Many speculative theologians are afflicted with the former, and many Sufis with the latter. They believe that he must be believed or that he must be obeyed, yet in their pursuit of knowledge

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Is there any spiritual station or state above faith in Allah and His Messenger? Does faith encompass every station and state commended by Allah and His Messenger? Is faith to be described as a light that Allah places in a servant’s heart, enabling him, when it enters his heart, to distinguish truth from falsehood?

Is there some means by which faith is first attained—such as seeing righteous people, sitting with them and keeping their company, learning to perform a particular act, or something else? If its initial attainment has a cause, what is that cause? And what are the means—in their proper order—by which faith is strengthened until it reaches perfection?

Should one begin with renunciation until one practices it soundly? Or with knowledge until one becomes firmly grounded in it? Or with worship until one has fully exerted oneself? Or should one combine these according to one’s ability? How, then, does one attain the reality of the faith praised by Allah and His Messenger?

Explain to us the means by which the reality of faith is attained, detailing their various kinds, and describe the person who possesses it—may Allah be pleased with you.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The term “faith” is used both without qualification and with qualification. When used without qualification, it encompasses everything Allah and His Messenger love of a servant’s inward and outward words and deeds. This is the understanding generally held by the early generations and leading scholars among the Companions, the Followers, and their followers, who hold that faith consists of words and deeds, increases through obedience, and decreases through disobedience. They include within its meaning all acts of obedience, both obligatory and voluntary. This is the position of the vast majority of scholars of hadith, Sufism, speculative theology, and jurisprudence among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

This includes what may be called spiritual stations and states, such as patience, gratitude, fear, hope, reliance upon Allah, contentment, reverent fear, turning to Allah, sincerity, affirming Allah’s oneness, and other such qualities.

Among the evidence for this is the hadith recorded in the two Sahīh collections, in which the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Faith has sixty-odd—or seventy-odd—branches. The highest is the declaration that none is worthy of worship but Allah; the lowest is removing something harmful from the road; and modesty is a branch of faith.”

He thus mentioned the highest branch of faith: the declaration that none is worthy of worship but Allah. Nothing is better than this declaration, as reported in al-Muwattaʾ and elsewhere from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who said:

“The best supplication is the supplication on the Day of

ʿArafah, and the best that I and the prophets before me have said is: ‘None is worthy of worship but Allah alone, with no partner. His is the dominion, and His is all praise, and He has power over all things.’”

In al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere, he is reported to have said:

“Whoever dies knowing that none is worthy of worship but Allah will enter Paradise.”

In the Sahīh, it is reported that he said to his uncle as death approached:

“My uncle, say, ‘None is worthy of worship but Allah’—a declaration with which I may plead your case before Allah.”

The evidence is abundant and mutually reinforcing that the greatest good deed is affirming Allah’s oneness, just as the worst evil deed is associating partners with Him. This is the sin that Allah does not forgive, as He, the Exalted, says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whom He wills.”

Affirming His oneness is the good deed that necessarily brings bliss to the one who possesses it. This is established in the authentic hadith concerning the two determining causes: that which entails bliss and that which entails misery. Whoever dies testifying that none is worthy of worship but Allah will enter Paradise, whereas whoever dies associating anything with Allah will enter the Fire. In the hadith, he also described this declaration as the highest branch of faith.

In the two Sahīh collections, it is reported that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to the delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays:

“I command you to have faith in Allah. Do you know what faith in Allah is? It is to testify that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, to establish prayer, to give zakat, and to pay one-fifth of the spoils.”

He thus included these deeds within faith, while also including them within Islam in the authentic hadith of Gabriel. When Gabriel came to him in the form of a Bedouin and asked him about faith, he replied:

“Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death, and to believe in divine decree, both its good and its evil.”

He then asked him about Islam, and he replied:

“It is to testify that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah

 إلَى أَنْ قَالُوا:
 يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يُصَدِّقَ بِقَلْبِهِ وَلَا يُظْهِرَ بِلِسَانِهِ إلَّا كَلِمَةَ الْكُفْرِ مَعَ قُدْرَتِهِ عَلَى إظْهَارِهَا فَيَكُونُ الَّذِي فِي الْقَلْبِ إيمَانًا نَافِعًا لَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ وَقَالُوا: حَيْثُ حَكَمَ الشَّارِعُ بِكُفْرِ أَحَدٍ بِعَمَلِ أَوْ قَوْلٍ: فَلِكَوْنِهِ دَلِيلًا عَلَى انْتِفَاءِ مَا فِي الْقَلْبِ وَقَوْلُهُمْ مُتَنَاقِضٌ؛ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا كَانَ ذَلِكَ دَلِيلًا مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِانْتِفَاءِ الْإِيمَانِ الَّذِي فِي الْقَلْبِ امْتَنَعَ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْإِيمَانُ ثَابِتًا فِي
translated_text:
and to establish prayer, give zakat, fast Ramadan, and perform pilgrimage to the House.” In a hadith in al-Musnad, he said:

“Islam is outward, while faith is in the heart.”

The foundation of faith lies in the heart and consists of the heart’s affirmation and action—its acknowledgment through assent, love, and submission. Whatever is in the heart must manifest its necessary effects and implications in the limbs. If a person does not act accordingly, this indicates its absence or weakness. Thus, outward deeds are among the necessary effects and implications of the heart’s faith. They confirm, indicate, and bear witness to what is in the heart. They are a branch and a constituent part of faith considered in its entirety. Yet what is in the heart is the foundation of what the limbs do. As Abū Hurayrah—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“The heart is a king, and the limbs are its soldiers. If the king is good, its soldiers are good; if the king is corrupt, its soldiers are corrupt.”

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is reported to have said:

“Indeed, there is a piece of flesh in the body: when it is sound, the rest of the body is sound because of it; and when it is corrupt, the rest of the body is corrupt because of it. Indeed, it is the heart.”

For this reason, some groups thought that faith resides exclusively in the heart, and that the deeds of the limbs do not fall within its meaning, but are merely its fruits and consequences, which indicate its presence. Their extremists—such as Jahm and his followers—went so far as to say that a person may believe in his heart while uttering nothing but words of disbelief, despite being capable of making an outward profession, and that what is in his heart would nevertheless constitute faith that benefits him in the Hereafter. They also said that whenever the Lawgiver judges someone to be a disbeliever on account of a deed or statement, it is because that deed or statement indicates the absence of what is in the heart.

Their position is contradictory. If that is evidence necessarily entailing the absence of faith from the heart, then it is impossible for faith to be present in

the heart alongside evidence that necessarily entails its absence. If, however, it is not evidence, it cannot be used to establish inward disbelief. Allah, glorified is He, explains in several places that faith is realized and confirmed through outward and inward deeds. For example, He says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

“Those who establish prayer and spend out of what We have provided for them.”

“It is they who are truly believers.”

He also says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. It is they who are truthful.”

And He, the Most High, says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger and, when they are with him on a matter of common concern, do not leave until they have asked his permission.”

And He, the Most High, says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning their disputes, then find within themselves no unease over what you have decided and submit completely.”

If someone says, “This indicates that faith is absent when these things are absent; it does not indicate that they are part of faith,” the reply is: This is an acknowledgment that inward faith is absent when outward matters such as these are absent. Thus, one cannot claim that the heart can contain faith incompatible with disbelief without any outward manifestation, whether in speech or action. This is the point to be established—and that acknowledgment confirms it.

This is because, when what is in the heart is firmly established, it necessarily affects what is outward; the two cannot be separated. A firm resolve to act, together with full ability, necessarily brings about the action within one’s power. Thus, if love for Allah and His Messenger is firmly established in the heart, it necessarily entails loyalty to His allies

translated_text:
and enmity toward His enemies.

“You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day having affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers, their sons, their brothers, or their kindred.”

“Had they believed in Allah and the Prophet and what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies.”

This necessary connection is inescapable. Some have erred by supposing that no such connection exists, just as others have erred in considering it possible for a firm resolve to coexist with full ability without action. They have even disputed whether a person is punished for an intention without acting upon it.

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained that an intention unaccompanied by whatever action the person is capable of performing is not a firm resolve. A firm resolve must be accompanied by whatever action lies within the person’s ability. Pardon applies to someone who contemplated an evil deed but has not committed it—not to someone who intended it, did what was within his power, but was unable to achieve his aim. An example is someone who intended to kill his companion and fought him until one of them was killed. Such a person is punished because he intended the deed and carried out whatever part of it was within his power. Whoever understands the necessary connections between inward and outward matters will be freed of many doubts concerning issues such as these, over which people have differed greatly.

One question remains: Does the term “faith” designate only the foundation, or both the foundation and its branches?

The precise answer is that the unqualified term encompasses both. When used in conjunction with another term, the name alone may be singled out for that designation; it may also encompass only the foundation when that alone is specified. The designation “tree,” for example, encompasses the root and branches when present. If the branches were cut off, the designation “tree” would encompass the root alone. Likewise, the designation “Hajj” encompasses everything prescribed within it, including essential pillars and obligatory acts

and recommended acts. It remains a complete Hajj without the recommended acts, but is deficient when obligatory acts whose omission is compensated for by a sacrifice are left out.

The Lawgiver (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) does not deny a person’s faith for omitting something recommended, but for omitting something obligatory: the person has neglected what is required for faith’s perfection and completeness, not merely something recommended. The terms “perfection” and “completeness” may refer to either obligatory or recommended perfection. Thus, some jurists distinguish between a complete ritual bath and one that fulfills the minimum requirements. Accordingly, when the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) says:

“There is no faith in one who is not trustworthy,”

and:

“A person who commits unlawful sexual intercourse is not a believer while committing it,”

or makes similar statements, this is because something obligatory within faith is absent, not because its recommended perfection is absent.

Faith has constituent parts, and people differ in their degree of faith, just as they do in Hajj and prayer. Hence, he (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Those with a speck’s weight of faith in their hearts, and those with a barley grain’s weight of faith, will be brought out of the Fire.”

When, however, the term “faith” is used with a qualification—as in the words of Allah Most High:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds,”

and His words:

“Those who believed and were mindful of Allah,”

and the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Faith is to believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, and resurrection after death,”

and similar expressions—it may be said that faith encompasses these matters, and that conjoining them to it is an instance of conjoining the particular to the general, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“and His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael,”

and His words:

“And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, son of Mary.”

Or it may be said that the meaning of a term varies according to whether it is used alone or alongside another term. This is the case with “the poor” and “the needy”: when either is used alone, it includes the other, but when they occur together, they denote two distinct categories, as in the verse on zakat. Undoubtedly, the branches of faith stand in relation to its foundations as two terms joined by a conjunction, while their relation to faith in its entirety is that of a part to the whole. This is where dispute and confusion have arisen over whether deeds are included in faith, since they are mentioned alongside it using a conjunction.

Similarly, some of faith’s higher branches or loftier forms, such as certainty and knowledge, may be mentioned alongside faith using a conjunction, suggesting a distinction between them. Thus, one may say, “This is the highest form of faith”—meaning that certainty and knowledge are higher than faith unaccompanied by such certainty and knowledge. As Allah Most High says:

“Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees.”

It is well known that people differ in faith and affirmation themselves: in their strength and weakness, their breadth and specificity, their persistence and continuity, what they entail and what contradicts them, and other aspects. One of the two forms is therefore distinguished by a name indicating its superiority over the other, while in such usage the term “faith” continues to denote the other category. The same occurs in comparable cases, as when one says, “Human beings are better than animals,” or “Human beings are better than other living creatures,” even though human beings are included among the living creatures mentioned in His words:

“Indeed, the worst of living creatures in Allah’s sight are the deaf and dumb who do not reason.”

Once this is understood, wherever an acceptable statement describes something as superior to faith, it merely gives precedence to a particular form over faith in general, or to some of its higher branches over the rest,

 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى:

 فَالْإِيمَانُ الَّذِي يَهَبُهُ اللَّهُ لِعَبْدِهِ سَمَّاهُ نُورًا وَسُمِّيَ الْوَحْيُ النَّازِلُ مِنْ السَّمَاءِ الَّذِي بِهِ يَحْصُلُ الْإِيمَانُ 
{نُورًا نَهْدِي بِهِ مَنْ نَشَاءُ مِنْ عِبَادِنَا}
 وَقَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{فَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِهِ وَعَزَّرُوهُ وَنَصَرُوهُ وَاتَّبَعُوا النُّورَ الَّذِي أُنْزِلَ مَعَهُ}
 وَأَمْثَالُ ذَلِكَ وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ الْمُؤْمِنَ يُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ الْحَقِّ وَالْبَاطِلِ بَلْ يُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَعْظَمِ الْحَقِّ لَكِنْ لَا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يُقَالَ: بِأَنَّ كُلَّ مَنْ لَهُ إيمَانٌ يُفَرِّقُ بِمُجَرَّدِ مَا أُعْطِيَهُ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ بَيْنَ كُلِّ حَقٍّ وَكُلِّ بَاطِلٍ.
translated_text:
and the term “faith” may encompass both categories or be restricted to one of them, as explained above. As has been said, “Most disagreement among rational people arises from the terms they use.”

Section

As for the question, “Is the quality of faith a light that Allah casts into a servant’s heart, so that when it enters his heart, the servant recognizes truth and falsehood?” the answer is:

Allah Most High has said:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is that of a niche containing a lamp.”

Ubayy ibn Ka‘b and others said, “The likeness of His light in the believer’s heart.” The passage continues up to His words:

“And whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.”

He Most High also says:

“Is one who was dead, then We gave him life and granted him a light by which to walk among people, like one who is in darkness?”

Thus, Allah called the faith He bestows upon His servant a light. The revelation sent down from heaven, through which faith is attained, is likewise called:

“A light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants.”

He Most High also says:

“So those who believe in him, honor him, support him, and follow the light sent down with him.”

There are other passages of this kind. Undoubtedly, the believer distinguishes truth from falsehood; indeed, he discerns the greatest truths. Yet it cannot be said that everyone who possesses faith can, merely through the faith he has been given, distinguish every truth from every falsehood.

translated_text:
Section

As for his question, “Is there a cause for faith’s initial emergence?” undoubtedly, it arises through a cause: listening to the Quran; observing believers and reflecting on their lives; learning about the Prophet’s life and miracles—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and reflecting on them; contemplating the signs of Allah Most High; reflecting on one’s own circumstances; or experiencing the pressing needs that Allah brings upon a servant, compelling him to humble himself before Allah, surrender to Him, and seek refuge in Him.

One cause may bring about one aspect of faith, while another brings about another. Indeed, everything that occurs in the world must have a cause. The causes of faith and its branches sometimes come from the servant himself and sometimes from someone else. For example, Allah may provide someone with a person who calls him to faith, enjoins good upon him, forbids him from evil, and explains to him the signs, arguments, and proofs of the religion. There are also events that befall him, upon which he reflects and from which he takes admonition, along with other causes.

فَصْلٌ:
وَأَمَّا قَوْلُهُ:
 فَالْأَسْبَابُ الَّتِي يَقْوَى بِهَا الْإِيمَانُ إلَى أَنْ يَكْمُلَ عَلَى تَرْتِيبِهَا؟ هَلْ يَبْدَأُ بِالزُّهْدِ؟ أَوْ بِالْعِلْمِ؟ أَوْ بِالْعِبَادَةِ؟ أَمْ يَجْمَعُ بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ عَلَى حَسَبِ طَاقَتِهِ؟

{فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ}

translated_text:
Section

As for his question, “What are the means by which faith grows stronger until it reaches perfection, and in what order should they be pursued? Should one begin with renunciation, knowledge, or worship, or combine them according to one’s ability?”

The answer is: One must have the obligatory measure of faith, worship, and renunciation. Beyond that, people differ in their levels of faith just as they differ in its branches. Each person should pursue what is within his reach and give priority to the more excellent deeds he is capable of undertaking.

People differ in this regard. Some find acquiring knowledge easier than renunciation; others find renunciation easier; and still others find worship easier than either. What is prescribed for each person is to do whatever good he can, as Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

When the branches of faith compete for his attention, he should give priority to what is more pleasing to Allah and what he is better able to perform. He may be more capable of performing a less excellent deed than a more excellent one, and may gain more from the former than from the latter. It is therefore better for him to pursue what benefits him more, since that is better in his particular case. He should not pursue what is better in absolute terms if it is beyond his ability or so difficult that it causes him to miss what is better and more beneficial for him.

An example is someone who recites the Quran at night, reflects upon it, and benefits from his recitation, whereas prayer is burdensome for him and he derives no benefit from performing it; or someone who benefits more from remembering Allah than from reciting the Quran.

أَمَّا الْأَوَّلُ:
 فَإِنَّ الزُّهْدَ. . .

translated_text:
Thus, whatever deed is more beneficial to him and more obedient to Allah is better for him than forcing himself to undertake a deed that he performs inadequately rather than properly, thereby missing what would benefit him more.

It is well known that prayer is more emphatically enjoined than reciting the Quran, and that reciting the Quran is better than remembrance of Allah and supplication. It is also well known that remembrance of Allah in the particular acts to which it belongs—such as bowing and prostration—is better than reciting the Quran in those positions, and that remembrance, recitation, and supplication at sunrise and sunset are better than prayer.

Renunciation is the opposite of desire, just as hatred is opposed to love and aversion to willing. Both willing and aversion have various forms, whether considered in themselves or in relation to their objects. Renunciation, likewise, may be considered from two perspectives: what is renounced and renunciation itself.

As for the former, renunciation … (1)

As for renunciation itself, which is the opposite of desire and consists in aversion and hatred, its prescribed form consists in the servant’s aversion, hatred, and love being governed by Allah’s love, hatred, pleasure, and displeasure. He therefore loves what Allah loves, hates what Allah hates, is pleased with what Allah is pleased with, and is displeased with what Allah is displeased with. In this way, he follows not his own desires but his Master’s command.

Many who renounce worldly life have turned away from its excesses without turning toward what Allah and His Messenger love. Such renunciation is not what Allah and His Messenger command. Thus, there have been ascetics among the polytheists, among the People of the Book, and among the followers of religious innovation.

وَمِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَزْهَدُ لِطَلَبِ الرَّاحَةِ مِنْ تَعَبِ الدُّنْيَا وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَزْهَدُ لِمَسْأَلَةِ أَهْلِهَا وَالسَّلَامَةِ مِنْ أَذَاهُمْ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَزْهَدُ فِي الْمَالِ لِطَلَبِ الرَّاحَةِ إلَى أَمْثَالِ هَذِهِ الْأَنْوَاعِ الَّتِي لَا يَأْمُرُ اللَّهُ بِهَا وَلَا رَسُولُهُ وَإِنَّمَا يَأْمُرُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ أَنْ يَزْهَدَ فِيمَا لَا يُحِبُّهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَيَرْغَبَ فِيمَا يُحِبُّهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ فَيَكُونُ زُهْدُهُ هُوَ الْإِعْرَاضُ عَمَّا لَا يَأْمُرُ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَرَسُولُهُ أَمْرَ إيجَابٍ وَلَا أَمْرَ اسْتِحْبَابٍ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ مُحَرَّمًا أَوْ مَكْرُوهًا أَوْ مُبَاحًا مُسْتَوِيَ الطَّرَفَيْنِ فِي حَقِّ الْعَبْدِ وَيَكُونُ مَعَ ذَلِكَ مُقْبِلًا عَلَى مَا أَمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ وَرَسُولُهُ وَإِلَّا فَتَرْكُ الْمَكْرُوهِ بِدُونِ فِعْلِ الْمَحْبُوبِ لَيْسَ بِمَطْلُوبِ وَإِنَّمَا الْمَطْلُوبُ بِالْمَقْصُودِ الْأَوَّلِ فِعْلُ مَا يُحِبُّهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَتَرْكُ الْمَكْرُوهِ مُتَعَيَّنٌ كَذَلِكَ بِهِ تَزْكُو النَّفْسُ؛ فَإِنَّ الْحَسَنَاتِ إذَا انْتَفَتْ عَنْهَا السَّيِّئَاتُ زَكَتْ فَبِالزَّكَاةِ تَطِيبُ النَّفْسُ مِنْ الْخَبَائِثِ وَتَعْظُمُ فِي الطَّاعَاتِ كَمَا أَنَّ الزَّرْعَ إذَا أُزِيلَ عَنْهُ الدَّغَلُ زَكَا وَظَهَرَ وَعَظُمَ.
فَصْلٌ:
وَأَمَّا طَرِيقُ الْوُصُولِ إلَى ذَلِكَ:
 فَبِالِاجْتِهَادِ فِي فِعْلِ الْمَأْمُورِ وَتَرْكِ الْمَحْظُورِ وَالِاسْتِعَانَةِ بِهِ عَلَى ذَلِكَ فَفِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: {الْمُؤْمِنُ الْقَوِيُّ خَيْرٌ وَأَحَبُّ إلَى اللَّهِ مِنْ الْمُؤْمِنِ الضَّعِيفِ وَفِي كُلٍّ خَيْرٌ احْرِصْ عَلَى مَا يَنْفَعُك وَاسْتَعِنْ بِاَللَّهِ وَلَا تَعْجِزَن وَإِنْ أَصَابَك شَيْءٌ فَلَا تَقُلْ لَوْ أَنِّي فَعَلْت لَكَانَ كَذَا وَكَذَا. وَلَكِنْ قُلْ قَدَّرَ اللَّهُ وَمَا شَاءَ فَعَلَ؛ فَإِنَّ لَوْ تَفْتَحُ عَمَلَ
translated_text:
Some people renounce worldly life to find relief from its toil. Others do so to seek handouts from worldly people and escape their harm. Still others renounce wealth in pursuit of ease. These and similar forms of renunciation are not commanded by Allah or His Messenger. Rather, Allah and His Messenger command a person to renounce what they do not love and desire what they love. His renunciation thus consists in turning away from whatever Allah and His Messenger have not enjoined, whether as an obligation or a recommendation—whether it is forbidden, disliked, or permissible such that doing it and leaving it are equally preferable for that servant. At the same time, he must devote himself to what Allah and His Messenger have commanded.

Merely abandoning what is disliked without doing what is loved is not what is sought. The primary aim is to do what Allah and His Messenger love. Abandoning what is disliked is likewise necessary; through this the soul is purified. For good deeds flourish when evil deeds are removed from them. Through purification, the soul is cleansed of impurities and grows in obedience, just as crops, when cleared of weeds, flourish, rise, and grow.

Section

As for the way to attain this, it lies in striving to do what is commanded, abandoning what is forbidden, and seeking Allah’s help in doing so. In Sahīh Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both. Strive for what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘If only I had done this, such-and-such would have happened.’ Rather, say, ‘Allah has decreed, and He has done what He willed,’ for ‘if only’ opens the way to the work of

Satan.”

The Sunan collections relate:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled against a man, who then said, ‘Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Allah reproaches a person for helplessness, but you must act prudently. Then, if a matter overcomes you, say: “Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.”’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus commanded the servant to strive for what benefits him and to seek Allah’s help in doing so. Striving for what benefits him means exerting himself in goodness, which is worship. For the servant is commanded to seek everything that benefits him. He is only forbidden to seek what harms him—even if he believes it benefits him—as when he seeks forbidden things, which harm him, or pursues an inferior course that does not benefit him.

Allah Most High has permitted believers wholesome things, which benefit them, and forbidden them unwholesome things, which harm them. Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best. May Allah bestow blessings and abundant peace upon Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

original_text:
قَالَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ - طَيَّبَ اللَّهُ ثَرَاهُ -:
فَصْلٌ:
وَأَمَّا الْإِيمَانُ:
 هَلْ هُوَ مَخْلُوقٌ أَوْ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ؟ . فَالْجَوَابُ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةَ نَشَأَ النِّزَاعُ فِيهَا لَمَّا ظَهَرَتْ مِحْنَةُ الْجَهْمِيَّة فِي الْقُرْآنِ هَلْ هُوَ مَخْلُوقٌ أَوْ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ؟
 وَهِيَ مِحْنَةُ الْإِمَامِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ عُلَمَاءِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَقَدْ جَرَتْ فِيهَا أُمُورٌ يَطُولُ وَصْفُهَا هُنَا لَكِنْ لَمَّا ظَهَرَ الْقَوْلُ بِأَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ كَلَامُ اللَّهِ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ وَأَطْفَأَ اللَّهُ نَارَ الْجَهْمِيَّة الْمُعَطِّلَةِ صَارَتْ طَائِفَةٌ يَقُولُونَ إنَّ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَهُ مَخْلُوقٌ وَيُعَبِّرُونَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ بِاللَّفْظِ فَصَارُوا يَقُولُونَ أَلْفَاظُنَا بِالْقُرْآنِ مَخْلُوقَةٌ أَوْ تِلَاوَتُنَا أَوْ قِرَاءَتُنَا مَخْلُوقَةٌ وَلَيْسَ مَقْصُودُهُمْ مُجَرَّدَ كَلَامِهِمْ وَحَرَكَاتِهِمْ بَلْ يُدْخِلُونَ فِي كَلَامِهِمْ نَفْسَ كَلَامِ اللَّهِ الَّذِي نَقْرَأُ بِأَصْوَاتِنَا وَحَرَكَاتِنَا وَعَارَضَهُمْ طَائِفَةٌ أُخْرَى فَقَالُوا:
 أَلْفَاظُنَا بِالْقُرْآنِ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقَةٍ فَرَدَّ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد عَلَى الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ وَقَالَ: مَنْ قَالَ: لَفْظِي بِالْقُرْآنِ مَخْلُوقٌ فَهُوَ جهمي وَمَنْ قَالَ: غَيْرَ مَخْلُوقٍ فَهُوَ مُبْتَدِعٌ.
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah bless his resting place—said:

Section

As for faith: is it created or uncreated?

The answer is that disagreement over this issue arose when the Jahmiyyah’s inquisition began over whether the Quran was created or uncreated. This was the ordeal suffered by Imam Ahmad and other Muslim scholars. Much occurred during it that would take too long to describe here.

However, when the position that the Quran is Allah’s uncreated speech prevailed, and Allah extinguished the fire of the Jahmiyyah, who deny His attributes, a group began saying that the speech Allah had sent down was created. They expressed this in terms of “utterance,” saying, “Our utterances of the Quran are created,” or, “Our recitation,” or, “Our reading is created.” They did not mean merely their own speech and movements; rather, they included in their statement the very speech of Allah, which we recite with our voices and movements.

Another group opposed them, saying, “Our utterances of the Quran are uncreated.” Imam Ahmad refuted both groups, saying: “Whoever says, ‘My utterance of the Quran is created,’ is a Jahmī; and whoever says, ‘It is uncreated,’ is an innovator.”

original_text:
وَتَكَلَّمَ النَّاسُ حِينَئِذٍ فِي الْإِيمَانِ فَقَالَتْ طَائِفَةٌ:
 الْإِيمَانُ مَخْلُوقٌ وَأَدْرَجُوا فِي ذَلِكَ مَا تَكَلَّمَ اللَّهُ بِهِ مِنْ الْإِيمَانِ مِثْلَ: قَوْلِ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ فَصَارَ مُقْتَضَى قَوْلِهِمْ أَنَّ نَفْسَ هَذِهِ الْكَلِمَةِ مَخْلُوقَةٌ وَلَمْ يَتَكَلَّمْ اللَّهُ بِهَا فَبَدَّعَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد هَؤُلَاءِ وَقَالَ: قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{الْإِيمَانُ بِضْعٌ وَسِتُّونَ شُعْبَةً أَعْلَاهَا قَوْلُ لَا إلَهَ إلَّا اللَّهُ}

 كَمَا يَرَى الشَّيْءَ فِي الْمَاءِ وَالْمِرْآةِ رُؤْيَةً مُقَيَّدَةً لَا مُطْلَقَةً أَوْ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَإِنْ أَحَدٌ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ اسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ حَتَّى يَسْمَعَ كَلَامَ اللَّهِ}
 كَانَ مَعْلُومًا عِنْدَ جَمِيعِ مَنْ خُوطِبَ بِالْقُرْآنِ أَنَّهُ يَسْمَعُ سَمَاعًا مُقَيَّدًا مِنْ الْمُبَلِّغِ لَيْسَ الْمُرَادُ بِهِ أَنَّهُ يَسْمَعُ مِنْ اللَّهِ.
 وَمِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّهُ يَسْمَعُ صَوْتَ الْقَارِئِ مِنْ اللَّهِ ثُمَّ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مَنْ
translated_text:
People then began discussing faith. One group said, “Faith is created,” including in this what Allah had spoken concerning faith, such as the statement, “There is no god but Allah.” Their position thus implied that this very statement was created and that Allah had not spoken it. Imam Ahmad declared these people innovators and said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Faith has sixty-odd branches, the highest of which is saying, “There is no god but Allah.”’ Can the statement ‘There is no god but Allah’ then be created?”

His meaning was that whoever declared this statement created without qualification thereby implied that Allah had not spoken it. Likewise, whoever said, “Our utterances, recitation, and reading of the Quran are created,” thereby implied that Allah had not spoken the Quran He sent down; that the revealed Quran was not Allah’s speech; that Gabriel had brought down something created, not Allah’s speech; and that Muslims were reading a created Quran that was not Allah’s speech.

Yet it is necessarily known as part of the religion of Islam that the Quran Muslims read is the speech of Allah Most High, even when it is heard from someone conveying it on His behalf. For speech may be heard from the one who speaks it, as Moses heard it without an intermediary. This is hearing in an unqualified sense, just as one may see something in an unqualified sense. Or it may be heard from someone conveying it on the speaker’s behalf, in which case it is heard in a qualified sense—just as something is seen in water or a mirror in a qualified, rather than unqualified, sense. Or, as the Most High said:

“And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah.”

Everyone addressed by the Quran understood that he would hear it in a qualified sense from the person conveying it; what was meant was not that he would hear it from Allah.

يَقُولُ:

 لِأَنَّ الْكَلَامَ لَا يُسْمَعُ إلَّا مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ؛

translated_text:
say that the Lord’s voice has come to dwell within the servant. Others say that it has become manifest in him without dwelling within him. Others say, “I say neither that it has become manifest nor that it has come to dwell within him.” Others say that the voice heard is uncreated, or eternal. Still others say that two voices are heard from him: one created and one uncreated.

Among those who say that it is heard from Allah are those who maintain that one hears the eternal meaning subsisting in the Lord’s essence while also hearing the newly produced voice. These say that one hears both the eternal and the newly produced, just as the others say that one hears two voices, one eternal and one newly produced.

Another group said, “People have not heard Allah’s speech, either from Allah or from anyone else.” They argued that speech can be heard only from its speaker. Some of these said that a reproduction of it is heard; others said that an expression of it is heard, not a reproduction. Among those who say that it is created are those who said, “Two things are heard: the created speech; the one who created it; and the servant’s voice.”

All these positions are invented innovations. The early generations held none of them, and all are false according to both revelation and reason. Yet those who held them were driven to them by ambiguity in words and confusion over meanings.

When someone says, “I heard Zayd’s speech,” or, “This is Zayd’s speech,” this refers to the speech he uttered, in both its wording and its meaning, whether it is heard from him or from someone conveying it on his behalf. The distinction between the two situations is nevertheless understood: when it is heard from him, it is heard in his voice; when it is heard from someone else, it is heard in the voice of the person conveying it, not in the original speaker’s voice, even though the wording is that of the original speaker.

With an accompanying indication, one may also say, “This is so-and-so’s speech,” even when it has been translated into different wording. Thus Allah recounts in Arabic the speech of people from the various nations whose words He relates, even though they originally spoke in Hebrew or Syriac

translated_text:
or Coptic or another language. These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that disagreement arose among the people of Sunnah and hadith over “the two issues of the Quran and faith” because of ambiguous expressions and meanings liable to confusion. A group of scholars who adhered to the Sunnah, including al-Bukhārī, the compiler of al-Sahīh, Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazī, and others, said, “Faith is created.” They did not mean any of Allah’s attributes by this. Rather, they meant the actions of His servants. The imams of the Muslims agreed that the actions of Allah’s servants are created. Yahyā ibn Saʿīd al-Qattān said, “I have always heard our companions say, ‘The actions of Allah’s servants are created.’”

Some people came to think that al-Bukhārī and these scholars had opposed Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other imams of the Sunnah. Al-Bukhārī suffered an ordeal because of this, and some liars even claimed that, when al-Bukhārī died, Ahmad ibn Hanbal ordered that no funeral prayer be offered for him. This is an obvious lie, for Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Bukhārī—may Allah have mercy on him—died about fifteen years after Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Ahmad ibn Hanbal—may Allah be pleased with him—died in 241 AH, whereas al-Bukhārī died in 256 AH. Ahmad ibn Hanbal loved al-Bukhārī and held him in great esteem and respect. As for the esteem in which al-Bukhārī and others like him held Imam Ahmad, this is well known.

When al-Bukhārī composed his book on the creation of the actions of Allah’s servants and included chapters on this subject at its end, he mentioned that both groups—those who say that our utterance of the Quran is created and those who say that it is uncreated—are affiliated with Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal

Another group—including Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī, al-Qādī Abū Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā, and others who say that they hold the creed of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the imams of Sunnah and hadith—said: “Ahmad and others disliked the expression ‘my utterance of the Quran,’ because lafz means throwing away and casting aside.”

Yet they have not understood what the imams of the Sunnah, such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others like him, actually taught. We have explained the statements of the early generations and the imams, including Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others, at length elsewhere.

As for al-Bukhārī and those like him, they are among the people most knowledgeable about the positions of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the other imams of the Sunnah. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other leading scholars. Al-Khallāl also recorded this in his book al-Sunnah (The Sunnah), and Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Battah recorded some of it in al-Ibānah (The Elucidation). Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mandah likewise recorded much of it in his writings on “the question of utterance.”

Abū Muhammad ibn Qutaybah al-Dīnawarī said: “The people of hadith did not differ over any aspect of their creed except the question of utterance.” Ibn Qutaybah then explained that lafz (“utterance”) can denote the act of uttering, as the verbal noun of “to utter”; it can also denote speech itself, which is the servant’s act and voice and is created. As for Allah’s own speech, which His servants utter, it is not created.

Likewise, regarding “the question of faith,” Ahmad ibn Hanbal never said that faith is uncreated. Nor did Ahmad or any other member of the early generations say that the Quran is eternal. Rather, they said: “The Quran is Allah’s speech, revealed and uncreated.” Neither Ahmad ibn Hanbal nor anyone among the early generations said that any of the servant’s attributes or actions are uncreated—not his voice when reciting the Quran, his utterance of the Quran, his faith, his prayer, or anything of that kind.

Later scholars, however, split into many groups over this matter. Among those who said, “Our utterance of the Quran is uncreated,” some also stated without qualification that faith is uncreated. Others described both utterance and faith as eternal. Some distinguished between verbal expressions of faith and deeds, saying that the verbal expressions are uncreated and eternal, whereas the deeds of faith are created.

Concerning deeds pertaining to faith, some say that those which are forbidden are created. As for acts of obedience, such as prayer and the like, some say that they are uncreated, while others withhold judgment and do not say that they are

Others say that it is created, and that He created it separate from Himself, as held by the Jahmiyyah, Najjāriyyah and Mu‘tazilah. Others say that it is an eternal meaning subsisting in the Divine Essence, as held by Ibn Kullāb and al-Ash‘arī. Others say that it consists of letters and sounds, as held by Ibn Sālim and a group of others. Still others say that He began to speak after not having spoken, as held by Ibn Karrām and a group of others.

The correct view among these is that of the early generations and the imams, whose statements I have presented at length elsewhere.

When the Inquisition arose, Ahl al-Sunnah maintained that Allah’s speech is uncreated, whereas the “Jahmiyyah,” including the Mu‘tazilah and others, maintained that it is created. Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb al-Qattān was a man of merit and learning. He used his knowledge to refute the Jahmiyyah and Mu‘tazilah who denied the divine attributes, and explained that Allah Himself is above the Throne, discussing this at length. Yet he did not entirely free himself from the specious argument of the Jahmiyyah. Rather, he supposed that the Lord cannot be characterized by acts of choice dependent on His power and will. Thus, He does not speak by His will and power, nor does He come to love a servant and be pleased with him after his faith and obedience, or become angry and displeased with him after his disbelief and disobedience. Rather, He loves and is pleased with those whom He knows will die as believers, or is angry and displeased with those whom He knows will die as unbelievers. Nor does He utter one statement after another.

Yet Allah, exalted is He, has said:

“Indeed, the likeness of Jesus in the sight of Allah is that of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he was.”

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“So when they provoked Our anger, We exacted retribution from them.”

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked what pleased Him, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

translated_text:
And He, exalted is He, has said:

“It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne.”

This is a fundamental matter that has been discussed at length elsewhere. The purpose here is merely to draw attention to the grounds for disagreement among Muslims over “issues such as these.” Once this is understood, we must affirm what the Quran and Sunnah affirm and deny what the Quran and Sunnah deny.

An ambiguous expression that does not occur in the Quran and Sunnah must not be applied affirmatively or negatively until its intended meaning is clarified. Thus, if someone says, “The Lord occupies space,” or “does not occupy space,” or “He is in a direction,” or “is not in a direction,” the response is: These expressions are ambiguous. Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah uses them, whether affirmatively or negatively, nor did any of the Companions or those who followed them in righteousness affirm or deny them.

If by your statement you mean that something created encompasses Him, that it is not He who upholds the Throne and its bearers by His power, and that He is not the Most High, the Most Exalted, the Most Great, the Magnificent—whom no vision can encompass, while He encompasses all vision, and who, glorified is He, is greater than all things—then He does not occupy space in this sense. But if you mean that He is distinct from His creatures, exalted above them, above His heavens and over His Throne, then He, glorified is He, is indeed distinct from His creation. This was stated by the imams of the Sunnah, such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh and other leading figures of Islam. It is also established by authentic transmitted evidence and clear reason, as explained at length elsewhere.

The same applies to the expression “direction”: if by direction one means an existing entity that encompasses the Creator, or

translated_text:
on which He depends, then everything that exists other than Allah is created. Allah is the Creator of all things; everything besides Him is dependent upon Him, while He has no need of anything besides Himself. But if he means that Allah, glorified is He, is above His heavens, over His Throne, distinct from His creation, then this is correct, whether expressed using the word “direction” or otherwise.

The same applies to the expression “compulsion.” If someone asks, “Is the servant compelled or not?” the response is: If by compulsion he means that the servant has no will, no power, or no action of his own, then this is false. The servant performs his voluntary actions through his own power and will. But if by compulsion he means that He is the Creator of the servant’s will, power, and action, then Allah, exalted is He, is indeed the Creator of all these.

If someone asks, “Is faith created or uncreated?” he should be asked: What do you mean by “faith”? Do you mean something belonging to Allah’s attributes and speech, such as His saying, “There is no god but Allah,” and His “īmān” (affirmation of truth), indicated by His name al-Mu’min (the Affirmer of Truth)? If so, it is uncreated. Or do you mean something belonging to the servants’ actions and attributes? The servants are all created, and all their actions and attributes are created. A servant who was brought into existence and created cannot possess an eternal, uncreated attribute. No one who understands what he is saying would claim this.

Once clarification is sought and the distinctions are made, guidance becomes evident and the way becomes clear. It has been said: Most disagreements among rational people arise from words having more than one meaning. In these and similar matters over which people frequently dispute, affirming or denying them, a precise explanation distinguishes error from what is correct. People are obliged to affirm whatever the Book and the Sunnah affirm, and whatever is negated by the Book

and the Sunnah, they must negate. Regarding anything that the Book and the Sunnah neither affirm nor deny, they must ask the speaker to clarify what he means. Whoever affirms what Allah and His Messenger have affirmed is correct, and whoever denies what Allah and His Messenger have denied is correct. But whoever affirms what Allah has denied, or denies what Allah has affirmed, has mixed the religion of truth with falsehood. He must therefore distinguish the truth in his words from the falsehood, follow the truth, and abandon the falsehood.

Whatever contradicts the Book and the Sunnah also contradicts sound reason, for sound reason does not contradict authentic revelation, just as the teachings transmitted from the prophets, peace be upon them, do not contradict one another. Yet many people imagine that these contradict one another. Such people are among those who differ over the Scripture:

“Indeed, those who differ over the Scripture are in deep discord.”

We ask Allah to guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom He has bestowed His favor—the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

Section

“Qualifying one’s profession of faith is Sunnah.”

This is the position of our scholars and most of Ahl al-Sunnah. The Murji’ah and the Mu‘tazilah, however, say that such qualification is impermissible, since it constitutes doubt.

Qualification means saying: “I am a believer, if Allah wills”; “I am a believer, I hope”; “I believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers”; or: “If by faith you mean that which renders my blood inviolable, then yes. But if you mean:

‘The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned,’

then Allah knows best.”

There are three views here. The first is that qualification is obligatory, so an unqualified assertion is impermissible. This view is stated by al-Qādī in ‘Uyūn al-Masā’il, among other sources. The second is that qualification is recommended, while an unqualified assertion is permissible from another standpoint. The third is that both are permissible, each from a particular standpoint. The statement that qualification is Sunnah means only that it is permissible, in refutation of those who prohibit it.

If we say that it is obligatory, al-Qādī’s reasoning is that, if we could categorically assert that we are believers, this would amount to categorically asserting that we are destined for Paradise, since Allah has promised Paradise to the believers. Yet we cannot categorically assert that the promise of Paradise applies to us, because this is conditional upon dying in faith, and only Allah knows that,

: فَحَقِيقَةُ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ أَنَّ الْإِيمَانَ اسْمٌ لِلْعِبَادَةِ مِنْ أَوَّلِ الدُّخُولِ فِيهِ إلَى أَنْ يَمُوتَ عَلَيْهِ فَإِذَا انْتَقَضَ تَبَيَّنَ بُطْلَانُ أَوَّلِهَا كَالْحَدَثِ فِي آخِرِ الصَّلَاةِ وَالْوَطْءِ فِي آخِرِ الْحَجِّ وَالْأَكْلِ فِي آخِرِ النَّهَارِ؛ وَقَوْلُ مُؤْمِنٍ عِنْدَ الْإِطْلَاقِ يَقْتَضِي فِعْلَ الْإِيمَانِ كُلِّهِ كَقَوْلِ مُصَلٍّ وَصَائِمٍ وَحَاجٍّ؛ فَهَذَا مَأْخَذُ الْقَاضِي. وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ بَعْدَهَا فِي الْمُعْتَمَدِ 
" مَسْأَلَةَ الْمُوَافَاةِ "
 وَهِيَ مُتَّصِلَةٌ بِهَا وَهُوَ أَنَّ الْمُؤْمِنَ الَّذِي عَلِمَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ يَمُوتُ كَافِرًا؛ وَبِالْعَكْسِ؛ هَلْ يَتَعَلَّقُ رِضَا اللَّهِ وَسَخَطُهُ وَمَحَبَّتُهُ وَبُغْضُهُ بِمَا هُوَ عَلَيْهِ أَوْ بِمَا يُوَافِي بِهِ.
 وَالْمَسْأَلَةُ مُتَعَلِّقَةٌ بِالرِّضَا وَالسَّخَطِ:
 هَلْ هُوَ قَدِيمٌ أَوْ مُحْدَثٌ؟
translated_text:
and likewise, faith is only realized by remaining faithful until death, and this cannot be known.

For this reason, Ibn Mas‘ūd said: “Why did he not entrust the former to Allah, just as he entrusted the latter?” This refers to the report cited as evidence: a man said in his presence, “I am a believer.” Ibn Mas‘ūd was told, “This man claims that he is a believer.” He replied, “Then ask him whether he is in Paradise or in the Fire.” They asked him, and he said, “Allah knows best.” ‘Abd Allāh then said, “Why did you not entrust the first matter to Allah, just as you entrusted the second?”

I say: Further evidence for the obligation to qualify one’s profession of faith may be drawn from ‘Umar’s statement: “Whoever says that he is a believer is an unbeliever; whoever claims that he is in Paradise is in the Fire; and whoever claims that he is learned is ignorant.” When the opponent argued that qualification is needed only for a future event whose occurrence is uncertain, he replied: “The answer is that there is indeed a future event here whose occurrence is uncertain: dying in faith. The parts of faith are interconnected, so it is like a single act of worship.”

I say: In essence, this position holds that faith denotes an act of worship extending from the moment one enters it until one dies upon it. If it is invalidated, its beginning is shown to have been invalid—as when one loses ritual purity at the end of prayer, has intercourse at the end of Hajj, or eats at the end of a day of fasting. The unqualified designation “believer” implies fulfilling faith in its entirety, just as do the designations “one who prays,” “one who fasts,” and “one who performs Hajj.” This, then, is the basis of al-Qādī’s reasoning.

After this discussion in al-Mu‘tamad, he addresses the related “question of one’s state at death”: in the case of a believer whom Allah knows will die an unbeliever—and vice versa—do Allah’s pleasure and anger, love and hatred, relate to the person’s present state or to the state in which he dies? This question is connected to whether His pleasure and anger are eternal or arise anew.

translated_text:
The second basis is that the designation, when used without qualification, implies completeness, which the speaker cannot know he possesses. Thus,

[Abū al-‘Āliyah said: “I met thirty of Muhammad’s Companions, all of whom feared hypocrisy for themselves. Not one would say, ‘My faith is like Gabriel’s faith.’”] (1)

For a man to declare that his faith is complete is to make a claim about something he does not know. This is the meaning of Ibn al-Munazzil’s statement: “The Murji’ah say that their good deeds are accepted, whereas I do not testify to that.” This reasoning can support making qualification obligatory. It is also al-Qādī’s second basis: his opponent argued that, since qualifying one’s profession of Islam is impermissible, the same must apply to faith.

He replied: “The answer is that Islam consists simply of the two testimonies of faith, which he has pronounced, whereas faith comprises words and deeds, as indicated by the saying, ‘Faith has seventy-odd aspects.’ He cannot be certain that he has fulfilled them all.”

The third basis is that such a claim amounts to praising oneself, whereas Allah has said:

“So do not claim purity for yourselves.”

This can support recommending qualification; otherwise, a person may lawfully describe himself as he actually is, even if this entails praise. It may also support making qualification obligatory.

Al-Athram said in al-Sunnah: “Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated to us: ‘I heard Yahyā ibn Sa‘īd say: “Everyone among our companions whom I met or heard about qualified his profession of faith.”’” Al-Athram said: “I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh being asked about qualifying one’s profession of faith: ‘What is your view of it?’ He replied: ‘As for me, I do not disapprove of it… (2) I qualify it out of fear and caution, not out of doubt, as they claim. Qualification concerns only deeds.’”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said: “Allah has said:

‘You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills.’”

That is, this qualification does not express doubt. The Prophet also said

translated_text:
—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“And indeed, if Allah wills, we shall join you.”

That is, he had no doubt about this, yet he qualified his statement. He also mentioned the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“We shall be raised from the grave, if Allah wills.”

He also mentioned the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“Indeed, by Allah, I hope to be the one among you who fears Allah most.”

He said: “All of this supports qualifying one’s profession of faith.”

I said to Abū ‘Abd Allāh: “So it seems that you see no harm in omitting the qualification?” He replied: “If the person holds that faith consists of words and deeds, and that it increases and decreases, then I find this less objectionable.” Then Abū ‘Abd Allāh said: “Some people’s hearts are too weak to make this qualification.” He expressed amazement at them and spoke at length; I have omitted those remarks.

Ahmad’s words thus indicate that the qualification concerns deeds—this is the “second basis”—and that it does not arise from doubt about the foundation of faith. This resembles the “third basis” and implies that omitting the qualification is permissible.

As for saying without qualification, “I am a believer,” this is valid if one means the foundation of faith rather than its completeness, and having entered into it rather than having attained its fullness. Likewise, someone who has begun Hajj or fasting may say, “I am a pilgrim,” or “I am fasting.” The same applies to the unqualified statement, “I believe in Allah and His messengers,” and to the statement, “If you mean such-and-such…” The point is that permission to describe oneself using a verb entails permission to use the corresponding noun when the context makes the intended meaning clear.

On this basis, one may understand what is reported from a companion of Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, as well as the report of al-Hārith, who said, “I am truly a believer,” and the report of the delegation who said, “We are the believers”—although both chains of transmission are open to question.

translated_text:
He was asked:

What is the meaning of the Prophet’s hadith—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—:

“When a person commits unlawful sexual intercourse, faith leaves him and remains above his head like a canopy. When he ceases that act, faith returns to him.”

It was narrated by al-Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd. Is someone a believer while committing unlawful sexual intercourse, or not? Have any of the imams understood this hadith according to its apparent meaning, or have they unanimously agreed to interpret it otherwise?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Regarding a sinful Muslim—such as someone who commits unlawful sexual intercourse, steals, drinks alcohol, or the like—people fall into “three groups”: two extremes and a middle position.

One extreme holds that such a person is not a believer in any respect and is not included within the general scope of the rulings attached to the designation of faith. Some who hold this view say that he is a disbeliever, like a Jew or a Christian. This is the position of the Khawārij. Others say: “We assign him a position between the two positions: the position of a sinner, who is neither a believer nor a disbeliever.” These are the Muʿtazilah.

These groups maintain that those who commit major sins will remain in the Fire forever and that none of them will ever emerge from it. This is among the “doctrines of the people of innovation” contradicted by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness. Allah Most High says:

“If two groups of believers fight, make peace between them.”

Then, further on, He says:

“The believers are but brothers, so make peace

between your brothers.” Thus, He called them believers and designated them as brothers despite their fighting and the aggression of some against others. Allah Most High also says:

“Then a believing slave must be freed.”

If someone frees a sinful slave, that emancipation fulfills the requirement by scholarly consensus.

For this reason, the scholars of the early generations state in their formulations of creed: “We do not declare anyone among those who face the qiblah a disbeliever on account of a sin, nor do we exclude him from Islam on account of a deed.” Unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, and drinking alcohol were established against certain people during the Prophet’s lifetime—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—yet he did not treat them as disbelievers or sever the bonds of allegiance between them and the Muslims. Rather, he flogged one and cut off another’s hand, while seeking forgiveness for them and saying: “Do not help Satan against your brother.” All the rulings of Islam rest upon this principle.

The second extreme is the view of those who say: “Their faith remains just as it was, without diminishing.” This rests on the premise that faith is nothing more than assent and firm conviction, which have not changed; only their observance of Islam’s prescriptions has diminished. This is the position of the Murji’ah, the Jahmiyyah, and those who follow their path. It too contradicts the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the earliest Muslims and those who followed them in righteousness. Allah Most High says:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He also says:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned”—through to His words—“It is they who are truly believers.”

He also says:

“And it increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us.’”

And He says:

“So that they might increase in faith beyond the faith they already had.”

And He says:

“It has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.”

And the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Faith has seventy-odd branches. The highest is saying, ‘There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah,’ and the lowest is removing something harmful from the road.”

He also said to the delegation of ‘Abd al-Qays:

“I command you to have faith in Allah. Do you know what faith in Allah is? To testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and to pay one-fifth of whatever spoils you acquire.”

The early generations unanimously agreed that faith consists of words and deeds, and that it increases and decreases. This means the affirmation and actions of the heart, followed by the speech of the tongue and the deeds of the limbs. The heart’s affirmation is firm assent to Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, and the Last Day. This includes believing in everything the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—brought.

People differ in this respect. Some affirm it as a whole without knowing its details, while others affirm it both as a whole and in detail. Some remain constantly mindful of this affirmation and keep it present in their hearts, while others become heedless of it and lose awareness of it. Some gain clear insight into it through the light and faith Allah casts into their hearts. Others are firmly convinced on the basis of evidence against which a doubt might arise, or through firm reliance on the authority of others.

This affirmation is followed by the actions of the heart: loving Allah and His Messenger; venerating Allah and His Messenger; supporting and honoring the Messenger; fearing Allah; turning to Him in repentance; being sincere to Him; relying upon Him; and other such states. All these actions of the heart are part of faith. Affirmation and conviction necessarily give rise to them, just as a cause necessarily produces its effect. Conviction is followed by the speech of the tongue, and the heart’s actions are followed by bodily deeds, such as prayer, zakah, fasting, Hajj, and the like.

In light of this, the balanced position—that of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah—is neither to deny the designation “believer” without qualification nor to confer it without qualification.

Thus we say: “He is a believer whose faith is deficient,” “a sinful believer,” or “a believer by virtue of his faith and an evildoer by virtue of his major sin.” It may also be said: “He is not a true believer,” or “His faith is not genuine.” Every statement made in the Quran and Sunnah must be accompanied by something that clarifies its intended meaning. Some rulings depend only on the foundation of faith, such as the validity of manumission as expiation, bonds of allegiance, mutual inheritance, and similar matters. Others depend on both its foundation and its branches, such as deserving praise and reward, forgiveness of sins, and similar matters.

With “this principle” understood, the report in the Sahīh records the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—as saying:

“A fornicator is not a believer at the time he commits fornication; a thief is not a believer at the time he steals; a person is not a believer at the time he drinks wine; and a person is not a believer at the time he seizes valuable plunder as people raise their eyes to him.”

The additional wording narrated by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī is authentic and explains the well-known narration.

The questioner’s words, “Did any of the imams understand the hadith according to its apparent meaning?” can mean different things. If he means that its apparent meaning is that the fornicator becomes a disbeliever and is entirely stripped of faith, then none of the imams understood the hadith in this way. “Faith leaves him and is like a canopy above his head,”

translated_text:
does not leave him entirely, for a canopy shades the person beneath it and remains attached and connected to him in some way. But if by its apparent meaning he means what is actually understood from it, as we shall explain, Allah willing, then yes.

The scholars of the early generations generally affirm these hadiths and let them stand as transmitted. They disapprove of interpretations that divert them from the intent of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Disapproval of interpreting the hadiths containing threats of punishment has been reported from Sufyān and Ahmad ibn Hanbal—may Allah be pleased with them—and a great many other scholars. Ahmad explicitly stated that a hadith of this kind must not be interpreted in a way that diverts it from its intended apparent meaning.

Al-Khattābī and others have offered strained interpretations, such as their statement: “Its wording is declarative, but its meaning is prohibitive”—that is, a believer ought not to do such a thing. They also say: “Its purpose is to threaten and deter, not actually to negate faith.” They justify such wording by the resemblance and closeness between his condition and that of someone devoid of faith. They also say: “What is absent is only the perfection and completeness of faith, or its prescribed practices and fruits,” and so forth. The shortcomings of all these interpretations are plain to anyone who examines them closely.

The truth, then, is this: he has not lost the assent that distinguishes him from a disbeliever. Yet had this assent remained unchanged, he would affirm that Allah has forbidden this major sin, that He has threatened severe punishment for it, and that He sees and observes the person committing it. He—glorified and exalted is He—in His greatness, majesty, loftiness and grandeur, detests the person committing this act. If the person truly grasped all this, he could not commit the act. Whenever he commits this sin, therefore, one of “three things” must be present.

translated_text:
Either his belief is unsound: he believes that the apparent meaning of the threat does not reflect its actual meaning and that its purpose is merely deterrence, as the Murji’ah maintain; or that this is forbidden only to ordinary people, not to the spiritual elite, as the Ibāhiyyah (antinomians) maintain; or he holds some similar belief that takes a person outside the fold of Islam.

Or he is heedless and oblivious to the prohibition, the greatness of the Lord, and the severity of His punishment.

Or his desire is so excessive that it overpowers what faith demands and prevents faith from producing its proper effect. His belief thus becomes submerged and overpowered, like reason in someone asleep or intoxicated, or the soul in someone asleep. Clearly, “faith”—faith in its true sense—does not remain as it was, for it is no longer firmly established and manifest in the heart. The unqualified designation “believer” applies only to someone whose faith remains intact and produces its effects.

In some respects, it resembles the soul of someone asleep, for He—glorified is He—“takes souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died during their sleep.” A sleeping person is therefore dead in one respect and alive in another. Likewise, someone intoxicated or unconscious possesses reason in one respect but lacks it in another. If someone says, “An intoxicated person is not rational; when he sobers up, his reason returns to him,” he speaks truthfully, even though we know that such a person is not like an animal: his reason is concealed, whereas the animal has none. Indeed, anger may drive a person to a state in which his reason and judgment desert him. A report states:

“When Allah wills to carry out His decree and ordainment, He deprives those endowed with reason of their reason. Once He has carried out His decree and ordainment, He restores their reason so that they may take heed.”

The reason upon which religious accountability depends has not been taken away. What has been taken away is the reason by which one manages one’s affairs rightly in this world and the Hereafter.

translated_text:
Likewise, the adulterer, the thief, the drinker of intoxicants, and the looter have not lost the faith by virtue of which they are entitled not to remain eternally in the Fire, for which intercession and forgiveness may be hoped for them, and by virtue of which they retain the rights of marriage and mutual inheritance. But they lack the faith that entitles them to deliverance from punishment, the expiation of sins, the acceptance of acts of obedience, and Allah’s honour and reward—the faith by virtue of which they deserve praise and approval.

This makes clear that the hadith is to be understood according to its apparent meaning, in a manner befitting it. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

What is the meaning of the Prophet’s statement (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“No one who has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise”?

Does this hadith apply specifically to believers or to disbelievers? If we say it applies specifically to believers, our claim is untenable, because believers enter Paradise by virtue of their faith. If we say it applies specifically to disbelievers, what purpose does the hadith serve?

He replied:

The wording of the hadith in al-Sahīh is:

“No one who has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise, and no one who has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart will enter the Fire.”

A person whose arrogance is incompatible with faith will not enter Paradise, as Allah says:

“Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell in humiliation.”

This includes the arrogance of Iblīs, Pharaoh, and others whose arrogance was incompatible with faith. Likewise, the arrogance of the Jews and those of whom Allah says:

“Whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, did you grow arrogant, rejecting some and killing others?”

All arrogance is incompatible with the faith one is required to have. Whoever has an atom’s weight of arrogance in his heart fails to do what Allah has required of him and to refrain from what He has forbidden him. Rather, his arrogance leads him to deny the truth and hold others in contempt. This is the “arrogance” that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) explained when he was asked in
